506.title: /continual-progress — trackable, always-PR’d, continually-committed work
506.content: Skill continual-progress: Make in-flight work trackable by others in real time — open a PR from the first commit, push small coherent increments continuously (never hoard uncommitted work), keep a live status checklist in the PR body, and post brief intent on the PR + any overlapping sibling PRs. Use on any multi-step or long-running task, especially when siblings/agents or the author may need to follow, cherry-pick, or take over mid-flight. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Sibling agents and the author can only coordinate with work they can see. This skill makes every in-flight task trackable in real time: the PR is open from the first commit, progress lands as a stream of small pushed commits, and the PR body carries a live status checklist. It is the visibility complement to /coordinate (which triages across PRs); this one governs how your own PR stays legible while you work.

507.title: The four invariants
507.content: . | Always have an open PR (from commit #1). Branch, make the first (even stub) commit, push, open the PR — before further work. The PR is the durable, visible artifact; the chat session is ephemeral. Never accumulate work on a local branch with no PR. Never ask permission to open one — branch, commit, push and PR are all pre-authorised. | Commit + push small, coherent increments — continuously. Each logically distinct change is its own commit (a single fix, a single module, a single unit of work). Push after each commit (or every 2–3 if moving fast). A watcher should be able to git log your branch and see a legible, bisectable trail — not one giant drop. Target: no more than ~20–30 min of work between pushes on a long task. | Keep a live status checklist in the PR body. Maintain a - [ ] / - [x] checklist of the task’s sub-parts in the PR description (or a pinned top comment), updated as each increment lands. A sibling or the author should be able to read the PR body and know exactly what is done / in-flight / remaining — without reading the diff or asking in chat. | Post brief intent — on your PR and overlapping siblings. One short intent line on PR-open (“doing X on <files>; will touch <scope>”); a one-line comment on any sibling whose scope overlaps (“starting <theme> on <files>; flag conflicts”). Don’t stream comments — update the checklist (invariant 3) for routine progress; comment only for genuine coordination (overlap, a blocker, a handoff-relevant finding). Defer to /coordinate for the full cross-PR triage protocol. New work posts its intent only after the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work” has been run and recorded in the workplan work item. | . Bean edits are pushed to the state branch, not the PR . Work item and workflow-instance edits (beans/defs/*.md, beans/workflows/*.json) do not belong in the PR’s commit set. The code PR contains code, test, and documentation changes destined for main. Work-plan progress, work item claims, status updates, and notes are written directly to the work-plan store through its configured Tool (work-plan-store; on a git state branch, bun run cat state:push per work-plan-store-git-branch). The PR description references the work item via Closes-bean: <id> (or in the status checklist), but commits on the PR branch must not bundle work item file edits. This avoids merge conflicts on work item files and prevents work-plan edits from triggering code CI workflows.

508.title: The fifth invariant, and the one agents get wrong
508.content: . | Do not hold a green change proposal back waiting for someone to look at it. This is the rule that gets inverted in the name of care, and inverting it is not caution — it is a blocked reviewer. | . An agent that has built something it cannot fully verify — a rendered page, a diagram, a UI — must not leave it open and ask the human to confirm from a preview first: . A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it, and a preview pasted into chat is a strictly worse proxy than the deployed thing. Holding the merge does not transfer the verification to them — it withholds the only form in which they could do it, and asks them to adjudicate from a screenshot. Link the PAGE, never the site root . When you ask somebody to look at a rendered artefact, link the artefact. Not the site it is on, not the preview’s front door — the exact URL of the thing you changed. Linking the root makes the reader reconstruct a route the agent already knew, and every extra click is a cost passed to a reader who may type with difficulty. It also hides a real failure: an agent that links the root has not checked that its page is reachable at all. So: . | One link per thing to look at. Two changed pages is two links, each labelled with what to look for on it — not one root and a sentence of navigation. | Deep-link past the index. If the change is on /docs/<iris-replica>/kg-to-portal.html, that is the URL, not /docs/<iris-replica>/. | Take it from the preview’s page list, never from memory or a source path: a branch slug is exactly the kind of string that is almost right. The rule, and where the list comes from, is staging-review §”The deep-link rule”. | The root is the right link for precisely one thing — a change to the landing page itself. | . This is the same rule as the invariant above, one step further on. A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it; they also cannot assess it from a link to somewhere near it. What to do with the thing you could not verify . Say it in the body, and merge anyway. ## Not verified is a real section and an honest one; an unmerged proposal is not a substitute for it. Reversibility is what makes this safe — a docs or content change is one revert away, and the cost of reverting is far below the cost of a human blocked on a decision they have no artefact for. A pipe discards the exit code — so a piped run cannot verify anything . cmd | tail makes $? the status of tail. Every claim that a command PASSED must come from a run without a pipe, or from ${PIPESTATUS[0]}. This is mechanical rather than a matter of care, because care does not prevent it. A command whose output sounds like a failure, run through a pipe, reads as a silent pass, and one whose output sounds like a pass hides a failure; a silent pass is what this repository treats as worse than a loud failure. So: when the question is “did this pass”, run it bare. When you want both the output and the verdict, run it twice or capture the status first. Reading a verdict off prose you piped is the same error as quoting a count from prose. A template is not a page — verify the BUILD, not the source of it . The invariant above says a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. This is its twin, and it is the one an agent breaks: . An agent cannot assess a rendered artefact from the template that generates it. A correct template and a correct page are different claims, and only the second is what a reader loads. Every source gate can pass over a defect that exists only in the build’s output. For example, a Liquid -%} that strips the space between two attributes makes Kramdown stop treating a block as HTML and escape it into visible text, while unit tests, lint, type checks, gates, e2e and accessibility suites all read valid sources and pass. So the rule is mechanical, not a matter of diligence: . | When the artefact is a built page, the evidence is the built page. Build the site and read the output. Reading the template proves the template. | A screenshot of a scratch render is not a screenshot of the build. If the real build cannot run locally (here the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway — a pass-through _layouts/default.html is enough to see what Kramdown did. Stub the part that cannot run; never substitute the part under test. | State which one you looked at. “Rendered and checked” is ambiguous between the two, and the ambiguity is where this hid. | . check:escaped-markup, run in docs-site.yml against the assembled _site/, covers the escaped-markup case, because the assembled site is the only place the answer exists. It does not retire the rule: the next defect of this shape will be in whatever the build does that no source gate can see. The exceptions, and none of them is “I am unsure” . | Never merge red. A failing or unrun required check is a real blocker. | Never merge over an unresolved review thread you have not answered. | Where the repository requires explicit merge permission, that wins, and nothing here relaxes it by a word. Some folios require an explicit “merge it” from the author for every merge to the default branch. There the rule reads: get it green, get it mergeable, say once that it is ready, then stop — do not re-ask on a timer, and do not let “not merged yet” become a reason to stop pushing. | . Green means handed to the Merge Steward — an agent never merges to main here . The merge policy for folio-assistant. It is the “explicit merge permission” case above, made into a hand-off rather than a question: . | Never merge to main yourself — not with gh pr merge, not with the MCP merge tool, not after a green run, not under a standing “merge it” from earlier in the session. | When CI is green on EVERY job (the run list, not the PR page — see prepare-merge §”NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”; on a draft, the fast tier), and when the queue allows (§”Pace the ready marking” below): mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha> — the full sha of the head that went green, so a push after it is visibly not what was declared ready. | The Merge Steward session (“Separation”) merges. It brings main in, runs regen, re-checks and merges. That is its lane, not yours. | If it reports red, it is yours again: fix, push, wait for green on every job, then re-label and comment ready: <new head sha>. | . Wherever a merge does happen, it is the merge-to-main sub-process: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for that merge, recorded, then the merge. So “merge anyway” in §”What to do with the thing you could not verify” reads here as mark it ready anyway, and “merge it as soon as it is green” in the fix-forward section below reads as hand it over as soon as it is green. The point of both is unchanged: a green PR is not held back. Pace the ready marking — the runner pool is shared . The Actions runner pool is shared across the owner’s repositories. A draft PR runs only the fast tier, and marking it ready starts the full tier, about 10 jobs. So the number of PRs marked ready at once is what fills the queue: . | Open every PR as a draft. | Mark it ready only when its own change is done and its fast checks pass. | Check the queue first: gh api "repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/runs?status=queued" --jq .total_count. If it is more than about 2 queued runs per runner (5 runners on 2026-10-24, so more than about 10), hold the marking and check again later. | At most 3 ready, CI-pending PRs per agent per repository. Hand one over or let it finish before you mark another. | A fix that unblocks other work may jump the line: a link in the repin chain, or a fix for a red main. | . Holding a PR as a draft for pacing is not holding back a green PR: the fast tier is green, and the hand-off above waits for the full tier. Two green PRs can merge into a red main, and the answer is to fix forward . A PR is tested against the main it last merged, not the main it lands on. Two PRs that are each green can still combine into a failure that neither branch contained, and no regen on either branch can see it. The policy is to fix forward, not to add a merge queue or an “up to date” requirement. So: . | Watch main’s CI after every merge of yours, not only your PR’s — whoever pressed the button. “My PR was green” does not mean main is green. | A red main whose failure your diff did not cause is still yours to fix when you find it. Establish the cause from the failing run and each parent’s history first, then regenerate or repair in a small PR of its own, and merge it as soon as it is green. | Do not blame the last merge because it is the last merge. Check whether the parent was already red. | .

509.title: Why — the failure modes this prevents
509.content: . | Stepped-on work. A branch that hoards uncommitted work collides with siblings the moment it lands. Continual push surfaces intent from minute 1 so siblings triage around it. | Lost work on session reclaim. Cloud sessions are ephemeral; an uncommitted change vanishes when the container is reclaimed. Push it. | Opaque progress. “What’s the status?” should be answerable from the PR body, not a chat scrollback. The checklist is the source of truth. | Un-takeoverable tasks. If you go idle/blocked, a sibling can pick up a continually-committed, checklist-annotated PR; they cannot pick up an opaque local branch. | .

510.title: Checklist (run this as you work)
510.content: . | PR open? If not: branch → stub commit → push → open it now. | Anything uncommitted older than ~20–30 min? Commit + push it. | Does the PR-body status checklist reflect the current state? | Any sibling whose files I just started touching un-notified? One intent line (not a stream). | Blocked or going idle? Update the checklist + a one-line “blocked on X / handoff-ready” note so a sibling can continue. | .

511.title: Relationship to other skills
511.content: . | pr-description: what the PR body says ABOVE the status checklist (the problem, why, approach, constraints, solution, usage, what is not done), for a reader who was not here. | /coordinate — cross-PR triage (scope map, sibling intent, cherry-picks, ledger). continual-progress keeps your PR legible so /coordinate (yours or a sibling’s) has something to triage. | A folio’s own AGENTS.md may carry these rules for that repository, and a stricter merge gate — litlfred/qou §”Branch + PR workflow” is the worked case. This skill is the platform-side statement; where a folio is stricter, the folio wins. | /todo-manager — the session work-plan; the PR-body status checklist (invariant 3) is its externally-visible projection, so a watcher needs no access to the session’s work item queue. | .

513.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
513.title: Contributor feedback on a working draft
513.content: Process_ContributorFeedback · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . A document is still being written, and the Authoring Committee gives feedback on it in a shared Contributor Feedback sheet. This is what happens to ONE change set, one row of that sheet: a member starts it with a title, the sections it is about and their feedback; the agent proposes a direction; an Editor lets the agent edit; the agent makes the edit in the row’s one pull request, whose staging preview shows what changed; the committee answers on the row; and an Editor lets the agent merge. If the row’s feedback changes after the agent wrote its proposal, the proposal is marked stale and the row’s Ready for agent goes back to No, so the agent proposes again and an Editor decides again. The sheet’s colours follow the lanes: Blue for the committee, Green for the agent, Orange for the Editor. Skill: review-sheet-script. i i i i i i i i i

514.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft

515.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
515.title: Lanes — who acts
515.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Authoring Committee | authoring-committee | The people writing the document with the editor: contributors, each with their own Contributor Feedback column (Blue). They start rows, give feedback and answer the preview. They recommend; they do not set the Ready columns. | . | Authoring agent | authoring-agent | Writes only Green cells and the Agent tab. Proposes a direction for each row, edits the document in the row’s one pull request once an Editor says so, and merges it once an Editor says so. | . | Editor | editor | The one lane that decides, through the Orange Ready columns, which only the people in the sheet’s EDITORS list may set. Ready for agent lets the agent edit; Ready for merge lets it merge. | . | QA reviewer (independent) | qc-reviewer | Whoever runs the QA gate: an agent session that did not write the row’s pull request, or a person. Never the authoring agent’s own session. Writes only QA gate (change set) on the Agent tab. | .

516.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
516.title: Steps
516.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Start a change-set rowTask_StartRow | Authoring Committee | review-sheet-script | A member adds a row on the Contributor Feedback tab: a title, the Selected Sections it is about (a dropdown from the document’s table of contents) and their feedback in their own Blue column. The script gives the row its Change-set id and links each section. | . | Propose a directionTask_Propose | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | Reads: the row (Title, Selected Sections, the Contributor Feedback columns, Disposition) and the sections it names. Writes: a proposed direction in Feedback (agent) (Green), and the row’s feedback basis on the Agent tab, so the script can tell when the feedback has moved on. A question for people goes in Feedback (agent) as a Decision needed block with options and a recommendation, and the row’s Agentic status becomes Needs human; a chat card may repeat it, but the sheet is the record. An answered question leaves the feedback: its decision is added to the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab, shown in Disposition (agent), whose decision history is appended to and never removed. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Set Ready for agent to YesTask_ReadyForAgent | Editor | review-sheet-script | An Editor agrees the direction and sets the row’s Ready for agent (Orange) to Yes. Person-only: the agent never sets it. | . | Edit the document in the row’s pull requestTask_EditInPullRequest | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | One row, one branch, one active pull request: the agent edits on the row’s branch and opens its pull request, or updates it when the row comes round again. A closed pull request the committee wants back is reopened, or replaced by a new one on the same branch; earlier ones stay listed in Agentic status. Agentic status (Green) says where it is, and Staging review opens the preview’s what-changed page. Before the preview is staged, the agent writes the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab: one line per feedback item, starting from the people’s Blue Disposition, after an optional Overall statement; the sheet shows it in Disposition (agent) and flags any item without a disposition, or one that differs from the people’s. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Review the preview and answerTask_AnswerPreview | Authoring Committee | review-sheet-script | Members read the preview and answer in their Blue columns, or leave them as they are when the change is right. They record the row’s Disposition (Blue): Pending, Accepted, Partially accepted, Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate or Out of scope. | . | QA gate: review dispositions against the people and the pull requestTask_QaGate | QA reviewer (independent) | review-sheet-script | Reads: the change set’s Disposition (change set), the people’s Blue Disposition and feedback, the pull request’s diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every feedback item has one disposition; that each agrees with the people’s Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted item has the change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate or Out of scope item has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set) on the Agent tab, first line “Passed <head sha>: …” or “Failed <head sha>: <why>”, and QA report (change set), the report’s link. The sheet shows the gate under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Set Ready for merge to YesTask_ReadyForMerge | Editor | review-sheet-script | An Editor sets the row’s Ready for merge (Orange) to Yes once the QA gate has passed for the pull request’s head commit. Person-only. Set earlier, the agent does not merge until the gate passes, and its feedback says so. | . | Merge the pull requestTask_Merge | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | The agent merges the row’s pull request, and Agentic status says merged. The change set’s Dispositions blurb, as it stands when Ready for merge is set to Yes, is the summary: it goes into the merge, and closes the change set’s issue. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Close the change set: the issue, then the sheet rowTask_CloseChangeSet | Authoring agent | review-sheet-agent-columns | Closing is one step with two tools, GitHub and the review sheet. The agent closes the change set’s issue on GitHub, with the merge or the reason it closed unmerged, then records Agentic status Closed (or Change merged) on the Agent tab through Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn). The sheet script then hides the row and strikes the whole row through (“make sure complete changeset rows are hidden so not cluttered and that text of that whole row is crossed out”). The agent never hides or strikes a row by hand, and never deletes one: reopening the issue and writing a new status shows it again. Hiding and striking are formatting only, which the review-log watcher ignores. A change set closed without a merge, at a person’s request, takes this step too. | .

519.title: /coordinate — multi-agent / multi-PR coordination
519.content: Skill coordinate: Coordinate work across multiple in-flight Claude PRs working toward a shared goal. Post intent + asks on related PRs, identify cherry-pickable work, respond to code-review comments on your own PR, periodically triage sibling PR activity (new comments, CI status, new commits), watch main + newly created branches/PRs, escalate inconsistent findings to the author, and keep a coordination ledger up to date. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . When several Claude branches are converging on the same long-term goal (e.g. “reach the precision target”, “close all violators of a rule”, “infrastructure overhaul”), each agent has only its own context. Without coordination they will: . | duplicate work (two agents both implementing the same helper), | silently diverge (one renames a symbol, another keeps the old name, the merge conflicts), | miss cherry-picks (one agent already wrote the template the others need), | accept inconsistent findings without flagging them to the author, | accept review-tool feedback without checking it against the actual artifact / sibling change proposal’s — pull request’s (PR’s) — framing (e.g. accepting an off-by-one “fix” that contradicts a definition another PR is also using), | miss new sibling PRs that opened mid-session (new branches landing on main with overlapping scope). | . /coordinate is the protocol that prevents this. None of the agents has all the answers; they look to the author for clarification on inconsistencies, and they cherry-pick from each other.

520.title: Workflow rule reminder
520.content: This skill assumes you’ve already created a branch + opened a PR for the work tranche being coordinated. Per continual-progress (STRICT, supersedes default “no auto-PR” guidance for this repo): always create a branch and open a PR at the start of every work tranche — ASAP, and never ask the user “want me to open the PR?” Branch + PR creation is pre-authorized; the only git action needing explicit permission is the merge. Commit early, commit often. Small structured commits cherry-pick cleanly; big mixed commits do not. Exception: integration-watcher batch audit-job sweeps may use a single bulk commit.

521.title: When to invoke
521.content: . | Start of a session where the user mentioned other branches/PRs by name (e.g. “coordinate with claude/foo and claude/bar”). | Whenever you start a new substantive task in a multi-PR effort — before making code changes, post intent on the relevant PRs. | When you finish a substantive task — post progress + concrete cherry-pickable artefacts (file paths, function names, templates, fixtures). | Periodic triage between substantive commits (§7) — even with no external trigger, sibling PRs may have landed commits or comments that change your scope. Run a quick triage every ~3–5 commits or when you finish a task and pick up the next one. | When main lands new commits during your session — if any touch the same files, blocks, or scripts you are editing, treat as a sibling PR for §3 classification purposes. | When a code-review comment lands on your own PR (gemini-code- assist, copilot-pull-request-reviewer, codex, or human reviewers) — see §5 Responding to review comments. | When you encounter a finding that contradicts another PR’s framing — write the disagreement up explicitly, post it to both PRs, and tag the author for resolution. | A COLLISION — coordinate. A merge conflict caused by a sibling’s landed work is not merely a thing to resolve; it is the signal that two sessions are editing one subject. Resolve it AND coordinate. | A POTENTIAL collision, seen in the work items — coordinate. Before you start a topic, and at each triage, scan for an in-progress work item whose scope overlaps yours. That is the cheapest collision to find, because it is the one found BEFORE either of you has written anything. How to read a sibling’s state out of the store, and the boundary of that inference, is bean-coordination §”Where a sibling session is visible from” — not restated here. | When you START any new unit of work — before the first edit. A new story, epic, feature or task work item, an issue, CRDM Phase 6, a workplan tranche, or a handover pickup runs the collision review in §”Starting new work” below, scaled to its blast radius, and records it in the workplan work item. | .

522.title: Inputs
522.content: . | The current PR number (your branch). | A list of sibling branch names or PR numbers (the user gives this, or list the open PRs labelled in-flight with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool). | The shared goal in 1–2 sentences. | .

523.title: Where each section lives
523.content: This skill was 732 lines and the Protocol was 478 of them — an agent reads the whole thing before acting, and at that length it skims. The Protocol now sits beside this file. Nothing was deleted and no step was renumbered, because other skills cite coordinate §0a and coordinate.md §8a and those citations have to keep resolving. | section | where | . | workflow rule, when to invoke, inputs | here — read before you start | . | Protocol §1–§11 — the eleven coordination steps | coordinate/protocol.md | . | output, anti-patterns, §11 STATUS.md, §12 same-goal coordination, related skills | here | . Coordinating: read this file for whether and when, then protocol.md for how.

524.title: Output
524.content: After invocation, you should have: . | Read every sibling PR’s body and changed-files list. | Posted at most one coordination comment per sibling PR (intent + asks), unless you’ve made progress that warrants a separate progress comment. | Triaged every open review-tool thread on your own PR (§5) and posted a single consolidated status comment. | Run a §7 periodic triage every 3–5 of your own commits, capturing new sibling-PR comments + commits + CI status in one table. | Run §8a (git fetch origin main) at each triage cycle and react to any main-landed changes that touch your scope. | Run §8b (newly-opened PRs / branches) at each triage cycle and prompt the author when a new sibling overlaps your scope keywords. | Identified the next concrete, non-overlapping task on your own workplan and started on it. | (Optional) Created or updated docs/coordination/<goal-slug>.md with the current state. | Escalated any inconsistencies via §6 with @<author> tagging. | .

525.title: Anti-patterns
525.content: . | ❌ Post a coordination comment that just summarises your own PR. Sibling agents already read your PR body. | ❌ Pick the same task as a sibling without posting first. Even if their PR has been quiet, the human author may have given them a verbal lead. | ❌ “Resolve” an inconsistency by rewriting your finding. Escalate to the author. | ❌ Accept a review-tool fix without verifying it against the artifact and sibling-PR conventions. Bot suggestions can flip conventions silently. | ❌ Reply per-thread on a 6-comment review pass. Use one consolidated status comment + per-thread accept / reject-with-reason flags. | ❌ Skip §7 triage between commits because “I would have heard if something landed” — you wouldn’t. Sibling agents work in parallel and rarely interrupt each other. Run the triage anyway. | ❌ Silently merge / cherry-pick from main without §8a classification. Main commits can also be inconsistent findings. | ❌ Add a newly-opened PR to your scope without prompting the author (§8b). The author may want it independent. | ❌ Long prose. Coordination comments are tables, file pointers, and one-line asks. | .

526.title: §11 STATUS.md + master ledger pattern
526.content: A repeated flip-flop episode (a claim asserted and retracted across several sessions) motivates a more structured coordination layer that overlays this skill: . | Root STATUS.md — single dashboard listing every goal + pointer to its master ledger + active PRs. | Master ledger per goal — docs/coordination/<goal>.md holds the durable narrative: current canonical status, open tasks, flip-flop history, sessions log. | Per-goal queue — the beans queue (beans/); each open task is one entry. | . When /coordinate runs, it now ALSO: . | Reads STATUS.md to find which goal(s) the current PR touches. | Reads the goal’s master ledger to identify the current canonical status — overrides recent commit claims if the ledger records a retraction. | Reads the queue to find sibling tasks in flight. | References the ledger session log when posting intent comments on sibling PRs, so the comment is grounded in the durable record, not just session memory. | . See session-intent for the session-start / session-end ledger + queue update protocol — /coordinate is the sibling-PR arm; /session-intent is the durable-state arm. They are run together at session start.

527.title: §12 Multi-agent same-goal coordination
527.content: Multiple agents MAY work the same goal in parallel. Per author directive: agents coordinate with the user on goals, not with each other on task-level locks. Model: . | Goal = product (author’s directive). User-level concern. | Queue = per-goal item list (the beans queue). | Tasks are NOT exclusively claimed. Two agents may attack the same task with different methods — both threads have value. | Coordination is with the USER on goal-level decisions, not agent-to-agent on task-level locks. | . When you detect a sibling agent on your task . Signals: . | The queue entry has co_assignees populated, OR | A sibling PR (listed with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool) has commits touching your task’s scope files within the last 24h, OR | The ledger session log shows another agent declared intent on the same task ID. | . Workflow: . | Do not silently abandon. Your independent attack is valuable. | Post intent on the sibling PR (this skill §3) so the sibling sees you’re also working it. | Ask the user with AskUserQuestion whether to keep both threads or have one stand down. Include rich context per AGENTS.md §User accessibility — quote what each agent is doing, what method, what’s been found, cost of running both. | If user says one stands down, the standing-down agent appends partial results to the ledger and updates queue status: "open" (releasing the task). The continuing agent may pick up the partial results. | . Watching for sibling-PR contradictions . Per §8 of this skill: at each triage cycle, look for sibling-PR commits or comments that contradict your branch’s framing. Per §6: escalate inconsistent findings to the user. Do not silently adopt the sibling’s framing without an §6 conversation.

528.title: What actually reaches a sibling
528.content: Do not assume you can message a sibling session. Measured from a cloud session with eleven siblings live on one repository: . | channel | reaches a cloud sibling? | . | list_sessions | sees them — id, title, branch, task summary | . | ListAgents | no — “no other Claude session is running on this machine” | . | SendMessage | no — the send is refused, target not reachable | . | a committed work item | yes — every session reads the store at session start | . | a PR or issue comment | yes — to whoever looks, and it is durable | . So list_sessions tells you WHO is working and on WHAT, and then the message has to travel through something committed. The practical order: . | list_sessions (or the work items) to find WHO overlaps and how. | Write the coordination INTO the artefacts they will read — the work item, the PR body, the issue. A work item is the strongest, because bean-coordination §”The store on main is the one every sibling reads” makes it the one surface every session opens. | Only then consider a direct message, and only for a sibling ListAgents actually lists. | . A spawned helper is reachable, and the owner’s authority is not relayed . The table above is for a session without the remote-session tools. A session that has create_session and send_message (the claude-code-remote server) can seed a helper session and message a cloud session it lists. Reaching it does not give it the owner’s authority: a helper’s permission layer may refuse pushes, messages back and even reads when its task arrived from another session, and it must refuse a relayed ruling (such as a merge window) as the owner’s. That refusal is correct. conduct/security/zero-trust-handover §”Who the principal is” puts a message relayed from another session on the NOT-the-principal list. So, when you seed a helper session: . | Quote the owner’s own words verbatim in the seed prompt, with the session they were typed in, and say which part the helper serves. The helper then knows what was asked, though it still cannot treat the words as instructions the owner gave it. | Relay no rulings. A merge window, a re-pin consent, or an answer to an owner decision binds the session it was given in. Tell the helper to open PRs and leave them green, not to merge. | Tell the owner, in your own turn, that each helper may ask for confirmation in its own session, and name the sessions. That is the only way the owner’s authority reaches it. A helper that stops to ask is working as designed. The ask is not a failure to route around. | Give the helper a lane it can finish without the owner: a work item store or a set of repositories, the lanes of its siblings, and the report-back channel (send_message to the coordinator). | Carry the interaction-modality rule in every seed prompt and subagent brief, and require the helper to pass it on. A helper that asks the owner directly must present every question twice in order — first the full question in chat (context, what differs, every identifier expanded, ≤ 4 numbered or lettered options with pros/cons/downstream/reversibility, recommended option first and marked (Recommended), and stated default on silence), then the tappable card (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, ask_question, or post_widget) with the same option labels — never in prose alone and never asking the owner to type. A subagent or a sibling running beside a live discussion returns any owner question to the coordinator in the hand-back-to-discussion schema format. See opening-brief §”Briefing a sibling or a subagent — pass interaction-modality on (STRICT)”. | . Eleven sessions is the normal case, not the exception . Measured with eleven sessions on one repository, each merging main on a loop: one branch took four base merges in three hours, three of them conflicted. The rate IS the environment; coordinate earlier, not merge harder. The worked example: a voice landing in a directory being deleted . A branch migrated every voice from <instance>/voices/ to <instance>/skills/voices/. Mid-flight, main landed a NEW voice in cat-harness/voices/ — the directory the branch removes. Git’s rename detection then placed the new file inside another voice’s folder. Nothing was wrong with either piece of work. What was missing was that neither session knew about the other, and the work items said so the whole time: the migration’s work item was in-progress and names the directory. A work item scan by either session would have caught it before a line was written, which is exactly why the trigger above is worth having.

529.title: Crossing into a sibling’s subject — permitted, and what it costs
529.content: Crossing into a sibling’s stream is allowed, but coordinate, watch for collisions, and avoid duplicating work. Two rules follow. 1. The stream that owns a milestone’s WORK may repair the milestone. A checker must not rewrite a milestone — a gate that guesses replaces a stale belief with an invented one. A session that has re-measured the goal’s whole surface may. So the line is checker vs. session, not owner vs. non-owner. A session repairing somebody’s milestone re-measures every line it rewrites, in a fresh container, by running the thing — and says which clause it could not verify. 2. Crossing is permitted; colliding silently is not. Cross freely, but the crossing is what triggers this skill rather than what excuses skipping it. The collision surface is FILES, and it is predictable before you touch one . A work item scan finds sessions working the same subject. It does not find two sessions about to edit the same file from different subjects: . | file | why two sessions want it | . | scripts/stale-paths-baseline.json | two lines long. Every milestone repair removes its own entry. Two repairs in flight = a conflict whose wrong resolution silently empties a file whose stated property is that it shrinks rather than fossilises — and an empty baseline fails every finding, “which is the safe direction” only if somebody notices. | . | a shared work item | every stream appends its own outcome. “An append cannot collide” is false when two sessions append, because both land at EOF. | . | generated dirs (auto-docs/, skill-instructions/, kg-qa sidecars) | nobody edits them, everybody regenerates them. Take main’s copy and re-run the generator — never hand-merge. For test/results/**, bun run cat qa:resolve-conflicts: those are derived QA results whose record is on the qa-reports branch. | . | test/attestations/** | judgements, not generated — no generator can reproduce one. Read both sides and keep both unless they are the same judgement; see prepare-merge §”Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/”. | . Name the files you will touch, not just the work items, when you post intent. A sibling can dodge a file; it cannot dodge a subject it cannot see. Duplicated work is measured in what was already pushed, not in what is open . Before re-deriving a measurement, check whether a sibling’s pushed commit already carries it: an open PR’s diff is a fact, and reading it costs one call against a session’s worth of re-measurement.

530.title: Starting new work — a collision review, recorded before the first edit (STRICT)
530.content: This section is the rule’s only home. bean-coordination, session-intent, continual-progress, opening-brief, issue-working and crdm-requirements-workflow point here. They do not restate it. When it runs — the start of any new unit of work . Run the review once, before the first edit, whenever you start: . | a new story, epic, feature or task work item; | work on an issue, before you announce the branch; | CRDM Phase 6, implementation; | a new tranche of a workplan; | a pickup of someone else’s work from a handover. | . A pickup runs its own review. The previous session’s review is dated, and PRs may have opened since it was written. How deep — scale the review to the blast radius . The review is proportional. The question is how much other work your change can collide with, not how big your diff is. | A platform refactor gets the full review: all five steps, with messages to the owners. A platform refactor is a change to something that many pages, generators or open PRs depend on: . | shared layout and includes: _includes/, docs-ui.css, docs-ui.js, the navbar; | a generator whose output is committed or published, such as gen-ig-pages.ts or gen-navbar-include.ts; | a schema, a BPMN process, a workflow or a gate that other work is checked against. | . A ten-line change to a shared include collides with every PR that regenerates it. | A small, local story still runs steps 1 and 2, quickly. When they find nothing, record “no overlap found” in the work item, together with what you checked: the PR search, the work item search, and the terms you used. That takes about two minutes and one work item note. | Only an overlap triggers steps 3 and 4. If steps 1 and 2 find a sibling on your files or your subject, name its owner and message it, whatever the size of your change. | . “No overlap found” with no record of what was checked is not a review. The next session cannot tell it from a review that was skipped. The work item trigger above catches a sibling working on the same subject. §”The collision surface is FILES” catches two sessions editing the same file from different subjects. A refactor causes both kinds at once, which is why it gets the full review and does not rely on either trigger. The five steps, in order, before any file is edited . | List the open PRs and the files they change. Use the list change proposals forge-operation Tool, then list changed files for each PR. Intersect the result with the files your work will touch. A PR that changes only generated files you will also regenerate is not a collision; say so and move on. | Scan the in-progress work items for overlapping scope. Use beans list --status in-progress --search <term>, and search the subject as well as the ids: the file names, the generator, the page type. A work item id finds nothing when the overlapping work has no work item of its own; see bean-coordination §”The trigger is STARTING WORK”. | Name the owning sessions. Use list_sessions, the Claude-Session: trailers on each PR’s commits, and bun run cat sessions --since <window>. bean-coordination §”Where a sibling session is visible from” says how far that inference goes. | Message each owner with your intent and your asks. State what you will change, phase by phase, and the files each phase touches. Then ask two things: which order do we land in, and who owns each overlapping file. Send it through a channel that actually reaches them; §”What actually reaches a sibling” says which ones do. A PR comment also leaves a durable copy. | Record the review in the workplan work item before editing. Write down each overlapping session, its PRs and work items, the files you share, and the phases affected; or “no overlap found” and what you checked. A review that exists only in the chat is gone when the container goes, and the next session has to run it again. | . Phases that overlap a sibling wait. They wait until the sibling has agreed an order, or until its overlapping PR has landed. Phases that touch none of the sibling’s files can go ahead, and the review says which ones those are. Worked example: a platform refactor . A refactor moving the per-page nav, the harness bar, icons, scripts and the IG chrome CSS into shared cached assets touches the layout of every page. Before any edit, the review found active sibling work on every layout file the plan needed: a navbar session (four PRs on docs-ui.css, docs-ui.js, the navbar include, harness_details.html, head_custom.html), and two IG sessions on gen-ig-pages.ts. The review went into the work item, the three owning sessions were asked for an order, and the only work that started touched none of their files. Without the review, five PRs would have been rebased into a refactor of the files they were editing.

531.title: Related skills
531.content: . | bean-coordination — the committed store siblings read, how to claim, and how far a sibling’s state can be inferred from it. The DETECTION half of this skill’s work item trigger lives there. | delivery-summary — what to post after a feature lands (one PR scope). | watch — passive monitoring of upstream branches. | diff — per-block change report (one PR scope). | session-intent — session-start / session-end ledger + queue update protocol (the durable-state arm of coordination). | pending-show — read-only display of current session’s pending work (todos, intent, queue assignments). | prepare-merge-auto — autonomous merge pipeline (uses this skill’s sibling-coord pattern). | specification-management — governance of specification requirements, linking CRDM and spec-kit to the bootstrap Requirement definition. | . /coordinate complements them: it is the active cross-PR protocol — including handling of code-review comments on your own PR — not a passive watcher and not a single-PR summary.

532.title: Flag-bearer reflections
532.content: Lessons from acting as flag-bearer across many sibling PRs on a shared goal. Apply when you hold the flag. | Build the ledger hub FIRST, then post. Create docs/coordination/<goal>.md with: the direction (one boxed statement of the target), the common infra everyone rows toward (cheat-sheet step table, watcher queues, dashboards, a falsification anchor), and a per-PR “which way to row” roster with report-back slots. Post intent only after the hub exists, so every comment can link one canonical place. This is what makes “make sure all use common infra” actionable rather than a slogan. | Tailor per-PR; then LISTEN. A flag-bearer that only broadcasts is half-doing the job. Pull each sibling’s current state (a background Explore agent reading PR bodies + last comments is ideal), and fold their findings back as sharpenings to your own plan. Record sharpenings in the ledger and amend the workplan — do not silently keep the stale plan. | Anchor the cluster to one falsifiable target. Give every sibling a shared regression target. It turns “which way to row” into a checkable claim and prevents divergent re-derivations. | Push-race coordination with background agents. When a background sub-agent and you both push to the same branch, wrap every push in a fetch → rebase → retry loop: for i in 1 2 3 4; do git push && break || { git fetch origin <br> -q; git rebase origin/<br>; sleep $((2**i)); }; done. The agent’s commits may already be in your local history (shared working dir) — check git log before assuming a divergence. | Billing-CI is noise — do not let it derail coordination. If CI fails setup-phase (≤5 s, simultaneous, no logs) on every push while local validation stays green, recognise the billing signature (litlfred/qou AGENTS.md “CI billing failures”), note [skip-ci: billing], and keep working; never re-diagnose it as a code problem or pause the cluster for it. | .

535.doc: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio
535.title: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio
535.content: Process_CopyIntoFolio · strict · 8 step(s) . Taking an asset from an upstream knowledge graph into your own folio so you can edit it, comment on it or raise todos against it — without touching the upstream source and without losing where it came from. This is the fourth knowledge-graph affordance (copy-into-folio in kg-affordances). Like copy-out-materialized.bpmn for held library items, it is TWO WRITES AND A REFUSAL, gated up front by write capability: . | Check whether the session holds a write capability (git-push, github-api, or github-connector). When none is available, degrade cleanly to read-only inspection (browse) and emit the KgAsset declaration snippet with source pre-filled rather than failing mid-procedure. | Read the asset and its origin (instance, path, ref) from the source knowledge graph without mutating the source. | Copy the asset into the target folio, declare it in the folio’s assets[], and stamp KgAsset.source ({ instance, path, ref } — AssetSourceSchema in schemas/kg/kg-node.ts). source absent means authored locally (a third state), so omitting source on a copy is the defect this process exists to prevent. | Verify the declared asset via check:declaration-resolution (check:declared-assets), then hand off to the folio author to edit, comment or raise todos on their copy. | . i i i i i i i i

541.title: Working on materialized content — copy it out
541.content: Skill copy-out-materialized: Materialized content is read-only. To work on it you take a copy into your own folio/, and the copy records what it is a copy of — the local-provenance edge, which is not the upstream one. Named by: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes . Materialized content is a copy of somebody else’s bytes, and this repository does not edit it in place. The contents of a materialized <stub>/<sub-graph> are immutable, and the rule is enforced: to work on them, copy them into your own folio/. Diagram: copy-out-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

542.title: What the rule protects, and what it does not
542.content: It protects the CLAIM. A materialized record asserts “these bytes are what upstream published”. Editing them in place leaves that assertion standing over bytes it no longer describes — and check:materialized-fixity is what catches one that happened, by hashing the bytes against the digest the record carries. It does not protect against the copy being wrong, stale or badly chosen. Those are the five gates’ job, at materialisation time (materialize-remote), and a copy-out re-opens none of them: you are copying something this repository already decided it may hold.

543.title: Who may copy out
543.content: Any reader. This is deliberately not a permission: refusing a copy would not protect the original, because the original is protected by being read-only. A gate here would only stop people working. What copying out does NOT confer is the right to publish. The copy inherits its source’s restrictions and copyright verdicts, and it is a new artefact in your folio whose publication is your folio’s decision, judged the way any other authored content is.

544.title: Where the copy goes
544.content: Into the copier’s own folio/, with provenance — never a scratch area, which makes the copy publishable by accident: a directory nobody declared is a directory nobody gates.

545.title: The copy records what it is a copy of
545.content: This is the part that is easy to leave out and impossible to reconstruct later. materialization.provenance is a pair: . | field | points at | . | upstream | the remote thing — a URI, upstream | . | local | the original in this repository it was taken from | . A copy-out writes local. It does not overwrite upstream, and it does not reuse upstream for the local original. Without local, one rename later a copy is indistinguishable from original work. That is the whole failure this step exists to prevent, and nothing downstream can repair it: the information was never written down.

546.title: The copy is NOT read-only
546.content: A materialized node is frozen because it is a claim about somebody else’s bytes. A copy in your own folio/ is yours, makes no such claim, and is ordinary authored content — so it is writable, and its directory’s readOnly is false. If it were frozen too, the copy-out would achieve nothing, and the next person would need a copy of the copy.

547.title: The exception is “say what you did”, not a list of who may skip
547.content: The exception — for publication workflow purposes and the like — is a rule, not an allowlist of writers that would go stale: . A step that rewrites a materialized artefact records the new fixity in the same change. Then check:materialized-fixity passes and the record describes what is actually there. A step that rewrites without updating fixity fails, correctly, because it has forked upstream without saying so — which is exactly what the rule exists to prevent. The check asks a question about BYTES and never about who wrote them, so it needs no attribution of a commit to a process step. Where it applies . refresh-materialized.bpmn’s Task_Apply is the one step in the declared corpus that rewrites bytes a materialization record describes, so it writes the new fixity in the same change; otherwise a correct run of it would fail the gate as an unannounced edit. No publication process writes to materialized content. kg-to-portal.bpmn’s S_Sign signs a subgraph cut from the KG — derived content, not held upstream bytes. So the publication case is a rule with no instance yet, stated here rather than drawn as a step no diagram does, because a declared-but-absent step makes a consumer report a clean run over nothing.

548.title: What to check afterwards
548.content: . | bun run cat check:materialized-fixity — the original still hashes to its recorded digest. If it does not, the copy-out was an edit in place. | bun run cat check:read-only-graphs — your folio’s directory is not accidentally declared read-only, and the source’s still is. | .

550.doc: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else's bytes
550.title: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes
550.content: Process_CopyOutMaterialized · strict · 5 step(s) . Somebody wants to change content this repository holds a read-only materialized copy of: copy it into their own folio/, recording which original it came out of. Materialized content is read-only, and that is enforced, not advised. STRICT, and the reason is narrow. Only one step here is a gate, and it is Gateway_Frozen: whether the target is read-only at all. Everything after it is mechanical. What makes the process strict is that skipping it does not fail loudly — an edit in place succeeds, and is only caught later by check:materialized-fixity hashing bytes against the digest their record carries. A process whose omission looks exactly like compliance cannot be advisory. The copy-out re-opens NONE of the five materialisation gates. Those were answered when this repository decided it may hold these bytes at all (materialize-remote.bpmn); copying something already held is not a second acquisition. What the copy does inherit is the restrictions and copyright verdicts — the copy is a new artefact in the copier’s folio, and publishing it is that folio’s decision. The three states, the five gates and the provenance pair are folio-assistant-core/schemas/materialization.ts. Nothing here restates them. i i i i i

556.title: Corpus — committing an accepted edit
556.content: Skill corpus-commit-contract: The contract the corpus role is held to when an accepted edit is committed into it: take the write only on the editor’s acceptance, as one change with its QA sidecars, under the commit-hygiene requirement and with no relaxing of that policy. The narrowest contract the editing diagram requires. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: Editing and HCI validation . corpus (declared below this layer) is played by a mechanical actor: the versioned content store, which is written to and decides nothing. A role played by a machine is still a role, and its skills are its contract: the responsibilities it must perform, which a test can hold it to. This skill is the part of that contract this layer’s diagrams rely on, and nothing more.

557.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
557.content: Lane_Corpus in editing-hci-validation names this role and holds one activity, Task_Commit. What that lane’s documentation and the task’s say is the whole contract.

558.title: What it must do
558.content: . | Receive the write only after the editor accepts. Task_Commit is reachable from no path except Gateway_EditorDecision’s accept branch (the lane’s documentation). A change the editor discards, or one that has not reached the editor, never reaches the corpus. | Take the change together with its QA sidecars. “Only now does the change become corpus content, together with its QA sidecars” (the task’s documentation): the block and the findings about it arrive as one change. | Hold the commit to the commit-hygiene requirement (req:commit-hygiene), and allow no relaxing of it: the task’s policy is relaxable="false", because this is the one step that is irreversible in a way nothing upstream is. | .

559.title: Not its responsibility
559.content: Drafting the change, validating it, or deciding whether to accept it. Those happen in the author’s, the pipeline’s, the reviewer’s and the editor’s lanes before anything reaches the corpus. Resolving the bean afterwards is the work plan’s.

560.title: Tests
560.content: The test in tested-by: drives the editing process with the harness’s workflow engine and checks line 1 (the commit is enabled only after accept), and checks that the diagram binds the lane to this role and carries line 3’s policy. Line 2 and the content of the commit-hygiene statements are not exercised: no code in this layer performs the commit.

562.title: Corpus-Grep Skill
562.content: Skill corpus-grep: Pre-declaration corpus check. Before declaring any item “open”, “gap”, “TODO”, “open problem”, “pending derivation” — or asserting in chat that something is unresolved in the corpus — run the four-path grep checklist. A source file’s ## Status note lags the corpus by weeks; the corpus is the source of truth. An item is open only after all four paths come back empty (modulo the originating file itself). Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Disambiguation. This skill formalizes the backward check (“has this already been resolved somewhere in the corpus?”). Its forward complement is the formalize-first discipline (“can a structural claim prune the hypothesis class before I run a wide search?”). Run corpus-grep before declaring an item open; run formalize-first before launching an expensive numerical scan. The two are duals — backward against known results, forward against the hypothesis class.

563.title: Role
563.content: Gate every “this is open / unresolved / a gap” declaration behind a mechanical four-path search of the corpus. The originating source file’s status note (## Status, Open question, Phase 3 open, a TODO in a code or formal-source file, a PR-description “still open”) is not authoritative — prior agents routinely land a resolution as an audit doc, an adjacent chapter’s block, an implemented witness script, or a coordination ledger entry weeks before the source file’s note is updated. This skill catches that lag.

564.title: When to run this skill (STRICT)
564.content: Run the checklist before any of the following land in a durable artifact (audit doc, content block .md/.ts, code or formal-source comment, PR description, coordination ledger) or are asserted as fact in chat: . | “X is open” / “Open X” / “open problem” / “open question” | “TODO: derive X” / “pending derivation” / “still missing” | “this is a gap” / “no proof exists” / “not yet implemented” | “X is not wired into compute” / “nothing computes X” | . If you are about to type any of those about a corpus topic, stop and run the four paths first.

565.title: When NOT to run it (scope boundary)
565.content: The checklist gates factual corpus-status claims only. It does not gate, and must never be used to suppress: . | Skeptical assessments — “this looks fitted”, “this is numerology”, “hidden degrees of freedom here”. | Outside-view critique of a derivation’s rigor. | Reception / publishability / referee forecasts. | . Those are critical-distance judgments (see the repo’s Critical-distance license), not open-item declarations, and are never gated by this skill. Voicing them in chat does not require running corpus-grep first.

566.title: The four-path checklist (run all four)
566.content: | # | Path | What it catches | . | 1 | grep -rln <topic> docs/audits/ | Owner-authorised resolutions land as audit docs ahead of the source file’s status note being updated. | . | 2 | grep -rln <topic> content/ (full tree) | Related conjectures / propositions cross-cut chapters: a block in one chapter may answer a question raised in another. | . | 3 | grep -rln <topic> folio-assistant/computations/ | Implemented code may already discharge the content. | . | 4 | docs/coordination/<theme>.md | The coordination ledger — a prior agent may have already closed the item. | . Search the full content/ tree, not just the chapter you started in. The whole point of path 2 is that the resolution lives somewhere you did not expect.

567.title: Mechanical recipe
567.content: Pick a TOPIC that is the keyword / regex of the claim (an identifier, a label fragment, a phrase — e.g. delta_lambda, bring_color, c_3.*Taylor, kashaev.*density). Then run all four paths in one sweep: . TOPIC='delta_lambda' # ← keyword or regex for the claim under test for d in docs/audits content folio-assistant/computations docs/coordination; do if [ -d "$d" ]; then echo "=== $d ===" grep -rln -e "$TOPIC" "$d" 2>/dev/null fi done . Prefer the harness Grep tool (output_mode: "files_with_matches", one call per path or a single call with path set to the repo root and a glob) over shell grep when running inside an agent — results integrate with the permission UI and file links. The shell snippet above is the portable fallback. Widen the topic if the first pass is empty: try a synonym, the formal declaration name, the block label, the function name, and the witness-JSON key. A single spelling is not a clearing.

568.title: Decision procedure
568.content: . | Any non-trivial hit in (1)–(4) ⇒ the item is NOT open. Read the hit, then document the existing resolution instead of declaring a gap. Cite the file (audit doc / block .md / witness / ledger entry) that resolves it. | All four empty, modulo the originating file itself ⇒ you may declare the item open. “Modulo the originating file” means: a hit that is only the source file you are auditing does not count as a clearing — it is the very note you already mistrust. | Unsure whether a hit is the resolution ⇒ open the file and read it. A filename match is a lead, not a verdict. Treat a hit as resolving only if it actually discharges the claim (an audit verdict, a proved block, a passing witness, a ledger “CLOSED”). | .

It is invoked by, and consistent with, these codified instances: . | The folio’s own AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, where it states the rule for its corpus. | A content type’s own audits, which apply the checklist to their declarations. For a paper folio these are the science layer’s proof-gap-audit §K (proof-gap declarations), compute-author and compute-audit (before declaring a statement “not wired into compute”) and lean-environment-setup (before declaring a capability unavailable). | .

571.title: Covered is not reachable — and check:tools cannot tell you which
571.content: Skill covered-is-not-reachable: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism is reachable from no Tool node. Read before concluding from check:tools that a command is reachable, and before adding a Tool node or a maintains claim. Named by: Code node review, Code change and review . A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing. check:tools reports the skill as covered and is right to: coverage is a relation between a Tool and a skill, never between a Tool and a command. For example, kg-export can be satisfied by a publishing node, a serving node and schema carriers while no node runs an export; translation-manager by extract, inject, status, signoff and validate nodes while none reaches the round-trip QA.

572.title: The two questions, kept apart
572.content: “Does this skill have a Tool?” — bun run cat check:tools, and bun run cat tools:coverage for which of the uncovered ones warrant one. “Is this command reachable by asking the graph?” — no instrument answers this yet; it has to be measured by hand. A skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Do not use the first question to answer the second: the cause of an invisible mechanism is structural, because nobody asks the second question.

573.title: What to do when you meet one
573.content: Add the node for the mechanism. Then two things not to do: . | Do not widen an existing node’s satisfies to make the gap look closed. That makes the graph assert a node does something it does not. | Do not give the new node the same I/O as an existing one unless it really is a substitute. Alternatives are derived from a shared skill plus an identical I/O signature (deriveAlternatives), and export-then-publish-then- serve are complementary steps, not competing arms. | .

574.title: Two reasons NOT to write maintains
574.content: maintains.artefact is a single path. A generator that writes one file per subject — gen-skill-docs, gen-schema-docs, gen-block-jsonld — has no single artefact to name. A declaration naming one file out of tens is worse than absent: it looks like a complete provenance record. A maintains claim asserts the artefact is published. Verify that by reading the build, not by assuming: cat-harness/ns.jsonld is a real claim because .github/workflows/docs-site.yml writes it. Remove a claim in the same change that retires its artefact: a claim outliving its artefact is the same 404 from the other side. An artefact nobody publishes is exactly the 404 the drift check exists to prevent. And the drift check only covers its own producer . kg:schema:check reconciles maintains both ways, but its unproduced direction runs only over artefacts whose declaring Tool invokes bun run cat kg:schema, because a maintained artefact is not necessarily produced by the schema exporter. So a maintains claim on any other producer’s artefact is unchecked: it can rot to a 404 and nothing notices. The fix — not yet built — is to assert every declared artefact is present after _site/ is assembled, with could-not-determine kept distinct from present.

575.title: Adding a Tool type is fail-closed, and that is deliberate
575.content: check:tools refuses a command-line input whose type could express a shell payload, against the membership list in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts. A newly added type is absent from that list and therefore unsafe by default. Adding it is a deliberate step, not an oversight to route around — and the fix for an enumerable input is the enum, never a looser type that happens to pass. Where the enum duplicates a union declared elsewhere, guard it in both directions: satisfies catches a member that stops being valid, and a conditional type catches a member added to the union and not here. An unavoidable duplicate is fine; an unchecked one is not — see directory-conventions.

576.title: Five cases, most invisible to the instruments
576.content: | case | what exists | what is missing | what sees it | . | 1 | a skill | a Tool | check:tools, tools:coverage | . | 2 | a skill and Tools for its neighbours | a Tool for the mechanism | nothing — this skill | . | 3 | a mechanism | any skill stating the capability | nothing | . | 4 | a skill, a mechanism, a Tool | a command — it runs in-process only | nothing | . | 5 | a skill, a mechanism, a command | anything that invokes it | nothing | . Case 5 is case 4’s inverse — the entry point is present and the callers are absent — and it is discussed under §Reachability is PLURAL below, because the useful question there is how many dispatch points this should have. A script whose only references are its own usage string and a line of skill prose telling a human what to type is case 5: its mechanism is inlined in prose.

577.title: The third case: a mechanism with no skill at all
577.content: A generator that renders theme and avatar nodes into the site’s stylesheets is a textbook maintains pair, and yet no generic skill need state the capability. tools:coverage cannot see this: it enumerates skills and asks which lack Tools, so a capability nobody has stated is absent from the list it walks. (site-presentation-assets is the skill that now states that one.) . satisfies requires at least one skill, so a node cannot be written without one: . | Do not stretch a neighbouring skill to make the node validate. The resulting satisfies edge is simply false. | Do not write the skill as a wrapper for the command. A skill states a capability generically and names no script; one that exists to give a script somewhere to point is a Tool with front matter. | . Authoring the skill is a design act — a claim about the platform’s capability vocabulary, inherited by every dependent instance — so it goes to the owner rather than being decided in passing. Write the skill before the nodes. Once the gap is closed, remove any note announcing it: an agent that believes a stale gap either avoids the capability or rebuilds it.

578.title: The fourth case: a mechanism with no command, reachable in-process only
578.content: Cases 1–3 are about a missing node or a missing skill. This one has both, and is still unaskable: the mechanism has no command, so no CI job and no person can run it. For example, checkFolioProfile in pipeline/profile-check.ts catches what schema validation structurally cannot — a block valid against its own schema but wrong for the folio’s content profile, because adapters partition disjointly while profiles nest. Its only caller is the MCP tool registration, so it is reachable by an MCP-connected agent and by nothing else: not a gate, not a sweep, not a person at a shell. Every instrument that asks “can this be reached” answers yes. Ask which callers, not whether. “Reachable from MCP” and “reachable from CI” are different claims, and a durable verdict needs the second. Giving a library function its first command . Prefer a qa-sweep axis to a one-off check script: a sweep verdict is durable where a printed one is not — a printed verdict cannot distinguish “wrong since it was written” from “broken in the commit under review”. Watch the library’s defaults. checkFolioProfile resolves through readFolioProfile, which turns an undeclared profile into "paper" — correct for a validator, which validates against the wider vocabulary, and wrong for a reporter, which must use readDeclaredFolioProfile or report pass on a folio that declares no content type at all. A library’s defaulting is usually what erases the third state. When you give a library function its first entry point, the value it resolves for its own use is not the value a verdict may report. Check which of the two you are reading — by running it, not by reading it.

579.title: Reachability is PLURAL — “which caller should this have?” presumes one
579.content: One mechanism can have several dispatch points, so the question to ask is not which caller should this have but: . What should be able to start this — and is each of those a trigger or a Tool? . The two are different objects, and which one a dispatch point is follows from who initiates: . | dispatch point | it is a | because | . | a named command | Tool | a caller invokes it; that is what a Tool node IS | . | a BPMN activity | trigger | the process fires it when the step is reached | . | a QA sweep axis | trigger | the sweep fires it per subject | . | a schedule or a watcher | trigger | time or an event fires it | . None of them is an alternative to another, by the same argument deriveAlternatives makes about sharing a skill: they are different ways the same work gets started. Enumerating the dispatch points also finds the ones already built. For each candidate, check whether it exists (an activity may already carry the skill, so workflow_next already hands it to an agent), whether it is possible (a sweep cannot run a check whose verdict originates outside it), and only then what is missing. Presented as a choice, the options waste proposals; enumerated as dispatch points, they are a short audit with one action. Read the mechanism’s entry point before proposing dispatch points. A name and a position in a diagram say what something is for; an argument list says what it does — for example, whether it performs a check or only records a verdict somebody else produced.

580.title: The same failure one level out: a KIND, not a mechanism
580.content: Ask what is missing of a kind of node and the same mistake appears: counting kg-qa sidecars over the work item store, finding zero, and calling work items unaudited when several gates audit them. Coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for — see audit-coverage, with bun run cat audit:coverage as the second question.
