793.title: discussion — settling what an agent cannot read off disk
793.content: Skill discussion: Settle which harness, and which repositories, when no file says: the output is a document conforming to discussion.output.schema.json. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . An agent that has just read bootstrap’s README.md knows the shape of a harness and nothing about this one. Two questions have no answer in any file it can reach: . | which harness this repository should become: bootstrap itself, or any Harness built on it; | which repositories are involved — where the dependency is read from, where the new declaration is written to, and whether they are the same. | . Only whoever asked for the harness can answer them, so the agent asks. This skill says what the asking must produce. processes/discussion.bpmn narrows the candidates and then calls human-agent-discussion, the one reusable way bootstrap asks a person anything, with no default allowed.

794.title: Inputs and outputs
794.content: |   |   | . | in | discussion.input.schema.json: what the agent already knows, and which of the two unknowns is open | . | out | discussion.output.schema.json: harness, repositories[], outcome, determinedBy, answeredBy, and the exchange that produced it | . Both are plain JSON Schema in schemas/, readable with nothing installed. The task is finished when a document conforming to the output schema exists, not when a conversation has taken place. The participant may be a person or a sibling agent that already holds the answer; the output records which (kind: person | agent), as human-agent-discussion says.

795.title: First, say where you are
795.content: Before narrowing anything (A_DetermineWhere), determine the three things human-agent-discussion requires before any question: . | the Process: Initialize a harness, inside Determine the harness and repositories. A Bootstrapping Agent can be nowhere else (FR-2); | the Roles: itself as the Bootstrapping Agent; the person it will ask as the Requestor. A request relayed by somebody else leaves the Requestor undetermined; | the context: what the request said, and what the checkout holds. | . One that cannot be determined is never filled with a default: it is asked about first, and the harness question waits.

796.title: Rules
796.content: Ask the fewest questions that settle it. Narrow the candidate list from context first (a repository whose root already holds a declaration, <name>.json, is not a blank slate) and put the rest as one question with the candidates named. A question a reader must go and research is not ready. Never infer the answer from a default. If nothing is known, the output’s determinedBy is asked, not assumed. assumed is permitted only for a default the README states, and assumption then names it. Record repositories as pairs, not as a list. read from and written to can be the same repository or two; the point of determining them is to know where the declaration lands. Never infer written-to from push access. A remote repository is read-from until the Requestor authorizes writing to it (confirm-harness). A refusal is an outcome. If the participant declines, that is outcome: "unsettled" with what was asked and what is still open — not a guess, and not an error.

804.title: /dispatch-agent — parallel dispatch with a live 2-minute status heartbeat
804.content: Skill dispatch-agent: Dispatch one or more background sub-agents against parallel research/build fronts with a STANDARDIZED live progress contract, and monitor them on a 2-minute heartbeat. Every dispatched agent emits consistent DID/DOING/NEXT/BLOCKERS blocks with real log output (not static “still running”); the parent extracts the latest block from each agent every ~120 s and posts one consolidated synthesis table. Use when the user says “dispatch agents”, “fan out”, “run these in parallel with monitoring”, “give me status every 2 minutes”, or when you are about to launch ≥ 2 background Agents on independent work. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Agent activity log, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down, A refused merge-train member, Merge to main, A merge train, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . The expensive failure mode of multi-agent dispatch is going dark: you launch N background agents, then can’t say what any of them is doing until it completes 20 minutes later. This skill fixes that with two halves that MUST be used together: . | Agent-side progress contract — every dispatched agent emits a consistent, machine-greppable progress block on a fixed cadence, with live evidence (log tails, exit codes, counts), never a static “still working on it”. | Parent-side 2-minute heartbeat — the parent extracts the latest block from each running agent every ~120 s and posts ONE consolidated synthesis table to the user. | . Do not dispatch without both: an agent that skips the contract cannot be synthesized, and a parent that skips the heartbeat leaves the user blind.

805.title: 0. When to use
805.content: . | Launching ≥ 2 background Agent calls on independent fronts (research routes, per-file proofs, per-isotope compute). | The user asks for periodic status (“update me every 2 minutes”, “keep me posted”, “monitor these”). | A single long agent whose progress the user wants to watch live. | . For a single quick synchronous agent whose result you need before the next step, skip this — just call Agent(run_in_background: false).

806.title: 1. Agent-side progress contract (PASTE THIS into every dispatched agent)
806.content: Append the block below verbatim to every agent prompt you dispatch through this skill. Fill in <LABEL> with a short stable tag (≤ 16 chars, kebab-case: a3-offblock, ctil-root, a4-interface) — the parent keys the synthesis table on it. ## PROGRESS REPORTING CONTRACT (STRICT — the parent monitors you on this) Your label is: <LABEL> Emit a progress block **as a plain-text assistant message** (not a tool call) at EVERY meaningful step, and **at least once every ~90 seconds of wall time** even mid-step. Use this EXACT shape so the parent can grep and synthesize it: ### ⟦PROGRESS⟧ <LABEL> · step N DID: <what you just finished — CONCRETE evidence only: file paths, lean exit codes, real-sorry counts, git shas, row counts, the tail of a log. NOT "worked on the proof".> DOING: <the step in flight right now. If a command is RUNNING, quote the last 3–8 relevant lines of its output / the key live metric (elapsed, % done, current goal state, error so far). NEVER a canned "still running" — show the live log.> NEXT: <the single concrete next action you will take.> BLOCKERS: <none | the precise blocker (missing lemma name, 403, ENOSPC, evicted oleans, ambiguous spec).> Rules that keep updates LIVE, not semi-static: - **Tee every long command to a log and quote its tail** in DOING: `<cmd> 2>&1 | tee /tmp/<LABEL>-<step>.log` then put the last lines in the block. A Lean check, a python compute, a git op > ~10 s all qualify. - **Advance the step counter** every block; never repeat an identical block twice — if nothing changed, say what you are still waiting on and quote the newest log line. - **Evidence or it didn't happen**: every DID line names a file / exit code / count / sha. No vague verbs. - When you finish, emit a final block with marker `### ⟦DONE⟧ <LABEL>` carrying the verdict (closed / scope-(a) / scope-(b) / bean-the-gap), the exact .lean path(s), lean-direct exit code, real-sorry count, and the branch you pushed. Why this exact shape: the parent’s extractor (below) greps for the ⟦PROGRESS⟧ / ⟦DONE⟧ markers and pulls the DID/DOING/NEXT/BLOCKERS lines. Consistent markers → one-line-per-agent synthesis with zero guessing. Deviating from the marker or the four keys breaks the monitor. This contract is additive to the task’s own discipline (anti-fit, lean-direct verification, zero-sorry, bean-the-gap). It governs how the agent reports, never what counts as done. An agent still may not launder a fit or fake a closure to make its DID line look better — honesty over a pretty status.

807.title: 2. Dispatch procedure
807.content: Where the work comes from. A handover report hands its unstarted items over as DISPATCH LINES — one fixed sentence per work item, per handover-report rule 7: . Do bean folio-assistant-<id> on branch <branch-to-create> of repo <owner>/<repo>. Take the front from that line rather than inventing a scope: the work item carries its own Done-when, so the agent’s result can be judged, which a theme does not allow. If you are dispatching work that has no work item, work item it first. | Scope each front to one independent agent (no shared files between agents — worktree isolation makes parallel file writes safe; use isolation: "worktree" whenever agents mutate the tree). | Assign each a <LABEL> and paste the §1 contract block into its prompt, plus the task-specific brief (verification recipe, discipline, git/branch/PR rules — do not re-derive these; reuse the project’s standing lean-direct recipe and “push branch, parent PRs+merges” convention). | Name the skills that govern the front in the brief, by path, and quote the rules they set that the work could touch — rendering, layering, what is forbidden. An agent cannot follow a rule it was never pointed at. Always include interaction-modality (and hand-back-to-discussion) in every dispatched brief, and require the child to pass it on to any subagent it spawns: never ask the owner a question in prose alone without a tappable card (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, ask_question, or post_widget) after the full chat block (≤ 4 options, recommended first, stated default on silence), or return the question to the coordinating session in the hand-back-to-discussion schema format. If the skills are served over MCP and the server is unreachable, read them from the mounted layers (<layer>/skills/**) instead: an unreachable server is never a reason to work without them. | Launch all agents in a single message (multiple Agent tool calls) so they run concurrently. Record each returned agentId ↔ <LABEL> mapping in a scratch note (/tmp/<session>-dispatch-map.txt) so the heartbeat can label rows even before an agent’s first block lands. | Immediately arm the heartbeat (§3). Do not end the turn without it. | .

808.title: 3. Parent-side 2-minute heartbeat
808.content: 3a. The extractor (targeted — never read the full JSONL) . Reading an agent’s whole *.output transcript overflows context. Extract ONLY the latest progress block per agent. Save this once as scripts/agent-progress.py (or inline it): . #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Usage: agent-progress.py <tasks-dir> # Prints the latest ⟦PROGRESS⟧/⟦DONE⟧ block from each agent's *.output JSONL. import json, re, sys, glob, os tasks = sys.argv[1] for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(tasks, "*.output"))): aid = os.path.basename(f)[:-7] last = None try: for line in open(f): try: o = json.loads(line) except Exception: continue for c in (o.get("message", {}).get("content") or []): if isinstance(c, dict) and c.get("type") == "text": t = c.get("text", "") if "⟦PROGRESS⟧" in t or "⟦DONE⟧" in t: # keep only from the last marker onward idx = max(t.rfind("⟦PROGRESS⟧"), t.rfind("⟦DONE⟧")) last = t[t.rfind("###", 0, idx):] if idx >= 0 else t except FileNotFoundError: continue done = last and "⟦DONE⟧" in last print(f"===== {aid[:12]} {'[DONE]' if done else '[live]'} =====") print((last or "(no progress block yet — agent still spinning up)").strip()[:900]) print() . Run it against the session tasks dir: python3 scripts/agent-progress.py "$TASKS_DIR" where $TASKS_DIR is the tasks/ folder holding the <agentId>.output files (the dispatch tool result names each output_file; its parent dir is $TASKS_DIR). 3b. The cadence . Every ~120 s while any agent is still [live]: . | Run the extractor. | Post ONE consolidated synthesis to the user — a compact table, one row per agent, newest block only: . | label | DID (evidence) | DOING (live) | NEXT | BLOCKERS |——-|—————-|————–|——|———-| . Keep it to one screen. If a block is stale (same step counter as last heartbeat and > 3 min old), flag it ⚠ stale and note you’ll SendMessage the agent to nudge it. | Re-arm the next 120 s tick, then end the turn (do not busy-wait). | . Cadence mechanism — do NOT foreground-sleep (blocked). Use one of: . | ScheduleWakeup with delaySeconds: 120, prompt: "/dispatch-agent heartbeat", reason: "2-min agent status heartbeat" — the standard dynamic-loop tick. Call ScheduleWakeup({stop:true}) once every agent is [DONE]. | If the harness surfaces agent-completion notifications, those also wake you; run the extractor on each and treat it as an off-cadence heartbeat, then re-arm the 120 s fallback so quiet stretches still tick. | . The 120 s tick is a fallback heartbeat; completion notifications arrive on their own. 3c. Nudging a silent agent . If an agent shows (no progress block yet) for > 3 min, or its step counter hasn’t advanced across two heartbeats, SendMessage(to: <agentId>, ...) with a one-line nudge: “Emit a fresh ⟦PROGRESS⟧ block with the live tail of whatever is running.” An agent that has genuinely hung (evicted oleans, ENOSPC) will surface it as a BLOCKER once nudged.

809.title: 4. On completion
809.content: When an agent emits ⟦DONE⟧ (or the harness notifies completion): . | Drop it from the [live] set; keep its final block in the synthesis as a [DONE] row. | Verify before trusting the DONE line. The agent’s self-reported “sorry-free / exit 0” is a claim — the parent re-runs lean-direct on each edited .lean itself (exit 0, no declaration uses 'sorry') before merging, exactly as for any dispatched Lean work. A green DID line never substitutes for the parent’s own verification. | When all agents are [DONE]: post a final consolidated synthesis (verdict per front + the merge/next-step queue), ScheduleWakeup( {stop:true}), and end the heartbeat. | .

810.title: 5. Anti-patterns (each is a skill violation)
810.content: . | Going dark — dispatching background agents without arming the heartbeat. | Semi-static updates — “agent still running the proof” with no log tail, no step counter, no evidence. If a command is in flight, the block MUST carry its live output. | Reading the full transcript — tailing/cat-ing the *.output JSONL into context instead of using the targeted extractor. | A brief with no governing skills — dispatching a front without naming the skills that rule it (§2 step 3). The agent then decides a design question the owner already ruled on, and the PR carries it in. | Trusting the DONE line — merging on an agent’s self-reported “exit 0” without the parent’s own lean-direct re-verification. | Wrong cadence — 5-minute or “when I remember” ticks when the user asked for 2 minutes. Honor the literal cadence. | .

812.title: dmn-authoring
812.content: Named by: Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, SWOT situation analysis, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, Options analysis, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, Authoring a document, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Board: place a note . Skill id: dmn-authoring · Package: workflow · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn step Decision logic · DMN tables, in the Business analyst lane. Author DMN decision tables — a DAK’s clinical decision logic, and the tables that back this repository’s own computed gateways.

813.title: Inputs and outputs
813.content: schemas/skills/dmn-authoring/: . | in — decisionName (required), inputVariables (required), sourceLogic | out — dmnFile, decisionTableCount, ruleCount, hitPolicy | .

814.title: A computed gateway is not a chosen one
814.content: In this repository a DMN table has a second job: an exclusive gateway carrying <cat-harness.processes:decision ref="decisions/<file>.dmn#<Decision_Id>"/> has its branch computed from the table rather than picked by the agent. workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at such a gateway. Asserting the answer would defeat the point of writing the table. You pass facts — e.g. { failCritical: 0, failMajor: 2 } from qa_sweep totals — and the table returns the branch. Adding one means adding the .dmn, the cat-harness.processes:decision ref, and nothing else: the loader checks that every outcome the table can return names a real outgoing flow, so a table that can route somewhere the diagram cannot go is a load error rather than a surprise at the moment of decision.

815.title: The FEEL subset this interpreter implements
815.content: src/workflow/decision-table.ts implements a deliberate subset: - (any), literals, comparisons, and one-of. It refuses ranges, not() and function calls rather than mis-evaluating them. Write within that subset: a table using a construct the interpreter rejects fails at load, rather than being mis-evaluated at the moment of decision.

816.title: Three states belong in the table
816.content: Encode “could not determine” as an outcome in its own right — pages-live-gate.dmn returns live, not-yet and unknown; folio-intent.dmn returns ask when the filesystem cannot decide. A gate whose only outcomes are pass and fail forces an unmeasured input to be rendered as one of them, and it is always rendered as pass. If your decision has an input that may be unavailable, give it a branch.

817.title: Hit policy
817.content: Say it explicitly. FIRST is the usual choice here and is what folio-intent.dmn uses — rules are ordered, the first match wins, and the ordering is then part of the logic and must be reviewed as such.

818.title: When a layer above transforms it
818.content: A layer built on this one may render decision tables for human review or derive other artefacts (questionnaires, for instance) from them. Then the DMN is a source artefact, not documentation of one; that layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics and the caveats, and this one names no layer above it.

820.title: Docs generation
820.content: Skill docs-generation: How a checkout of this harness generates and publishes its docs site: regenerating derived references, composing the docs layers and each instance’s site into one Jekyll source, building it with just-the-docs, the post-build passes, the TypeDoc API reference, the knowledge-graph export, and the full-replace publish to gh-pages and its branches/ previews. Named by: Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive . The docs site is one Jekyll site built from the checkout’s sources and published to gh-pages. The host checkout’s .github/workflows/docs-site.yml runs it on a push to the default branch that touches its inputs, or on dispatch. Its steps, gateways and alerts are drawn in docs-site-publish.bpmn.

821.title: Regenerate derived references
821.content: Nothing derived is published from a committed copy. Before the build, each generator rewrites its pages from source, among them: . | What | Command | . | Pages derived from branch-kept graphs | bun run cat derive:publish | . | Skill contract reference | bun run cat schema:docs | . | Skill instruction pages | bun run cat skills:docs | . | Content-backed docs pages | bun run cat docs:pages | . | Graph projections and viewers | schema:viz, library:viz, … | . | Handler and translation indexes | handler:index, translation:index | . | BPMN drawings and process pages | render:bpmn, processes:viz | . Several are Tools in tools/ that satisfy this skill (schema-docs, skill-docs, bpmn-render); a Tool’s declaration says what it reads and writes.

822.title: Compose one source
822.content: cat-harness-tools/scripts/compose-docs.ts --out ./_docs lays the checkout root’s docs/ over cat-harness/docs/, the base. An instance that builds a site of its own then has its Tool compose that site into the host source at <instance>/. For example, the FHIR IG layer’s stage-ig-sites.ts --compose-into ./_docs stages each IG whose instance records its source. Which instances compose is data in their declarations. The result is one site with one sidebar, one search and one language selector.

823.title: Build
823.content: bundle exec jekyll build --source ./_docs --destination ./_site runs Jekyll 4 with the just-the-docs remote theme and the gems in .github/pages-jekyll/Gemfile. Post-build passes then run over _site: . | each composing Tool’s own pass (for IGs, build-ig-site.ts --dedupe-ids); | mount-instance-docs.ts, which mounts every other instance’s rendered pages under its kind; | the inline PDF viewer, set-html-lang.ts, search-split.ts and minify-site.ts; | the TypeScript API reference, built into _site/api by TypeDoc through .github/actions/typedoc-api. | .

824.title: Export the knowledge graph
824.content: kg-export.ts writes the instance’s graph to <stub>/<stub>.jsonld, with a .json copy so that Pages serves a JSON media type. harness-schema-export.ts writes its schema, and kg-viewer.ts writes the viewer. Where each endpoint lives and which media type it carries: serving-renderings and instance-publication. The instance that owns the site root is site.landing in index.config.json (index-config).

825.title: Check and publish
825.content: check:maintained-artefacts, check:escaped-markup and publish-verify.ts check the built tree. publish-gh-pages.sh then replaces gh-pages wholesale. Before each push attempt it copies in every open pull request’s branches/<slug>/ preview (restore-staging.ts). After the push, restore-staging.ts --verify confirms that the previews survived. Any failure opens or comments on one publication-manager alert, and the next clean publish closes it.

826.title: Previews
826.content: .github/workflows/feature-staging.yml builds the same site for a pull request and publishes it under branches/<slug>/, replacing only that directory. It removes the preview when the pull request closes.

827.title: Locally
827.content: bun run cat preview:site builds the site in a sandbox. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/generate-schema-manifest.ts writes build/schema-manifest.json for the viewer and the MCP server. Paper PDFs and Lean API docs belong to the paper layer: see build-pdf and lean-html-docs where that layer is mounted.

830.title: Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive
830.content: Process_DocsSite · strict · 11 step(s) . Builds the docs site from this checkout’s sources and publishes it to gh-pages (.github/workflows/docs-site.yml). Publishing replaces gh-pages wholesale: anything on the branch that this build did not produce is gone unless restored, so the open pull requests’ staging previews are copied in before the replace and checked on the deployed branch after it. The site is published whatever the built-site checks find: they run before the push and are judged after it, so a finding turns the run red with the site already live. A refused security gate or a failed deploy stops the run, and a check that could not tell counts as a failure (ci-health). Every failure, from a refused security gate to a lost preview or a failed check, goes through one alert to the publication manager, and the next clean publish closes it. Mechanical throughout; there is no human lane. i i i i i i i i i i i

836.title: document-authoring
836.content: Named by: Authoring a document, Data sharing agreement document life cycle . Author a document folio: policy guidance, a standard, a report, a handbook — anything whose content is structured prose rather than machine- checked mathematics.

837.title: What a document folio is
837.content: The same content model as a paper, minus the formal layer: . folio/<slug>/ <slug>.ts the document manifest (chapters, in order) <chapter-dir>/ <chapter-dir>.ts the chapter manifest (sections, in order) <block-root>.ts one block manifest <block-root>.md that block's narrative body <block-root>.qa.json QA sidecar (machine-written; never hand-edit) . A block is the unit of authorship, review, feedback and QA. Its .ts carries the metadata — label, title, uses[] — and its .md carries the prose. They are separate files so a reviewer’s diff is over prose, not over a manifest.

838.title: The kinds you may use
838.content: prose, recommendation, example, remark, algorithm, simulator, equation, diagram, figure, table (the document-profile nodes in block-kinds/). Not definition, theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, conjecture, proof. Those seven are the paper profile: their assertion is a formal mathematical claim backed by a .lean sibling, and a document folio has no Lean toolchain to check one. content_profile_check enforces this, and content_validate runs it on every pass. If you find yourself wanting a theorem, you want one of two things: . | a normative statement — a recommendation, a requirement, a rule. See normative-statements for how to carry one in this profile, and read it before reaching for a math kind. | an actual theorem — in which case this folio is a paper. Change the instance’s index.config.json entry to "contentType": "paper" deliberately (the index is the one config), and know that you are taking on Lean and TeX as dependencies. | .

839.title: Adding a block
839.content: . | Find the section it belongs to. content_list shows the tree. A block only reaches the output if a section’s blocks[] names it — writing the files is not enough, and a block nobody lists renders nowhere and is swept by nothing. | Write <root>.ts — the builder call for the kind, with label, optional title, and uses[]. | Write <root>.md — the prose. GitHub-flavoured Markdown; tables, footnotes and raw HTML all survive to the output unchanged, because the document render path assembles Markdown rather than translating it. | Add the root name to the section’s blocks[], in reading order. | content_validate before you consider it done. | .

840.title: uses[] is editorial, and it is yours to maintain
840.content: uses[] lists the blocks a reader must already have read to follow this one. It is a judgement about narrative order, not a mechanical fact — nothing derives it and nothing should. In a paper folio there is a machine-derived formal graph alongside it; in a document folio there is not, so uses[] is the only dependency signal the corpus carries. Every ordering metric, every impact question (“what has to change if this recommendation changes?”), and the reading-order review read it. List direct neighbours only. If A needs B and B needs C, A lists B.

841.title: Rendering
841.content: document_render_md assembles the whole folio into one Markdown file — run it to inspect ordering before you render anything else. document_render_html and document_render_pdf go through pandoc; the PDF path uses an HTML engine (weasyprint, prince, wkhtmltopdf) and never falls back to LaTeX. If no engine is installed it says so.

842.title: What belongs in the folio, and what belongs here
842.content: Subject matter — the actual recommendations, the vocabulary, the chapters — lives in the folio repo, as content. This platform holds the formalism. If you are about to add a domain constant or a subject-specific rule to folio-assistant, you are in the wrong repository.

844.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
844.title: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
844.content: Process_Ingestion · advisory · 4 step(s) . Accepts an upload, records its extracted metadata in the knowledge graph, and catalogues the asset in library/ — held if materialized, referenced if not. THE BASIC FLOW, with very little process context assumed. Accept, extract the metadata into the KG, ask whether the asset is materialized, place it in library/<slug>/. It calls NO subprocess and makes no content-type decision. THE ID Process_Ingestion IS KEPT ON PURPOSE: methodology-from-source.bpmn’s Call_Ingest names it, and so does every higher-layer process that refines this flow. Refinement is by INVERSION — a refining process calls this one as its first step and continues with its own work; nothing here names a refinement, because the corpus has no BPMN extension point and a harness diagram naming a higher one would be an upward edge. The document pipeline (rungs, the four ingest phases, the L1 completeness gate, promotion, the summary queue) is such a refinement, in the layer above. i i i i

846.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
846.title: Lanes — who acts
846.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Contributor (human or agent) | user | Whoever puts the file in the queue.“HUMAN OR AGENT” IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT A HEDGE: both place files here. That is why Task_Place is a plain bpmn:task rather than a userTask — asserting a human performs it would contradict the lane’s own role graph, which is what activity-fulfilment-kind exists to catch.WHAT THE LANE IS ACCOUNTABLE FOR, and where it ends. Choosing a route, writing the bytes into the DECLARED queue of the instance that will own them, and discharging afterwards whatever that route could not — the web form has no working tree, so no pre-commit hook and no generator runs on it. The lane does NOT ingest and does not clean the queue: it hands over, and Lane_1 takes it from there. upload-routes carries the routes and their obligations. | . | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | ingestion-agent | Runs the basic flow from the metadata step to the placement in library/, unattended: every decision in it is decidable from the material and its declarations. It asks one question — is the asset materialized? — and that is answered from the materialization state vocabulary (schemas/kg/materialization-state.ts), not by judgement. It does NOT choose a reader for the bytes, derive sections or blocks, or describe images: those are a refining process’s work, which calls this flow first.THE FLOW ENDS IN THIS LANE. The asset catalogued in library/ — held, or recorded as referenced — is the terminal state, and every knowledge-graph reference to it resolves through library/ from here; a refining process continues from it rather than being drawn into this one. There is no separate corpus lane: it would hold only the end event, and a lane with no activity has no performer to describe. | .

847.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
847.title: Steps
847.content: Every one of the 4 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Place it in uploads/ by a declared routeTask_Place | Contributor (human or agent) | upload-routes | THE FIRST LINK: everything downstream of here takes a file that is already in the queue, so without this step how the file got there is governed by nothing.WHAT THIS STEP IS. The basic flow’s ACCEPT step: choosing an arrival route, writing the bytes into the declared queue of the instance that will own them, and discharging what that route does not discharge for you. The routes, what each writer owes, and the two that are mechanisms against the one that is a persona are in the upload-routes skill; upload-url composes the forge URL for the web route from the declaration rather than from a literal, because a hand-written one can 404.WHY A PLAIN bpmn:task AND NOT A userTask. A userTask asserts a human performs it, and this lane is “Contributor (human or agent)” because both do; asserting human-only would be an activity-fulfilment-kind contradiction. A plain task asserts nothing about the performer.WHY THE BEAN OP IS note AND NOT claim. Placing a file claims nothing; it adds to a queue. What it owes the work plan is visibility. A note against the ingestion bean is what makes the queue’s growth something another session can see. | . | Extract its metadata into the KGTask_ExtractMetadata | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | asset-extraction | THE METADATA STEP. What enters the knowledge graph is the asset’s INDEX — what it is, how big, what type, when it says it was written — and, for a container, what is in it; its contents do not go in unless somebody asks, with a reason. The tool is cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-assets.ts, writing a folio-extraction/v1 record (schemas/content/extraction.ts).The media type is sniffed from the leading bytes, never taken from the extension. | . | **Place the asset in library//**`Task_PlaceInLibrary` | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | library-ingestion | The materialized branch. The asset lands in library/<slug>/ with its metadata record, its provenance and its fixity. The folder name IS the citation key, so a citation and a directory are the same string.The upload is then RETIRED, not left and not deleted: it moves to fsh-guts/uploads/ beside a sidecar naming where it came from and when, and check:uploads-retired finds one that was not. A refining process that derives content from the bytes does so before that retirement; library-ingestion carries the rule. | . | Record it in library/ as referencedTask_CatalogueReference | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | library-ingestion | The referenced branch. Nothing is fetched and no bytes are written: the catalogue record says where the asset is and that we hold none. A reference is not a fetch — it stays navigable without being held, and materializing it later is materialize-remote.bpmn’s decision, with its purpose and five gates, not this flow’s. | .

848.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
848.title: Decisions
848.content: Every one of the 1 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Materialized?Gateway_Materialized | Answered from the materialization state (schemas/kg/materialization-state.ts): materialized means the bytes are here; referenced means we know where they are and hold none. unknown is not a third branch here because a node must DECLARE its state — there is no default — and an asset this flow cannot classify is recorded as referenced-with-a-reason rather than placed as if held. Collapsing referenced into materialized is the failure the vocabulary exists to stop: corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a referenced node placed as held reads as present to every consumer. | materialized → Place the asset in library//**referenced** → Record it in library/ as referenced | .

850.title: Document Intake
850.content: Skill document-intake: Process uploaded documents (PDFs, scans, LaTeX, structured/normative guidelines, etc.) from uploads/ into structured content objects. Handles OCR extraction, environment detection, structural analysis, and content-object generation. Supports multi-stage pipelines: raw upload → extracted text → structured blocks → .ts/.md content objects. Named by: Getting started, Evidence for a recommendation, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph . Bib human-review integration. Track per-upload ingestion status beside the upload’s records in uploads/<document-id>/ (identified passage, formalised?, matched?) and link each upload to the references.ts entry it sources. An upload that supplies a cited source moves that ref to source-in-repo (agent-identified passage; no human photo) and then through the bib-human-review ladder to validated. Existing uploads/ follow the same agent-sourced path.

851.title: Overview
851.content: This skill manages the uploads/ directory as an intake pipeline for converting raw documents into structured content objects. It handles: . | Scanned PDFs / images — OCR extraction → text → blocks | LaTeX source — environment extraction → blocks | Structured / normative guidelines — normative structure → blocks | arXiv papers — fetched source → blocks (delegates to paper-importer) | Arbitrary documents — best-effort structural analysis | . The key distinction from paper-importer: this skill owns the full lifecycle of uploads/, including tracking processing state, partial extractions, and multi-pass refinement. Paper-importer focuses on the final content-object generation step.

852.title: When to Use This Skill
852.content: . | User says “upload”, “scan”, “process document”, “intake” | User drops a file into uploads/ | User mentions a guideline, standard, or normative document | User wants to convert a raw document into content objects | Files appear in uploads/ that haven’t been processed yet | .

853.title: uploads/ Directory Convention
853.content: uploads/ <document-id>/ intake.json ← what arrived and where from (folio-intake/v1) <document-id>.dc.json ← what it is: title, type, subject (folio-dublin-core/v1) original.pdf ← raw upload (PDF, scan, etc.) original.tex ← or LaTeX source extracted-text.md ← OCR or parser output (intermediate) extracted-blocks.json ← structured extraction (intermediate) mapping.json ← label/section mapping decisions README.md ← human notes about the document . The two records an upload writes . The description is a Dublin Core record; the intake records the capture and points at it. Both are validated by the registry (check:kind-validators). intake.json — folio-intake/v1, cat-harness-tools schemas/library/intake.ts: . { "$schema": "folio-intake/v1", "doc_id": "example-doc-2016", "record": "example-doc-2016.dc.json", "source": { "upstream": "https://...", "capturedAt": "2026-03-25T10:00:00Z", "capturedBy": "folio-assistant document adapter: the upload form" }, "files": [ { "path": "original.pdf", "bytes": 123456, "sha256": "…", "type": "upload", "role": "original-bitstream" } ] } . An intake names what it is a capture OF: a catalogue item (a folio-catalogue-node/v1 id), a Dublin Core record, or — only when neither exists — its own title. source is ProvenanceSchema (upstream for a URL, absent for a direct upload) plus the capture moment. <document-id>.dc.json — folio-dublin-core/v1: . | upload field | Dublin Core | . | title | dc.title | . | type (guideline, paper, report, standard) | dc.type | . | domain | dc.subject | . | normative level | dc.type qualified normativeLevel | . | detected format (pdf, latex, scan, docx) | dc.format | .

854.title: Pipeline Stages
854.content: Stage 1: Upload (→ uploaded) . Place raw files in uploads/<document-id>/. Create intake.json with source metadata. Files are committed to git for reproducibility. Record the licence in intake.json when you know it. The ingestion pipeline’s licence step runs before any extraction, because library/ is committed content and refusing a source after deriving from it is a deletion nobody may take unasked. That step sees only the upload: the licence record in intake.json (the same stated / unknown record a library manifest carries in meta.licence, cat-harness-tools schemas/library/source-licence.ts) and whether a LICENSE file sits beside it. bun run cat ingest prints its verdict before the first arm runs, and after the arms it writes a recorded licence into the staged entry’s licence.json — the authored sidecar gen-library-jsonld carries into meta.licence (the manifest itself is generated, so a licence written there would not survive a regeneration). It never overwrites a licence.json already there; a mismatch is printed as a conflict. | verdict | when | what to do | . | stated | licence: { status: "stated", id, basis } | nothing — basis says where it is stated | . | unknown | licence: { status: "unknown", searched: [...] } | nothing now; the places tried are the record | . | undetermined | no licence recorded (a LICENSE sibling is named, not read) | ingestion proceeds, and says so — undetermined is never reported as cleared | . It never reads a licence out of extracted text; that is a later check’s job. Supported formats: . | PDF — academic papers, scanned guidelines, reports | LaTeX — .tex source bundles | HTML — web-published guidelines, standards | DOCX — Word documents | Images — scanned pages (PNG, JPG, TIFF) | . For academic papers, prefer the MCP fetch path: when the session network allows the upstream host, use paper-search-mcp (arxiv / PubMed / bioRxiv / medRxiv) or openalex-paper-search (alex-mcp; OpenAlex catalog) rather than curl/WebFetch. The MCP tools return canonical metadata and the PDF in one call, eliminating the OCR-then-extract-then-name dance. See paper-importer.md §Phase 1 (in the science layer) for the per-tool routing table. Sandboxed Claude-Code-on-the-web sessions (github-only allowlist) cannot reach those hosts; in those sessions, queue the fetch onto a normal-network machine per bib-qa/qa-tags.md §Batch intake pipeline. Stage 2: Extraction (→ extracted) . Convert raw format to extracted-text.md: . For PDFs, always start with cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py — do not reach for a Python PDF library directly. It walks a fallback ladder (pdftotext → pypdf → pdfminer.six → a zero-dependency content-stream extractor → OCR) and, when it cannot read a file, tells you which rung failed and why instead of returning an empty string: . python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py FILE.pdf -o extracted-text.md python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py FILE.pdf --diagnose # structure only . Exit 0 = text; exit 2 = no text layer (a scan); exit 3 = a parser problem on a file that does have text. Two failure modes it prevents: . | A silent empty extraction reads exactly like a scan, a broken library, and a malformed PDF. The script separates them by inspecting the PDF structure (CCITTFaxDecode / JBIG2Decode / DCTDecode counts against /Font), so “swap libraries” vs “you need OCR” is decided by evidence rather than guessed. | A broken native extension kills the whole pipeline. pypdf and pdfminer.six both fail via pyo3 PanicException when cryptography’s Rust bindings are broken — and that is a BaseException, so an ordinary except Exception does not catch it. Every rung is guarded accordingly, and the zero-dependency rung exists for this case. | . | Format | Extraction method | . | PDF (text) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py (ladder; pdftotext when available) | . | PDF (scan) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-extract.py → exit 2, then cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py (Tesseract) or Claude vision | . | LaTeX | Direct parse (strip preamble) | . | HTML | Readability + turndown | . | DOCX | Pandoc → markdown | . | Images | Claude vision API | . | PDF (tables/figures) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py → tables.json (see Stage 3) | . | PDF (sections) | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-structure.py → structure.json + sections/*.md (see Stage 3) | . For scanned documents the script’s OCR rung fires automatically if tesseract and pdftoppm are installed (apt-get install -y tesseract-ocr poppler-utils); it names whichever is missing. Where OCR is unavailable, or where layout carries meaning (headings, lists, tables, boxes), fall back to Claude’s vision capability, which reads structure that OCR flattens. Output: extracted-text.md — raw markdown with preserved structure. Stage 3: Structural Analysis (→ structured) . Analyze extracted text for formal environments and document structure. The three producers this stage actually runs . These scripts build the corpus’s structure.json, sections/ and ocr/ trees. Stage 2’s pdf-extract.py writes loose text, not the greppable sections/ tree the corpus-grep checklist reads. | script | writes | notes | . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-structure.py | library/<doc-id>/structure.json + sections/NN-slug.md | metadata (a page-1 title GUESS, authors, arXiv/DOI from the page-1 stamp, and the PDF Info dictionary as docinfo), TOC from the PDF outline, or else inferred from the layout (see the note below), per-section text split. The page-1 guess is never the entry’s title: l1-document-ingestion §”A manifest’s title” gives the order (catalogue record → referenced.json → PDF /Title → slug) | . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py | library/<doc-id>/ocr/page-NNN.txt | pdftoppm -r 300 -png then tesseract; per-page cache; script auto-detected via Tesseract’s own OSD | . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-candidates.py | library/<doc-id>/candidates.json | pure regex, imports no PDF library; proposals, never content — nothing here writes to content/ and nothing here creates Lean | . python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py FILE.pdf --outdir library/<doc-id>/ # only if scanned python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-structure.py FILE.pdf --outdir library --ocr python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-candidates.py library/<doc-id>/ . How they fit together: . | pdf-structure.py READS OCR, it never runs it. Its --ocr flag consults the cache pdf-ocr.py wrote, gated on text_is_unusable() (under 120 chars/page, or under 55 % letters — mojibake). So on a scanned document the order is pdf-ocr.py first, pdf-structure.py --ocr second. Run them the other way round and the sections come out empty. | An OCR’d document whose structure was never re-run is invisible to the section grep. Its text is in ocr/ but sections/ holds a stub, and its structure.json does not record "text_source": "ocr". Re-run pdf-structure.py --ocr on it. | The backends are optional and their absence is reported, not guessed. pdf-structure.py prefers PyMuPDF (better text on maths, real outlines) and falls back to pypdf; the Dockerfile ships pypdf only, deliberately, so the image stays BSD-licensed against PyMuPDF’s AGPL. Check with python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-ocr.py --check. | With no outline, the TOC is inferred from the LAYOUT, and the artefact says how. diagnostics.toc_inferred_method is contents (a printed contents page, its page labels moved to physical pages by finding the titles in the body), font (lines set in a heading style: larger, bold, capitals or italic, numbered or not) or regex (text patterns — the last resort, used for OCR’d text, which has no fonts). Weight a regex TOC lowest. Each inferred entry also carries confidence (0..1) and evidence — which independent checks agreed: listed on the contents page, found in the body near the page it names, set in a heading style, numbered. Trust the high ones; look at the flagged ones before citing them. An inferred TOC is used only when it passes the concentration check, its mean confidence is at least 0.6, and no more than a quarter of the sections it would cut are empty; otherwise the entry is split one section per page (granularity: "page", with the reason in structure_note) — l1-document-ingestion §”The route pdf-structure.py takes itself”. The same artefact carries figures — the list of figures and tables, each caption with confidence and evidence (cited in the text, in its numbering run, a graphic on its page) — with numbering gaps in diagnostics.figure_sequence_gaps; and, when the document has a printed contents page, diagnostics.toc_alignment: entries the body no longer carries, numbered sections the contents omits, and page mismatches. On a draft, read these as findings about the document. Every page also has a printed label: pages[] (physical index, the label a reader sees, which sources agreed), page_label on TOC entries and figures, and label_start/label_end on sections. Cite the label, not the physical index; diagnostics.page_label_conflicts lists pages where the PDF’s own labels disagree with what is printed. Before changing cat-harness-tools/scripts/_pdf_headings.py, run python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/toc-benchmark.py before and after: a rule that fixes one document and costs two is visible only there. The numbers, the methods compared and what could not be run are in cat-harness/docs/research-and-analysis/toc-extraction.md. | . For academic papers: . Same as paper-importer Phase 2 — detect theorem/definition/lemma environments, sections, cross-references. For structured / normative guidelines: . This table is for a paper folio only. In a document folio definition is a math kind whose lean field is required, so a guideline recommendation mapped onto it will not validate; and proposition and conjecture are math kinds that content_profile_check rejects. There a normative statement is a recommendation block, with its strength as a code in a declared code list: load normative-statements from the folio-document-adapter package. Many guideline and standards documents have a recurring normative structure that maps onto content-block kinds: . | Guideline element | Content block kind | Notes | . | Recommendation (numbered, boxed) | definition | Normative statement | . | Evidence / rationale summary | prose | Supporting narrative | . | Remarks | remark | Implementation notes | . | Good-practice statement | proposition | Consensus-based | . | Research priority | conjecture | Open questions | . | Background | prose | Context sections | . | Evidence-quality table | diagram | Quality assessment | . When a document distinguishes normative levels (e.g. L1 = what to do, L2 = how to do it), map the normative statement to a definition block and the implementation guidance to a prose block tagged with the level (e.g. ["implementation", "L2"]). The exact level taxonomy is domain-specific; record it in the upload’s Dublin Core record as dc.type qualified normativeLevel. Domain-specific guideline handling (e.g. a particular standards body’s recommendation grammar) belongs in a domain adapter bundle, not the generic paper adapter. This skill detects the shape and hands off the domain-specific mapping rules to the relevant adapter: for prose folios, folio-document-adapter, whose normative-statements holds the recommendation grammar. Tables and figures — run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py . Text extraction destroys tables. A GRADE evidence table or a boxed recommendation comes out of Stage 2 as a run of prose, and nothing downstream can recover that it was a grid. python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py FILE.pdf -o uploads/<document-id>/ python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-tables.py --check # which backends are installed . Writes tables.json (pdf-tables/v1) beside structure.json, with each table’s cell matrix, column edges, caption, containing section_id, and a GFM rendering that can be pasted straight into a content block — the LaTeX pipeline already converts a GFM table to \begin{tabular}. Tables split across a page break are rejoined when their column geometry matches; stitched_from records what was merged, so check it on any table whose rows look like two tables. Read status before you read tables. The three ways to get no tables are distinguished on purpose, and tables is null — not [] — whenever nothing actually looked: . | status | Exit | Means | . | ok | 0 | a backend looked; tables: [] means the document has none | . | n/a-no-backend | 5 | pip install pdfplumber (or camelot-py) | . | n/a-no-text-layer | 2 | a scan — its tables are pixels; see Stage 2’s OCR route | . Needs pdfplumber or camelot-py, both pure PyPI installs with no model weights. Docling is the better parser and is not this: its weights come from HuggingFace, which is 403-blocked in sandboxed sessions, so it is a workstation/CI stage whose artefacts get committed — the docling capability probe reports it absent here rather than letting a session believe it ran. Output: extracted-blocks.json — array of detected blocks with provisional kinds, titles, and content; tables.json for the layout-bearing parts that do not survive as text. Stage 4: Mapping (→ mapped) . Interactive step — present extracted blocks to user for review: . | Show block count by kind | Let user rename, reclassify, skip, or merge blocks | Let user define chapter/section structure | Let user set the target paper ID | Generate mapping.json with confirmed decisions | . Stage 5: Content Generation (→ generated) . Generate content objects under content/<paper-id>/: . | .ts manifests via content/schema/builders.ts | .md content in project markdown conventions | Chapter .ts manifests with section structure | Paper .ts manifest (new or updated) | . Tag all generated blocks with: . tags: ["imported", "source:<document-id>"] . Add meta.source referencing the upload: . meta: { source: "uploads/<document-id>", originalSection: "3.2", importedAt: "2026-03-25T..." } .

855.title: Structured-Document Processing
855.content: Detecting normative structure . Normative guidelines often follow predictable patterns: . RECOMMENDATION N: <recommendation text in bold/box> Remarks: - Implementation note 1 - Implementation note 2 Summary of evidence: <narrative text> Evidence-quality table: <quality assessment> . Label conventions for guidelines . | Element | Label pattern | Example | . | Recommendation | def:<doc>-rec-<N> | def:example-rec-1 | . | Evidence summary | prose:<doc>-evidence-<N> | — | . | Remark | rem:<doc>-remark-<N> | rem:example-remark-1 | . | Good practice | prop:<doc>-gps-<N> | prop:example-gps-1 | . | Research priority | conj:<doc>-research-<N> | conj:example-research-1 | . Cross-referencing recommendations . Recommendations often reference each other and external evidence. Map these to uses[] in content objects: . export default definition({ label: "def:example-rec-3", title: "Recommendation 3: ...", uses: ["def:example-rec-1"], // references Rec 1 tags: ["imported", "source:example-doc-2016", "L1", "normative"], meta: { source: "uploads/example-doc-2016", strength: "strong", quality: "moderate", } }); .

856.title: Integration with Other Skills
856.content: | Skill | Integration point | . | paper-importer | Delegates Phase 5 generation for academic papers | . | content-validation | Validates generated content objects | . | editor | Reviews generated narrative content | . | scientific-accuracy | Checks extracted statements | . | ontologist | Maps terminology to glossary | .

857.title: Resuming Partial Processing
857.content: Where processing stopped is read from what EXISTS, not from a status field (intake.json has none). To resume: . | uploaded — intake.json is there | extracted — extracted-text.md (or an extraction record) is there | structured — extracted-blocks.json is there | mapped — mapping.json is there | generated — blocks tagged source:<document-id> exist in the content | . Start from the first stage whose artefact is missing. This allows multi-session processing of large documents.

858.title: Checklist
858.content: Before marking intake complete: . | Raw files committed to uploads/<document-id>/ | intake.json and <document-id>.dc.json validate (check:kind-validators) | extracted-text.md reviewed for OCR errors | extracted-blocks.json reviewed and confirmed by user | tables.json written, status checked (not silently n/a), and any stitched_from table spot-checked against the PDF | All content objects generated with correct builders | Blocks tagged with ["imported", "source:<document-id>"] | Chapter/section structure matches document | Cross-references mapped to uses[] | Content validation passes (content_validate) ``` | .

860.title: document-publishing
860.content: Named by: Authoring a document, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Release a draft for public comment . Take a document folio from corpus to published artifact — without a TeX installation.

861.title: The pipeline
861.content: folio/** → document_render_md → build/<slug>.md → document_render_html → build/<slug>.html → document_render_pdf → build/<slug>.pdf . One assembly step, then pandoc. Run document_render_md first and read it: it is the only place the whole document appears in reading order in one file.

862.title: Before rendering
862.content: Run, in this order, and fix what each reports before moving on: . | content_validate — schema, constraints, and profile conformance. A document folio that has acquired a math block or a .lean sibling fails here. | qa_sweep — the QA axes over each block’s sidecar. | document_render_md — read the assembly. Look for: sections that came out empty (a block written but never listed in blocks[]), blocks in an order that does not read, and the > **Missing block:** marker, which means a section names a root that failed to load. | .

863.title: PDF without LaTeX
863.content: document_render_pdf drives pandoc with an HTML engine — weasyprint (recommended), prince, or wkhtmltopdf. If none is installed it reports which are missing and stops. It does not fall back to latexmk, even on a machine that has it: a document folio is defined by not requiring TeX to publish. document_render_html needs only pandoc, so it works when the PDF path cannot. When you are drafting rather than publishing, prefer it.

864.title: Styling
864.content: Both HTML and PDF accept css, a stylesheet path relative to the repo root. Keep it in the folio repo, not here — a house style is content, and the platform ships no default beyond pandoc’s. The same stylesheet drives both outputs, so a print rule (@page, page breaks, running heads) belongs in it alongside the screen rules rather than in a second file that drifts.

865.title: Release files: the public-comment PDF and the offline .docx
865.content: scripts/document-export.ts is the publication pipeline’s FILE step. It runs the same assembly as document_render_md, and it gives the same result locally as on any CI runner, because the commit is the only input that changes: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/document-export.ts release --document <slug> [--out <dir>] [--release <id>] [--date YYYY-MM-DD] . | file | what it is | . | <slug>-public-comment-<sha7>-<date>.pdf | the frozen, line-numbered review draft | . | <slug>-public-comment-<sha7>-<date>.docx | the same draft as Word, whose sha256 goes in the release references (public-comment-channels) | . | <slug>-offline-<sha7>.docx | the editing copy: Track Changes on, one Word bookmark per chapter, section and block | . | <slug>-export-<sha7>.json | document-export/v1: commit, date, tool versions, and each file’s format, filters, parameters, sha256, pages, lines and bookmarks | . | <slug>-…-latest.{pdf,docx,json} | the same files under stable names, overwritten by every export, so a link to one always serves the newest | . | index.html | the Export page: every file above with its format, the filters and parameters it was made with, size, date, and links to this export and to its latest copy | . pdf or docx builds only that half. The PDF is the .docx laid out by LibreOffice (soffice --headless), not a print of the site. That way the two files have the same pages and line numbers (Word line numbering, continuous), and pdf-line-map.py reads the PDF as it reads a Word-made review PDF. It needs pandoc, LibreOffice and poppler (pdfinfo, pdftotext), and never TeX. It refuses a working tree with uncommitted changes under folio/, because the stamp would name a commit the file does not come from (--allow-dirty marks the stamp -dirty). The date defaults to the commit’s date, so two runs at one commit write the same .docx bytes. The PDF differs only in LibreOffice’s creation timestamp. Bringing an offline edit back . An author edits the offline copy in Word with Track Changes on and returns it with every change still pending. A change accepted before upload looks like the original text and carries no author. python3 -I folio-assistant-core/scripts/docx-offline.py changes <edited.docx> --repo . \ --out <changes.json> --summary <pr-body.md> [--apply [--commit]] . | The file’s folio-source-commit must exist in the repository, or nothing is merged (exit 2). | Each paragraph belongs to the last folio_<sha1(label)[:16]> bookmark before it. The name is recomputed from the source commit’s review-anchors.json, so run bun run review:anchors before exporting. | --apply edits the block’s .md in the working tree, carrying each insertion and deletion onto the matching line or table cell so emphasis, links and list markers around it survive. A block whose .md changed since the source commit is a conflict and is left alone. A paragraph that matches no line (a heading, a split or merged paragraph) is manual. Neither is guessed at; both are listed in the summary with the original and the proposed text. | --commit makes one commit per block (`offline edit: (, )`), so a review can take or drop each. Run it on a branch `offline-edit//`, and open the pull request with `--summary`'s file as its body. | Word comments come back on their block, in the report and the summary. Formatting-only changes are ignored. | .

866.title: A large document loads its text as data
866.content: build-document-site.ts publishes a document of 200 or more blocks (LAZY_THRESHOLD) as a shell plus data, because one page of every block is too heavy to use. | file | holds | who reads it | . | en/<slug>/index.html | headings, every block anchor, a placeholder per block, [edit]/[feedback] as data, comment-note counts | readers | . | <slug>/blocks/NNN.json | each block’s rendered HTML, 40 blocks per chunk, in document order | the shell, as the reader nears a block, then the rest in idle time | . | en/<slug>/index.hydrated.html | the whole document on one page | file:// opens (fetch fails, so the shell goes there), readers without JavaScript, tools (block-screenshots.ts) | . | <slug>/pc-notes.json | each block’s comment list (a public-comment folio) | a comment note, when opened | . | outline.json lazy | the hydrated page, the chunk count, and each block’s chunk | the rendered-impact predictor, which names the chunk a change alters | . Pages are under the page locale, en/, and data is not. scripts/document-site-route.ts says where each one goes. The name follows the knowledge graph’s own pair: a subgraph publishes index.jsonld, which references its members, and index.hydrated.jsonld, which holds them inline. The document page is the same pair: index.html references its blocks, index.hydrated.html holds them. A link to a block (#prose:…) or to a term inside one (#term-…) loads that chunk first and lands on it. --lazy always|never overrides the threshold. Two rules for anything that reads the document page: . | Want the text? Read index.hydrated.html when it exists. The shell has placeholders where the text goes. | Find blocks by their anchor (<a id="<label>">). It is on both pages. | . Searching the document’s comments is the dashboard’s job, not the page’s.

867.title: What is not implemented
867.content: The pandoc tools (document_render_*) have no citations, no bibliography, no glossary and no automatic cross-reference numbering: \cite{…} passes through verbatim, so write references as Markdown links or footnotes for that path. The site build (build-document-site.ts) does render \cite{a,b} as a muted [a, b] (each key linked to its entry with --bibliography-url) and :defterm / :refterm as a term and its link; it has no cross-reference numbering either. Cross-references do work: every labelled block emits an HTML anchor, so [see the scope statement](#rec:scope) resolves in both HTML and PDF. Use the block’s label, not a heading-derived anchor, which changes whenever the title is edited.

868.title: Release
868.content: Publication authorisation is the base process’s, not this skill’s: Task_AuthorizeRelease and Task_PublishRelease are non-relaxable in draft-to-publication.bpmn and no content type can opt out of them. Render, review, then take the release decision through the workflow — workflow_next will tell you what is enabled. A public comment release is a full build . A site build is a preview (a pull request’s branches/<slug>/: only what the change reaches, every whole-corpus index borrowed from main) or full (the main deploy, a public comment release, a release: every index rebuilt). See cat-harness skill feature-staging, section “Build types”. Before pc:release freeze, dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, so the frozen copy’s search index and slices describe the draft rather than main. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json.

870.title: document-structure
870.content: Named by: Authoring a document, Data sharing agreement document life cycle . Decide and maintain the chapter/section skeleton of a document folio.

871.title: Structure is authored, not inferred
871.content: Nothing derives the outline from the prose. Three manifests hold it, and each is an ordered list: . | File | Holds | Order means | . | folio/<slug>/<slug>.ts | chapters: ChapterRef[] | reading order of chapters | . | <chapter>/<chapter>.ts | sections: Section[] | reading order within the chapter | . | a section’s blocks: string[] | block root names | reading order within the section | . A block reaches the output iff some section names it: a block whose .ts and .md exist but that no blocks[] lists renders nowhere. Adding the name to blocks[] is part of adding a block.

872.title: Sections may nest exactly one level
872.content: subsections[] on a section carries another section, whose blocks[] render under a deeper heading. One level only — the renderers flatten at that depth, so a third level silently loses its blocks rather than nesting further. If you need a third level, you need another chapter.

873.title: Chapter granularity
873.content: A chapter is the unit a reviewer is asked to read in one sitting, and the unit the work plan tracks. Prefer more, smaller chapters over few large ones: a chapter is also the unit that gets rewritten.

874.title: Adding a chapter
874.content: . | mkdir folio/<slug>/<chapter-dir> | Write <chapter-dir>/<chapter-dir>.ts — title, optional label, and sections[] (which may start empty). | Add { dir: "<chapter-dir>" } to the document manifest’s chapters[], in the position it should be read. | content_validate. | bun run review:anchors, so the review sheet’s Selected Sections list and every comment’s placement see the new chapter. | . Every document folio declares review:anchors and check:review-anchors from its first commit (review-anchors-from-folio.ts --document <doc>; the --library/--source flags only when it was seeded from a library file). The section list is what a review sheet’s dropdown reads; a folio without it leaves a linked sheet empty. See review-sheet-script, “Linking a sheet to a repository”. The directory name is the chapter’s slug; it appears in build output and in every path a reviewer sees, so name it for what the chapter is about rather than for its position. A ch3- prefix is a rename waiting to happen the first time something moves.

875.title: Back matter: glossary and acronyms go at the end
875.content: Owner, 2026-11-02: every document opens on its title and summary, never on a reference list, and the same skeleton holds across documents: . | Part | Chapters, in order | . | Front | title page and front matter (acknowledgements, publication data), executive summary or abstract, how to use | . | Main | the numbered chapters | . | Back | Annexes or Appendices, then Glossary, then References | . Acronyms are a section of the Glossary chapter, never a chapter of their own. An acronym is a glossary term’s SKOS notation (folio-glossary/v1), so the acronyms list is one view of the glossary graph: the Glossary chapter holds the terms first and the acronyms after them. When a source publication prints its glossary or abbreviations up front (WHO handbooks often do), the folio still puts them at the back. Move the section into the glossary/ chapter by moving its block files (blocks resolve from their chapter’s directory) and keep every label: review comments, review sheets and contributor logs cite them. Then regenerate or update review-anchors.json, and fix any <chapter>/<block> paths in L1-coverage or glossary-table registries. bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/back-matter-order.ts --document <doc> warns when a document breaks this. It is warn-only: moving a chapter in an existing document is its editor’s call.

876.title: Reordering
876.content: Move the entry in chapters[] — nothing else. Do not rename directories to encode order: labels, uses[] targets, feedback records and QA sidecars all key on names, and a rename breaks every one of them for a change that the manifest already expresses. Then bun run review:anchors, as after adding one. After any reorder, re-read uses[] across the moved chapter: an editorial edge that pointed backwards may now point forwards, which is a real finding about reading order rather than a mechanical detail.

878.title: Domain fencing — keeping one folio’s rules out of everybody’s platform
878.content: Skill domain-fencing: How a domain-specific rule is kept out of the platform without being lost — the opt-in axis mechanism, why a profile is not a fence, and the test for whether a rule generalizes at all. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . Skill id: domain-fencing · Package: graph-management . Detangling a repository and detangling a rule set are the same practice. A rule that is true of one folio is harder to see than a stray import because nothing fails: it never fires for anyone else, or fires wrongly.

879.title: The mechanism: an opt-in axis
879.content: folioOptionalAxes() in pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts. A folio opts in through its config, inline in its index.config.json entry: . { "qaAxes": ["q-usage"] } . Without that, the axis’s criteria are absent from the registry — not registered-and-skipped, absent. There is nothing to run and nothing to report. The q-usage watcher states its own fencing, and it is the model to copy: . “Folio-optional axis. The q-usage criteria encode a substrate deformation parameter q and its regimes — one folio’s mathematics, not a platform concern. They are registered only when the folio opts in.” . A domain-regime axis and a structural axis are different axes, and a node can pass one while failing the other. Do not conflate them.

880.title: A profile is not a fence
880.content: detangler-archimedean-wall and the four wall criteria (wall-side-correct, wall-base-ring-minimal, wall-side-statement, wall-side-proof) are fenced behind qaAxes: ["archimedean-wall"], because they read a .lean file and name one folio’s chapters — one folio’s mathematics, not a platform concern. profiles: ["paper"] is not a fence. A profile says what KIND of folio can answer the question. It does not say WHOSE question it is. Every paper folio has a .lean to read, so a profile alone admits all of them to a criterion about one folio’s chapters. A domain rule needs an opt-in axis even when it already carries a profile: the two restrict different things. One axis per domain, not one per criterion. The five wall criteria open together on archimedean-wall, so a folio adds one key and cannot end up half-fenced. A single domain criterion inside an otherwise-generic axis is fenced by a conditional spread of a one-element array, not a gated domain. Gate the registry and the watcher bucket together. A bucket built from an unfenced array names a criterion the registry never registered — a watcher axis reporting on nothing and looking clean. WATCHER_CRITERIA_BY_AXIS and DETANGLER_WATCHER_CRITERIA both spread conditionally. Discovery is registry-driven. A fenced axis’s checkers are not discovered when the axis is closed, so fencing does not strand them as orphans. Direct callers keep working, and should. q-usage-audit.ts calls checkWallSide and checkBaseRingMinimal by function, not through the registry. Fencing governs what the platform asserts every folio must be measured against; a folio’s own audit may compute what it likes, having already decided the wall applies. |   | wall in registry | in the one-voice bucket | wall checkers discovered | . | no qaAxes | 0 | 0 | none | . | qaAxes: ["archimedean-wall"] | 4 | 4 | wall-side-correct, wall-base-ring-minimal | . Verify against a synthetic folio root, in a subprocess. The registry reads its config ONCE at module load, so OFF and ON are not both observable in one process. scripts/tests/folio-optional-axes.test.ts does this and pins both states; removing the conditional spread turns it red.

881.title: The shape of the repair: the mechanism stays, the data leaves
881.content: detangler-topic-coherence had a hardcoded DETANGLER_CHAPTER_KEYWORDS table; the table moved out to a folio-supplied topic-keywords.json, and the criterion stayed. repo-partition.ts has the same open problem: roughly 400 of its 1,180 lines are one repository’s exception list inlined into a generic algorithm.

882.title: The test for whether a rule generalizes
882.content: The examples are drawn from the science layer’s audits, described here rather than named; that layer links this skill from its side. Three questions, in order, and the first one that answers settles it: . | Does the rationale survive translation? A proof-gap audit’s reasons for extracting a shared sub-derivation — inconsistent edits later, inflated graph energy, hiding that the shared thing is worth naming — are the duplicate-module argument word for word. It generalizes. | Is the domain in the mechanism, or only in the vocabulary? A proposition-consolidation audit’s overlap rule is set-overlap arithmetic with a kind list bolted on; strip the list and the rule stands. Its near-duplicate rule normalises boxed LaTeX with bound-variable renaming and Levenshtein distance — the shape generalizes, the detection does not. | Would the platform need the domain installed to run it? A Lean completeness audit needs Lake, imports, sorries and axioms. No. | . A rule that fails all three is a folio’s rule, correctly located: fence it and say so.

883.title: Record the residue, do not quietly drop it
883.content: When a rule is lifted, the part left behind is a finding, not waste. A critical-path analysis splits cleanly: its union-of-two-relations model generalizes and lives in edge-kinds-and-blast-radius.md; its GENERAL / SPECIALIZED-STATEMENT / SPECIALIZED-PROOF / MIXED taxonomy does not, and stays where it is. The taxonomy is the interface-versus-implementation distinction restated for propositions; saying so keeps a future reader from lifting it a second time.

891.title: dsa-catalogue-status — Set the catalogue status when an agreement changes or ends (P14.5)
891.content: Skill dsa-catalogue-status: Set the life-cycle status (adms:status, W3C DCAT 3 §6.4.30) on a Data Sharing Agreement’s DCAT 3 catalogue record when the agreement is amended, renewed, terminated, or expires, while keeping all published versions readable at their immutable URLs (DSA building block B3, process step P14.5 Task_SetStatus). Named by: Data sharing agreement document life cycle . Skill id: dsa-catalogue-status · Package: folio-document-adapter · Process: folio-assistant-core/processes/content/dsa-document-lifecycle.bpmn (Task_SetStatus, P14.5) · Checker: folio-assistant-core/scripts/check-dsa-hash.ts (bun run cat check:dsa-hash) . When a Data Sharing Agreement is amended, renewed, terminated or expires (P14 in dsa-document-lifecycle.bpmn), its W3C DCAT 3 catalogue record must reflect its life-cycle status without deleting or overwriting any previously published version.

892.title: Using W3C DCAT 3 §6.4.30 (adms:status)
892.content: W3C DCAT 3 §6.4.30 specifies adms:status (http://www.w3.org/ns/adms#status) on dcat:Resource with the ADMS status vocabulary (http://purl.org/adms/status/): . | In force / published release: "adms:status": { "@id": "http://purl.org/adms/status/Completed" } . | Draft under negotiation or review: "adms:status": { "@id": "http://purl.org/adms/status/UnderDevelopment" } . | Superseded by an amended version (dcat:previousVersion points here): "adms:status": { "@id": "http://purl.org/adms/status/Deprecated" } . | Terminated or expired agreement (P14.5 Task_SetStatus): "adms:status": { "@id": "http://purl.org/adms/status/Withdrawn" } . | .

893.title: Preservation of immutable versions
893.content: . | Never delete or alter the signed legal text of an ended version: historical grants and audit logs continue to verify the SHA-256 digest of the version that was in force when a data access occurred. | Update only the catalogue life-cycle status (adms:status) (or publish the superseding version linked via dcat:previousVersion) and re-run bun run cat check:dsa-hash to confirm that every version’s legal text digest and dcterms:source citation remain intact. | .
