1033.title: Glossary terms
1033.content: Skill glossary-terms: Add terms to an instance’s glossary: local SKOS terms (folio-glossary/v1) with a definition, a code and links to external SKOS concepts, and references to whole external schemes. Rendered on the glossary/ page; gated by check:glossary. Authored terms go to gettext (.pot) for translation; a paper’s glossary is one more scheme. Named by: Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph . A glossary can reference external SKOS schemes, and that is the preferred way.

1034.title: Where terms go
1034.content: Core declares the glossary directory in folio-assistant-core.json. Its graph typology is perInstance, so every folio built on core has a glossary/. Each *.glossary.json is one SKOS concept scheme, $schema: "folio-glossary/v1" (folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts).

1035.title: Reference first, define second
1035.content: | you have | write | . | a term somebody else already defines in SKOS (ISCO-08, an EU authority table, a W3C vocabulary) | a local term with exactMatch (or closeMatch, broadMatch, narrowMatch) to the external concept IRI. Do not copy its definition. | . | a list of external terms this folio uses | members: the external concept IRIs, emitted as a skos:Collection | . | a whole external scheme | a remoteGraphs entry in the declaration with graphTypologies: ["glossary"]: known about, not held | . | a term only this folio defines | a local term with prefLabel, definition, and notation for its code | .

1036.title: Three states, never two
1036.content: . | authored: a person wrote or approved the definition. It must have one. | candidate: extracted from a source and not yet curated. It may have no definition, and the page marks it. | could-not-extract: the source names a term the extractor could not read. It carries a reason a person can act on. | . A candidate is never presented as a definition. An extractor writes candidates; only a person moves one to authored. A paper’s definition block counts as that person: its author wrote the definition and marked it (see “A paper’s glossary” below).

1037.title: How a term is linked: the workflow
1037.content: Terms are linked across the glossary, the narrative and the knowledge graph with a few shared joins, not a framework. One join key: the SKOS term (its id, or its IRI from another instance). Everything else points at it, and nothing copies it. | thing | how it names the term | . | the defining site | the term’s source: its glossary row (an L1 section line, or the document’s glossary table block). One node-kind structure for every term. | . | a narrative block that explains the term at length | the block’s defines: [<term id>] (and :defterm[...]{#id} inline). Provenance, not a second definition. | . | other uses in prose | nothing to write: matched at build time (term-passages.ts) and linked by --link-terms | . | an acronym | notation on the term, never a second list. The acronyms table is drawn from it (glossary:table). | . | an organization | focus (W3C ORG), shared ones in smart-ra organizations.glossary.json | . | an ArchiMate element | the element’s skosConcept property (glossary-archimate.ts) | . | a BPMN lane or task, DMN decision, skill, Tool | the generated candidate schemes (glossary-extract.ts); exactMatch when one is the same concept | . | a FHIR code | exactMatch / closeMatch to the CodeSystem concept; the code stays a CodeSystem | . | an external glossary | exactMatch to its IRI, members, or a whole scheme in remoteGraphs | . Where terms come from. | Ingesting a source (L1, DTH, DAK): bun run cat glossary:from-source reads its glossary and abbreviations sections into verbatim candidate terms with source: <file>#L<line> (l1-document-ingestion). No per-handbook script. | Authoring in the narrative (dth-hrh): the glossary file is edited, and the chapter is drawn from it (glossary:table, or the folio’s own build). A block that explains a term lists it in defines. | External: reference, don’t copy (below). | . What a reader gets. Every authored-scheme term has a page (glossary:page, glossary/instance/<instance>/<scheme>/<term>/). It shows the definition and acronym, Defined in (its glossary row), broader, narrower (computed), related terms, matches, ArchiMate elements, and In the narrative: the blocks that explain it, then those that use it. A Capitalized label in prose links to that page when the document build passes --link-terms, which dth-init sets for every DTH. Warnings, never failures. bun run cat glossary:links reports a source that is missing from a mounted layer, and a defines id that no scheme holds. With --all it also lists terms the narrative never uses. The acronym report is glossary:acronyms.

1038.title: Conventions
1038.content: Every folio follows these; none re-decides them. The instance namespace. A term’s IRI is <instance namespace>glossary/<scheme id>/<term id>. The instance namespace is built from the instance’s declaration (iriBase, version, and the stub of a sub-instance) by instanceNs in folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-page.ts; schemeIri and termIri are in folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts. For example: . | instance | namespace | . | folio-assistant-core | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/ | . | ihris (its own site) | https://litlfred.github.io/ihris/ihris/ns/ | . The namespace is never the asset’s path: moving the asset must not move the term. A term is minted by the instance that owns its source. A scheme and its terms live in the namespace of the instance whose root holds the SOURCE ASSET, not of the instance whose glossary/ directory holds the file: . | In a folio with sub-instances, that is the sub-instance (instanceNs(<sub-stub>), under the folio’s own publication root). It is never the root instance, even when the glossary/ directory is declared at the root. In ihris, a term drawn from ihris-manage is minted in ihris-manage’s namespace, not ihris’s. | A code list extended by several packages belongs to the instance that DEFINES it. Say so with the scheme’s own source (a repository path in that instance). Each term’s source still points at the package that contributed it. | A scheme whose terms are sourced in several instances and that names no defining source is refused, never guessed: split it, one scheme per instance. folio-assistant-core/glossary/ holds two platform schemes for that reason, core’s and cat-harness’s. | No two instances share a namespace, and a scheme IRI is unique across every instance. | . check:glossary enforces all of this (schemeOwner and collect in glossary-page.ts, and the checks in glossary.test.ts); glossary-extract.ts mints extracted terms by the same rule. When a check fails, fix the generator or split the authored scheme. Never edit the output. One ConceptScheme per code list. This follows schemas/code-list.ts (codeListToSkos): “a code is addressable and two lists may share a code without sharing a concept”. The same code in two lists gives two concepts. A relation between them is a SKOS match, never a merge. The basis of a match is recorded, never assumed. A match comes from a mapping the repository verified, such as a FHIR ConceptMap whose equivalence implies one: . | equal/equivalent gives exactMatch; | wider/subsumes gives broadMatch; | narrower/specializes gives narrowMatch; | nothing else gives a match. | . Any other basis needs the owner’s explicit acceptance. One example is a ValueSet that binds a local code list to the external code system itself, so that the local code is the external code. Once accepted: . | the scheme’s description names the basis and the ruling; | the builder lists the accepted systems explicitly; | QA recomputes the matches from the same source. | . ihris’s ISCO-08 lists to ESCO are the worked example. An IRI built from a publisher’s pattern but never dereferenced says so.

1039.title: Then
1039.content: bun run cat glossary:page writes the index, docs/glossary/index.md (the authored terms with A–Z and a filter box, the counts, the sources, schema.org DefinedTermSet JSON-LD, and a link to every asset type’s page), one page per asset type at docs/glossary/<type>/index.md (skills, tools, bpmn-activities, dmn-decisions, schema-fields: that type’s extracted terms, with A–Z and a filter box), and one SKOS JSON-LD file per scheme under docs/assets/glossary/. Each term is on exactly one page. bun run check:glossary is the gate: it fails on a document that does not validate, on a stale page, and on a page over its size budget (64 KB for the index, 1 MB for an asset type’s page). A page over budget is split further, never given a bigger budget. The harness’s swimlane-role terms (swimlane-glossary, the swimlane-glossary skill) are one more source the page links to, not copies of.

1040.title: Extracted terms
1040.content: glossary:page also extracts a candidate term from every knowledge-graph asset that carries a title and a description (folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-extract.ts): skills, Tool nodes, BPMN tasks and call activities, DMN decisions, and schema fields with a doc comment. One scheme per asset type per instance (kg-skills, kg-tools, kg-bpmn-activities, kg-dmn-decisions, kg-schema-fields), written to generated/<instance>/<type>.glossary.json inside core’s glossary/. | They are generated. Never edit them: fix the asset, then re-run. | The kg- scheme prefix is reserved for them. An authored scheme that takes it fails check:glossary. | A definition is the asset’s own text, verbatim. An asset with no description gives a candidate with no definition. | To promote one, author a term in a glossary of your own with a definition you have checked, status: authored, and the same source. | BPMN lanes and roles are not extracted: the swimlane ledger carries them. | Extracted terms are on their asset type’s page, never on the index, and each carries the “candidate, extracted” badge. Only authored terms go into the schema.org DefinedTermSet, which is on the index. | .

1041.title: Ordered glossaries — logical order, not A–Z
1041.content: Some glossaries (bootstrap’s, for one) are read top to bottom: each term is defined only by terms above it, and never by itself. Do not sort them A–Z. | ordered: true on a glossary says its terms array IS the order. Each term’s requires lists the local ids its definition uses; the schema refuses one that is later, itself, or not in the glossary. checkDeclaredOrder (schemas/dependency-order.ts) is the same check for any authored order. | In SKOS the order is a skos:OrderedCollection (memberList as an RDF list), each use is dcterms:requires, and isDefinedBy — the schema or standard that defines the term — is rdfs:isDefinedBy. | On the page an ordered scheme is its own numbered section at the top of the index, with its “Uses” links, and is not repeated under the A–Z bar. | A schema whose $defs carry uses IS an ordered glossary, read by termsOfSchema in glossary-page.ts: the definitions stay in one place, the schema, and the glossary cannot drift from it. They are authored, not candidate: a person wrote and approved them in the schema’s source, and the collector only reads them out. | The uses list is authored, not inferred. A text matcher over the definitions is a guard that the list and the prose agree (graph.test.ts); a word can appear without being used as a term. | .

1042.title: Translation: authored terms only
1042.content: bun run cat glossary:pot writes one gettext template per scheme that has an authored term, to translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.pot under cat-harness’s declared translation-sources directory, beside the BPMN templates in processes/, through the same pipeline (formatPot, the same timestamp-blind comparison); the translation status page counts them. bun run cat glossary:pot:check is the gate. | Only authored terms are extracted: prefLabel, each altLabel, and the definition, in the source language (en when given per language). A candidate reaches a template once a person promotes it. | The term’s IRI is the translator comment, never a msgid. It stays the same in every language; only labels and definitions are translated. | translations/<locale>/glossary.po is a different file (terminology hints for translation-block-qa). Do not confuse it with the glossary/ directory. | . Translations and the per-locale pages . A translation is a .po beside its template: translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po. bun run glossary:page reads every such file (readGlossaryTranslations, through glossary-pot.ts’s potPath) and produces two things: . | a page per locale, docs/<locale>/glossary/index.md, listing every authored term with its translated label, alternative labels and definition. An entry with no translation shows the source text marked (untranslated) — never silently English, never dropped — and the page states how many terms are fully translated; | language-tagged SKOS: the published <instance>--<scheme>.skos.jsonld carries skos:prefLabel and skos:definition once per language (@language), the source as en. | . check:glossary covers both, stale and orphan alike. A translation is UNOFFICIAL until a person signs it off. Every glossary .po says so in its header and records Last-Translator: folio-assistant agent (drafted, unofficial) when an agent drafted it; every locale page carries translation_status: unverified. Keep code, identifiers and standard names (BPMN, SKOS, ODRL, PROV-O, JSON, IRI, $schema, needs) as written, and give each capitalised defined term ONE rendering per locale across every scheme. Subject areas and fixed translations . Owner, 2026-11-07 (glossary review, “scoped fixed terms”). Three fields and one rule, in schemas/glossary.ts: . | field | where | meaning | . | subject | scheme, optionally a term | the subject area the translations bind in (dcterms:subject), a local id: harness-vocabulary, digital-health-trust, who-health-guidance. A term’s overrides its scheme’s; with neither, the term binds only within its own scheme. | . | translationStatus | term | per locale, official or unofficial; a locale not listed is unofficial. It records sign-off, never the translation. | . | (none) | the scheme’s .po | the translation itself. | . A fixed translation is derived, never flagged: an authored term whose scheme catalogue holds a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr for its prefLabel (isFixedTranslation). There is no #, fixed flag and no label in the JSON, so the .po stays the one place a translation lives. Precedence applies within a subject area. Across the layers an instance needs, the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term’s translation for its subject area, and an instance layer only adds. A match in a different subject area — the harness’s policy (策略) in a health guide’s sentence (政策) — is a sense check note for a person, never a violation. translation:glossary:check reads these fields. Use scopeNote for the prose a reader needs; it is never compared.

1043.title: Source glossary first
1043.content: When a folio is written from a source document (a WHO handbook, say), its terms come from that source’s own glossary before anyone writes one. | Latest edition. Use the most recent edition in the library. If it lacks something an older edition has, use the older one and say so on the term. | Verbatim, as candidates. Extract every glossary entry as a folio-glossary/v1 term, status candidate, the definition copied word for word with its page. Keep the source’s spelling as an altLabel when the prefLabel is normalised. | Read the PDF when the ingest missed it. A glossary the library entry does not hold (a missed section, a missing indicator sheet) is read from the PDF, and the scheme says so. | Structure the source gives is kept. Modules, indicators and the like become concepts too, linked (broader, related) to the glossary terms they cite. | Record what the source never defines. A term the source uses but does not define is a candidate with no definition and a scopeNote saying so, not a definition we write. | Place the scheme with the source. It lives beside the document’s library entry (for WHO publications, in the WHO publications IG), so every folio that cites the source shares one scheme. | Use the source’s words downstream. Blocks, diagrams and ArchiMate names use the source’s terms and link to their concepts, not a paraphrase. | . A conflict between the source’s definition and another scheme’s is raised as an issue on the repository that owns the other scheme, quoting both. Neither is chosen by the agent.

1044.title: Deprecating a term: a change set, decided later
1044.content: Replacing one term with another (for example “Core Data Element” replacing “MDS-HRH”) is proposed, not applied. The agent records a change set with the old term, the new term, the reason, and every place the old term appears. It changes no text and no glossary entry. An agent review, started later by an editor, decides it. Once decided: . | the old term stays in the scheme, so old links still resolve, with a scopeNote saying it is deprecated and why, and related to the new term (folio-glossary/v1 has no deprecated status yet; adding one is a schema change, not part of this rule); | the folio’s own prose moves to the new term; | quoted source text is never changed: a quote keeps the term it was published with. | .

1045.title: A paper’s glossary
1045.content: The paper builder (folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-glossary.ts, skill glossary-build) also writes the paper’s terms as one folio-glossary/v1 scheme, paper-<paper directory>, into the glossary directory the paper’s OWN instance declares. The page picks it up through collect() like any other scheme, so the IRIs are in that instance’s namespace (a sub-instance’s for a paper in a sub-instance, never the root’s). | the owning block | its :defterm paragraph | status | . | kind: "definition" | found | authored: the author wrote the definition | . | any other kind | found | candidate: extracted from a theorem, remark, … | . | any | not found | could-not-extract, with the reason | . The definition is the :defterm paragraph, verbatim, with directives replaced by their labels. The slug is the term’s notation. Never edit the scheme: edit the paper and re-run the builder. An instance that declares no glossary directory gets a notice and no scheme; add { "id": "glossary", "path": "glossary/", "dependents": "reproduce", "graphTypologies": ["glossary"] }.

1046.title: Organizations and acronyms
1046.content: An organization (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, a national regulator) is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus: SKOS’s foaf:focus link from the concept to the organization, which is typed with W3C ORG. The concept keeps the words: prefLabel is the full name, notation is the acronym, and altLabel holds other spellings. The organization keeps the facts about the organization. { "id": "who", "prefLabel": "World Health Organization", "notation": "WHO", "definition": "…quoted from its source…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "type": "FormalOrganization", "homepage": "https://www.who.int/", "subOrganizationOf": ["un"] } } . | type is a W3C ORG class: Organization, FormalOrganization, OrganizationalUnit or OrganizationalCollaboration. | subOrganizationOf names a local term that has a focus, or an organization’s IRI. sameAs links the same organization in another register, such as ROR or Wikidata. Give an identifier only when you have checked it; never guess one. | Without iri, the organization’s IRI is <term IRI>/_focus. | . One home per organization. An organization that several handbooks use (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, UNICEF, USAID) is defined once, in the shared reference architecture’s organizations scheme. A handbook lists it under members and does not copy it. An organization only one handbook names, such as a country’s regulator, stays in that handbook’s glossary. An acronym is scoped to its meaning. Use the document’s own expansion, and check it in context. In the WHO product catalogue handbook, “FDA” is the Rwanda Food and Drugs Authority, not the US Food and Drug Administration. When the document’s acronym would mislead a reader, record it as a candidate and raise it in the document’s review log. Do not fix the quoted text yourself. Finding the acronyms that are missing. The QA criterion acronym-in-glossary warns, block by block, about an acronym that no glossary the folio can see holds as a notation, prefLabel or altLabel. It warns and never fails. For the whole folio, with counts and the expansion the document gives (its abbreviations table, or “Long Name (ACR)”), run: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-acronyms.ts --folio folio . Each row is a candidate for a person to decide on. Words set in capitals (RESOURCES in a figure), plural forms (GTINs) and the folio’s own ids (PC-R-05) are left out.

1047.title: Architecture elements: the model drawn from the graph
1047.content: A reference architecture’s elements live in the knowledge graph, and the ArchiMate model is drawn from it, with the relationships on each glossary term. A term that names an element is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus that is the element: its ArchiMate type, and its relationships to other terms’ elements. { "id": "client-registry", "prefLabel": "Client Registry", "definition": "…quoted from the document…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "archimate": "ApplicationComponent", "relationships": [ { "type": "Realization", "target": "client-identification" }, { "type": "Access", "target": "client-record", "accessType": "read" } ] } } . | archimate is the element type, as ArchiMate’s exchange format names it. | relationships[].type is one of ArchiMate 3.2’s eleven. target is a local term whose focus is an element, or an element’s IRI. accessType is only for Access. | In JSON-LD the element is <term IRI>/_focus, typed archimate:<Type>, and each relationship is a predicate such as archimate:serving. | . The Tool archimate-from-glossary (bun run cat archimate:from-glossary --instance <dir> --model <id> [--write] [--prune] [--check]) makes the model agree. It matches each element by its skosConcept property, never by name. It names and documents the element from the term, creates any element the model lacks (on no view: place it in Archi, or with archimate-detangle), and adds the relationships the terms list. A type that disagrees is reported, and a person decides. A relationship between linked elements that no term lists is removed only with --prune. Archi keeps the layout: no box moves. Its report counts the elements that still point at no term. An authored ArchiMate model is never a source of the glossary. Never write a term, label, definition, focus or relationship into a glossary from a model someone authored in Archi. The words come from the source documents; the model only depicts them. The one exception is a model that was ingested: received from elsewhere and held as a source under the instance’s library/. Such a model can seed the glossary once with --seed --from library/<entry>/<file>.archimate (--write to write). Every term an element of it already points at, and that has no focus yet, takes the element’s type and its relationships to the other linked elements. From then on, the glossary is the source. The Tool refuses --seed on any model outside library/. The read-only “depicted by” links on a term’s page (glossary-archimate) read the model’s skosConcept on each build and write nothing into the glossary, so they are allowed.

1048.title: Not here
1048.content: A clinical code system is FHIR CodeSystem/ValueSet, not a glossary: convergence stops at SKOS. A glossary term may exactMatch a clinical concept; it does not become one.

1049.title: glossary-terms (skill)
1049.content: The skill glossary-terms as its source file folio-assistant-core/skills/library/cataloguing/glossary-terms.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

1050.title: Goal review — cold start, sweep a window, prioritise against stated goals
1050.content: Skill goal-review: Cold start, then review a time window of activity — sibling sessions, the work plan, issues, change proposals, branches, CI — and prioritise what it finds against goals stated in the owner’s words. Inputs are the window, the goals, the scope and the axes; the output is a synopsis (closed, open, needs doing, with effort), a priority queue per goal with selectable next actions, and the instruction gaps met on the way, each recorded as a work item. Use when asked “what happened”, “what is stalled”, “what should we do next for X”, or at the start of a session that inherits parallel work. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . This is a review, not a plan. It reads everything and writes only work items for the gaps it finds. Picking up the queue it produces is pickup; declaring intent is session-intent; this skill sits before both and feeds them.

1051.title: Inputs — four, all stated before the first read
1051.content: | input | what it is | default if the owner gives none | . | window | the time period to sweep, as a duration or two instants | the last 4 hours | . | goals | the outcomes to prioritise against, in the owner’s words | the store’s goal milestones, offered in the closing question (§”No goals given”); only if there are none, ask, or review without a queue and say so | . | scope | which repositories and stores are in the sweep | the checkout you are in and its forge repository | . | axes | which kinds of activity to read | all six below | . Keep the owner’s wording for a goal verbatim through the whole report. A goal paraphrased by the agent is a different goal, and the reader cannot tell which one the queue was built for. No goals given — but the store may already hold them. With no goals given, list the open milestones (beans list -t milestone), each title verbatim, and offer them as the queue basis in the closing question. Say which milestones quote the owner (their body carries the owner’s own words) and which are a milestone’s wording only — a title is the owner’s words only where it says so, and presenting one as such is the paraphrase this section forbids, one level up.

1052.title: Cold start — before any durable read
1052.content: Run the instance’s cold-start line (the top of AGENTS.md), so the work-plan Tool is in hand and primed. | The line can be wrong. If it fails, the fallback Tool for the work plan still exists — find it through the tools graph, do not stop — and the failure is the first instruction gap to record. | Fetch every branch, not just the default. Most of a window’s activity is on sibling branches that have not merged. | . Then fix the window’s two edges as commits on the default branch: the last commit before the window opened and the head now. Every “before → after” measurement below is a diff between those two.

1053.title: The six axes, and what each one can and cannot tell you
1053.content: 1. Sibling sessions. ASK THE SESSION API FIRST. List the sessions; where it answers, it gives what no inference can — each session’s session_status, and a task_summary that carries a held question in plain text. Fall back to commit trailers when it does not answer, and report “could not determine” when neither does. Never present the fallback as the method. Reading the listing. It is ordered by creation, not activity, so in-window sessions are interleaved with ones last active weeks earlier. Page until a whole page was created before the window opened, then stop — a session cannot be updated before it exists, so no later page can hold an in-window row. A reader who does not know the order either stops at page 1 or pages forever. The listing is large (~75 KB per 40 sessions): parse it, do not read it, and note the JSON sits inside an untrusted wrapper line. Read status_bucket / session_status and task_summary; a summary on a session that requires action is a held question — quote it, it is the sweep’s most valuable line. The trailer route, for when it is needed: the durable identity of a session is the trailer it leaves on its commits. Sweep the window’s commits across all branches for those trailers, group by session, and record for each: commit count, first and last commit, and the branches whose tip it wrote. A session’s state is then read from its branch: an open proposal that is green, red, conflicted, or one that merged. Say plainly that this is inferred. 2. Branches. Refs with commits in the window, each with its count ahead of the default branch and its tip session. A branch that is ahead by zero has merged; one ahead by sixty-five is a workstream the default branch cannot see (axis 4 says why that matters). 3. Change proposals (pull requests). Two lists: closed in the window, with merged distinguished from abandoned; and open, sorted by last update. For each open one, read the merge state, the CI outcome on the current head, the last comment, the reviews, and whether the body or last comment carries a question to the owner — quote the question. “Green” means every check on the head passed; a head with no checks is not green. 4. The work plan. Diff the store between the window’s two edges: items added, and every status transition (todo → completed, in-progress → completed, todo → in-progress, anything → scrapped). Then two measurements the store’s own status field cannot give you: . | Claims without activity — items in-progress with no change in the window. in-progress records a claim; it does not record that anyone is working (bean-coordination §”A quiet claim”). | Items that exist only on a branch. The store is committed per branch, so a long-running proposal can carry an entire epic the default branch has never seen. Sweep the open branches’ stores too, or the review is blind to the largest workstream. Compare against origin/main, never a bare main — the local ref is whatever this container last checked out, and nothing moves it. A session fetches origin/main and fast-forwards its own branch; the local main just sits there, often thousands of commits stale, and a count against it can be wrong by two orders of magnitude in the direction that manufactures a crisis. And if you cannot confirm the baseline is fresh, report could not determine rather than a count. An unverifiable baseline is not a measurement — §Rules, rule 1, applied to the ref. Confirming it is cheap: . # Resolve the default branch, then FALL BACK — `origin/HEAD` is unset in some # clones, and without the fallback this exits 128. # `session-start-coord-sweep.sh` does the same. DB="$(git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null | sed 's@^origin/@@')" [ -n "$DB" ] || DB=main git fetch origin "+refs/heads/$DB:refs/remotes/origin/$DB" git rev-list --count "refs/heads/$DB..origin/$DB" # 0 = the local ref is usable . An explicit refspec, not a bare git fetch origin $DB: the bare form updates refs/remotes/origin/$DB only when remote.origin.fetch happens to cover it, and exits 0 when it does not. Then compare by work item ID, never by file diff against a merge base. Even with a fresh origin/main, git diff --diff-filter=A origin/main...origin/<branch> -- beans/defs diffs against the merge base, which predates everything main gained since — so the count of “added” work items inflates with how far behind the branch is. The check, ids on the branch minus ids anywhere on main (archive included): . ids() { git ls-tree -r --name-only "$1" beans/defs | sed -n 's#.*/folio-assistant-\([a-z0-9]\{4\}\)--.*#\1#p' | sort -u; } comm -23 <(ids origin/<branch>) <(ids origin/main) # beans on the branch and nowhere on main . A large file-diff count from a far-behind branch is the stale-base signature, not a hidden epic — measure by id before reporting either. | . 5. Issues. Updated in the window, and the full open set for classification. Measure it; do not expect a size. 6. CI on the default branch. Runs in the window by workflow and outcome. A red default branch reclassifies every “stalled” proposal, so read this before judging any of them. Compare the tool’s span with the window. check:ci-health reads the last 100 runs and says what span they cover (“100 recent run(s) spanning 13.4h”), which can be shorter than the window. The uncovered part is could not determine (rule 1), reported as such with its extent. To cover it, page the forge’s workflow-run listing for the default branch by created back to the window’s start (the actions_list tool, or GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs?branch=<default>&created=>=<start>); check:ci-health takes no --since. Where a check fails, sidecars and generated files are the first suspect — for instance a QA sidecar not regenerated after its skill was edited.

1054.title: Classify against the goals — judgement, marked as judgement
1054.content: For each goal, in this order: . | Assign the items from every axis that advance it. Assignment is a judgement; say so once, and quote the item’s own title so the reader can disagree. An item can serve two goals; a goal can have none. | Critical path — the items in dependency order, from what the goal waits on first. Read dependencies from item bodies, not from the blocked_by field alone: dependencies are often only prose. | Blocked on the owner — items whose next step is a decision. Quote the question verbatim from the item; a paraphrase is a second question. | Done in all but name — items whose body says everything is finished but whose status is not completed. Report them; never resolve a sibling’s item (bean-coordination). Where the body says “not resolving unilaterally, awaiting the owner”, that is the owner’s line to close, and it is the same rule seen from the other side. | Effort — S (under an hour of agent work), M (a session), L (several sessions or an epic), with “blocked” as a separate mark, because a blocked S is not small. | Contradictions — two items or rulings that cannot both be followed. Name both and stop there; the owner reconciles them. | . Goals that are not in the store are a gap. If the owner’s goals exist nowhere as objects — no milestone, no epic carrying the goal’s words — every future review re-does this classification from scratch. Record that as a work item and offer the fix as an option; do not create the objects unasked.

1055.title: Output — three parts, in this order
1055.content: 1. Synopsis of the window. Counts first, each with how it was measured: proposals merged and abandoned, still open by state (green, red, conflicted, stale); work-plan transitions by kind; items added; claims without activity; issues touched; CI outcome on the default branch; sessions seen and how. A count in prose without its measurement is a claim (turn-reporting); a table is the right shape. 2. A priority queue per goal, ordered by the critical path. One line per item: id, what it is in six words, effort, what it waits on. Split into do now (nothing waits on the owner), owner decides (with the question), and close or scrap (done in all but name, superseded, expired notices). 3. The instruction gaps, each as a work item. A gap is anything the instructions said that the sweep could not do as written, said two ways, or did not say at all. Create the item with the measurement in its body and the rule it concerns named; parent it to the process epic. Do not create one per stale item — that is a queue entry, not a gap. Then one question, selectable. The queue will surface several owner decisions. Ask one in full — context, options, recommendation first and marked, a stated default — and give a count of the rest (interaction-modality §4.1). A reader on a low-dexterity profile (interaction/) answers by choosing a number.

1056.title: Rules
1056.content: . | Could not determine is never rendered as clean. Sessions the API cannot see, a store on a branch you did not fetch, a check that did not run — each is reported as unknown, and unknown outranks “nothing found”. | Measure at the window’s edges, not from prose. A body that says “nothing remains” is evidence; the status field is a claim; a count you remember from an earlier turn is neither. But a COMMITTED CHECK’S OUTPUT is not prose, and re-deriving it is strictly worse than quoting it. A check’s finding was produced by code with a test behind it; your inline version of the same question has neither. So quote the finding and name the check that produced it — bun run cat health, check:anchor-names, whatever it was — and re-derive only what no committed check answers. A re-derivation that finds MORE items than the instrument hands the owner a larger permission than any instrument justified, and deletion-requires-confirmation assumes the list put to a person is true. Where the rule exists as code (stagingSlug in schemas/sdlc/staging.ts, for a staging slug), import it. Not the same as “read the published survey” below. That is about a SIBLING’S sweep and the reason is duplicated effort. This is about an instrument’s computed finding and the reason is correctness — a wrong number reaching a person who acts on it. | Read the owner’s rulings out of the items and carry them forward. An item can be blocked only in name — the ruling already in a sibling’s body. Quote it and move the item to do now. | A window boundary is an artefact. A bulk edit just before the window makes everything look untouched; a bulk edit inside it makes everything look active. Say when a count is dominated by one commit. | Generated files inflate every count. Diff stats, files changed and commits touched all double where sidecars, exports or rendered diagrams regenerate; count the authored change and say the rest is generated. | The report is not durable; the gaps are. The synopsis lives in the turn and, if it must outlive the session, on the issue that asked for it. The work items are what the next agent inherits. | Do not pivot into the queue. The owner asked what to do next, not for it to be done; the first queue item is the next question, and picking it up is a separate, declared intent. | .

1057.title: What falsifies a review
1057.content: . | A proposal the review called green that a reviewer finds red on the same head: the CI read was of the wrong commit. | An item the review placed on a goal’s critical path that the owner says serves a different goal: the assignment was a paraphrase. | A “stalled” session that was in fact mid-turn: the inference from its branch was stated as fact. Re-read axis 1; the word is inferred. | .

1058.title: Read the published survey before deriving one
1058.content: bun run cat survey:owed first, so that parallel sessions do not each re-derive the same sweep. The command answers in four states, and each says what you owe: . | it says | you do | . | none published | the whole window is yours. A determined empty, not an error. | . | covered | read the survey; do not re-derive it. | . | a delta | survey only to..origin/main — normally a handful of commits. | . | unusable | a published survey’s upper edge is unreachable here (rewritten history, another branch). Survey the whole window. | . When you finish a sweep, publish it: . bun run cat survey:publish --from <sha> --by <session> --axis beans="…" --axis ci="!not looked at, and why" . An axis written name=!reason records one you did not cover. That is a first-class answer: a survey of four of six axes is useful, and a reader must be able to tell which two it says nothing about; recording only what you did lets a partial survey read as a complete one. The window’s two edge commits are recorded, so staleness is decidable rather than guessed. An unreachable upper edge is reported as unusable and never as covered, because siblings trust a covered survey instead of looking. This does not claim the window and does not divide the axes between sessions. It is an artefact: one session writes what it found, and a later one decides for itself whether that still covers its question.

1059.title: Tools this skill reaches for
1059.content: Reached through the tools graph the instance declares, never by a remembered path: the work-plan CLI and its manual fallback; the forge API for proposals, issues and CI runs; version-control history for trailers, branch tips and the window’s edges; and the session API where it can see siblings. Where one is absent, the axis it serves is reported as could not determine.

1060.title: goal-review (skill)
1060.content: The skill goal-review as its source file cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/goal-review.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

1061.title: Graph detanglement — the practice, not the migration
1061.content: Skill graph-detanglement: Drive a tangled graph toward a clean partition, so a sub-graph can be split off when it grows too large or when a business reason separates it. The staged practice — declare in place, detangle, isolate, extract — and the seventeen moves for measurement, ordering, judgement and enforcement. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Skill id: graph-detanglement · Package: graph-management . A repository grows until part of it wants to leave. Sometimes the reason is size, sometimes it is semantic — “split only where consumers or cadences differ” (docs/concepts/architecture/migration-plan.md). Either way the move is the same and the mistake is the same: treating the split as a migration to be executed rather than a practice to be run. This skill is the practice. Its subject is any graph with directed edges whose nodes are being partitioned: TypeScript modules into repositories, blocks into chapters, skills into packages.

1062.title: The one rule, at four scales
1062.content: At block scale — pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts, the detangler-no-dependency-cycle criterion: . “a cycle is reorder-invariant — when two blocks each uses: the other, or a longer loop closes, NO chapter ordering removes the forward edge. A cycle signals a genuine structural tangle: prune one dependency edge, merge the mutually-defining blocks, or factor the shared content into a third block both depend on.” . At repository scale — scripts/repo-partition.ts, the gate’s own failure message: . “A repo may not import one that depends on it. Either the CLASSIFICATION is wrong — check the target’s layer before the importer’s — or the import is.” . At knowledge-graph scale — kg-detangle.ts (bun run cat kg:detangle), over the instance stack each <instance>.json declares in needs. The repository and knowledge-graph scales share ONE verdict function, schemas/kg/layer-direction.ts. An edge is wrong-direction exactly when its target layer is not among what the source layer declares it may reach — ALLOWED for repos, needs plus itself for instances — and no reasoned permit names it. An instance with no needs is undetermined, reported in its own column, never read as clean. The function stops at direction: whether an allowed edge is a restatement or essential is the adjudicator’s call, so those edges stay unclassified with the verdict as their basis. The direction count is the one detangle number that is GRADED, and it is graded in a gate of its own — bun run cat kg:detangle:direction, blocking in CI. Everything else this tool measures stays pinned: kg:detangle:check fails on a stale or orphaned sidecar and never on a number, because the carve is an adjudication a person makes and grading it would be the tool overruling the adjudicator. A module’s bucket is taste. An edge whose target layer is not among what the source layer’s <instance>.json says it may reach is a contradiction between two declarations, which no adjudication makes consistent, so it is the one thing here a machine may refuse. Two flags, two scripts, two CI steps, so a red run says which question broke. Two things that gate reports and refuses to grade, both because grading them would be grading a could-not-determine: . | undetermined edges — an endpoint’s instance declares no needs. Failing on these would be the gate deciding a layering nobody declared. | the denominator — the count is over the edges that resolve. Dangling refs are excluded before any edge is classified, so a 0 is “0 among the edges that resolve”. The gate prints the excluded count and its breakdown, so a pass cannot hide an edge that failed to resolve. | . It is not check:partition’s second opinion. That tool’s root is one instance, so it partitions a future layout by path rule among that instance’s own modules; this checks the present layout against declared needs across instances. Either can be green while the other is red, and Phase I.1 of the migration plan needs both. At term scale — a glossary declared ordered (logically tight, non self-referential). Each term’s requires must point UP, and checkDeclaredOrder in schemas/kg/dependency-order.ts names every forward, self and missing use. It is the block-scale rule with terms for blocks: a forward requires is a forward edge, and two terms defined by each other are a cycle no ordering removes, so the moves are the same three — drop the use, merge the two terms, or factor the shared idea into a term above both. The rule and its form on the page are in glossary-terms §”Ordered glossaries”. Same rule, four scales, two vocabularies. Prune, merge, or factor into a third are the only three moves, and “the classification is wrong” is the fourth possibility the block- and term-scale versions do not have because a block’s chapter is not in doubt the way a module’s layer is. Everything below is machinery for finding out which of the four you are looking at.

1063.title: The four stages, and each is a gate
1063.content: Nothing moves until the stage before it measures zero. The stages are not advice about sequencing; each is a state the graph is in. 1. Declare in place . The sub-graph is declared where it already sits. Still inside the repository, still connected, nothing moved. The declaration gains a directory entry with its graphs[] kinds; a sub-graph that owns its own layout gains a nested declaration (beans/beans.json, todos/todos.json) whose paths resolve against its own directory, so the whole graph relocates by moving one folder. Declaring is cheap and extracting is expensive. The methodology graph typology is defined by exactly this property: “extractable (somebody else’s work, adopted, so it lifts out with its declaration when the field moves on)”. 2. Detangle . Drive cross-edges toward zero. This is the long stage and the rest of this skill is about it. 3. Isolate . The sub-graph carries its own declaration, its own namespace, its own published artefact. bootstrap/ is the demonstrated case: its own declaration, its own bootstrap: namespace — the prefix IS the stub, see kg-export §”A prefix is the stub” — its own graph document. 4. Extract . Only once edges are zero and the declaration stands alone. A directory move rather than a file-by-file sift. The five-point gate is in docs/concepts/architecture/migration-plan.md Phase II and is not restated here. For a Knowledge Graph leaving as its own repositories — a content repository and a tools repository — the rest of the method, from splitting the tools out to the cutover, is kg-separation and its process kg-separation.bpmn.

1064.title: The seventeen moves
1064.content: Measurement . 1. Read the unassigned column before the edge count. A low edge count over an unclassified corpus is the same false comfort as a green check over an empty one: “these are not cross-edges — they are edges this tool declined to judge. Do not read them as clean.” The same false comfort at a different join is covered-is-not-reachable: a skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Read that skill before concluding a corpus is covered. 2. The count rises when the measurement improves, and that is correct. Folding previously-unjudged edges in raises the wrong-direction count. A detangling count that only ever falls is not being measured honestly. 3. Quote both numbers, not only the one that improved. An edge can move rather than vanish. 4. An assignment is verified by re-running, never by being locally reasonable. The obvious move, even the one the tool’s own message asks for, can raise the count. Ordering . 5. Move the shared target first, then the importers. Classifying leaves before their shared schema targets adds edges; moving the targets first does not. 6. A schema moves with its script, or you mint the edge you meant to retire. 7. Declaration and readers first, files second. Update the declaration and every consumer while the files are still where they are, verify green, and only then git mv. The reverse order makes every gate red at once with no way to tell which failure is which. 8. Some fixes are two steps and only work in one order. Reclassifying handlers alone can make the composition root cross the line to mount them; a step that is edge-neutral by itself (resolving routes by variable specifier) can be what makes the reclassification a net win. Judgement . 9. Read what a module is FOR, never what directory it sits in. Layer is not by directory, and a name says what something is for while an argument list says what it does. 10. The triage question, in either of two equivalent forms. “Does it act on the PLATFORM or on CONTENT?” and “does it need a folio to have anything to do?” A sharper cut: needed to RUN a process is tooling; DESCRIBES one is core. And for the renderable side: if it renders, it is not the harness’s. 11. Check the TARGET’s layer before the importer’s. The gate’s failure text says so. 12. A keyword classifier gives false signals on filenames, and will keep reclaiming. fsh in fsh-guts.ts matches the FHIR-Shorthand keyword; content in content-type.ts sends marker machinery to core. Every keyword assignment is provisional against a read of the module, and removing a misclassification needs an exact entry rather than deleting the old one, because a rule that classifies by name will keep reclaiming it. 13. Inverting a dependency does not remove the edge if the new holder sits in the same layer. 14. The fix is not an exemption, it is the right owner. An exemption is what you write when ownership is genuinely ambiguous, and then it carries its reason inline. Enforcement . 15. A check is an error only once its count is zero, and enforce per axis. Turning a red gate on teaches the next agent to append || true (see the ruff comment in code-quality-gates.yml). 16. Watch the new gate FAIL before trusting it. Re-introduce the defect deliberately and see exit 1. A gate that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that passed. 17. Merge main before trusting a local green; CI builds the merge ref. A gate that passes locally and fails in CI can be a newer, stricter gate on the merge commit, not flakiness.

1065.title: Declare a falsifier, and mean it
1065.content: State in advance the result that would show the classification wrong (for example, “if classifying these RAISES the cross-edge count, the classification is wrong rather than the tool”). When it fires, read the new edges rather than arguing them away, and change the plan. A falsifier that never fires is decoration.

1066.title: Measurements that are not measurements
1066.content: . | A measurement you know to be inconclusive is not a measurement. If an earlier rule (an exact list consulted first) means your change never applied, say the experiment was inconclusive. | An edge that several passes called intractable is an edge nobody read. Open the file before deferring it. | A grep that under-reports reads exactly like a clean result. A pattern like from "\.\./*skills/ cannot match ../../skills/, and an export {} block can hide consumers that tsc finds. | Enumerate dispatch points before proposing a mechanism. It is how you find the ones already built, and as an audit it survives a bad hit rate where a choice between guesses does not. | .

1067.title: What the metric will not tell you
1067.content: From the editorial side, measured on a real corpus: . “an unconstrained search cleared 66 of 236 forward references — and a narrative review of its 53 moves found 18 of them made the paper worse. Reducing the metric and improving the reading are different objectives, and they diverge often enough that the difference is not a rounding error.” . “Expect the reviewed yield to be roughly a third of what the raw metric promises, and prefer it.” . So: a guard is not an objective. Pinned nodes, atomic families and container boundaries constrain the search, and split and merge are never auto-dischargeable — they rename things and ripple through every reference.

1070.title: A sub-graph wants to leave
1070.content: Process_GraphDetanglement · strict · 8 step(s) . Part of a repository wants to leave, for size or a semantic reason: four gated stages measure it out of the graph before anything moves, and an administrator authorises the extraction. THE FOUR STAGES ARE GATES, NOT ADVICE: nothing moves until the stage before it measures zero, and they are drawn because a rule in prose is one an agent under pressure talks itself past. Each gate here is a DECISION TABLE: workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at a cat-harness.processes:decision gateway, so the branch is computed from the counts a tool already produced rather than asserted. THE SHARPEST GATE IS Detangled?, AND IT IS SHARP BECAUSE OF ITS RULE ORDER. unassignedEdges &gt; 0 returns unknown BEFORE the cross-edge rule is reached, so a zero cross-edge count over an unjudged corpus cannot be read as a pass: unassigned edges are edges the tool declined to judge, not clean ones. A person can skip that rule; a table cannot. EVERY GATE HAS A THIRD STATE AND NONE OF THEM RENDERS IT AS CLEAN. Declared in place? answers unknown on a declaration that did not parse rather than “not yet”, because one says the work has not started and the other says nobody can tell. Detangled? answers unknown on an incomplete measurement. Both route to End_Unknown, which is a REFUSAL to advance — the process stops rather than proceeding on a guess. DECLARING IS CHEAP AND EXTRACTING IS EXPENSIVE, WHICH IS THE POINT. Stage 1 moves nothing: the sub-graph is declared where it already sits, still inside the repository, still connected. STAGE 2 IS A LOOP, AND THE LOOP IS LOAD-BEARING. Prune, merge, factor, or reclassify returns to Measure rather than to the gate, because an assignment is verified by RE-RUNNING and never by being locally reasonable. The four moves are the only four: the first three are the block-scale rule, and “the classification is wrong” is the fourth the repository scale adds because a module’s layer is in doubt the way a block’s chapter is not. ISOLATION IS NOT ZERO EDGES. A sub-graph with no inbound edges can still carry no declaration, no namespace and no published artefact, and lifting that directory produces a repository that cannot say what it is. bootstrap/ is the demonstrated case and the shape to match. THE EXTRACTION IS A PERSON’S DECISION, AND THE LANE SAYS SO. Authorise the extraction sits in the Administrator lane because an extraction moves durable artefacts out of a repository, and deletion-requires-confirmation is not a courtesy the agent may waive: the agent reports what would move, and waits. The administrator lane is the one whose activities change the substrate every other diagram’s lanes bind to, which is exactly what a repository cut does. i i i i i i i i

1076.title: Graph rendering: one set of rules for every drawn graph
1076.content: Skill graph-rendering: Draw any graph in a harness (schemas, processes, a folio’s block graph and any formal relation its content type adds, a detangle partition) so the picture is derived, checkable and readable. Ten rules, which engine to lay a graph out with and why, and how each graph typology here applies them. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . Skill id: graph-rendering · Package: graph-management . One set of rules applies to every drawn graph, so that each drawing does not follow conventions of its own. This skill is the general part. It says what any drawing of a graph owes its reader. The per-graph skills say how one generator meets it: uml-overview for schemas, bpmn-authoring for processes, and content-graph for a folio’s blocks. A drawing is how a person READS a graph. graph-detanglement is how the graph is RESTRUCTURED, and it needs the drawing: a partition you cannot see is a partition you argue about from numbers alone.

1077.title: The ten rules
1077.content: The failure each rule prevents is stated beside it. | Draw from a declared graph, never by hand. Every node and edge in the picture is read from a source: a schema, a declaration, a BPMN file, a uses[] list, a dependency cache. A wrong picture is fixed at its source. A hand-edited diagram is overwritten on the next run, and a check fails while it is stale. | Groups are declared sub-graphs. A box around nodes is a named sub-graph (a directories[] entry, a chapter, a package), never a grouping the renderer invented. | No empty box without a reason. A node drawn with nothing in it reads as a rendering fault. A node with no fields to show carries one line saying why. A node whose shape could not be determined is drawn dashed, as a finding, never as a quiet empty shape. | Edge kinds are drawn distinctly and never merged. A graph has more than one kind of edge (edge-kinds-and-blast-radius). Editorial uses[] and a content type’s formal edges, enforced and prose-only references, and a field-carried link versus one declared elsewhere (the UML’s dashed bootstrap.processes:skill edge) each get their own line style and a legend. Merging two kinds into one line destroys the signal every metric on that graph is computed from. | Pick the layout engine by what the graph is, and write down why. See §”Layout engines” below. The choice is a claim with a measurement behind it, not a taste. | Offer two orientations from one source. A tall graph on a wide screen and a wide graph on a phone are both unreadable. Derive the second view from the first (landscapeOf in scripts/plantuml-render.ts) rather than keeping two sources that can drift apart. | Declare colour once. Colour a node by its family (for the UML: schema, scenario, process, state, test) in one stylesheet, and have every renderer read that stylesheet (uml-palette.ts). A second palette is a second answer free to disagree with the first. | Stamp the output with its source’s hash. A rendering whose staleness check needs the renderer is a check CI cannot run: Java, a browser, or a font set that measures text a pixel differently. Write the sha256 of the exact source text into the output and compare stamps. The UML and block-graph SVGs do this through scripts/plantuml-render.ts, which every PlantUML generator shares, with its pinned jar and one JVM for all diagrams. | Show it in a zoomable figure. On the site, use the bpmn-figure markup so docs-ui.js adds zoom, reset and full-width controls, and the export ones: download the SVG, download a 2× PNG, or copy it (as an image where the browser allows, else as SVG text, and it says which). A pages template missing layout: default renders with no site script and so no controls, and nothing reports it. There is ONE viewer, and every diagram on a folio or IG page gets it. It is mountFigure in docs-ui.js; mountFigures decides what is a figure. Do not write a second one for a new kind of page. Extend what mountFigures and inlineDiagrams recognise instead. It takes each way a page embeds a drawing: . | embedded as | taken by | where it appears | . | .bpmn-figure markup | always | the process pages | . | an inline <svg> | always (an icon-sized one, or one inside a link or nav, is not a figure) | Mermaid, an IG’s {% include x.svg %} (PlantUML) | . | <img src="x.svg"> | always; inlined first | UML overviews, workflow figures | . | <object data="x.svg"> | always; inlined first, and its fallback text becomes the name | the IG Publisher’s convention for a pre-rendered diagram | . | a raster <img> | only on a page that opts in with data-fa-figure-images, and only when the column has shrunk it | an IG’s .drawio.png architecture drawings | . The raster row is an opt-in because a raster image on the platform’s own pages is as often a card face or a photo. A site build that knows its images are drawings stamps the attribute on the page. The IG site build does this on every IG page, and its own skill (ig-site-links) says where. This skill names no instance, because the viewer belongs to the platform. At 100% a plain figure is shown at its own width, capped at the column. It is not stretched to fill the column. A figure that is wider than its column scrolls inside its card and never runs past the page’s edge. The viewer is keyboard-operable, because the profile is low-dexterity. Drag-to-pan is an accelerator, never the only way to pan (board-windows §”The floor”). The figure takes focus (Tab from its toolbar). While it has focus, the arrow keys pan it, + and - zoom, and 0 resets. An arrow key is taken only when the figure can scroll in that direction. Otherwise the page scrolls as usual. The tools layer’s test/ig-diagram-viewer.e2e.ts checks all of this on a fixture page. | Put the measurement on the drawing. When a graph is being partitioned, show each group’s detangle numbers (size, cohesion, links in and out) beside the group, so the picture and the metric are read together. The UML overview pages do this through detangleResultsDir (schemas/kg/detangle-sidecar.ts), the same function the detangler writes through. A number shown without its picture invites arguing about the number. | .

1078.title: Layout engines
1078.content: Measured on the UML overview. Re-measure before relying on it for a different graph. | engine | use it for | what it gets wrong | . | stored layout (BPMN DI) | a graph whose author placed the nodes | nothing to choose: never re-lay a graph that carries its own layout | . | ELK (!pragma layout elk in PlantUML) | the compact, portrait default; it routes edges around boxes | it lays everything top to bottom and ignores left to right direction and arrow hints (output byte-identical). Unconnected groups end up in one wide row. | . | ELK + hidden links | a grid of unconnected groups (an overview) | nothing, if the column count suits the orientation: ceil(√(n/2)) for portrait, ceil(√(2n)) for landscape | . | Graphviz dot, left to right, polyline edges | the landscape view of a connected graph | it can route a long edge across a box, which is why ELK stays the portrait default. Use nodesep 70, ranksep 160. | . | Graphviz with orthogonal edges | avoid | it places edge labels away from their edges and runs lines through boxes. | . | Mermaid (dagre) | a secondary view where CSS classes on nodes matter | the same model came out three times taller than ELK’s | . | Graphviz dot in the browser (WASM, unflatten then dot) | the interactive view a reader rearranges by dragging nodes (kg-subgraph-layout) | like ELK it sets unconnected clusters, and unconnected nodes in one cluster, on one rank: fold both into grids with invisible, marked anchors | .

1082.title: Guideline Updates
1082.content: Process_GuidelineUpdates · strict · 8 step(s) . Taking up a new version of a guideline, or a changed lower layer, is a re-pin and a review at once. The steward maps the affected layers and re-pins them in dependency order. For each re-pin, the adaptation team compares the old version, the new version and its own adaptations. A change that touches no adaptation or policy merges on the technical path. One that does goes to the adaptation committee, which decides for each adaptation whether to keep, revise or retire it. Revisions are ordinary content changes (Process_ContentChangeReview), and the re-pin merges with them. The loop runs until every layer is current. i i i i i i i i

1088.title: Hand back to the discussion
1088.content: Skill hand-back-to-discussion: A sibling agent, spawned during or working beside a live agent-human discussion, hands every card, question, decision, result, blocker or piece of context back to the discussion agent that is talking with the person, and never leaves it only in its own thread. The discussion agent asks the person (ask-the-person), marks every copy answered, and routes the answer back. A review sheet or issue in play is an extra channel. Use whenever an agent that is not the one talking with the person has something the person must see. Named by: Ask the person, Hand back to the discussion . The procedure behind Process_HandBackToDiscussion. It joins two rules that already bind: ask-the-person (how a question is put) and the relay paragraph of interaction-modality §4.1 (a relayed question says where the answer goes). This skill is the missing step between them: who puts the question, and how the answer gets back.

1089.title: Why
1089.content: A card posted only in a sibling’s own thread is not seen by the person, who is talking with the discussion agent elsewhere; the decision stalls, or reaches the person only by reconstruction. A feedback channel in play (a review sheet, an issue) is used as well.

1090.title: The two roles
1090.content: | role | who | does | . | Discussion agent (session-coordinator) | the agent the person is talking with right now: a project coordinator, the parent of a subagent, the session that spawned a swarm | shows the hand-back to the person, asks with ask-the-person, marks every copy answered, routes the answer back | . | Sibling (sibling-session) | any agent the discussion agent spawned, or one working beside it on the same goal: a project thread, a subagent, a workflow agent, a cloud session | composes the hand-back once, with the analysis it alone has, and acts on the answer | . You are a sibling when your brief names a discussion agent, or when you were started by another agent while a person was talking with it. A sibling that is not sure hands back anyway: one extra copy costs a line, and a missed card costs a stalled decision.

1091.title: The brief names the discussion (spawning agent)
1091.content: An agent that spawns a sibling during a live discussion puts the discussion link in the brief (definitions.discussion of the input schema): who the discussion agent is, how to reach it, the standing card rules, and any feedback channel in play (a review sheet’s id and tab, an issue). See process-state §”A coordinator that briefs a thread”. A sibling has nothing else that tells it.

1092.title: Input and output
1092.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In (the hand-back): from (title, link, process), to (the discussion link), kind (decision, question, context, result, blocker), a one-sentence summary, ask (the ask-the-person input, unchanged, for a decision or question), context (for the others), links, channels (always discussion, plus any of own-thread, project-chat, review-sheet, github-issue, github-pr), answerRoute, blocking, and supersedes when it replaces an earlier one. | Out (the record): shown (every copy, discussion first), state (open, answered, withdrawn, superseded, informed), the ask-the-person output, chosen, quote, answeredIn, marked (the strike-through edit per copy) and deliveredBack (proof the answer reached the sibling, with citesPerson). | .

1093.title: Steps — sibling
1093.content: . | Compose once. A question is the full ask-the-person input: what will differ, context, every option lettered with a one-line trade-off, the recommendation and why, what happens with no answer. The discussion agent must be able to show it without opening your thread. Context, a result or a blocker gets the same test. | Show it where you are. Post it in your own thread too (chat text, then the card), so the tappable card sits beside the work. Your own thread is never the only copy. | Mirror it to the feedback channel in play. When a review sheet governs the work, write the “Decision needed” block into the row’s agent column and set Agentic status to Needs you (the document layer’s review-sheet-script skill, §”A question to people goes in the sheet”). An issue or PR in play gets a comment. These are extra copies, never instead of the discussion. | Hand back to the discussion agent with the host’s route: . | host | route | . | Claude projects thread | message_coordinator (or message_thread to the discussion thread), the hand-back as plain prose in the schema’s order: summary, question, lettered options with trade-offs, recommendation, if silent, link to your thread | . | subagent (Agent tool, workflow agent) | your final report: the hand-back as a fenced json block that validates against the input schema, then a one-line summary. 1094.title: Steps — discussion agent

A question goes through Process_AskThePerson unchanged: the chat text in full first, then the card with the same letters. Never “see the card in thread X”. | Context, a result or a blocker that needs no answer: post it, state informed, done. | Take the answer from any copy. A sheet’s “Decision needed” block is replaced by the decision and who made it, and Agentic status moves on. A withdrawn or superseded hand-back is marked the same way with the reason. | A rule-level answer goes into the governing skill in the same turn (symbiotic-interaction §2). | .

1103.title: Handover report
1103.content: Skill handover-report: Write a handover report: a templated snapshot of an agent’s current state, committed as a work item note, so that a session or subagent that stalls, runs out of context, or loses its container can be picked up by another agent without re-deriving anything. Use it when you are told a stall is likely, at the end of every long arc, before a risky or long-running step, and whenever a steward asks for one. Its reader is stalled-agent-triage. Named by: Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . An agent’s state lives in three places that do not survive it: the chat, its scratchpad, and uncommitted work in its worktree. A handover report moves the parts that matter into the repository, as a committed work item note, so the next agent starts from fact rather than from guesswork. To produce one under time pressure, follow prepare-for-handover: it commits and pushes first, then writes this report citing the pushed SHAs. This skill is not agent-handoff, which hands one task to a named agent in another environment. A handover report is a snapshot of everything one agent is holding, written for whoever turns up next, which may be no one in particular.

1104.title: When to write one
1104.content: . | When told a stall is likely. Write it first, before continuing any work. A report written after the stall is never written. | Before a long or risky step: a 30-minute regenerate, a big merge, a disk-heavy run. | At the end of an arc, even a successful one, if anything stays open. | When a steward or the owner asks. | . Write it short and early, then update it. A 20-line report pushed now is worth more than a complete one that never lands.

1105.title: Where it goes
1105.content: A work item note on the work item you are working, or on its epic if you hold several: . bun run cat beans:note <bean-id> --title "handover: <role> <date>" \ --body-file <file> --branch <your-branch> bun run cat beans:notes # rewrites the index; commit both files git add -A && git commit && git push . One file per branch per work item, so two agents writing handovers never conflict (bean-coordination §”Adding to a bean — a note, not an append”). Write it in your own worktree. Some tools write into the main checkout instead; if you are a subagent, check git status there afterwards. Push it, even onto a draft PR or a red branch. An unpushed report does not exist.

1106.title: The template
1106.content: Mix narrative with formal content. The tables are what a triage agent parses; the prose is what a person reads. ## Handover report: <role> (<session or agent>) - **Session:** <session URL, or the parent session plus agent id> - **Written:** <UTC time>, <why: stall expected / end of arc / asked> - **Role and mandate:** <one line; the owner rulings that bound you> ### Where I'm going (current arc) <2–4 sentences: the goal, the epic it serves, and what "done" looks like.> ### Done so far - <outcome, with PR, commit or bean> ### Next in queue 1. <next concrete step: command, file, PR> 2. … ### In flight | item | kind (PR / branch / bean / process run) | state | next action | owner |---|---|---|---|---| ### Blockers and dependencies | blocker | waits on | since | expires / re-check |---|---|---|---| ### Decisions pending (owner) - <question, with options and your recommendation, so it can be asked cold> ### Unpushed or at-risk state - <scratchpad files, local commits, running jobs, and whether each is reproducible> ### Dispatch lines (copy-paste, one per unstarted item) Do bean folio-assistant-<id> on branch <branch-to-create> of repo <owner>/<repo>. Do bean folio-assistant-<id> on branch <branch-to-create> of repo <owner>/<repo>. ### How to resume <the first three things the next agent should do, in order> .

1107.title: Rules
1107.content: . | Facts with provenance. Write “CI red on abc123 (check X)”, not “CI is flaky”. Give SHAs, PR numbers and work item ids, never “the branch”. | Say what is NOT pushed. Unpushed commits, scratchpad plans and running background jobs are exactly what a stall destroys. Name each one, and say whether it can be rebuilt. | Owner rulings verbatim, with the date. A ruling paraphrased in a handover becomes a different ruling by the second handover. | Never put secrets in it. Name secrets, never give their values. | Blocks follow bean-blocking: what it waits on, since when, and when to re-check, so a stale block can be told from a live one. | Update in place. Re-run beans:note on the same branch and work item, which gives the same file. Do not append a second report. | Every unstarted item gets a DISPATCH LINE, in one fixed sentence. Do bean folio-assistant-<id> on branch <branch-to-create> of repo <owner>/<repo>. It is a format, not a suggestion: write it verbatim with the three slots filled. Why one sentence, and why these three slots. A dispatch is read by somebody with no context — the owner pasting it into a new session, or a steward handing out work. The three slots are the minimum that makes it actionable alone: the WORK ITEM says what and carries its own Done-when, the BRANCH stops two agents landing on one ref, and the REPO is required because an agent’s session may be scoped to a different one. Drop any slot and the recipient has to come back and ask. Three rules: . | Name a branch that does not exist yet, and say so. A line naming a finished branch sends an agent to a dead ref. | One work item per line. Not a theme, not “the three remaining X”. The work item is what carries the Done-when, and a line that names a theme hands over a judgement instead of a task. | Order them, and say what is ordered. If a line must follow another, write that above the block — not inside the sentence, which stays fixed. A hidden prerequisite makes a list of dispatchable work items worse than a list of the one that is ready. | . dispatch-agent governs what happens AFTER the line is sent — the progress contract and the heartbeat. This rule is only about writing the line so the work can be handed on at all. | .

1109.title: A harness’s default rendering
1109.content: Process_HarnessRendering · strict · 7 step(s) . Renders a harness instance as its default interface: its left-hand nav and docs on its own theme’s art, and a board of its todos and beans from which a reader reads, reviews and, when a write tool is available, proposes changes into the publication review. The theme art goes behind every docs page. Read-only is the floor. Whether the reader may write is a question about the tools the session has (git-push, github-api, github-connector) and the reader’s permissions, so the gateway reads capabilities and never assumes one write path. A change a reader proposes enters the content change review in folio-assistant-core (content-change-review.bpmn); this process enables that review and does not replace it. i i i i i i i
