2041.title: Glossary: Schema fields, F–L
2041.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2476 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 187 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 500 terms and is 294 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 500 shown . F G H I J K L

2050.title: Glossary: Schema fields, D–E
2050.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2476 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 187 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 191 terms and is 114 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 191 shown . D E

2054.title: Glossary: Schema fields, S
2054.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2476 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 187 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 250 terms and is 145 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 250 shown . S

2057.title: Glossary: Schema fields, A–C
2057.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2476 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 187 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 507 terms and is 304 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 507 shown . A B C

2062.title: Glossary: Schema fields, M–O
2062.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2476 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 187 (SKOS). One of 7 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 219 terms and is 131 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 2667 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 219 shown . M N O

2067.title: Glossary: Schema fields
2067.content: Candidate terms extracted from every schema field with a doc comment: <Declaration>.<field> as the label, the comment’s first paragraph as the definition. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap-tools 45 (SKOS) · cat-harness-tools 2476 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 187 (SKOS). Split by first letter. 2708 terms are too many for one page within its budget of 1.0 MB, so they are on 7 pages by the first letter of the label. The ranges are fixed, so a term’s address does not move as terms are added. A label that does not start with a letter is on the first page. | A–C: 507 terms | D–E: 191 terms | F–L: 500 terms | M–O: 219 terms | P–R: 540 terms | S: 250 terms | T–Z: 501 terms | .

2069.title: quality of the evidence
2069.content: In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. Also called: certainty of the evidence, confidence in the estimates of effect . The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout.

2175.doc: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution
2175.title: Health Workforce Education and Training Institution candidate
2175.content: An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. Also called: Health workforce education and training institution . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 2201.title: Remuneration candidate
2201.content: Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 2215.title: Public Health Workforce candidate
2215.content: The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. Also called: Public health workforce . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 2421.title: Facility Type candidate
2421.content: Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. Also called: Facility type . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 89; PDF page 103). 2436.title: Facility/Institution Ownership Type candidate
2436.content: Classification for ownership type: • Publicly-owned: Facilities owned or controlled by a governmental unit or a public corporation (where control is defined as the ability to determine the general corporate policy) corresponding to the institutional sector “government units” defined in the System of National Accounts 2008. • Not-for-profit privately-owned: Facilities that are legal or social entities created for the purpose of producing goods and services, whose status does not permit them to be a source of income, profit, or other financial gain for the unit(s) that establish, control or finance them, corresponding to the institutional sector “non-profit institutions serving households” defined in the System of National Accounts 2008. • For-profit privately-owned: Facilities that are legal entities set up for the purpose of producing goods and services and are capable of generating a profit or other financial gain for their owners corresponding to the institutional sector “non-financial corporations” defined in the System of National Accounts 2008. Also called: Facility/institution ownership type . From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 2454.title: Gender candidate
2454.content: Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. This includes norms, behaviours and roles associated with being a woman, man, girl or boy, as well as relationships with each other. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). 2473.title: F
2473.content: Facility Type candidate Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. 2474.content: Gender candidate Gender refers to the characteristics of women, men, girls and boys that are socially constructed. This includes norms, behaviours and roles associated with being a woman, man, girl or boy, as well as relationships with each other. As a social construct, gender varies from society to society and can change over time. Gender is hierarchical and produces inequalities that intersect with other social and economic inequalities. The handbook cites its reference 48 for this entry. | Facility Type (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Facility types are categorized following the system of health accounts through the classification of health care industries. These enable arrangement of country-specific institutions in common, internationally applicable categories. The categories are as follows: Hospitals (HP.1) Hospitals comprise licensed establishments that are primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic and treatment services that include physician, nursing and other health services to inpatients and the specialised accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals provide inpatient health services, many of which can be delivered only by using specialised facilities and professional knowledge as well as advanced medical technology and equipment, which form a significant and integral part of the provision process. Although the principal activity is the provision of inpatient medical care they may also provide day care, outpatient and home health care services. The tasks of hospitals may vary by country and are usually defined by legal requirements. In some countries, health care facilities need in addition a minimum size (such as a number of beds and medical staff to guarantee 24-hour access) in order to be registered as a hospital. Residential long-term care facilities (HP.2) The category of Residential long-term care facilities comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing residential long-term care that combines nursing, supervisory or other types of care as required by the residents. In these establishments, a significant part of the production process and the care provided is a mix of health and social services, with the health services being largely at the level of nursing care, in combination with personal care services. The medical components of care are, however, much less intensive than those provided in hospitals. Providers of ambulatory health care (HP.3) This item comprises establishments that are primarily engaged in providing health care services directly to outpatients who do not require inpatient services. This includes both offices of general medical practitioners and medical specialists and establishments specialising in the treatment of day-cases and in the delivery of home care services. Health practitioners in ambulatory health care primarily provide services to patients who visit the health professional’s office, or the practitioners visit the patients at home. Consequently, these establishments do not usually provide inpatient services. Ancillary services (HP.4, including transportation, emergency rescue, laboratories and others) This category comprises establishments that provide specific ancillary type of services directly to outpatients under the supervision of health professionals and not covered within the episode of treatment by hospitals, nursing care facilities, ambulatory care providers or other providers. Included are providers of patient transportation and emergency rescue, medical and diagnostic laboratories, dental laboratories and other providers of ancillary services. These specialised providers may charge patients directly for their services rendered or may provide these ancillary services as benefits-in-kind under special service contracts. Retailers (HP.5, including pharmacies) This item comprises specialised establishments whose primary activity is the retail sale of medical goods to the general public for individual or household consumption or utilisation. Establishments whose primary activity is the manufacture of medical goods, such as making lenses, orthopaedic or prosthetic appliances for direct sale to the general public for individual or household use, are also included, as is fitting and repair done in combination with sale. Note: Due to special medical safety and quality regulations, retailers of over-the-counter medical products and other providers of medical goods are subject to licensing and/or pharmaceutical authorisation in order to be eligible to provide their activities. Non-health care products such as cosmetics, dietetic products and natural products are excluded from health expenditures. Providers of preventive care (HP.6) This category comprises organisations that primarily provide collective preventive programmes and campaigns/public health programmes for specific groups of individuals or the population-at-large, such as health promotion and protection agencies or public health institutes as well as specialised establishments providing primary preventive care as their principal activity. This includes the promotion of healthy living conditions and lifestyles in schools by special outside health care professionals, agencies or organisations. (108) Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 90; PDF page 104). Public Health Workforce candidate The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. 2482.title: Q
2482.content: quality of the evidence In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout. Remuneration candidate Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 2684.title: A
2684.content: ArchiMate model from the glossary candidate, extracted Make an ArchiMate model agree with the instance's folio-glossary/v1 terms whose focus is an ArchiMate element: elements matched by their skosConcept property (never by name) take the term's prefLabel and definition, a term with no element gets one on no view, and the relationships the terms list are added. A type that disagrees is reported, never changed. A relationship between two linked elements that no term lists is reported, and removed with --prune along with the lines that draw it. No box or line is moved. Without --write it only reports; --check fails when anything would change. --seed goes the other way once, and only from an ingested model held under library/ (--from): an authored model is never a source of the glossary. 2685.content: Bibliography page candidate, extracted Render every reference in the checkout (each declared references directory's folio-reference/v1 nodes and each catalogue directory's Dublin Core records) as the bibliography page and one page per sub-graph, each with its BibTeX, CSL-JSON, RIS and Dublin Core JSON-LD exports and a per-reference export, at the route of the visualiser core declares for it. Block edit and feedback links candidate, extracted Each labelled block's links back to where it can be changed: [edit] opens the block's Markdown source in GitHub's editor on main, and [feedback] opens a new GitHub issue about the block, from the folio's .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/block-feedback.yml when it has one (prefilling only the fields it declares: block, section, source, page, url) or as a plain issue whose body carries the same facts. The document build draws these on every block; this Tool prints them as JSON for one block or all. Governed by the block-actions skill. BPMN workflow engine candidate, extracted Run a declared BPMN process as an instance: workflow_start opens one for a subject, workflow_next reports what is enabled, workflow_complete records a step or answers a decision (a DMN-computed one from facts) and REFUSES a step that is not enabled. State is committed under the work plan, so which edge was taken is a record, not a memory. Tools of cat-harness-tools · source cat-harness-tools/tools/bpmn-engine/bpmn-engine.ts#bpmn-engine . Build the review sheet's Apps Script and a document's Config tab candidate, extracted Builds Code.gs (--script), the one Google Apps Script every review sheet runs (from review-sheet.gs), and one document's Config tab rows (--config), filled from the folio's review/public-comment/sheet-sync.json, its review anchors and the draft's pdf-line-map.json. The script keeps a public-comment review sheet's links and joins current: each comment No. links to its comment page; Sections, Page and Line no(s) link to the page of the frozen review draft; Review Change Sets joins its comments, suggested revisions, feedback and dispositions, each No. n linking to its row; and on both tabs Agentic status lists each pull request of the change-set, linked, with its status and what it changed, from the Agent tab. It reads the document's URLs, tab and column names and data from the sheet's Config tab (visible, locked to the owner), which the agent writes from these rows. A person pastes the script (one file) into the sheet once (Extensions > Apps Script) and runs installTriggers; from then on the sheet rebuilds itself within about a minute of an edit, with no agent. With "mode": "drafting" in the config it builds the drafting sheet instead: one Contributor Feedback tab where each row is a change set (ids assigned by the script), Sections picked from the document's table of contents and linked to it, and Issue and Agentic status from the Agent tab. 2686.title: C
2686.content: Catalogue a library from its bibliography candidate, extracted Write one folio-dublin-core/v1 record and one folio-catalogue-node/v1 item per library entry that the source ledger joins to a CSL-JSON reference, into the folio's declared catalogue directory, so gen-library-jsonld reads the title from the catalogue's dc.title instead of falling to the PDF or the slug. The join is exact: a ledger row naming the entry's structure.json source file, one reference id, and the same sha256 where both record one. Unjoined entries are reported and left alone. Sign the package and/or each asset candidate, extracted THE TRUST ANCHOR IS GDHCN, SPECIFIED BY THE WHO SMART TRUST IG. READ OFF THAT IG rather than from general knowledge: a GDHCN trustlist distributes KEY MATERIAL as W3C DID documents, and says nothing about what you wrap your bytes in — the health-certificate envelope is a separate specification in the same IG, and a document package is not a health certificate. So what is settled is where a verifier GETS THE KEY, not what it verifies. A portal that can fetch the bytes but not reach the trustlist cannot verify, which is unknown and not a failure — air-gapped is a declared deployment value, so that case is answered rather than assumed away. Still OPEN and unread: the rotation and revocation model, and whether a document-package signature can be expressed for a GDHCN-aware verifier at all. Two schemes with different properties remain to choose between, and the trustlist does not choose between them. A PACKAGE signature over the manifest verifies the SET — nothing added, removed or altered — and must be reissued whenever any file changes. A PER-ASSET signature verifies one file independently, which is what an edge cache serving one asset can actually check, and it cannot detect a removal because there is nothing left to verify. They compose; composing them is the safer and more expensive default, and it is the deployment's choice rather than the pipeline's. 2705.title: Glossary: BPMN activities, A–D
2705.content: Candidate terms extracted from every BPMN task and call activity: name as the label, its own <documentation> as the definition, the element id as the code. Each is the asset’s own text, verbatim and not curated, and carries the badge “candidate, extracted”. A person promotes one by authoring it. Authored terms are on their owning instance’s page, and those pages, the counts and the sources are linked from the glossary index. From: bootstrap 38 (SKOS) · bootstrap-tools 7 (SKOS) · cat-harness 616 (SKOS) · folio-assistant-core 244 (SKOS). One of 3 pages of this type, split by the first letter of the label: all parts. Size: this page holds 281 terms and is 231 KB before compression, fetched in one request, within its budget of 1.0 MB. There is no search index: the filter below runs over this page, and the A–Z bar jumps within it. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 902 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 902 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin. Per term. Every term on this page is unmapped on fhir, and unmapped on skos, unless its entry says otherwise. No entry says otherwise. Filter terms . 281 shown . 0–9 A B C D

2706.content: 1 · Declare in place (nothing moves) candidate, extracted A <name>.json entry with its graphs[] kinds. A sub-graph that owns its own layout gains a NESTED declaration whose paths resolve against its own directory, so the whole graph relocates by moving one folder. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/graph-detanglement.bpmn#Task_Declare . 1 · Declare it in place, with its seam candidate, extracted <name>/<name>.json with name, version, repository (the planned home), livesAt (where it sits today), needs, and only the directories that exist, each declared with its files in one commit. <name>/platform.ts from the first commit, so no climb out of the directory ever needs rerouting. Scaffolded by init-folio --staged <path>, which writes those two files and nothing at the host root; never --instance, which writes a whole repository. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn#Task_Declare . 1–3 · Declare, detangle, isolate candidate, extracted The graph-detanglement practice, all of its gates: declared in place, zero wrong-direction edges on every axis, and standing alone with its own declaration, namespace and artefact. A plain task on purpose, not a call to graph-detanglement.bpmn: that process ends in its own authorise-and-extract steps, which here are stages 9-13 of this one, and calling it would run them twice. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/kg-separation.bpmn#Task_Detangle . 10 · Re-point: livesAt, seam, mount or subscription candidate, extracted In the new repository livesAt goes (absent means it sits at the root of repository) and platform.ts points at where the platform now is. The host consumes it as a remote mount (a source.remote instance in its root index.config.json) if it imports its code, or a subscription if it only reads its content, pinned to a commit while staging. Additive: the host keeps its copy. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn#Task_Repoint . 10 · Seed both repositories candidate, extracted Seed main, then bring the content and the tools in as reviewed pull requests with their history, so neither repository's first commit is unreviewable. The seed includes every publisher the declaration promises (sub-kg-lifecycle stage 10): a qa directory with storage needs .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml, the caller of the tools layer's layer-qa-publish.yml, and test/results/ ignored. Without it the declared store is never written, and once the layer stops committing its results no reader finds them. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/kg-separation.bpmn#Task_Seed . 11 · Parent consumes, additively candidate, extracted The parent pins the pair (a commit while staging, a version once released) — a code dependency as a source.remote instance in its root index.config.json (remote-mount skill), never a submodule — repoints its imports, and keeps its own copy until it is green with the dependency declared. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/kg-separation.bpmn#Task_Consume . 11 · Verify on a fresh clone candidate, extracted bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <branch> (Tool sub-kg-verify-clone): clone into an empty scratch directory with submodules and any sibling it needs, install, and run its own gates. Green, red or unknown, and unknown is never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a missing module shows here. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn#Task_FreshClone . 12 · First release candidate, extracted Tag each repository, publish /v<major>/. From here the two are versioned independently; a tools release lists the content majors it supports. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/kg-separation.bpmn#Task_Release . 12 · Owner confirms: freeze the in-repo copy candidate, extracted The agent reports the files that would move, their size, the new repository and the commit the copy matches, then asks: (1) freeze it in the kept trashcan now, (2) keep in place until the first release, (3) show the file list first. Default if there is no answer: (2), nothing moves. A green fresh clone is the precondition for asking, not the answer. Non-relaxable. The host keeps a FROZEN copy in the kept trashcan, not a refreshed mirror and not a deletion; the live copy is the remote mount or subscription set up at stage 10. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn#Task_ConfirmCutover . 13 · Cutover: freeze the copy in the kept trashcan candidate, extracted Only on the owner's answer (1) at step 12. The in-repo directory moves, as one relocation, under separated/<name>/ in the kept trashcan, on its own branch (a plain mv, git rm --cached, state:push; the trashcan skill says how), with ONE note carrying movedFrom, movedOn, the new repository and the commit the copy matches. Frozen: never refreshed, never rendered; a reader wanting the live content follows the note to the new repository. On main this is one revertable commit removing the directory. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn#Task_Cutover . 13 · Cutover: retire the parent's copy candidate, extracted The one commit worth reverting, made only after the parent consumes the release and every identifier dereferences. It retires the parent's copy, frozen, never refreshed and never rendered, rather than deleting it. Where the copy goes is the sub-kg-lifecycle skill's stage 13; this diagram does not name that store, because the published graph must not. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/kg-separation.bpmn#Task_Cutover . 2 · Grow it in place candidate, extracted The content type's own authoring process runs here, against the staged instance. Many sub-KGs never leave; this task can last as long as the graph does. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn#Task_Grow . 2a · Measure — unassigned column FIRST candidate, extracted bun run cat check:partition. Read the unassigned column before the edge count, and quote BOTH numbers rather than only the one that improved. The edge count can rise when the measurement improves (previously unjudged edges are folded in); that is correct. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/graph-detanglement.bpmn#Task_Measure . 2b · Prune, merge, factor — or the classification is wrong candidate, extracted The only four moves. Move the shared TARGET first and the importers after; check the target's layer before the importer's; a schema moves with its script. The fix is never an exemption, it is the right owner. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/graph-detanglement.bpmn#Task_Move . 3 · Isolate — own declaration, namespace, artefact candidate, extracted Only once cross-edges measure zero: give the sub-graph its own declaration, its own namespace and its own published artefact, as bootstrap/ has (its own declaration, bs: namespace and graph document). Nothing moves yet; the sub-graph now stands alone in place. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/graph-detanglement.bpmn#Task_Isolate . 3 · Push generic down first candidate, extracted Move what is generic into the harness below before the seam is closed, and consolidate what the sub-KG needs into the harness it instantiates. Wrong-direction edges hide in declarations and data as well as imports: run check:import-direction, check:reference-direction and check:process-bindings. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/sub-kg-lifecycle.bpmn#Task_PushDown . 4 · Extract — a directory move, not a file-by-file sift candidate, extracted Only once edges are zero and the declaration stands alone: move the sub-graph out as one directory move, not a file-by-file sift. Its nested declaration resolves paths against its own directory, so moving the folder moves the graph. The five-point gate is in migration-plan.md Phase II. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/graph-detanglement.bpmn#Task_Extract . 4 · Identity: version, iriBase, nodeSchemas candidate, extracted The declaration carries name, version, iriBase, needs and nodeSchemas. A base move is bun run iri:sync -- --from <old base>, once; then iri:sync:check and check:node-iris are green. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/processes/kg/kg-separation.bpmn#Task_Identity . 4 · Route every climb through platform.ts candidate, extracted Every platform symbol the sub-KG uses is re-exported from <name>/platform.ts, so re-pointing the platform is a one-file edit. A merge from main is where new climbs arrive; reroute them here. Admit it to the train, record the train id candidate, extracted Writes the queue entry's trainId and placement (rule, class, rank) with who decided and when. A decision, so it is stored; the facts it was decided on are not. PRECONDITION, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the worktree carries no untracked, non-ignored file before the member is merged and the tree regenerated. git status --porcelain must be empty. The reason is specific: generated directory READMEs carry a per-subdirectory file count, and the writer counts the files GIT WOULD COMMIT -- git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard (bootstrap-tools/scripts/git-files.ts:23). --exclude-standard already keeps IGNORED junk out, which is the __pycache__ case that drove that line, but --others still counts an untracked file nobody has ignored. So a transient written by an earlier train step moves a committed count, readme:subgraphs:check goes red, and the red belongs to nobody. Train 6 hit this. The count is volatile for a second reason the precondition cannot fix: two members each adding a file write different integers to one line. Measured in bean y7b3 -- 76 of 300 replayed merges conflicted on beans/README.md, every one on the | defs/ | N files | line -- and the exposure is wider than that bean states: 54 generated READMEs across 14 instances carry 207 such rows (measured 2026-10-02). merge:main already resolves them (readme-generated-regions), so the cost falls on merges made by plain git. The chosen fix is bean ba9e: take the integer off main into the KG's _data layer, which classifies take-base and is therefore auto-resolved, leaving the README with a marker that is invariant until the directory crosses LIST_LIMIT. Not done here -- it spans the pinned bootstrap-tools submodule. BPMN activities of cat-harness · source cat-harness/sdlc/processes/merge-train.bpmn#Task_Admit . Agent pass on the changed rows candidate, extracted For each changed row, the agent pass of Contributor feedback on a working draft: Ready for agent = Yes gets its edit, Ready for merge = Yes its merge, and a Blue answer to a Decision needed question is taken up. Every new row (from an issue, a person or a TWG workbook), every row with an empty Feedback (agent) and every row whose Blue cells changed gets feedback in the same wake, in the fixed layout: the ask first (Decision needed: with lettered options, one recommended, and where to answer), then Proposed direction: and Next:, only the tags bold. The work stays inside the row's Selected Sections; a row with none gets a question asking which, and any edit outside them is named on an Outside the selected sections: line. PRs are named as repo#n, which the sheet script links, and it adds a Where to review line linking each selected section on the preview. The agent then runs tools/review-log-watch/lint.ts and fixes what it flags: a cell that breaks the layout, or a PR state that GitHub contradicts. The agent records its step on the Agent tab at once, with the real time. Previews follow main: by default (Config PREVIEW_REFRESH automatic) the agent runs tools/review-log-watch/previews.ts on every poll for every open change-set PR, and also when people act on a change set (new Blue feedback, Ready for agent set to Yes, or feedback asking to update the preview); with PREVIEW_REFRESH on-feedback, only then. Answer the other four gates candidate, extracted Restrictions, copyright, retention and source loss, each answered permitted, refused or unknown. What the licence permits for THIS bitstream, and separately whether it permits the derivation. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists in this repository and the ingestion pipeline does not read it. RETENTION.
