3049.title: IRIS, DSpace and Dublin Core
3049.content: Skill iris-dspace: How WHO IRIS uses DSpace and qualified Dublin Core — the three identifier systems, MeSH as a controlled vocabulary, bundles, and the containment path — and the requirements a tool reading a record must meet. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . Every claim here is read off one captured record: the DSpace full item record for wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng, transcribed at catalogue/records/wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng.dc.json. Nothing is asserted from general knowledge of DSpace. Where this file and the record disagree, the record wins. The type is folio-assistant-core/schemas/dublin-core.ts. It is generic: Dublin Core is ISO 15836 and DSpace is a platform. This file covers only what IRIS does with them.

3050.title: Scale
3050.content: From IRIS’s storage report (By Location → Entire Site) and home page, read 2026-09-20: . |   |   | source | . | items | 273,559 | the home page’s search placeholder | . | files | 1,057,223 | the storage report | . | storage | 361.55 GB | the storage report | . | top-level communities | 8 | the storage report | . Items and files are different denominators, so catalogue/catalogue.json carries them in separate fields, totalItemsUpstream and totalFilesUpstream. That is 3.86 files per item, because an item carries several bitstreams. totalBytesUpstream is derived: the report prints two decimals and no byte count, so the value is round(361.55 × 1024³), good to about ±5 MiB. It is GiB rather than GB because every per-community figure the report prints (238.58, 19.72, 34.84, 26.14, 25.71) reproduces exactly at 2³⁰ and none does at 10⁹.

3051.title: Three identifier systems
3051.content: The worked item carries all three: . | system | value | authoritative? | . | DSpace UUID | 18892cf3-5a4f-42a4-923c-a93f4a594dec | no — IRIS’s own, stable only while this DSpace instance is | . | Handle | 10665/332098 | yes — guaranteed by the Handle System, outside WHO | . | WHO govdoc | WPR/RDO/2020/003 | no — WHO’s publication number | . The library slug wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng is derived from the govdoc, the weakest key. A tool that resolves by Handle survives the source moving. A legacy handle is live in the record, and must not be deduplicated . dc.identifier.uri appears twice: . https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/332098 ← global http://iris.wpro.who.int/handle/10665.1/14518 ← regional, merged away . Regional IRIS instances were folded into the global one and both URIs were kept. The second is a real alternate identifier, and evidence that a source host can disappear (the sourceLoss gate’s worked example).

3052.title: Qualified, repeated, language-tagged
3052.content: Every field is element.qualifier. Four fields repeat in this one record (dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available, dc.identifier.uri, dc.subject.mesh), so Record<string, string> silently keeps the last value and drops the rest. There is a per-field language column, present on dc.title, dc.description and each dc.subject.mesh, absent on the author, the dates and the identifiers. An absent tag is not en: it is a value whose language nobody asserted.

3053.title: MeSH is a controlled vocabulary, not a keyword
3053.content: dc.subject.mesh = Publishing, Guidelines as Topic. These are NLM Medical Subject Headings, with their own identifiers and hierarchy at https://id.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/. A MeSH term can be resolved and subsumed (searching “Guidelines as Topic” should reach narrower terms); a free-text keyword can do neither. DcValue.authority records the distinction per value.

3054.title: An item is not a file: bundles
3054.content: DSpace groups bitstreams into bundles — conventionally ORIGINAL, plus TEXT (extracted), THUMBNAIL and LICENSE. Size and format are per-bitstream: the 2.68 MB in the record is the PDF’s, not the item’s. Bundles are why there are more files than items.

3055.title: Containment is a path, not a parent
3055.content: The breadcrumb: Home → 7. Regional Office for the … → Regional Office for the W… → Information products — four levels, two of them communities and one a collection. DSpace also lets an item be mapped into several collections, so “the” parent of a node does not exist. CatalogueNode.parents is a list of paths.

3056.title: What a later tool needs — as requirements
3056.content: | # | requirement | why, in one line | . | R1 | Resolve by Handle where one exists; treat UUID and govdoc as secondary | only the Handle is guaranteed outside WHO | . | R2 | Never deduplicate dc.identifier.uri | the second one is evidence of a host that vanished | . | R3 | Preserve repetition on every field, not a known list | four fields repeat in a single record; assume more do | . | R4 | Treat an absent language as unasserted, never as en | both states occur in one record | . | R5 | Carry dc.subject.mesh as a controlled value with its authority | it can be resolved and subsumed; a keyword cannot | . | R6 | Model bitstreams per bundle, with size and format on the bitstream | an item is not a file | . | R7 | Model containment as a list of paths | four levels deep, and multiple mappings are legal | . | R8 | Never infer metadata from the PDF when a record exists | OCR off a title page catalogued the WHO Editorial Style Manual as Abies | . | R9 | Record what the source says even when it contradicts the file | dc.description says 30 p.; the PDF has 33 | . | R10 | An item with no known collection carries parents: [] — never a guessed one | held-and-unplaceable is a STATE; inventing containment is unfalsifiable | . | R11 | Key a node by path when its UUID is not in the capture | an invented UUID resolves to nothing while looking authoritative | . | R12 | Keep the page captured and the identifier apart | /items/<uuid>/full is what was fetched; the Handle is what the item IS | . | R13 | A materialized claim must name bytes that EXIST, and something must check it | an unchecked claim can name no bytes and still pass as held | . | R14 | Read a storage figure in the units that round-trip its own bytes | IRIS prints “GB” for what its byte counts make GiB — a 7% error | . | R15 | Never fall back to a parent URL when an item has no upstream URI | “no upstream URI recorded” is the answer; the front page is a lie that resolves | . | R16 | A partial transcription must SAY it is partial | a truncated abstract that does not declare itself cannot be told from a short one | . | R17 | Hold what you hold: model the bitstreams whose bytes are here | the handbook lists 8 upstream; this repository has 1 | . | R18 | Do not “correct” a record that looks wrong | the English-titled editorial manual really does carry an Italian ISBN | . | R19 | A derived figure must round-trip the figure it was derived from | round(361.55 × 1024³) bytes must render back as 361.55 GiB | . | R20 | An item count and a file count are different denominators | 273,559 against 1,057,223 — a fraction built from the wrong one is off by 3.86× | . | R21 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (Upstream Skolemization) | minting https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx} at extraction leaves no blank nodes for a later pass to resolve | . | R22 | Append-only streaming partition writes | A 300,000 item corpus cannot accumulate uncompressed in working memory; write quads directly to partition file streams | . R8: where a library entry’s title comes from . who-pub-tps-931 shows why. Its structure.json carries title: "Abies" and authors_raw: "Cpe N" — OCR noise off a scanned title page of the WHO Editorial Style Manual. 9789241548960-eng has three renderings of one title from the PDF (Handbook forGuideline Development 2nd edition from joined title lines, GRC Handbook - second edition from PDF docinfo, and the real one) and no authority among them. The IRIS record settles both. A library entry’s title is taken, in order, from: . | the catalogue record: dc.title of the Dublin Core record that the catalogue node naming the entry (libraryId) points at through metadataRef; | referenced.json identity.title; | the PDF Info /Title (structure.json metadata.docinfo.Title), only when it is not junk such as Microsoft Word - …, a file name, untitled, or an arXiv stamp; | the slug, which check:library-qa then reports as title-missing. | . The page-1 front-matter parse is never a title. It may still feed search and the section files’ doc_title. The manifest records which source won as meta.title_source (for example dc-record) and where it came from as meta.title_from, so R8 can be checked. The resolver is cat-harness-tools/pipeline/library-title.ts; the library-ingestion skill carries the full rule.

3057.title: Covers: an artefact we made, filed where IRIS files its own
3057.content: The replica’s home page shows a cover beside each item in its Recent Submissions strip, and each library entry page shows it too. None of them came from IRIS. Each is page 1 of the item’s PDF, rasterised by cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-cover.py and filed as a THUMBNAIL-bundle bitstream — the bundle name DSpace uses for the thumbnails it generates. Nothing downstream can tell the two apart from the bundle name, so the bitstream’s materialization.note must say the cover was derived here. The PDF is either held in this repository or, for a referenced item, fetched by the iris-cover-pdfs GitHub workflow, matched against the sha256 its ORIGINAL bitstream records, rendered and discarded. Only the cover PNG is committed. folio-assistant-core/scripts/gen-covers.ts (bun run iris:covers) renders only covers the catalogue asks for: a node declares the THUMBNAIL bitstream and the script supplies the bytes. It refuses to write bytes for a THUMBNAIL whose materialization.note does not declare the derivation, since a tool cannot attest to its own output. bun run iris:covers:check compares the bytes, the recorded sha256 and the recorded pixel dimensions, re-rendering where the PDF is held. That is R13 for covers. A cover whose PDF is not held can be verified but not re-rendered. The WHO emblem is masked on covers . The site chrome carries no WHO mark until the replica is published under WHO. Covers are shown with the WHO emblem and wordmark blanked to flat grey before the PNG is written, so the committed bytes never contain it. Each THUMBNAIL bitstream declares the blanked rectangles and the reason as maskedRegions. A title that contains “WHO” is not masked: it is the work’s name. A cover whose publication gates block it is shown as cover withheld, not no cover.

3058.title: Getting a record
3058.content: DSpace 7 exposes /server/api/discover/search/objects, paged and filterable by dsoType, scope and facets; communities are listed at /community-list. The calls this repository makes, and what live IRIS accepts, are in iris-rest-feed; the code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts. A record derived from a PDF rather than transcribed from IRIS must be marked derived, so it can be replaced wholesale when the real record arrives with nothing downstream having believed it. Enumeration cost, subsetting and the characterisation that decides whether IRIS may be cited at all are in who-iris/sources/who-iris.json.

3060.title: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
3060.content: Skill iris-oxigraph: How to build WHO IRIS catalogue and Qualified Dublin Core metadata into partitioned N-Quads, and query it with Oxigraph — in Bun on the build side, in WebAssembly in the browser — including cross-graph joins and facet counts. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . The IRIS catalogue and its Dublin Core records are compiled into named graphs and queried with Oxigraph: natively in Bun at build time, and as WebAssembly in a browser. One SPARQL query can then join Dublin Core properties, catalogue containment and bitstream access gates — which DSpace Discovery cannot do in a single call.

3061.title: Build and query
3061.content: # Build from catalogue/nodes and site/dublin-core into dist/oxigraph/ bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts # Build from exported DSpace records (the CDN release's records/ tree) bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts --records <dir> --out <dir> # Load dist/oxigraph/who-iris-dataset.nq and run sample searches and facets bun run scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts bun test scripts/tests/iris-oxigraph.test.ts . scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts exports IrisOxigraphEngine (loadSpine, loadCommunity, searchSpine, complexSearch, facetCounts). The CDN exporter (scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts) calls the build over exported records and publishes each output file as graph/<file>.

3062.title: 1. Graphs and files
3062.content: The build writes, sorted and de-duplicated so unchanged inputs give byte-identical files: . | Tier 1, the spine — <https://iris.who.int/graph/spine>, in who-iris-spine.nq and .nq.gz. Hierarchy (dspace:Community, dspace:Collection), item Handles, titles, first creator, issued date, and bitstream descriptors with copyright verdicts. Loaded first. | Tier 2, one partition per community — <https://iris.who.int/graph/community/{id}>, in iris_who_int_graph_community_{id}.nq and .nq.gz. The full Dublin Core of that community’s items: MeSH authorities, abstracts, spatial coverage, govdoc numbers, ISBNs. Mounted on demand. | Catalogue and metadata graphs — <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> and <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata>, each in its own iris_who_int_graph_{catalogue,metadata}.nq(.gz), and merged in who-iris-dataset.nq and .nq.gz for server-side use and integrity checks. | subgraph-manifest.json — the spine and each community partition, with file names, quad counts and item counts. | queries.json — prepared SPARQL queries. | . Namespaces . | dspace: = https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace# — catalogue terms (Item, inCommunity, hasBitstream, fileName, …). | dspaceNs: = https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/ — Dublin Core value terms, including authority. | . No binary bytes in the graph . PDFs, cover images and archives are never stored as literals. A bitstream node carries only: . | dspace:fileName (e.g. "WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf") | dspace:mediaType (e.g. "application/pdf") | dspace:fileBytes (integer) | dspace:copyrightGate — the copyright gate’s verdict, e.g. "permitted" | . The bytes are fetched from the CDN.

3063.title: 2. Requirements
3063.content: | # | Requirement | Why, in one line | . | OX-1 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx}); the build fails if any blank node remains | no multi-document collisions, every node addressable, no normalizer pass | . | OX-2 | Store zero binary bytes in RDF | keeps WASM memory small; binaries are static files on the CDN | . | OX-3 | Join across named graphs with explicit GRAPH blocks | separates containment and rights from bibliographic description | . | OX-4 | Use Handle URIs as the item subject (https://hdl.handle.net/...) | identity resolves outside WHO’s servers | . | OX-5 | Treat bitstream rights as access gates | results can be filtered by whether the PDF may be downloaded | . | OX-6 | Partition by community | a client fetches only the slice it needs | . | OX-7 | Never scan whole-corpus text in SPARQL | full text belongs in a static inverted index | . | OX-8 | Preserve controlled-vocabulary authorities (dspaceNs:authority) | distinguishes MeSH headings from free keywords | . | OX-9 | Append-only streaming partition emission | bounded memory at 300,000 items. Not met yet: buildIrisDataset holds and sorts every quad in memory; StreamingPartitionWriter is defined but unused | .

3064.title: 3. SPARQL recipes
3064.content: Recipe 1: multi-condition search . Items in the Western Pacific community, issued in or after 2000, with a subject containing “guidelines”, and a PDF whose copyright verdict is permitted. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX dspace: <https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace#> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> SELECT DISTINCT ?handle ?title ?creator ?issued ?pdfName WHERE { # 1. Join Dublin Core Metadata GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:title ?title ; dcterms:creator ?crNode ; dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?crNode rdf:value ?creator . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?handle dcterms:issued ?issued } } # 2. Join Catalogue Hierarchy & Access Gates GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> { ?handle dspace:inCommunity ?comm ; dspace:hasBitstream ?bs . ?comm rdfs:label ?commLabel . ?bs dspace:mediaType "application/pdf" ; dspace:fileName ?pdfName ; dspace:copyrightGate "permitted" . } # 3. Multi-Field Filter Evaluation BIND(IF(BOUND(?issued), xsd:integer(SUBSTR(STR(?issued), 1, 4)), 0) AS ?year) FILTER ( CONTAINS(LCASE(?subject), "guidelines") && CONTAINS(LCASE(?commLabel), "western pacific") && (?year >= 2000) ) } ORDER BY DESC(?year) . Recipe 2: facet counts . Item counts per subject term and its authority. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX dspaceNs: <https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/> SELECT ?subject (COUNT(DISTINCT ?handle) AS ?itemCount) ?authority WHERE { GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?sNode dspaceNs:authority ?authority } } } GROUP BY ?subject ?authority ORDER BY DESC(?itemCount) ?subject .

3065.title: 4. Browser pattern: spine first, communities on demand
3065.content: import oxigraph from 'oxigraph'; // Where the graph files are served from, e.g. a release's graph/ directory. const BASE = '<graph-base-url>'; async function gunzipText(resp: Response): Promise<string> { const stream = resp.body!.pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream('gzip')); return new Response(stream).text(); } const store = new oxigraph.Store(); // 1. Fetch the spine and the manifest const [spineResp, manifestResp] = await Promise.all([ fetch(`${BASE}/who-iris-spine.nq.gz`), fetch(`${BASE}/subgraph-manifest.json`), ]); const manifest = await manifestResp.json(); // 2. Load the spine: hierarchy, title search and rights filtering work now store.load(await gunzipText(spineResp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); // 3. Mount a community when the user selects it. load() adds its named // graph without clobbering what is already in the store. async function mountCommunity(commId: string) { const partition = manifest.tiers.tier2_communities.partitions[commId]; if (!partition) return; const resp = await fetch(`${BASE}/${partition.fileGz}`); store.load(await gunzipText(resp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); } // 4. Run a prepared query locally for (const binding of store.query(myPreparedQuery)) { console.log(binding.get('title').value); } .

3067.title: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
3067.content: Skill iris-rest-feed: How to read changes from the WHO IRIS DSpace 7 REST API: the nightly “changed since” walk over Discovery, the weekly reconciliation that stands in for the deletions REST does not report, and the guard that stops a short listing from reading as a mass withdrawal. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . Changes are read from the DSpace REST API only. REST has no change feed with deletions, so a nightly walk is paired with a weekly reconciliation. The code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts; its tests run on fixtures in scripts/tests/iris-cdn.test.ts.

3068.title: What live IRIS accepts
3068.content: . | Discovery offers only five sortOptions: score, dc.title, dc.date.issued, dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available. sort=lastModified,DESC returns HTTP 422. | Changes are found with a Solr range query instead: query=lastModified:[<isoZ> TO *]. | The bound must be a Z-suffixed UTC timestamp. A +00:00 offset returns totalElements: 0. | .

3069.title: Endpoints
3069.content: | Use | Request | . | Changed items since cursor | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&query=lastModified:[{isoZ} TO *]&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Weekly full item listing | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Collection-scoped batch (initial load) | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&scope={collectionUuid}&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Communities / collections with parent | GET /server/api/core/{communities|collections}?page=N&size=100&embed=parentCommunity | . | One item with its files and collection | GET /server/api/core/items/{uuid}?embed=bundles/bitstreams&embed=owningCollection | . | Bundle bitstreams beyond page 0 | GET /server/api/core/bundles/{bundleUuid}/bitstreams?page=N&size=100 | . | A file’s bytes | GET /server/api/core/bitstreams/{uuid}/content | .

3070.title: Nightly: changedSince(cursor)
3070.content: . | Normalise cursor to UTC Z (new Date(Date.parse(cursor)).toISOString()) and run the range query above. | Page through the matching result set. | The cursor is inclusive: an item modified at that instant is read again, not missed. Re-reading an unchanged item writes the same bytes. | Return the items oldest first, de-duplicated by UUID. | . The cursor is the newest lastModified read, kept in state/cursor.json. A failed night does not advance it.

3071.title: Metadata changes without the PDF changing
3071.content: A PDF may stay the same while its Dublin Core changes. Records and files are handled separately: . | A record is re-read whenever its item appears in the walk. A PDF is re-fetched only if its DSpace MD5 changed. | Communities and collections are re-read in full every night (allContainers). A renamed collection changes no item, and DSpace 7 does not expose lastModified for these. An unchanged one serializes to the same bytes. | The weekly metadata check. The weekly listing pages carry each item’s metadata. metadataSha hashes it canonically, and any item whose hash differs from the one last ingested is re-read. That catches edits that did not move lastModified, without one fetch per item. | .

3072.title: Weekly: allItems and withdrawnOrHidden
3072.content: . | List every item ID Discovery returns. | Compare that list with the IDs the library holds. | Guard. If more than 1% of held items are missing, the listing is treated as faulty and nothing is marked. Possible causes are a paging fault, an outage or a Solr reindex. | Re-fetch each missing item by ID. Mark it withdrawn only if IRIS confirms it: withdrawn: true, or a 404 (gone), 401 or 403 (private). | .

3073.title: Fixity
3073.content: DSpace reports an MD5 checkSum for each bitstream. Downloaded bytes must match it before their SHA-256 is recorded. A mismatch quarantines the bitstream and reports it. It is never retried silently.

3074.title: Politeness
3074.content: Requests are made one at a time, with a User-Agent that names the project and its repository, and back off on 429 and 503. The initial load is paced to the budget stated in Task_StateBudget (processes/iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn), including maxRequestsPerSecond.

3075.title: A subset by reference: run.ts subset
3075.content: bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset catalogues part of IRIS without fetching any bytes (who-iris#207): for each item, the Dublin Core record as DSpace returns it and a referenced catalogue node whose ORIGINAL bitstreams link to https://iris.who.int/bitstreams/{uuid}/download. The subsets it reads live in scripts/iris-cdn/subsets/. | Which items. A handles file goes first (for example the IRIS items a DAK cites), then a Discovery query. The query is a field query on metadata (dc.title, dc.subject, dc.subject.mesh, dc.description.abstract), not a bare keyword. A bare keyword also searches the PDF text, so vaccine matches a report that mentions one in passing. | Write boolean operators in capitals. Solr reads a lowercase or as a word: HIV or immunization or vaccine matches fewer items than vaccine alone. | A Handle to an item: GET /server/api/pid/find?id=hdl:{handle} answers 302 to /server/api/core/items/{uuid}. | An ISBN or govdoc to an item: query=dc.identifier.isbn:"{isbn13}" or query=dc.identifier.govdoc:"WHO/HIV/2017.09". | A sample is one-row pages at seeded random offsets, so the same seed gives the same items. | No fixity is claimed. IRIS reports an MD5. A sha256 is recorded only once the bytes are fetched (R13), so the MD5 goes in the bitstream’s note. | Hand-made nodes win. An item whose Handle or UUID another node already carries is skipped and reported. The tool rewrites only its own nodes, the ones whose note starts “Catalogued by reference by scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset”, and only when they changed. | A token, when IRIS gives one, comes from the IRIS_DSPACE_TOKEN environment variable as Authorization: Bearer …. It never appears in an argument, a file or a log. | .

3077.title: Working an issue — announce, then re-check
3077.content: Skill issue-working: Working a tracked issue — announce the branch when you create it rather than when you finish, and re-check the issue for new AND edited comments while you work. Both rules are about the gap between your view of an issue and everyone else’s. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Two rules. Both exist because your view of an issue and everyone else’s diverge the moment you start, and neither side can see that it has happened.

3078.title: Announce the branch when you create it, not when you finish
3078.content: Comment on the issue with the branch name, the process and phase, and the work items claimed — at creation. Before it, run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”. A summary posted after the work lands is not a substitute. Until the first comment appears, a sibling session and a human both see an issue with nobody visibly on it, which is precisely the state the work plan exists to prevent and the one no sibling can detect. Announce once, on the single edge into implementation. A process that loops back into implement re-enters on the same branch, and re-announcing each time is noise that trains the reader to skip the announcements that matter.

3079.title: Re-check the issue while you work
3079.content: Checking once at session start is not checking. Requirements change while you are heads-down, and the comment that changes direction is the one you are least likely to see. Track what you have already read as two marks, not one: . | a comment-id high-water mark, and | the newest edit timestamp — because an edited comment keeps its id, and an edited requirement is a changed requirement. A high-water mark alone cannot see an edit at all. | . With no stored mark, everything counts as unseen. A fresh container has read nothing, and defaulting the other way is exactly how the comments that change direction get skipped — silently, because nothing distinguishes read from never looked.

3080.title: When the new material is a large chunk of work, stop
3080.content: Do not fold it into the current run. Say that this is a good stopping point for review, link the artefact, and confirm priorities before continuing. Absorbing it buries a scope change inside a diff nobody asked for, and spends the author’s next review on work they have not agreed to. A large new ask is a decision to hand back, under the usual discipline — context, options with their costs, a marked recommendation, then the question.

3081.title: What an issue is for, against its neighbours
3081.content: They are not synonymous, and conflating them is how an agent closes something it had no standing to close: . |   | what it carries | . | issue | stakeholder sign-off | . | change proposal | code review | . | work item | work-plan tracking | . Never close an issue without explicit authorisation from the analyst or stakeholder. Whether work is done is a judgement, and an agent must never assume completion on its own say-so — the same rule that stops you closing a work item a sibling is mid-flight on. That authorisation may be given in advance: an issue-close waiver, which names the issues it covers and expires. It is the stakeholder answering the same question earlier, which is the whole of what this rule asks for — never the agent supplying the judgement itself. confirmation-waiver.md. After each round of implementation, post a summary on the issue, not only on the change proposal: what was accomplished, what remains, and links to the updated content for review.

3082.title: Milestones and decision points go on the issue, as they happen
3082.content: A round can be long, and the owner follows the issue, not the session or the PR. So between round summaries, post on the issue at two kinds of moment: . | A milestone — a result the owner would want to know before the round ends: a method lands, a benchmark number moves, a tool turns out not to run here, an approach is replaced because measurement reversed it. | A decision point — whenever you put a choice to the owner in the chat, put it on the issue too, in the same shape: context, options with their cost, the marked recommendation, and what happens if nobody answers (interaction-modality). A choice made only in the chat leaves no record where the next reader looks. | . Not every push: a push is reported on the PR. An issue update is for what a stakeholder would act on. Each update must be readable on its own, because it is read days later without the session: status, approach in a line, findings with their numbers and provenance, what landed, and next steps — and a link to the previous update rather than a restatement of it.

3083.title: A sign-off on the issue becomes a record
3083.content: When a requirements document is signed off on its issue — approved, amended, rejected, deferred or cancelled — the comment is the evidence, not the record. The record is a requirement-signoff attestation in the attestations graph (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set>.attestations.json): who (kind, id, actor), at, scope, outcome, the stage it moves the requirement set to, the reason, and evidence — the comment’s permalink, …/issues/<n>#issuecomment-<id>. A sign-off given in chat is quoted on the issue first, dated, so the evidence link exists. The agent writes the record of a person’s decision; it never writes one for a decision nobody made, and check:requirements refuses approved or accepted without a human one.

3084.title: Before you publish that something does not exist (STRICT)
3084.content: An issue comment is published, and a false claim in one costs more than a missing true one: it sends the next reader off to verify an accusation, and the correction never reaches everybody the original did. So before an issue comment, PR body or commit message asserts that a file, a function or somebody’s cited precedent does not exist, re-read it from the remote — git show origin/main:<path> — in a command of its own, and check the open branches when the claim is nobody has built this. Grepping your checkout answers “is this in my base”, not “does this exist”, and a git fetch earlier in the same compound command is not a barrier when siblings merge every few minutes. bean-coordination §”Re-derive from the REMOTE” has the two guards. For the third case, a path that exists only on an open PR’s head, ask the open-work-lookup Tool.

3085.title: When the work has a BEAN and no issue (STRICT)
3085.content: A round summary is owed either way. With no issue, it goes on the change proposal AND into the work item — the work item is the durable artefact a sibling reads, and a summary that exists only in a PR thread is invisible to the work plan on main. And a work item that has an issue carries the link BOTH ways: a reader arriving at either object has to be able to reach the other, and a check reports the ones that cannot. When to open an issue at all is crdm-detect §”Issue association” — scan before creating one, and never create one without permission. This section is about what is owed once the work exists, not about manufacturing an issue for every work item.

3092.title: Knowledge graph affordances — browse, materialise, instantiate, copy-into-folio
3092.content: Skill kg-affordances: The four affordances of a conformant knowledge graph — browse, materialise, instantiate and copy-into-folio — which capabilities each requires, how each writing verb degrades cleanly when no write capability is available, and how copying an asset stamps KgAsset.source provenance. Named by: Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Execute Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . A person or an agent arriving at any conformant instance has four verbs available on what they find: . | browse — explore the graph, its subgraphs, its skills, its processes, its schemas and its assets without mutating anything. | materialise — pull a remote harness closure or a subscribed subgraph onto local disk at a pinned commit or recorded digest. | instantiate — scaffold a new folio or harnessed repository from the harness so it can author and publish its own graphs. | copy-into-folio — take a node or asset from a knowledge graph into your own folio (assets[] or folio/), stamp KgAsset.source provenance, and edit, comment or raise todos on your copy. | .

3093.title: The four verbs and their capability floor
3093.content: Three of the four verbs write, and an agent in a read-only container, a viewer on a static site, or a session without repository credentials cannot perform a write. Each verb therefore declares its capability requirement up front and degrades cleanly rather than failing halfway through a procedure. | verb | write capability required | process | governing skills | Tools | read-only degradation | . | browse | none (git-read or published HTTP/files only) | — (stateless read) | kg-navigation, directory-conventions | skill-list, skill-fetch, search-graph, get-neighbors, kg-graph-export | none needed — browse is the read-only floor and must remain completely useful with zero write capabilities | . | materialise | one of git-push, github-api, github-connector (to persist lock/record changes; local worktree write for --staging) | mount-dependency.bpmn, materialize-remote.bpmn | remote-mount, materialize-remote, kg-subscription | remote-mount (mount:remote), mount-from-lock, kg-retrieve-npm | run bun run cat mount:remote --plan or mount:remote:check to inspect the resolved closure and digests without writing | . | instantiate | one of git-push, github-api, github-connector | getting-started.bpmn, repo-conversion.bpmn | folio-init, getting-started, repo-conversion | folio-init (folio_init / bun run cat init-folio) | run folio-init with --dry-run (dry_run: true) to emit the full manifest and file plan as Markdown without touching disk or remote refs | . | copy-into-folio | one of git-push, github-api, github-connector | copy-into-folio.bpmn (for KG assets); copy-out-materialized.bpmn (for materialized library items) | kg-affordances, copy-out-materialized, directory-conventions | declaration-resolution (check:declared-assets), witness-conformance | inspect the upstream asset in place via browse, and emit the target KgAsset declaration snippet (with source pre-filled) so the user can apply it where they have write access | .

3094.title: Why browse requires zero write capability
3094.content: browse is the read-only floor of every conformant knowledge graph: . | On a published site (gh-pages or a CDN), browse reads the exported JSON-LD graph (kg.jsonld), the per-subgraph visualisers, and the rendered BPMN/DMN surfaces over plain HTTP. | In a checkout with an MCP server attached, browse uses skill-list, skill-fetch, search-graph and get-neighbors. | In a bare filesystem checkout with no server and no network, browse reads <name>.json at the instance root, resolves directories[] and assets[], and reads the files directly (kg-navigation). | . No step of browse may require git-push, github-api or github-connector. If a browse tool or visualiser refuses to run because write credentials are absent, that is a defect in the tool.

3095.title: Checking write capability before a writing verb
3095.content: Before starting materialise, instantiate or copy-into-folio, determine which write capability the current environment holds (scenarios/capabilities/): . | git-push — a working tree with push access to the target repository’s remote (git push --dry-run succeeds). | github-api — a GH_TOKEN / GITHUB_TOKEN or gh auth status capable of creating commits, branches or pull requests via the GitHub API. | github-connector — an MCP GitHub connector (push_files, create_or_update_file, create_pull_request) attached to the session. | . The three states of the capability check are kept distinct: . | Available (git-push, github-api, or github-connector present): proceed with the writing verb using the corresponding tool path. | Absent (probed and none of the three is present): take the read-only degradation branch (--plan, --dry-run, or in-place inspection plus an exportable snippet). Never silently drop the provenance or leave a half-written tree. | Could not determine (the probe itself failed for an environmental reason, such as an unreachable host): report could-not-determine with the probe error; do not report the capability as absent and do not attempt a blind write. | .

3096.title: copy-into-folio and KgAsset.source provenance
3096.content: When a folio owner or authoring agent copies an asset from an upstream knowledge graph into their own folio to adapt it, comment on it or raise todos against it, the process is copy-into-folio.bpmn. Like copy-out-materialized, copying a knowledge-graph asset into a folio is two writes and a refusal: . | Never touch the source graph. The upstream instance is read-only from the copier’s point of view; the arrow runs out of the source lane and never back. | Copy the bytes and declare the asset in the target folio’s <name>.json assets[]. A file copied into an undeclared scratch path is invisible to check:declared-assets and to the folio’s visualisers. | Stamp KgAsset.source (AssetSourceSchema in schemas/kg/kg-node.ts) on the target folio’s KgAsset entry: | . { "id": "adapted-guideline-table", "src": "assets/adapted-guideline-table.json", "role": "guideline-table", "source": { "instance": "litlfred/example-ig", "path": "assets/guideline-table.json", "ref": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567" } } . The three states of KgAsset.source . KgAsset.source ({ instance, path, ref? }) is how the graph tells a copy from original work: . | source state | meaning | . | present, and ref matches upstream | copied from instance at path and current with that upstream commit | . | present, and ref differs or is omitted | copied from instance at path, either adapted locally since ref or taken without a commit pin (staleness is checkable only when ref is recorded) | . | absent (undefined) | authored in this instance — a third state, never “copied from an unknown place” | . A copied asset MUST carry source: without it the copy is indistinguishable from locally authored work, and nothing downstream can reconstruct which instance it came from. Working on the copy in the target folio . Once the asset is declared in the target folio with KgAsset.source stamped and verified by bun run cat check:declaration-resolution (check:declared-assets), it is ordinary writable content of the target folio. The folio owner can edit it in place, attach review comments, or raise todos (todo-manager) against it without disturbing the upstream knowledge graph.

3098.title: Offering the knowledge graph
3098.content: Skill kg-contribution-offer: Ask whether agreed requirements should become knowledge-graph content, and as what — in a form the person can answer by selecting. Use at the end of CRDM sign-off, or whenever a body of agreed work could become a skill, a process, a schema or a work item and nobody has been asked. Offers “none” as a first-class answer. Named by: CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off . When a person is done with requirements on some workflow, ask whether and how to add them to the knowledge graph, and give options. CRDM sign-off is the usual moment: without this step, agreed requirements exist only as an issue and a conversation, and no later agent finds them.

3099.title: What this skill is NOT
3099.content: It is not a decision procedure for where a node goes. That is placement, and it is an agent’s procedure: which instance, which declared graph, which kind of node, which stub convention. Run it after this skill has an answer, not instead of it. It is not general guidance on asking questions. That is interaction-modality §4.1, and this skill does not restate it — it obeys it, and supplies what the options are here. It is not what to do when the author CORRECTS a rule. That is symbiotic-interaction §2, and it runs the other way: the node already exists, the author has just said it is wrong, and the correction is written into it in the same turn without an offer, because offering there asks the author to repeat a correction already made. The line between the two is one question: does the rule already have a home? A ruling on something already in the graph is an edit and needs no offer; a ruling that implies a node which does not exist is this skill’s case, unless the author named the destination themselves. The division in one line: . This skill decides what to offer. symbiotic-interaction §2 decides what needs no offering. placement decides where the answer lands. interaction-modality decides the shape of the asking.

3100.title: The rule
3100.content: The agent never picks a destination silently. An agent that decides on its own that a requirement “is really a skill” and writes one has made a node nobody asked for, in a graph somebody else maintains. If the person does not answer, the default applies — and the default creates nothing.

3101.title: One question, not two
3101.content: “Should this enter the knowledge graph at all” and “as what” are asked as one question: destinations as options, none among them, and a stated default. Two rounds cost a low-dexterity person a real interaction; listing none keeps the single question from forcing an answer.

3102.title: One question for the SET, not one per requirement
3102.content: A CRDM run can agree many requirements. Asking once per requirement is redundant entry (WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.7), so the offer names the set and asks once. If the person wants different destinations for different items, they say so and the agent asks follow-ups about the ones that differ. That path is opened by their answer, never assumed.

3103.title: The options are DERIVED, never invented
3103.content: The destinations are the graphs this instance declares, in <name>.json — read at the time of asking, never a list typed from memory. Not every declared graph is an authorable destination. A store that is incoming (uploads), derived (qa, health, translation-sources) or a record of something that already happened (issue-marks, memory) is not somewhere a requirement is authored into. Offer the graphs whose nodes a person writes: . | offer | because | . | a skill (cat-harness) | the requirement is a rule an agent must follow | . | a BPMN process (cat-harness) | it is a sequence with lanes and gateways | . | a schema (schemas) | it constrains the shape of data | . | a Tool (tools) | it is a capability with declared io | . | documentation (docs) | it is a design-memory asset — see below | . | a work item (beans) | it is work to be done, not knowledge to be kept | . | an fsh-guts proposal | it is a design not yet agreed — and see the warning below | . | folio content (folio) | it is subject matter, not platform | . | none | it is already captured by the issue and the code | .

3104.title: The design-memory asset, and the question that identifies one
3104.content: A design record — an asset produced while building a feature, accessing data, or managing or rendering a type of content, but not the content to be displayed — goes into docs/. One question separates this class from every other destination: . Was this produced while BUILDING something, rather than being the thing that was built? . A requirement set, an options analysis, a measured comparison, the reasoning behind a schema: each is an artefact of the work rather than its output. It is not subject matter, so it is not folio. It is not a rule an agent follows, so it is not a skill (a skill is read by an agent about to act; a design record by a person asking why is it like this). It is not work outstanding, so it is not a work item. It is memory, and docs/ is where an instance keeps memory a person reads. Not fsh-guts . fsh-guts is the declared non-rendered trashcan, whose content may be thrown away or lost. A proposal not yet agreed can afford to be lost; the reasoning behind something already built cannot. WHOSE docs/ — the owning instance’s, not the repository’s . docs/ is not one place. It is a declared graph, and the instance that owns a harness, feature or tool owns its detailed information, design and planning. Ask placement Step 1’s question: which instance owns this? A design record for a cat-harness feature files in cat-harness/docs/; one for a folio’s own subject matter does not belong in the platform at all. What else belongs there, and the line against a skill . Besides the design record, docs/ holds: . | how to reach the data a piece of content describes — endpoints, credentials policy, shapes, quirks of a source; | everything past the competence line, which is the sharp test: | . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, and an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls are documentation. Conversely, a rule an agent must follow, filed in docs/, is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Where in that instance’s docs/ is placement’s question, not this one. none is a real answer: a requirement whose whole content is “the button should be blue” becomes a commit and nothing else.

3105.title: What the agent does with the answer
3105.content: . | Run placement for the chosen kind — it decides instance, graph and node kind, and catches a hardcoded path or a literal naming one folio. | Create a work item for the authoring work, parented to the feature’s epic. The offer produces a decision, not a node; writing it is work, and work is a work item before it is a file. | Record the answer where the next agent will see it — on the issue, with the round summary issue-working already requires. | . On none, record that too (“asked, answered none, because the requirement is carried by the code”): otherwise it is indistinguishable from never having asked.

3106.title: Related
3106.content: |   |   | . | the shape of the asking | interaction-modality §4.1 | . | a correction to a rule that already exists — no offer | symbiotic-interaction §2 | . | where the answer lands | placement | . | the process step | crdm-signoff.bpmn | . | the round summary that records it | issue-working | . | why work becomes a work item first | todo-manager | .
