3610.title: public-comment
3610.content: Named by: Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft . Skill id: public-comment · Package: folio-document-adapter · Process: folio-assistant-core/processes/content/public-comment.bpmn (Process_PublicComment), which calls its change phase public-comment-change.bpmn (Process_PublicCommentChange) · Tool: folio-assistant-core/scripts/public-comment.ts · Schema: folio-assistant-core/schemas/public-comment.ts. Run a public review of a document folio. A frozen, line-numbered draft goes out. Comments come back as spreadsheets, form exports, letters and GitHub comments. Each comment is placed on the block it is about, triaged, weighed by a review committee and decided by an editor. Where a decision changes the document, the change lands on a feature branch whose staging preview shows the text before and after.

3611.title: The one fact everything rests on: a comment cites the REVIEW VERSION
3611.content: A reviewer writes “§3.4.5, p.22, l.618–624”. Those numbers exist only in the PDF the reviewer read. Word computes pages and lines at layout time and stores neither. Once an editor changes the folio, the numbers no longer describe the current text. So the review version is frozen in the library, and the folio is extracted from it in two halves: . | docx-structure.py reads the structure from the .docx: headings, lists, tables, figures, footnotes, call-out boxes. | pdf-line-map.py reads the page and line of every item from the line-numbered PDF, by matching letters only. A miss is reported, never guessed. | docx-to-folio.ts writes the editable folio. Every block’s meta.source records its page, printed page and lines. review-anchors.json is the same index in one file, which is what the importer reads. | . Never regenerate the folio over editors’ work. docx-to-folio.ts refuses a non-empty folio without --force. The anchors keep resolving after edits, because they point at the frozen version, not at the current text. Read the alignment stats (pdf-line-map.json → stats) before trusting a comment’s anchor. The unaligned items are listed by method, not hidden.

3612.title: Intake: one store, four routes, nothing dropped
3612.content: The channels a release goes out on (an offline Excel sheet, a Google Form, a GitHub issue form), each limited to the release’s fixed references, and the path each one takes back to these routes, are the public-comment-channels skill’s. | route | command | anchor comes from | . | comment matrix (.xlsx) | import <file> | section, page, line or Table/Figure columns | . | online-form export (.csv) | import <file> --channel online-form | the same columns, per row | . | narrative letter or email | import-narrative <file> --reviewer … | section, page/line, table or quotation in each paragraph | . | committee or editor on GitHub | the github job, from an issue or PR comment | the pc: reference | . A consolidated review log . A secretariat often keeps one workbook for the whole review: a master log, a tab per large submission, and a contributors sheet. import reads every sheet that holds a comment table, records the sheet on each comment, and passes over a blank template tab. Pass --series <id> naming the log. A copy re-sent later is a different file holding the same rows, and each comment carries the log’s own row number (“No.”), so a re-import adds only the rows it has not seen. What the log already says is carried, not re-done: . | Status. “Accepted”, “Partially accepted”, “Not accepted”, “Noted” and “Deferred” arrive decided, with the log’s disposition as the reason and review-log as who recorded it. “Reviewed” arrives triaged. A refusal with no rationale arrives triaged and is listed as held, because the commenter is owed a reason. | Categorisations. Theme, stakeholder type, committee routing, a review question or priority (“Q9 - Conformance and testing”, “P1”) are kept in labels, verbatim and keyed by the column header. The three comment types stay type. | Consent. Read from the contributors sheet by name, and only the name and consent columns are read. “NAIR, Tapas” and “Tapas Nair” are one person. | . Rules that are not negotiable: . | A row that resolves to nothing is unplaced, not dropped. Triage places it (triage <ref> --to <label>) or leaves it as a general comment. | A narrative is split only where it cites something. Paragraphs that cite nothing stay together as ONE general comment. Inventing an anchor for them would put a reviewer’s words on a paragraph they never mentioned. | Re-importing a file is a no-op. Batches are keyed by sha256. | Privacy. The reviewer’s email is never written, and an address typed into a comment’s text is removed too. Their name is written only when they answered the acknowledgement question “Yes”. Keep the original spreadsheets OUT of the folio’s repository, because they hold emails. Record the batch, and keep the file in the review owner’s private store. | . The live review sheet: public comments, change-sets and feedback . A secretariat may keep working in the log after the import, as a shared Google Sheet. The master log is then split into tabs, joined by the log’s own row number, No. Exactly one tab is written by the agent. Every other agent-facing column is a formula over it, so the views stay current without anyone, person or agent, refreshing them. The model. There are two things to review: public comments (PCs) and change-sets (CSs). A PC brings its own Comment / issue and Suggested revision, which are the commenter’s words. Reviewers give feedback on either one, in Committee Feedback (initials) columns: on a PC in Review Public Comments, and on a CS in Review Change Sets. A reviewer may also change which working group (TWG) a CS goes to. “Ready for agent” and “Ready for merge” belong to a CS, so they are only on Review Change Sets. Columns are named here by header, never by letter: people move them. | tab | who writes it | holds | . | Public Comment Source | intake, copied from what each channel returned (locked) | Every column Grey, header and cells: it is the external source, copied mechanically, and nobody edits it. No., date received, channel, reviewer name, organisation, country / region, stakeholder type. Reviewers’ names and emails stay here and never enter the repository | . | Review Public Comments | people, plus formulas and the Apps Script | one row per PC. Grey, mechanical: No. (a link to the comment’s page), Sections, Page, Line no(s) / Table / Figure (each linked to the draft page), Comment / issue, the PC’s own Suggested revision. Green, derived: Change Set (a link to its Review Change Sets row: the agent’s suggestion, or the person’s Change Set (human)) and TWG (agent). Blue, people: Change Set (human) (another change set’s id, several ids, or new; wins over the agent’s, like TWG (human)), TWG (human) (a multi-select dropdown), Comment type, any number of Committee Feedback (<initials>) columns, Disposition, Status. Green, from Agent by the Apps Script (derived agentic content): Agentic status, one line per pull request of the PC’s change-sets, <repo>#n (status, completed) · what it changed (the repository in the link text, because Sheets’ link popup cuts the URL short) with the PR linked and the status and completion time bold, or the status alone when there is no PR. Green, from Agent: Staging review page (by the PC’s change-set) | . | Agent - Comments | the agent, and only the agent | one row per No.: No., Comment ref (the PC id), Agentic status, Agentic action taken, Agentic applied in, Agentic handled by, Agentic date actioned (a UTC time, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ, when the agent last finished work on the PC; the four Agentic columns after the status are the agent’s log of what it did on that PC; no view reads them), Change-sets (the change set or sets this comment belongs to) | . | Agent - Change Sets | the agent, and only the agent | one row per change-set: Change-set, Title, Pull request (change set) (any number of PR URLs, one per line), Staging review page (change set), What the PRs changed (change set) (one line per PR, in the same order: what that PR changes in the document), Agent completed (UTC, change set) (one line per PR, in the same order: when the agent last finished work on it, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ), Feedback basis (change set), Staging built (UTC, change set), PR head (change set), Staging built from (change set), Staging deploy (change set) (what the agent found on GitHub, so the script can flag a stale preview; skill review-sheet-script, “Checked by commit”). A change-set may have several PRs, and a PC in several change-sets shows all of theirs. A PR belongs to a change-set, not to a PC. A sheet with one Agent tab (comments in A–H, change sets from I) is read when the Config sets AGENT_CS empty | . | Review Change Sets | people, plus formulas and the Apps Script | one row per CS. Blue, people: Title: making a change set is human-controlled. A person makes a change set by typing a Title on an empty row, and the script gives it the next id; the agent’s title is only the first value of a row it adds. Grey: Change-set, and the Apps Script’s Sections and Pages (each linked) and joins: Public Comments (No. n (Status) · comment, status in bold), Suggested Revisions, PC Committee Feedback and Dispositions (No. n · text), each No. n linking to its row. Green: TWG (PCs), the PCs’ TWG (human), else TWG (agent) marked “(AI)”. Blue, people: TWG (CS) (multi-select), Committee Feedback (<initials>) on the CS. Orange: Ready for agent and Ready for merge (Yes/No, editors). Green, from Agent by the Apps Script (derived agentic content): Agentic status, as on Review Public Comments: one line per PR of the change-set, <repo>#n (status, completed) · what it changed, the status being the change-set’s PCs’ agentic statuses. Green, from Agent: Staging review page | . | RCS joins (live) | formulas (hidden) | live joins over Review Public Comments and Agent, kept for checking the Apps Script’s output | . Splitting an older sheet’s one Agent tab. Duplicate it, delete A–H on the copy and the change-set columns on the original, rename them, set AGENT and AGENT_CS in the Config, and give each an Instructions row. Then, in the same step, repoint every formula that read the old tab’s change-set columns: they become #REF! when those columns are deleted. They are Review Change Sets A3 (FILTER('Agent - Change Sets'!A3:B, ...), the Change-set and Title), the Staging review column of Review Public Comments (its lookup range becomes 'Agent - Change Sets'!A:D), and A2 of the hidden RCS joins (live) tab. Also unmerge row 1 on the copy: the Instructions cell was merged across B1 to the last column, so deleting A–H shifts that merge onto A1 and hides B1 (a write to B1 then lands in the hidden part and seems to vanish). Merge B1 across the new width again. Read row 3 of each tab for #REF! before saying it is done. Colour key. Blue: people decide. Orange: a release an editor gives (Ready for agent, Ready for merge). Grey: fixed, mechanical, or from the knowledge graph. Green: derived or written by the agent. Every green header is the same green; a header does not say “from Agent”. Locks. Grey and green columns, and every header, are protected; only the owner’s account (which the agent’s connector and the Apps Script run as) may edit them. Editors may change the blue and orange cells. Ready for merge is open to editors, so an editor’s Yes makes the agent merge. Why the CS inputs stay with their rows. Review Change Sets’ Change-set and Title are plain values, so people can type a Title and start rows (where they are still a spill of FILTER('Agent - Change Sets'!A3:B, ...), the script turns it into values once). The script keeps the rows: a Title-only row gets the next id, never reused across both tabs, and a change set the agent records that is not on the tab yet is added at the end. Rows are never reordered or deleted, so the typed cells beside them stay put. Once per sheet, the script also turns Title and Change Set (human) Blue and takes them out of the locks on the agent’s columns. A sorted or filtered view of PCs cannot hold inputs. Feedback columns are found by header. The agent and the views read every Review Public Comments column whose header starts with Suggested revision or Committee Feedback, and every Review Change Sets column whose header starts with Committee Feedback. A board adds its column beside the others and puts its own initials in the header. Never write a fixed column letter into a view. People may reorder the Review Public Comments tab, because Review Change Sets finds columns by name (MATCH on the first row). A renamed header that is looked up by name (No., Sections, Page, Comment / issue, Suggested revision, Status, Disposition, TWG (agent), TWG (human)) does break the view, and its formula, or the Apps Script’s sheet-sync.json, must be updated with the new name. How the views update. The formula columns are FILTER, VLOOKUP, BYROW and MAKEARRAY over Review Public Comments and Agent. Setting Ready for agent, adding feedback, or the agent writing an Agent row shows at once. Nothing is run to refresh them. Two things are not automatic: . | A new or retitled change-set reaches the sheet only when the agent rewrites Agent - Change Sets’ Change-set and Title from review/public-comment/changesets/. | A PC’s change-set (Agent - Comments’ Change-sets) is the change-set whose refs hold the comment. The agent rewrites it when a comment is moved between change-sets. | . What the agent watches. Feedback arrives two ways, and the agent reads both on Review Public Comments and Review Change Sets: . | the Committee Feedback cells and Review Change Sets’ TWG categorisation; | cell comments (Google’s Insert > Comment) anywhere on those two tabs, read with the spreadsheet’s comments included. A cell comment on a PC row is feedback on that PC. One on a CS row is feedback on that CS. | . A changed TWG categorisation on a CS is a re-routing, not an edit. The agent records it in the change-set’s record through the tool, and says so in the CS’s agentic status. When the agent runs. A sheet sync runs three ways: . | Scheduled. A scheduled task in the project runs it (for example, every 2 hours on weekdays). Each run is a fresh thread with no memory of earlier ones, so everything it needs is in the sheet, the records and this section. | Manual. Anyone asks for it (“sync the sheet”, “work the ready rows”) in a project thread, or presses Run now on the scheduled task. A thread may also fire the scheduled task itself. | Active mode. On demand only, and it lasts two hours. The owner asks for it in a project thread (“active mode on”). That thread then checks the sheet about every ten minutes, waking itself with reminders rather than a loop. It compares Review Change Sets’ Ready for agent, the feedback columns and the cell comments with what it saw last, and runs a sheet sync, or fires the scheduled task, when something changed. Two hours after it was switched on, it stops and says so in one line. The regular schedule keeps running throughout. A sheet edit cannot wake an agent by itself, so active mode is frequent checking, not a push. | . Each sync does the steps below, in this order. | Reconcile. For every change-set with a pull request (Agent - Change Sets’ Pull request), read each PR’s state from GitHub. Open: PR open, with its staging review page. Merged: Change merged, and clear the staging link, because a merged branch’s preview is gone and its link 404s. Closed unmerged: back to Not started, and say so in “agentic action taken”. Write the status on every PC row of the change-set. Rewrite the change-set columns from the change-set records as above, keeping each change-set’s row and the PR columns beside it. | Work the ready change-sets. For each Review Change Sets row with Ready for agent = Yes whose PCs’ agentic status is Not started or Needs human, or that has new feedback since its PR was opened: . | Find each PC by No.: the record whose public.source names the log’s sheet and that entry. A row with no record is set to Not in comment record, and the agent goes no further with it. | Review all of it before drafting: every PC in the change-set, with its Comment / issue and its own Suggested revision; every Committee Feedback cell and cell comment on those PCs; and every Committee Feedback cell, cell comment and the TWG categorisation on the CS itself. Feedback on the CS weighs on the whole change; feedback on a PC weighs on that PC’s part of it. | Propose the change the way every change is proposed: in its change-set (see Change-sets below), on a branch, with a PR. A PR already open for the change-set is updated rather than replaced. “Ready for agent” says the change-set is ready to draft. It is not the editor’s decision, and a comment’s status still moves only through this tool. Where the suggestions and feedback conflict, or one asks for something the document cannot say without a decision, set Needs human and write what is needed in “agentic action taken”. | Publish the branch’s staging preview (branches/<slug>/). | Write the Agent rows (skill review-sheet-agent-columns, which applies to any work on a change set, in a sync or not), and nothing anywhere else in the sheet: status (Working, PR open, Ready for review, Change merged), what was done, the blocks or sections changed, who acted (the agent and its session) and the completion time (UTC, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ) on each PC’s row; and on the change-set’s row the PR and branches/<slug>/en/review/ (Pull request, Staging review page), one line saying what the PR changes in the document (What the PRs changed) and the completion time (Agent completed), each on the same line as its PR’s URL. The PR body names the feedback it answered by tab, row and column header, never by a reviewer’s name. | . | Merge the released PRs. For each change-set with an open PR whose Review Change Sets row has Ready for merge = Yes (any editor may set it), and whose QA gate has passed for the PR’s head commit, merge it. The gate is run by a reviewer that did not write the PR (review-sheet-script, “The QA gate”); without a pass for the current head, the agent does not merge and its ⏳ line says why. Nor does it merge while any comment’s committee Disposition is still Pending (review-sheet-script, “Unconfirmed dispositions block the merge”). Only a PR in the folio’s own repository is merged, never one on a WHO repository. After the merge, set every PC row of the change-set to Change merged, clear its staging link, and comment on the PR’s issue. If the merge is refused (a session safety check, a conflict, a required review), set the rows to Merge blocked, write why in “agentic action taken”, and say so in the run’s summary. Do not route around a refusal. | . Which PR counts. Only a PR that edits the document for the change-set. A change-set record’s pr can name the PR that proposed the change-set, long merged. That is not a change PR. Read the PR’s diff or body before writing it to a row. The dashboard draws a staging link only for a PR that is open now, for the same reason (openPullRequests in scripts/public-comment-site.ts). Page links. Every page, section and line reference in the sheet opens the frozen review version at that page. The log cites printed page numbers; the PDF page is the printed page plus the front matter, read from the library entry’s pdf-line-map.json (pages.<pdf page>.printed). Use a short link: the folio’s site publishes a draft/ redirect to its library viewer, so a link is <site>/draft/#page=<n> rather than the full assets/vendor/pdfjs/web/viewer.html?src=… address, and a cell with many links stays small. The review sheet’s Apps Script . Links inside a cell’s text (sections, pages, lines, each No. n in a joined column) are kept by a Google Apps Script bound to the sheet, built by the Tool review-sheet-sync. How to build it, install it, check it works, and reuse it for another document’s public comment is the review-sheet-script skill. A change-set that already has an agent PR has Ready for agent = Yes, so the sheet never shows agent work nobody released. The agent never writes the Review Public Comments, Public Comment Source or Review Change Sets tabs except on the owner’s explicit instruction (such as releasing a change-set as above). It never sets “Ready for agent” or “Ready for merge” on its own, and it never copies a reviewer’s name or email from Public Comment Source, a feedback header or a cell comment’s author into the repository. The sheet is reached through the session’s Google Sheets connector. No credential for it is committed. Google cannot stop the owner’s own account editing any tab, so the one-writer rule is kept by the agent, not enforced by the sheet. Editorial change-sets may be drafted without waiting . A change-set is editorial when it changes only wording, numbering, cross-references, typos or house style, and no meaning: nothing a TWG or committee has to judge. The agent may draft an editorial change-set as a draft PR with a staging preview without waiting for Ready for agent. It records each step in the Agent tab as usual (review-sheet-agent-columns), with “editorial draft” in its status. | It still never sets Ready for merge, and nothing merges without it. | A change-set that mixes editorial and substantive asks is split: the agent drafts the editorial part, and the substantive part (a new definition, new guidance, a rewrite) goes to Needs human. | A house-style choice the document has not made yet (a spelling convention, say) is asked once with options, then followed; it is not guessed. | When unsure whether a change is editorial, it is not: wait for Ready for agent. | .

3613.title: Placing a comment: how much to trust the anchor
3613.content: anchor.method says how the place was found, and confidence says how far to trust it: . | caption (high): “Table 3.1” named a captioned block. | page (medium or low): a page with no usable line. A lines cell such as “Requirement 5” or “A14.01” names an item, not a line, so it is not read as one. Lands on the page’s first block in the cited section. | page-line (high, when the cited section agrees): the page is read as the printed page first, then as the PDF page index. Printed numbering restarts in the front matter, so the cited section breaks ties. “Section does NOT agree” in anchor.note is a triage signal. Check the comment. | quote (medium or low): a quotation found in the text. Low means it occurs more than once. The other places are in candidates. | section (medium): only the section resolved, by its number or by its title or acronym (“PHSP” is the Public Health Surveillance Platform). The anchor is the section label. | manual: a person placed it with reassign. | .

3614.title: The lifecycle, and who moves it
3614.content: received → triaged → assigned → recommended → decided → editing → incorporated, plus duplicate and withdrawn. Every move is a task in public-comment.bpmn or, for edit and incorporate, in its change phase public-comment-change.bpmn. transition() refuses any other move. Do not edit a comment’s status by hand: the dashboard counts statuses, and a hand-closed comment reads as adjudicated when no one decided it. | who (role) | does | how | . | intake agent (intake) | propose change-sets as records, with no issue (below) | public-comment-changesets.ts seed, propose | . | review coordinator (review-coordinator) | triage, place, mark duplicates, assign | triage, reassign, duplicate, assign | . | committee and editor | agree each change-set’s requirements, and change it, on its issue | the issue thread, and cs-* commands | . | committee member (reviewer) | recommend a decision, with a rationale | a GitHub comment pc: PC-0042 / recommend: accepted-modified, or recommend | . | editor (editor) | decide, with a reason unless accepted | decide: … on GitHub (editors only) or decide | . | author (author), human or agentic | once a comment is dispensed with a changing decision, make the edit on a feature branch | edit <ref> --branch … [--to <login>] | . | pipeline (build-pipeline) | build the change set’s staging preview, mark it incorporated on merge | staging workflow, incorporate | . Who can move a comment from GitHub. Both roles are read from the repository itself by default, so nobody maintains a list: . | Editor: the repository’s owner. Only the editor decides. | Committee: the repository’s collaborators (owner, member or collaborator). Adding someone as a collaborator on GitHub is the whole on-boarding. | . GitHub marks every comment with the commenter’s relationship to the repository, and that mark is what is checked. An editors or committee list in config.json replaces that role’s default with exactly those logins. Anyone may discuss a comment there, but the record is not open to everyone. The five decision codes: accepted, accepted-modified, not-accepted, noted, deferred. Every code but accepted needs a reason, because the commenter is owed one.

3615.title: Change-sets: an issue to agree it, a PR to approve it
3615.content: One editorial change often answers several comments, and one comment sometimes needs several changes. So a comment belongs to zero or more change-sets, and a change-set is discussed and made in two GitHub objects with different jobs: . | object | what people do there | . | the change-set’s ISSUE | discuss and agree the requirements: what the document should say, which comments the change answers | . | the PR that closes it | preview the change on staging, review it, approve the merge to main | . Requirements argued on a PR get lost when it is closed and reopened; a diff argued on an issue has nothing to point at. Keep each on its own object. One record, everything else rendered from it . review/public-comment/changesets/CS-012.json is the only record of a change-set: title, requirements, members, status, primary issue, every other issue that discusses it, its PR, and its history. Nothing else stores any of that: . | a comment’s change-sets are derived from the records, never written on the comment; | the change-set section at the top of its issue is rendered from the record, and a hand-edit to it is put back with a pointer to the commands; | the dashboard is built from the records. It is published per document at <site>/en/folio-assistant-core/public-comments/<folio>/<slug>/, the handler route every viewer follows (<base>/<handler>/<kind>/<subject>, the subject being the materialised document’s path in the folio) under the page locale, with its comments.json at the same route without the locale. public-comment-route.ts is the one place that says so: the site, the change-set issues and the rendered-impact predictor all ask it. | . The folio’s public-comment.yml workflow is the only writer, one run at a time, never cancelled half-way. People and agents ask; it writes. Two gates keep it honest: public-comment-changesets.ts check fails a PR whose records contradict each other (no network), and the nightly reconcile re-renders every issue from its record, opens or closes it as its status says, and opens the issue a change-set decided outside GitHub is owed. It reports and never deletes. The agent proposes; nobody is notified . Task_ProposeChangeSets (intake agent). An agent may draft every change-set, and drafting one opens nothing: a proposal has no issue, so 2,000 comments do not become 300 notifications nobody asked for. | seed --out seed.json lists the open or decided comments in no change-set yet, bucketed by section. A bucket is not a change-set. One section’s comments usually ask for several different changes, and one change (a term used throughout, say) spans sections. | Decide the changes. One change-set is one change a reviewer can approve or refuse as a whole. Good signs: the comments ask for the same edit, or for edits that must land together. Bad signs: the title needs “and”, or the requirements list unrelated edits. Cross-cutting themes (consent, a terminology standard, normative keywords) are ONE change-set touching several sections, not one per section: when several agents draft in parallel by section, run a merge pass over their drafts before recording. | Write requirements as what the text must do (“define actor once, in 2.1, and use it consistently”), not as the new text: the text is the PR’s job. | propose --file proposals.json records them ([{title, requirements, refs, anchor?}]), or add one at a time. Status: proposed. | . A comment the agent cannot place is left out, not forced in. It shows on the dashboard’s open, in no change-set tile. The issue appears when somebody engages . Task_GroupChangeSets. A change-set gets its primary issue the first time anybody engages with it: . | what somebody does | what the workflow does | . | presses Discuss on the dashboard (the change-set issue form, prefilled with the id) | adopts that issue as the primary one and renders the record at its top; their text stays below | . | recommends or decides on one of its comments, in any thread | records it, opens the primary issue, and quotes the tag there with a link back | . | mentions it, or one of its comments, in any issue | links that issue, and opens the primary issue (at most five from one mention; past that it replies with Discuss links instead) | . | opens a PR that links it by keyword (Closes CS-012, fixes/resolves CS-012, or a cs: CS-012 line) or closes one of its issues | records the PR, opens the primary issue if there is none, when the PR’s author is on the committee or an editor (judged as for tags; a PR by anyone else links nothing, and a merge counts whoever wrote it). A bare mention of CS-012 in prose links nothing, and a change-set already incorporated or closed is never re-linked to another PR: reopen its issue first | . | decides through the CLI | nothing at once; the nightly reconcile opens the issue | . People are disorganised, and that is fine. Any number of other issues may discuss a change-set: each is linked (the record’s issues), listed under Also discussed in on the primary issue, and told where the primary one is. Nobody’s own issue is rewritten, and a tag recorded in a linked issue counts exactly as one in the primary. An issue body is judged as its author’s: an edit to it by anyone else records nothing, so tags and commands go in a comment. Changing a change-set on its issue . In a comment, from the committee or the editor. Anyone else’s command is answered with why it changed nothing. | command | effect | . | cs-add: PC-0311, PC-0312 | add comments | . | cs-remove: PC-0107 | remove a comment | . | cs-title: … | rename | . | cs-requirements: then the text on the following lines | replace the requirements | . | cs-committee: <TWG> — <reason> | re-route the change-set to another TWG review committee, with a reason (Task_RerouteChangeSet, person-only; also reroute <CS-012> --to <TWG> --why "reason" --by <login>) | . | cs-merge: CS-087 | fold CS-087 in; its issue is linked, and closed with a pointer (or adopted, if this one had none) | . | cs-split: PC-0311, PC-0312 as New title | move those comments into a new change-set, which gets its own issue | . | cs-close: reason | no change is needed | . | cs-new: Title with a pc: line | a new change-set (the dashboard’s New change-set from the selected comments opens the form for it) | . A change-set’s committee is rolled up from its comments’ TWG routing unless a person in the committee or editor lane re-routes it by hand (cs-committee: <TWG> — <reason> or public-comment-changesets.ts reroute). Each move is recorded on the change-set (who, when, from, to, why) so re-ingesting comments never resets it, and the dashboard shows the new committee and the move history. Agents cannot re-route a change-set on their own (Task_RerouteChangeSet is a userTask in public-comment.bpmn). cs: CS-012 names the change-set where a thread discusses several. In a change-set’s issue a bare decide: accepted (or recommend: …) applies to all its comments; pc: PC-0042 first narrows it. Closing a primary issue by hand while its comments still need a change reopens it, with the list. Closing it when every comment is decided without a change closes the change-set. Reopening a primary issue puts its change-set back to discussing, whether it was closed or incorporated: a person reopening it is saying it is not done. reopen <CS-012> --note "why" makes the same move when the reopen event has already been handled. The issue forms . public-comment-changesets.ts install writes three forms and the two workflows into the folio’s .github/, from this layer’s templates/public-comment/. A form renders as ### Label and the value, and the tool reads it as the same lines a person would type, so there is one parser for both: . | form | for | reads as | . | Discuss a change-set (change-set.yml) | the dashboard’s Discuss link | cs: CS-012 and the discussion | . | New change-set (change-set-new.yml) | the dashboard’s picks | cs-new: Title, pc: …, cs-requirements: | . | Recommend or decide (comment-decision.yml) | a person who would rather not type a tag | pc: / cs:, recommend: or decide:, the reason | . Blank issues stay enabled: a person who ignores the forms is still linked by what they mention. The PR . | Branch from main, named for the change. Open the PR at the first commit (continual-progress), with Closes #<the primary issue> (or any of its issues, or Closes CS-012, or a cs: CS-012 line) in its body. Only those keywords link: a PR that mentions the id in passing, a pin bump say, does not. The PR’s author must be on the committee or an editor, judged by the author’s own login and association as tags are; merging it is allowed whoever wrote it. | Opening it moves the change-set to editing and its accepted comments to editing, with the branch and PR. Comments not yet decided, or decided not-accepted/noted/deferred, do not move. | Edit the folio’s blocks. An agent in the author role edits only what the decisions and the issue’s requirements say. Before the preview is staged, it writes the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the review sheet’s Agent tab, below the change set’s decision history (which is only ever added to): one blurb describing every disposition in the change set, one line per comment (No. 136: Accepted. <what was done>, after an optional Overall: line), starting from each comment’s Blue Disposition on Review Public Comments; the review sheet checks that every comment number in the change set has one (review-sheet-script). Before Ready for merge, an independent reviewer runs the QA gate: every disposition against the people’s Blue Disposition and the PR’s diff, and the staging QA report (review-sheet-script, “The QA gate”). Once an Editor sets Ready for merge to Yes, that blurb is the summary: in the merge commit and as the closing comment on the change set’s issue. | The staging preview is published to branches/<branch>/. The dashboard links each comment’s anchor on main (before) and on the preview (after). See staging-review. | Merging moves the accepted comments to incorporated. The change-set is incorporated, and its primary issue closed, only when every comment in it is settled (decided, incorporated, duplicate or withdrawn). If any is still undecided, the change-set stays open and so does its issue, and the workflow log says how many are left. A PR closed without merging puts the change-set back to discussing. | .

3616.title: The dashboard’s filters
3616.content: Status, Type, Section, Search and the count tiles filter both tables: the comments, and the change-sets above them. A change-set shows when any of its comments match, and its count then reads “10 of 18”. | Show its comments clears every other filter and shows all of that change-set’s comments. Any later Status, Type, Section or tile choice replaces it; the search box narrows within it. | Every filter change is a history entry, with the filters in the query string (?status=open&section=1.1.3). Back restores the previous view, and the URL of a filtered view can be pasted into an issue or a chat. | Closed in the Status box means incorporated, duplicate or withdrawn; the page says so above the tiles. | . This is the same review loop as any content change (content-change-review.bpmn), with a different intake. Reuse it rather than building a parallel review.

3617.title: Change-sets beyond public comment
3617.content: The change-set is the Change Set for ANY change to a folio: one that answers no comment has empty refs. It applies to the materialised folio/, never to the library/ source it was materialised from. Its PR carries rendered, one list per renderer of the rendered files the change alters, and review approves against those lists (skill rendered-impact).

3618.title: What not to do
3618.content: . | Do not answer a comment by editing the review version in library/. It is frozen, and every anchor depends on it. | Do not re-anchor by renaming a block. Labels are the anchors. 3632.title: The documents at their addresses: the primary step
3632.content: Skill publish-documents: The primary step of initializing a Knowledge Graph harness: every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document it names an address for (schemas, vocabulary, diagram vocabulary, graph export, each with its @context) is published AT that address, and the address answers. Checked first, right after the declaration is read. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . A Knowledge Graph harness is its JSON and JSON-LD. Its schemas say what a declaration and every node may be; its vocabulary says what each term means; its graph says what it holds. Each names itself with an IRI: a JSON Schema with $id, a JSON-LD document with @id. An IRI that answers 404 is a broken promise to everything that points at it. So this is the first step checked once the declarations are read, before any directory, README or site step.

3633.title: Which documents
3633.content: Read from the files, never from a list: . | every JSON file whose top-level $id lies under the declaration’s iriBase is a JSON Schema published at that $id; | every JSON-LD file whose top-level @id lies under iriBase is published at that @id. For bootstrap that is the vocabulary (ns.jsonld, at <iriBase>v<major>/ns/) and the diagram vocabulary (processes/ns.jsonld, at <iriBase>v<major>/processes/ns/, the namespace every diagram binds); | the graph export, built when the site is published, at the address its own @id names (bootstrap-graph-publication). | . Each document carries its @context inline, so publishing the document publishes its context. A harness whose documents name an external context publishes that context the same way, at its own IRI. No iriBase, no addresses. An instance that declares none has nothing here to publish, and says so rather than reporting a pass over nothing.

3634.title: Where each goes
3634.content: At the path its IRI names, with iriBase removed. An address ending in / (…/v0/ns/) gets the document as index.jsonld there, with an index.json copy beside it. A .jsonld gets a .json copy with the same bytes beside it, because many hosts serve .jsonld as a download. The .jsonld stays the real one: it is what the @id names.

3635.title: Two checks, four states
3635.content: | step | checks | done | not done | could not determine | . | schemas:staged | the site build puts each document at its address | every one is there, byte for byte | one is missing, or another file holds its address | the build could not run | . | schemas:published | each address answers | every one answers | one answers 404 | 403, 407, 5xx or no answer: that is about the way from here (a proxy, an access rule), not about the address | .

3636.title: The site is the vehicle
3636.content: The documents get to their addresses by the Pages site (publish-site): its workflow stages each one where its IRI says, and lists them all under “Published documents” on the README page (README.html). When schemas:published is not done, the site steps are how it gets done. The site is not the goal: a site that answers while one schema address does not has not finished initializing the harness. Where a toolset is available, its site check (site.ts --check) lists every address and what is staged at it, and init.ts reports both steps first.

3638.title: The site: an instance rendered for publication, and its address answering
3638.content: Skill publish-site: Give an instance a site: its Knowledge Graph rendered for publication at its site address, and the address answering. Four checks — a workflow publishes it, the gh-pages branch exists, Pages serves that branch, the address answers. How the rendering is staged and pushed is the toolset’s own process, not this skill’s. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . One abstract step. An instance with a repository is rendered for publication at its site address, and the address answers. How the rendering is staged, committed and checked is the toolset’s own subprocess (its render-to-GitHub-Pages skill and diagram), so this skill stays a list of checks. The site is how the documents reach their IRIs (publish-documents, the primary step), not the goal. Where the README page lands. At <site address>README.html, and the site address itself (index.html) is the landing page: by default a plain redirect to README.html, so a Harness that wants a different front page puts its own index.html or index.md at its root and changes nothing else. A page generated from the instance’s files says so at its top, and its footer points to what it was generated from, never to an editor for the published copy: that copy is replaced on every publish. The site address is the declaration’s iriBase when it declares one, otherwise https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/.

It must exist before Pages can be switched on; where it does not, the step says how to create it (an orphan branch with a placeholder page) | . | site:enabled | Pages is on, serving gh-pages at /. Switched on only by an authenticated forge CLI once the branch exists; otherwise the person gets the one step below | . | site:live | the address answers 200, and so does its README page, README.html. 404 after Pages is on usually means the workflow has not run yet. A 403, 407, 5xx or no answer is about the way from here: could not determine, never done | . When site:enabled cannot be done here, it goes to the person through human-agent-discussion, written so it can be followed without opening anything else: . Open https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/pages. Under “Build and deployment”, set Source to Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). It is free for a public repository. 3642.title: Publish verification, and the one alert
3642.content: Skill publish-verification: Verify what a publish produced, and alert the publication manager whenever any step after the publish button fails — the verifier set, how to add a verifier, what is in scope, and how the publication manager triages the one alert. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Human Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Agent activity log, The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use, Is CI actually working on the default branch?, Code change and review, The gates a change must pass before it can merge, Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down, Check a generated file still matches its source, Are the .jsonld siblings still in sync with their .ts manifests?, Merge the base branch in, Merge to main, A merge train, Which open pull requests have no CI run on their head?, Alert the publication manager, Verify the export before it is deployed, Publish and keep QA results on qa-reports, QA report signing, Is the repository itself healthy?, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Report a verdict on one tracking issue, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . The verifier set runs over the built site before it is deployed. It does not stop the deploy: its outcome is judged after the push, and any failure reaches the publication manager through the same single alert as every other step after the publish button.

3643.title: The two processes
3643.content: . | publish-verification.bpmn — the verifier set over the built tree, between the export and the deploy. Pass, fail, or could-not-tell; the caller deploys either way and judges the outcome after the push. | publish-alert.bpmn — ONE alert, called from every failure edge in docs-site-publish.bpmn: a refused security gate, a failed deploy, a lost preview, a failed built-site check. It reaches the role that already owns the release: the publication manager. | .

3644.title: The verifier set
3644.content: bun run cat publish:verify -- --dir <built site> [--report out.md] — scripts/publish-verify.ts. Exit 0 pass · 1 a finding · 2 could not tell. The caller treats 1 and 2 alike: an unverified release is not a verified one. Each verifier is one entry in VERIFIERS: an id, the question it asks, and a function from the directory to findings. Adding a verifier is adding an entry; the report, the exit code and the alert need no change. Give it a test that builds a document to break it, as publish-verify.test.ts does. jsonld-expand is the first: every JSON-LD document of ours is expanded by a real processor (jsonld.js, network refused). A key the @context does not declare is DROPPED by a processor, silently.

3645.title: A verifier the preview cannot ask is a release failure waiting (STRICT)
3645.content: The staging preview runs the same verifier set, so a preview is never greener than the release it previews. That promise breaks wherever the preview answers a different question. It serves the PUBLISHED search index (--search-index borrowed), so search-index there asks only “present and parsing”, never “does it cover the pages” — so a preview can be green while the release refuses it. So the preview asks the coverage question of the index it built, before swapping in the published one: publish-verify.ts --dir ./_site --only search-index. The rule, for any verifier added later: if the preview substitutes an input, the verifier runs on the preview’s own input before the substitution. A check only the release asks fails after merge, on main, where everyone pays for it. Deliberate exclusion is marked in what is built. search_exclude: true is front matter, and front matter is gone after Jekyll. head_custom.html writes <meta name="fa-search-exclude"> for it, and search-index leaves those pages out of the coverage denominator and COUNTS them in its finding. An exclusion the built page does not carry cannot be told from a truncated index, and the release check will refuse it, correctly.

3646.title: What is in scope
3646.content: A document is ours when its @context names our content context or binds a namespace in the own-namespaces code list. Everything else in the tree — an ingested IG’s artefact index, for example — is counted as out of scope, reported, and never able to block the release.

3647.title: Triage, for the publication manager
3647.content: The alert is a tracking issue labelled publication-manager: opened on the first failure, commented on for each later one (a comment notifies; an edit does not), closed by the next clean publish. The issue says which step failed and whether the site deployed: . | Nothing was deployed (the export, or verification) — the live site is the previous publish. Hold, or fix forward. | The site deployed and something after it failed (a lost preview) — it is live. Say so in the issue before fixing. | . The label names the role, not a person: no actor declares a GitHub account for publication-manager. Watching the label is how a person takes the role.

3655.doc: Publish and keep QA results on qa-reports
3655.title: Publish and keep QA results on qa-reports
3655.content: Process_QaPublish · strict · 7 step(s) . How a run’s derived QA results become a durable, commit-keyed record without being committed to main, and how that record is retired. You are in this process when CI has finished the gates for a push to main or a same-repository pull request (the publish path), or when the daily retention run fires (the prune path). Both are mechanical: nothing here judges a result, and nothing here decides mergeability. The record it writes is what a later --against <ref> reads as a baseline. A publish that did not happen makes that baseline UNKNOWN for every later change, which is why a red publish is still a red to fix even though it blocks nothing. Judgements are never written here: they stay on main in test/attestations/ (owner ruling D2 (a)). i i i i i i i

3657.title: Lanes — who acts
3657.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | CI/CD Pipeline | build-pipeline | Runs both paths as fixed programs. It decides nothing that needs judgement: whether a token can write is read from the event, whether a push was accepted is the push’s exit code (never its stderr — spike 3ds9 measured a harmless “push negotiation failed; proceeding anyway”), and what retention removes is planPrune’s rule. 3658.doc: Publish and keep QA results on qa-reports
3658.title: Steps
3658.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Derive the keyTask_DeriveKey | CI/CD Pipeline | qa-reports | qa:publish --github reads the event: a push to main publishes under main/<sha>/, a pull request under pr/<n>/<head-sha>/ — the head that was tested, not the merge ref. It also reads whether the token can write, which the gateway after it routes on. The key is main/<sha> or pr/<n>/<sha>. | . | Build the entryTask_BuildEntry | CI/CD Pipeline | qa-reports | First the working copy is produced (qa:refresh, bean 3hk4): while the checkout still tracks test/results/, the commit’s own copy is the record and nothing runs; once it does not, every declared QA writer runs into the empty tree, because the gates are in judge mode and wrote nothing a publish could carry. A refresh that leaves a writer failed, a family empty or a file unclaimed is INCOMPLETE: the job goes red and qa:publish --completeness refuses, so a partial tree is never stored as the commit’s record — the “Not stored” outcome, reached before any push. 3661.title: QA report signing — two routes, chosen by the performer’s reach
3661.content: Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use, Alert the publication manager, QA report signing, Test-plan execution, Adopting an upstream version bump, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Guideline Updates, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . A QA report becomes evidence when a third party can establish what was measured and who vouches for it. folio-test-run/v1 (schemas/sdlc/test-run.ts) answers the first: a data hash and a process hash, each all-or-nothing, plus the skill it tests, whose contract its recorded cases are checked against (test-run-conforms). This skill answers the second, and it has two routes because the participant doing the signing may not be able to reach anything: some machine actors are air-gapped, an API cannot be called from one, and a human actor signs instead. The subject signed is the QA report. This skill builds on signing. That skill holds what is true of any signature: who signs, what is signed, which suites a trust anchor accepts, key custody, the route, and what a verifier must check and record. This one keeps only what is particular to QA reports: the run hashes, the qa-reports branch, and the line between attestation and certification. Where the two overlap, signing is the rule.

3663.title: Reach is a property of the ACTOR, and unknown is a third state
3663.content: schemas/process/actor-reach.ts. | One vocabulary, two levels. An actor’s reach uses the same scale as the deployment’s network — internet, egress-restricted, air-gapped. There is no second scale, because two spellings of one fact drift apart. | Composition is asymmetric. An air-gapped deployment forces every actor air-gapped. A connected one forces nothing — a connected site may hold an isolated signing host. So an actor that declares no reach inside a connected deployment is unknown, not internet. | unknown routes to the human. A gateway that read could-not-determine as “use the API” would fail closed on the wire and open in the record: the call fails and what survives is an unsigned report that nothing marks as unsigned. Could-not-check is never green. | .

3664.title: Reach is declared, not a capability
3664.content: There is no network-egress capability. A capability is an environment probe — detection: { method: "command", … }, a thing you run to find out. Reach is an architectural fact, declared by whoever built the site. On an air-gapped host a failed probe is indistinguishable from an outage, and the safe reading of an outage (“retry later”) is the unsafe reading of an air gap. A capability would also carry the same fact as reach in a second place, free to disagree. What is a probe is whether an endpoint is configured: signing-api, an env-var detection. The DMN table reads both, because they answer different questions — can this host call out and is there anything to call. A configured endpoint on an air-gapped host is still uncallable.

3665.title: Declaration and execution are different mechanisms
3665.content: qa-report-signing.ts declares: . requiredCapabilities: [ { capabilityId: "signing-api", degradation: "fallback", fallbackRole: "publication-manager" }, ], . fallbackRole says which lane takes over when no capability can do it. It does not route anything, and nothing executes it; the gateway is what executes. They must agree — the declaration is what a reader and check:fallback-roles can see without executing anything; the gateway is what happens. Where they disagree, the diagram is what ran, and the declaration is the bug.

3666.title: Recording the attestation
3666.content: Record what signing §6 requires (suite, key, anchor, result, when checked) and, above all, which route signed it, not only that it is signed. The two are not interchangeable: one attests that a service with a key saw these hashes, the other that a person holding release authority did.

3667.title: Where the signed report goes: the qa-reports branch, next to its run
3667.content: A QA report is a derived record — it can be rebuilt from the tree and the data it hashed — so it is kept where every derived QA result is kept: the orphan qa-reports branch, in the entry keyed by the commit it judged (main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/), written through scripts/qa-store.ts and never by a hand git push. The signature and the route that produced it travel with the report, in the same entry, because a signature separated from the bytes it covers attests nothing a reader can check. Task_RecordAttestation in qa-report-signing.bpmn ends there. What does not go there. A certification — an accountable role’s Decision taken on a test report’s rollup — is a separate node, and it stays on main beside the attestations: it is a judgement, the same class as test/attestations/, and no regeneration can reproduce it. That decision belongs to the test-plan process, which calls this one to sign; this skill only signs. A read of a signed report follows the store’s rules: a miss is never read as “unsigned and fine”, and a store that cannot answer is UNKNOWN, which routes like unknown reach — to a person, never to a pass.

3675.title: QA reports — derived results on a branch, judgements on main
3675.content: Skill qa-reports: Where a QA result lives now. Derived verdicts go to the orphan qa-reports branch, keyed by commit, written by the CI job qa-publish. Judgements stay on main in the attestations graph. Gates compute and judge against a stored baseline, and a missing one is unknown. Read before you regenerate, commit, resolve, cite or delete anything under test/results/ or test/attestations/. A QA result is either reproducible or it is not, and that decides where it lives. A script verdict is a pure function of the tree: run the producer again and you get it back. A reviewer’s judgement is not, because no re-run can reproduce what an agent or a person decided. The two are split on that line: . |   | derived | judgement | . | what | every reviewer.kind: script entry: kg-qa/**, *.qa-results.json, witnesses, lsi/, tool-runs/, the health report | agent, human and baseline-pair attestations (a baseline is a judgement) | . | graph typology | qa (and health) | attestations | . | written to | <instance>/test/results/**, the working copy | <instance>/test/attestations/<family>/<mirrored subject path>.attestations.json | . | record | the orphan qa-reports branch, main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/ | main | . | schema | the family’s own | qa-attestations/v1, schemas/sdlc/qa-attestations.ts | . | on a merge conflict | take the base’s side (merge:main), then regenerate | a person reads both sides | . cat-harness and the content core do not commit the derived files. Where an instance still does, they are a copy on its way out, not the record. Do not regenerate one in order to commit it, and do not hand-resolve one. Every qa directory declares storage and is ignored by version control, so a new file there is not committed. Before an instance’s removal of its committed copy is pushed, bun run cat qa:verify-moved --key main/<head> must answer IDENTICAL. It compares every moved path’s blob id with the entry, and an entry it cannot read is UNKNOWN (exit 2), never a pass.

3676.title: The branch
3676.content: qa-reports (orphan; never merged; author folio-qa-bot) ├── index.json newest entry per ref ├── main/<commit-sha>/ one tree per main commit that published │ ├── manifest.json inputs, producers, the gates' result │ └── <instance>/test/results/** byte-identical to the checkout's layout └── pr/<number>/<head-sha>/… same shape, pruned 7 days after close . Everything goes through cat-harness-tools/scripts/qa-store.ts, and nothing else writes the branch. check:workflows fails a raw push (qa-reports-unretried). | command | does | . | bun run cat qa:fetch [--ref main\|<sha>\|pr/<n>] | read an entry | . | bun run cat qa:publish --ref main/<sha>\|pr/<n>/<sha> | write one. Fetch the tip, splice, commit-tree -p, push without -f, 3 attempts with backoff | . | bun run cat qa:refresh | produce the working copy a publish stores, and say whether it is complete (below) | . | bun run cat qa:publish --github --completeness <report> | CI’s form: derive the key, skip a fork PR with a ::notice, and refuse an incomplete refresh | . | bun run cat qa:prune [--apply] | retention, as a dry run unless --apply. Daily in qa-reports-prune.yml | . A read answers one of five states. hit exits 0, miss 1, usage 2, corrupt 3, unknown 4. A miss is never read as “no findings”. A reader must not turn an absent entry into an empty, clean directory. What qa-publish stores is produced in that job, not handed over by the gates. The gates are in judge mode and write nothing, so their checkout holds only what is committed. So qa:refresh runs first. While the checkout still tracks test/results/, it runs nothing, because the commit’s own copy is the record and main/<sha> must be byte-identical to it. Once nothing is tracked there, it runs every writer declared in QA_WRITERS (scripts/qa-refresh.ts) into the empty tree. Then it checks three things. A file no writer claims, a writer that produced nothing, or a writer that exited outside its declared exits makes the run INCOMPLETE: the job fails, and qa:publish --completeness refuses to store it. A partial entry is never published as the commit’s record. Adding a QA writer means adding it to QA_WRITERS, or the first CI run after its first file lands goes red naming the unclaimed path. qa-publish is a job, not a gate. It runs after gates whatever they concluded (the evidence of a red commit is evidence too). It is the only job holding contents: write, and bun run cat gates never runs it locally. Its red means the record was not stored, never that the commit is bad (ci-health). Diagram: sdlc/processes/qa-publish.bpmn, called from Task_QaPublish in code-quality-gates.bpmn. Whose branch: each layer publishes its own . The branch is the store of the repository that declares it. A layer repository that declares a qa directory with storage (test/results/, keyed by commit) keeps its results on cat/cat-harness/qa-reports of its own repository, keyed by its own commits. Its .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml calls the tools layer’s reusable layer-qa-publish.yml, which audits that one instance with the layer at the pushed commit and publishes main/<sha> or pr/<n>/<sha>. An index reads a mounted layer’s results from that layer’s store at the commit its lock pins (scripts/layer-qa.ts, readQaTreeAtCommit), and never from its own store. A pin the layer has not published is a miss naming the commit. cat-harness, and the instances it hosts (kgQaHomeFor “hosted”), are still written by the index’s qa-publish. A layer that stops committing test/results/ without a publisher keeps its verdicts nowhere, so setting a layer up includes the caller (initialization step 5, sub-kg-lifecycle stage 10 “its QA record”), and init-folio --instance writes it.

3677.title: Gates compute and judge
3677.content: A gate over the qa graph does not compare a fresh run against a committed file, because the committed file is not the record. Its --check form computes and judges, and writes nothing: . | A finding fails only if it is NEW against a baseline. The baseline is the committed working copy for now, and --against <ref> reads it from qa-reports (for example --against main). Inherited findings are counted and reported, but they do not fail this change. | A missing baseline is UNKNOWN. It is printed, it is never a pass, and it is never a fail, because an unwritten baseline is not this change’s defect. | The four judge states are ok (exit 0), finding (1), unknown (2) and error (2), from JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. An unknown from a source that would not read outranks a finding, because a sweep that was blind on one part has not cleared the others. | . Each script’s docblock says which form it is in.

3678.title: Attestations
3678.content: . | A writer moves judgements as it saves. If a writer finds judgements in a prior derived file and the store holds no entry for them, it moves them into the store as it saves. bun run cat qa:attestations:migrate does a whole instance at once, and :check exits 1 while any judgement is still only in a derived file. | A corrupt store reads UNKNOWN and is refused. No writer overwrites it, and no writer regenerates past it. | Two disagreeing judgements are a person’s to reconcile. The migration refuses that case, and so should you. Never take one side. | Commit the store file. It is authored content on main, the same class as a review verdict. | .

3684.title: Two of the three lanes are human, and that is the design
3684.content: A QC gate is a decision, and the processes put it in a reviewer’s lane — QC reviewer, PR reviewer / QC reviewer — not the build’s. The build’s lane runs the checks; the reviewer’s lane rules on them. The qc-reviewer role holds qa-reporting as a permission, and qa-reporting is also held by ci-pipeline and ig-publisher-service. That a build system and a human share a permission is deliberate: emitting a QA report is mechanical, ruling on it is not. editing-hci-validation.bpmn marks Task_ReviewFindings and Gateway_EditorDecision relaxable="false": the editor seeing the findings, and the decision itself, are the gate.

3685.title: Compute the gate, do not assert it
3685.content: Where a gateway carries <cat-harness.processes:decision/>, pass the facts — e.g. { failCritical: 0, failMajor: 2 } from qa_sweep totals — and let the DMN table return the branch. workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at such a gateway. decisions/draft-qa-gate.dmn is the table; dmn-authoring is how to change it.

3686.title: Severity is the gate’s vocabulary
3686.content: The corpus-wide convention, and what the tables read: . | critical — a broken reference: something names a thing that does not exist, and a consumer following it gets nothing. Blocks. | major — a missing join: intact, but a question has no answer. | minor — coverage. Has legitimate instances, so it must not gate; forcing a fake entry onto a real step is worse than the gap. | . unknown is never counted as a pass, and it is not promoted either — it counts at its own criterion’s severity: a check that did not run has not cleared.

3695.title: Ref stewardship — one ref, many writers, one steward
3695.content: Skill ref-stewardship: Steward a WATCHED REF — a long-lived branch many processes write and one consumer serialises. Covers what makes a ref need a steward at all, why a coalescing window is a different object from a hold, the four durable fields a window needs so a handover cannot double-push, and the rule that a steward stores decisions and reads facts live. Use for “gh-pages is cancelling its own deployments”, “two sessions pushed the same store branch”, “who owns writes to this branch”, “coalesce these pushes”, and before giving any ref a concurrency policy. Named by: Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, Merge to main, A merge train, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Guideline Updates . A watched ref is a long-lived branch that several processes write and that something downstream consumes serially. main is one. gh-pages is one. Each cat/cat-harness/* store branch is one. A feature branch is not — it has one writer and no downstream serialisation, and giving it a steward buys nothing and adds a single point of failure. A watched ref is main, gh-pages, or a branch a declaring directory’s storage (or source) names. There is no central table. A ref nothing declares is not a watched ref, and this skill does not apply to it.

3696.title: What a steward is FOR, and what it must not become
3696.content: role-model: nothing is a steward. An actor acts as one inside a process, for the duration of a lane, over one named ref. The ref is a parameter of the lane instance, not a property of the persona — which is why merge-steward names no ref in its own description and why a second contended ref can acquire a steward without a schema change. The rule it inherits from merge-queue: . A steward stores DECISIONS. It never stores a fact the host already knows. So a window may record when it opened, when it must close, who holds it, and who takes over. It must never record the ref’s tip SHA, a deployment’s conclusion, or whether the site is live. Those move, and a stored copy is a second answer that goes stale on the next push. MergeQueueEntrySchema.FORBIDDEN_FACT_KEYS refuses the tempting ones by name; a ref window is a sibling object under the same rule.

3697.title: A window is NOT a hold, and the difference is what ends it
3697.content: Per merge-queue §”A hold has an EXPIRY and a trigger”, a hold ends on the observation that lifts it, not a time. A hold whose reason you cannot restate from current facts is a habit. A coalescing window looks like a hold and is a different object: . |   | hold | coalescing window | . | what it is waiting for | a condition to become true | more arrivals | . | what ends it | the observation that lifts it | the clock, and a bound | . | why not the other way | a time cannot know the condition cleared | “no more arrivals” is only ever observable by waiting | . A window is timed because it waits on the absence of a future event, which has no observation; a hold waits on a present condition, which does. A hold that never ends starves, and a window that never closes starves identically. So a window carries a hard maximum and closes at it even while pushes keep arriving. A window that extends on every arrival is not a window, it is an outage with a timer.

3698.title: Coalesce into one write per window
3698.content: The shape, for a ref with n writers arriving in bursts: . | A write request does not push. It records its intent against the ref’s open window, opening one if none is open. | The window closes at its deadline — never later, whatever is still arriving. | The steward performs one write for the window, composing the requests. | Anything that arrived after the close belongs to the next window. | . Composition is only sound when the writes do not contend, and for a route-keyed store they do not: branch-store’s keyedBy: "route" gives each route one owning generator, so “nobody authored either side, so the newer generation wins”. Two requests for different routes compose by union. Two for the same route compose by taking the newer. The case that must still be reported: two same-route requests where different authors wrote both sides. Route keying says the newer wins, and that is correct for a regenerated page and wrong for authored content. A steward that silently takes the newer in that case has deleted the only signal that the two writers disagree. Report it; do not resolve it. Why a GitHub concurrency group is not a window . cancel-in-progress: false governs the RUNNING job, not the pending one, and GitHub cancels a PENDING job when a newer one queues for the same group. So a concurrency group keeps at most one pending run. It is not a queue, and cancel-in-progress: false is not coalescing — it protects the job in flight and silently drops the intermediate ones. It is worth having to protect the job in flight, and must not be described as coalescing. No concurrency setting can coalesce bursts of writes to a ref like gh-pages; that needs a steward.

3699.title: The window’s four durable fields — because of HANDOVER
3699.content: A window that lives in one agent’s head is lost at handover, and the next steward then either waits for a window that will never close or opens a second one and double-pushes. So the window is committed state, in the workflow-state graph under beans/workflows/, not a variable. The four fields are HoldSchema’s (schemas/sdlc/merge-queue.ts), for the same reason (bean-blocking’s ## Blocked on): a window with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one. schemas/sdlc/ref-window.ts is the type. Three fields are HoldSchema’s verbatim and the fourth is narrowed: . | field | for a window | without it | . | ref | the watched ref — HoldSchema’s waitsOn, narrowed from prose to a declared ref | a reader cannot tell which ref this window is for | . | since | when it opened | the deadline cannot be checked, only trusted | . | expires | the hard close — after since, enforced by refine | abandoned and open are indistinguishable | . | handoff | who takes it if this steward stops | the next steward cannot tell “mine to close” from “someone else’s in flight” | . Two more the type carries for the same reason. heldBy says whose window it is, and closedAt says whether the single write happened — absent means open OR abandoned, and expires is the only thing that tells those apart, so a reader must never take an absent closedAt for “still collecting”. There is no extend, and the object is strict, so an extra field is refused rather than ignored: expires is set once, at open, as a property of the type rather than a promise in prose. A hold’s expiry stops it outliving its justification; a window’s expiry is its justification, and also stops it outliving its burst.

3700.title: The two gaps a steward reports rather than fixes
3700.content: A declaration can disagree with the world in both directions, and a sweep that checks one direction reads as clean while the other is broken: . | a declared writer that no longer writes the ref — the declaration is stale; | a workflow that writes the ref and is not declared — the declaration is incomplete, and this is the one a grep over the declaration cannot find, because it is looking in the wrong file. | . For example, an action that defaults publish_branch: gh-pages writes the ref without naming it. Adding the missing line is the symptom; the fix is a gate comparing declared against measured and failing either way. And a sweep prints its denominator (generalise-the-fix §1.2a) — parsed 35 of 35 beside the verdict — and parses rather than matching text, since a plain string match also counts comments.

3701.title: What this does not do yet
3701.content: . | No steward runs over gh-pages. The ref is declared; until its producers write through branch-store’s route keying there is no window to hold. | No steward runs over the cat/cat-harness/* refs. They are seeded and declared and, per their declarations, “not authoritative”. A steward over a ref nobody reads from would be ceremony. | Nothing writes a window yet. schemas/sdlc/ref-window.ts types one and ref-window.test.ts holds it to the handover rules, but no steward opens one, because there is nothing to coalesce until the producers stop pushing directly. The type comes first so that a steward’s handover is tested before the steward exists. | The parity between the window and the hold is behavioural, not structural. SHARED_LEASE_FIELDS is the declared list and the test removes each field from both schemas and requires both to refuse. A key-list comparison would not work: a .refine() does not expose its inner object, and a parity check that silently compared two empty lists would pass forever. | .
