3703.title: Refresh materialized remote content
3703.content: Process_RefreshMaterialized · strict · 8 step(s) . Keep a materialized copy of remote content current: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both did — an archival copy is never re-fetched and gets a fixity check instead. One general process, used everywhere. REFRESH IS NOT RE-IMPORT: it needs three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally since, and what to do when BOTH did. upstream-pins.json answers the first for one caller and nothing answers the other two anywhere. An ARCHIVAL copy is not refreshed. Re-fetching it would defeat it: the copy exists to survive the source, so replacing it with whatever the source says today discards exactly the state it was keeping. What an archive gets instead is a FIXITY CHECK — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy. i i i i i i i i

3704.title: How it connects
3704.content: . | Called by: Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph | Calls: Adjudication | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

3705.title: Lanes — who acts
3705.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Contributor (human or agent) | user | Reached only when both upstream and local changed, which is the one case this process refuses to resolve by rule: which side wins depends on why the local edit was made, a fact only this lane has. | . | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | ingestion-agent | Runs whichever of the two paths Gateway_Purpose selects. On the working path it answers the two comparisons — upstream and local — whose combination Gateway_Both reads to decide whether a human must adjudicate; on the archival path it never compares to the source at all, since fixity asks only whether the copy itself rotted. | .

3706.title: Steps
3706.content: Every one of the 8 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | ARCHIVAL verify fixity — never re-fetchTask_Fixity | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Re-compute the digest and compare. An archive is NEVER re-fetched — the source is what it exists to survive, so replacing it with today’s version discards the state it was keeping. A mismatch means OUR copy rotted, and the remedy is restoration from a backup, not re-download. | . | WORKING what changed upstreamTask_Upstream | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Compare the recorded upstreamVersion against the source. could not reach the source is a THIRD answer and is never reported as unchanged — an unreachable source is the sourceLoss gate firing late. Reachability is asked by bun run cat sources:liveness <instance> against the node’s resolvable IRI, its Handle first: live, gone, or could not determine, never live on an error. | . | What changed LOCALLY sinceTask_Local | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | The half nothing answers today. A materialized copy that was edited in place is not a copy any more, and overwriting it silently destroys work whose existence the process never established. | . | Adjudicate the conflictTask_Adjudicate | Contributor (human or agent) | calls Adjudicationmaterialize-remoteadjudication | A human or agentic decision, never a merge rule. Which side wins depends on why the local edit was made, and a process that picked automatically would be choosing without the one fact that decides it. | . | Reconcile the two by handTask_Reconcile | Contributor (human or agent) | materialize-remote | Neither side wins whole: the contributor produces content that is neither the local copy nor the remote one, and THEN it is applied. Drawn as a separate step before Task_Apply rather than folded into it, because Task_Apply re-asks the five import gates against what is being materialized — and what is being materialized here is a hand-made artefact, which is exactly the case those gates should see rather than be told about. | . | Re-materialize and record new fixityTask_Apply | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | The gates are re-asked, not inherited: a licence can change, and a collection can grow past the size a caller agreed to.AND THE NEW FIXITY IS RECORDED IN THE SAME CHANGE. This step rewrites bytes that a materialization record describes, so leaving the old digest behind would make a CORRECT run of this process fail check:materialized-fixity as a mismatch — the gate reading “somebody edited held content without saying so” about the one process whose job is to replace it.This is the publication exception, stated as a rule rather than as a carve-out, because a list of permitted writers goes stale when a writer is added. The exception is NOT “these actors may skip the rule”; it is “say what you did”. A writer that updates the digest alongside the bytes passes, and the record then describes what is actually there. A writer that does not fails, correctly, because it has forked upstream silently. | . | Keep the edit, re-pinTask_KeepLocal | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | The local edit wins, so nothing is re-materialized — and the pin moves to the upstream revision that was compared against. Re-pinning is the half that is easy to forget and is the reason this is a step rather than an absence: without it the same upstream change is detected as new on every cycle, and a contributor is asked the same settled question for ever. The record says the copy is deliberately divergent FROM a named revision, which is a different claim from being stale against an unknown one. | . | Record the conflict: no decision, no re-pinTask_RecordConflict | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | materialize-remote | Both copies stay and the conflict is written down with what each side says. Deliberately does not re-pin, which is the one thing separating it from Task_KeepLocal: the question is unresolved, so it must be asked again next cycle. Recording is not optional here for the reason A_RecordEntry is not optional in an adjudication — a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a check that never ran, and a DEFERRAL nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a refresh that silently did nothing. | .

3707.content: Every one of the 3 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | working, or archival?Gateway_Purpose | Is this copy kept as a working copy or as an archive? archival only verifies fixity and never re-fetches; working asks what changed upstream. | archival → ARCHIVAL verify fixity — never re-fetchworking → WORKING what changed upstream | . | Both changed?Gateway_Both | Did the copy change both upstream and locally since it was fetched? yes goes to adjudicating the conflict; no re-materializes, re-asking the five gates, and records the new fixity. | yes → Adjudicate the conflictno → Re-materialize and record new fixity | . | Which side, and on what terms?GW_Outcome | Four answers, and they do four different things; without this gateway the process would ask which side wins and then discard the answer.defer is not local wearing a different hat: local decides and re-pins, so the same conflict stops being raised; defer deliberately does not decide and does not re-pin, so it is raised again next cycle. A process that could only decide would force a contributor with no answer today to invent one. | the remote wins → Re-materialize and record new fixitythe local edit wins → Keep the edit, re-pinneither whole — reconcile → Reconcile the two by handnot decidable today → Record the conflict: no decision, no re-pin | .

3709.title: External registry — confirming a source’s authority
3709.content: Skill registry-authority-contract: The contract the external-registry role is held to when a candidate source is checked against the body that publishes it: resolve the identifier through its own API and return the record, so authority is a resolved fact. When the answer is uncertain or absent the verdict is not invented here; the work plan records the citation as unverified. A role played by an external party is held to a contract, not handed instructions. Named by: Evidence for a recommendation . external-registry (declared below this layer) is played by an external actor: trusted registries and observatories outside this instance’s control. A role played by something we do not run is still a role, and its skills are its contract: what we rely on it to do. This skill is the part of that contract this layer’s evidence diagram relies on, and nothing more. The registry list, its endpoints and the API bindings are not settled (the diagram is a STRAWPERSON), so no registry is named here.

3710.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
3710.content: Lane_Trusted in evidence-retrieval names this role and holds Task_VerifyAuthority and Gateway_Authoritative. What that lane’s documentation and the task’s say is the whole contract.

3711.title: What it must do
3711.content: . | Resolve the identifier at the publisher, through the standard API of the body that publishes the candidate. | Return the record it holds, so the citation’s claim, its version and its date can be compared with what the publisher says (the task’s documentation lists the checks). | .

3712.title: What happens when it does not answer
3712.content: The decision is a readout of what the external API returns, not this instance’s call. When that answer is uncertain or absent, Gateway_Authoritative takes the no branch and Lane_WorkPlan opens a bean for the unverified citation. The lane does not invent a verdict, and the citation is neither dropped nor silently kept. Whether a publisher is one this folio has declared trusted is the folio’s judgement, not the registry’s.

3713.title: Tests
3713.content: The test in tested-by: drives the evidence process with the harness’s workflow engine and checks that a no from Gateway_Authoritative leads to the bean for the unverified citation and that no step in the registry’s lane is a decision of this instance’s. Lines 1 and 2 are the registry’s own behaviour, on endpoints not yet chosen, and are not exercised.

3718.title: Categorize and summarize (judgement)
3718.content: Every hit gets exactly one category and a one-line summary giving its state and why it is in that category: . | category | meaning | . | overlaps: coordinate | the same thing, or changes the same files or process; left alone, the two will collide | . | affected by | this work will change what that item sees or does | . | out of scope | related, but deliberately not part of this work; say why | . | unrelated | a false match; list it only if a reader might assume otherwise | . 3719.title: Ask
3719.content: Put one question to the user, in the order context, then options, then recommendation (interaction-modality §4.1). Do not link, block, merge or comment on another item before the answer. Coordinating is a commitment made on behalf of that item’s owners.

3727.title: Release epic planning
3727.content: Skill release-epic-planning: Plan and track releases using work item epics. Covers epic creation, story/task decomposition, release readiness tracking, and the relationship between epics and GitHub milestones. Applies to code releases, paper publications, and project milestones. Named by: Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, IRIS CDN initial load . A release epic groups all the work for a specific release version. This skill governs how to create, structure, and track them.

3728.title: Epic structure
3728.content: The work items hierarchy for a release: . epic: "Release v0.2.0" ├── feature: "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" │ ├── task: "Add Phase 4b to crdm-requirements-workflow.md" │ └── task: "Update phase table" ├── feature: "Release lifecycle skills" │ ├── task: "Create release-lifecycle.md" │ ├── task: "Create code-review-process.md" │ └── task: "Create branch-freshness.md" └── bug: "Fix 7 BPMN isMarkerVisible attributes" └── task: "Add isMarkerVisible to 5 files" . Bean types in a release context . | Type | Role in release | Granularity | . | epic | The release itself | 1 per release | . | feature | A capability area / user story | 1 per feature | . | task | A single PR-sized implementation unit | 1 per PR | . | bug | A defect fix included in the release | 1 per fix | . | milestone | A session-scoped work container | Not release-scoped | . Creating the hierarchy . # 1. Create the release epic beans create "Release v0.2.0" --type epic # 2. Create features under it beans create "CRDM Phase 4b prioritization" --type feature beans update <feature-id> --parent <epic-id> # 3. Create tasks under features beans create "Add Phase 4b to workflow" --type task beans update <task-id> --parent <feature-id> . Always check before creating — beans create is not idempotent. See todo-manager.md §”Check before you create”.

3729.title: Ordering within a release
3729.content: Apply the Phase 4b formalize-first rule from crdm-requirements-workflow.md: . | Structural/organizational work first | Process/policy formalization second | Implementation third | Visualization/UI last | . Within the epic, number features by dependency order. The first feature completed should not depend on any later feature.

3730.title: Release readiness
3730.content: Tracking readiness . The work items visualizer (<base>/beans/) shows open work items grouped by epic. A release is ready when its epic shows 0 open work items. Readiness checklist . Before moving from draft to pre-release: . | All must-have features resolved (all child work items completed) | All should-have features either resolved or deferred to next release | CI green on main (bun run cat gates) | All changed BPMN diagrams re-rendered | All changed docs pages regenerated | Changelog written (see release-lifecycle.md) | BA has reviewed accumulated changes | . Deferring to next release . If a should-have or nice-to-have feature won’t make the release: . # Move the feature bean to the next release epic beans update <feature-id> --parent <next-epic-id> . Record the deferral reason in the work item body: . beans update <feature-id> --body-append "Deferred to v0.3.0: not blocking v0.2.0" .

3731.title: GitHub milestone integration (optional)
3731.content: A GitHub milestone can mirror the release epic for stakeholder visibility: . # Create milestone gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/milestones --method POST \ -f title="v0.2.0" -f description="Release v0.2.0" # Assign PRs to milestone gh pr edit <number> --milestone "v0.2.0" . The milestone’s completion percentage gives stakeholders a progress view without needing access to the work items store.

3746.title: Remote-mount a harness
3746.content: Skill remote-mount: Bring a harness, and every instance it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a source.remote entry in the downstream’s root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration) and mountDefaults on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no .deps/, the transitive closure through needs and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states. Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Human Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Agent activity log, The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use, Is CI actually working on the default branch?, Code change and review, The gates a change must pass before it can merge, Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down, Check a generated file still matches its source, Are the .jsonld siblings still in sync with their .ts manifests?, Merge the base branch in, Merge to main, A merge train, Which open pull requests have no CI run on their head?, Alert the publication manager, Verify the export before it is deployed, Publish and keep QA results on qa-reports, Is the repository itself healthy?, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Report a verdict on one tracking issue, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Authoring a document, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Review and publish a folio, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . How a downstream folio gets the layers it is built on: . | no git submodules, ever; | no .deps/, because a dot directory collides with GitHub’s conventions and with this repository’s own dot-prefix guard; | a remote mount is a declared directory with a remote source, pinned to a full 40-character SHA; | the defaults live in the harness’s own declaration, so a downstream never restates the paths; | a downstream may override them by id, never by path; | mounts are resolved transitively across the dependency closure; | code arrives through the mounted code directories. | . |   | where | . | the process | mount-dependency.bpmn; the per-subgraph view is the remote and npm flows of mount-subgraph.bpmn | . | the schema | cat-harness/schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts, plus the remote, npm and hydrated members of SubgraphSource (schemas/kg/subgraph-source.ts); the per-pin index package is subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts | . | the tool | bun run cat mount:remote (--plan to resolve without writing), and bun run cat mount:remote:check (offline) | . | the entry point | bun run cat state:mount, which the session-start hook already runs | .

3747.title: Mount, subscribe or associate: choose first
3747.content: | you want | relation | what arrives | . | to build on a harness: run its scripts, import its schemas, read its skills as your own | remote mount (source.remote in index.config.json) | the harness’s declared directories and those of everything it needs, at one pin | . | to read another graph and hold chosen parts of it | subscription (subscriptions): the kg-subscription skill | a snapshot of its declaration, then parts you materialise one at a time through the five gates | . | to know of a harness and link to it | association (associatedHarnesses): the associate-harness skill | nothing | . | to retrieve or distribute as a package | npm distribution (kg-retrieve-npm, source.npm): the npm-kg-distribution skill | an npm .tgz tarball (unhydrated source or hydrated view) | . The test is whether your code imports theirs. If it does, mount. If you only read their content, subscribe: a subscription gates every part through copyright and purpose, and a mount does not, because the code it brings is the platform you are built on.

3748.title: The two halves of the declaration
3748.content: The harness side goes in the harness’s own <name>.json and is written once by the harness’s owner: . "mountDefaults": { "path": "cat-harness", "directories": ["schemas", "scripts", "skills"] } . What arrives is what the declaration NAMES: the declaration itself, the chosen directories, and the instance-scoped files in its assets (its README and AGENTS.md). A file the declaration does not name, such as a platform.ts beside it, never arrives. Code the mounted graphs import has to sit in a declared directory. Both fields are optional, and each absence has a meaning: . | path absent means the instance’s home path (livesAt.path, else its directory in its own repository). | directories absent means every declared directory whose content is in the checkout. A branch, family or remote source is somebody’s state, not part of the harness. | . The downstream side goes in the checkout’s root index.config.json, as the source.remote of the instance it brings in. Which instances a checkout instantiates, where each comes from, and the fallback for a folio with no index are index-config’s rule. This skill covers only what a remote source means once it is declared: . { "name": "<harness>", "source": { "remote": { "repository": "<owner>/<repo>", "ref": "<40-character sha>", "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "directories": ["schemas", "skills"] }, "bootstrap": { "skip": true } } } } } . The fields are a remoteMounts entry without its harness, because the instance’s name is the harness (RemoteSourceSchema in schemas/kg/index-config.ts). A folio with no index still reads remoteMounts on its declaration. Declaring a mount in both places is an error: readDeclaredMounts throws and names both files. bun run cat index-config:migrate --write moves the entries across. Every tool that writes mounts writes through writeDeclaredMounts, into index.config.json, and none writes remoteMounts. overrides is keyed by instance name, then by directory id: . | path moves an instance. | directories replaces its default list. An id may be one the instance declares in its <name>.json or from within one of those directories (a "subgraph": true entry of skills/skills.json, such as voices); both are resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories, the resolver every on-disk reader uses. A nested id mounts its own path alone. An id declared in neither place is refused, not dropped, and the refusal says where it looked. The same holds for the harness’s own mountDefaults.directories. An id may also be a concern name, a code from code-lists/concern-group.json such as sdlc. It expands to every kind-first member the instance declares, such as sdlc/processes/ and sdlc/skills/, read from each grouping kind’s own declaration file at the pin. Each member is locked as <directory id>/<code>. A code that none of the instance’s kinds declares is refused like any other unknown id. | After a review of hydrated metadata, `mount:remote –choose [:] --directories a,b --tools x,y` writes the choice into `overrides.` (the choice, never the state), so a fresh clone replays it. It ends the review: that instance mounts as files, so its `hydrated` is dropped. The pin and consent do not move. | skip leaves it unmounted, and the lock records it as an answer. | tools names Tools this instance declares, by id, and mounts each one runnable: its definition, its implementation and their import closure. The next section but one says what that brings. | hydrated: true (here, or on the entry for its harness) mounts each chosen directory as one file: its published index.hydrated.jsonld at the pin, a hydrated source. Read what is there, then choose what to mount as files. No declaration is laid down, and needs is not followed. Where that file comes from is the next section. With no directories, a hydrated mount offers every top-level in-checkout subgraph and ignores mountDefaults.directories on purpose: that list chooses which FILES a downstream gets, and a hydrated mount is the step before choosing. Each top-level file already carries its nested subgraphs inline (hasSubgraph), so a nested one is named only when you want it on its own. | .

3749.title: Hydrated: the index files are published per pin, in a package
3749.content: A pin’s subgraph index files (index.jsonld, index.hydrated.jsonld under <docs>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/) are published per pin in a package, and a hydrated mount fetches them through the Tool its source names (the hydrated source’s tool, which is remote-mount unless it says otherwise). | Not committed in each repository. The files are builtAtPublish: they are computed over the checkout’s other instances, so no commit can hold them current, and a committed copy turns every re-pin’s check red. | Not generated at mount time. The downstream would need the whole index, kg-export and the framing toolchain to read one file of metadata, which is the cost a hydrated mount exists to avoid, and two downstreams could frame two different files for one pin. | . What that means in practice: . |   |   | . | the package | <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>: the index files at their published paths, and subgraph-index.json (folio-subgraph-index/v1) giving each file’s sha256 and the repository, pin and harness | . | where | assets of the GitHub release subgraph-index-<sha> in the instance’s repository, with the tarball’s folio-binary-release/v1 record beside it. Every name is computed (subgraphIndexPackage in schemas/kg/subgraph-manifest.ts) | . | who publishes | the subgraph-index-package Tool, run on every push to main by the reusable workflow layer-publish-subgraph-index.yml (the tools layer); a harness opts in with one uses: line | . | what a mount checks | the pin’s git tree first (a commit that does carry the file still works); otherwise the package: the tarball against its record (size, sha256), the manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, each file against its sha256, then the same schema and subgraph-IRI check a tree file gets | . | the lock | a directory that came from the package records the tarball’s URL and sha256 and the file’s path in it (package), so mount:lock fetches the same bytes and refuses any others | . No release for the pin is missing, and the detail says the package was looked for. A package that fails a check is missing; one that could not be fetched is could-not-determine. Neither is ever an empty mount. The record travels with the tarball, so its digest proves the transfer, not the publisher: who may publish is the repository’s write access, the same trust the git tree at the pin already rests on.

3750.title: Tools: choose by id, mount runnable
3750.content: The workflow: load the Tools’ metadata, review it, then materialise a chosen set. The first step is a hydrated mount of the declaring instance’s tools directory. Its index.hydrated.jsonld holds every Tool whole, and each Tool is its own tools/<id>/ subgraph. The last step is tools on that instance’s override: . "overrides": { "cat-harness": { "tools": ["bean-query", "bpmn-checklist", "agent-memory"] } } . Three rules govern this step: . | A Tool brings both halves. Its definition is <tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts in the instance that declares it, by the folder convention in schemas/tools/tool-folders.ts. Its implementation is what its invoke names: . | inProcess.module, found in the declarer or in an instance whose needs names it (resolveImplementingPath’s rule; two holders is refused); | the script a bun run cat <key> command resolves to through the instances’ checkoutScripts. | . A bare runtime command (gh, beans) or manual brings no code. Both halves arrive with their import closure. A definition without its code is not a Tool you can run, and code without the modules it imports does not load: either way the checkout is half-working. | One closure walker. The closure is bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (scripts/check-closure.ts). check:tools-closure and the staging cone use the same walk. Do not write a second walker: two of them give two answers to “what does this code load”. | Directory granularity. The mount brings every declared directory the closure touches, whole. It takes the most specific declared directory (a nested one such as skills/voices mounts alone) and never a single file, so the lock schema is unchanged. A closure file in no declared directory, and an import that resolves to nothing, are refused with the file named. Neither is ever dropped. | . With tools named anywhere in a mount entry, each instance of that entry mounts the directories the closure touches, plus any its override names in directories. It does not mount its default list. A whole instance stays whole. A Tool id the instance does not declare at the pin is refused at plan time. tools together with hydrated is refused, because metadata brings no code. What it costs. A Tool folder is not a declared directory: tools/ is, and most definitions import its lib.ts. So a definition arrives with the whole tools directory, which holds every Tool’s definition. The cost that matters falls on the implementation side, which brings the directories its closure touches (in the tools layer, typically scripts and src). Without tools, the tools layer mounts every in-checkout directory it declares. The end-to-end check is the remote-mount test “load tools metadata, choose three Tools, materialise them” in the tools layer.

3751.title: Why the default path is the home path
3751.content: At its home path, a mounted instance keeps its position relative to its siblings. Two things then follow with no extra machinery: . | instanceRootsIn scans one level deep, so it finds every mounted sibling and needs resolves exactly as it does in the monorepo. | A relative import such as ../../cat-harness/schemas/… finds the file it names. | . Moving an instance by override is allowed, and the overlay still finds it through the lock (mountedInstanceRoots, mountScopeFor). The override is then responsible for any import that climbs out of the moved instance.

3752.title: The closure
3752.content: . | The harness’s declaration is read from the pinned tree, not from this checkout. | Each needs name is looked for in the same tree. | If it is not there, the planner looks for a gitlink at that tree’s root. A submodule entry is itself a pin, so a need on bootstrap resolves to litlfred/bootstrap at the gitlink’s SHA. The downstream gets the bytes and never a submodule. | A need the downstream already holds as a local instance is local: it is supplied by the checkout and never mounted over. | A need found nowhere is missing. It is never dropped. | .

3753.title: The lock, and the three states
3753.content: index.lock.json sits beside the downstream’s index.config.json and is committed. It is generated by mount:remote and never hand-edited, which is why it is a separate file rather than part of the index. Readers also accept the legacy name <name>.mount-lock.json, and both present is an error. It records: . | the pins it was written for; | for each instance: the repository, the SHA, how the pin was found (declared / same-tree / gitlink), the declaration’s digest, each directory’s tree digest, and declared instance assets (such as package.json); | what was not mounted, and why. | . The mounted bytes are not committed. With an index, each mount path is ignored by a generated block in the root .gitignore, written from the index (check:index-ignores is the gate). A path that block does not cover is reported as missing, never patched locally, because a local exclude is invisible to every other clone. In a folio with no index, a path its rules do not ignore goes into the worktree’s info/exclude. Mount path and route collisions. A mount with no path override lands at <name>/ in the downstream root, beside the downstream’s own directories, and its site routes sit beside the site-wide ones. To prevent collisions on disk and in route space: . | Reserved names: RESERVED_ROOT_AND_ROUTE_NAMES in schemas/kg/remote-mount.ts declares the one authoritative list of reserved root directories and site route names: ["skills", "tools", "docs", "assets", "glossary", "api", "payload", "branches/", "beans", "todos", "fsh-guts", "uploads", "test", "build", "_site", "_docs", "_kg"]. | Mount path check: checkMountPathCollisions (run during planning in mount:remote and by bun run cat check:mount-collisions) rejects any remote mount whose effective path (path or <name>/) collides with: . | a directory the downstream declares in its own configuration; | a reserved root or site route name; | another mount’s path. When a collision occurs, the error states how to fix it: “set path” (on the instance’s overrides.<name>.path in index.config.json or source.remote.overrides). | . | Route rules: . | Canonical: every visualiser is reachable at <base>/<harness>/<visualizer>/. Every generated link uses that form unless an alias is declared. | Alias: <base>/<visualizer>/ exists only when a declaration opts in via alias: true or alias: "<alias>" in its Visualisation declaration (coverage.visualiser). The site build refuses an alias that collides with another alias, a harness route, or a reserved site route, and names both claimants. | The route rule itself is in schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes”. | . | . Every instance ends in exactly one state: . | state | means | exit | . | mounted | on disk, hashing to the lock | 0 | . | unverified-approver | mounted, on consent no mountApprovers list checked | 0, reported apart | . | missing | not on disk, edited since mounting, not in the tree, refused, or the lock is for other pins | 1 | . | could-not-determine | the fetch failed, a declaration or lock is unreadable, or an instance is reached at two pins | 2 | . Could-not-determine outranks missing, and missing outranks mounted. A fetch that failed is never an empty layer. Re-pinning: from a checkout mounted from the lock . A re-pin is mount:remote --seed <name>=<owner/repo>@<sha> (it writes the pin and its consent into index.config.json), then mount:remote (it lays the bytes down and rewrites the lock). Do it in a checkout whose mounts match the lock: a fresh one, or one replayed by .github/mount-from-lock.sh. A mount with local edits is left untouched by the next mount, at its old commit, while the lock’s top-level pin moves, so CI would keep testing the old layer. --seed refuses while a mount it moves has such edits, and mount:check reports an instance entry behind its pin as missing. After the re-pin, check that the moved instance’s sha in index.lock.json is the new pin. The committer re-pins, locally, and CI only verifies. The person or agent who moves a pin does the whole re-pin in their own checkout: --seed, a fresh mount:remote, the regenerated agent surface (skill:commands, agent-memory, index:render), and the local checks. That same mount:remote then publishes the new lock’s layers cache ref (below) alongside the branch, with whatever credential pushes the branch. bun run cat layers:publish retries it, and --no-layers-publish skips it. CI never builds the ref when it exists: it fetches it and verifies it against the lock. Two writers are only fallbacks: . | the re-pin train, for layers nobody re-pinned; | main’s post-merge workflow, which rebuilds the ref for every push that changes index.lock.json. | . The layers cache: one fetch, every byte still verified . Replaying a lock fetches each pinned instance from its own repository. The layers cache is one git commit in the INDEX repository whose tree is the composed overlay a replay lays down: each locked directory at its mount path, each declaration and asset, and nothing an install, a state mount or a publish build wrote. | Ref: refs/cat/layers/<key>, where the key is the sha256 of the lock’s instances. refs/cat/layers/main moves with main’s lock. | Reader: mount:lock, and through it .github/mount-from-lock.sh, the session-start hook and every CI job, first tries ONE shallow fetch of the key’s ref, then of main. A layer whose copy verifies is laid down from it. A layer that does not verify, or a ref that is missing, is fetched from its own repository as before. --no-layers-cache (or CAT_LAYERS_CACHE=0) skips it, and CAT_LAYERS_URL points it at another remote. | Writer: the committer, through mount:remote or layers:publish. It refuses unless every mount reads current, then pushes the overlay. --main also moves main. --prune <n> keeps the newest n lock refs, main, and each --keep <key>, for example the lock of every open PR. | . The lock stays the sole authority. The cache is untrusted. Every byte taken from it is checked against the lock: the declaration’s and each asset’s sha256, and each directory’s treeDigest. These are the same checks a fetched byte passes. So a stale main still serves every layer that did not move, and a tampered ref costs time, never correctness. Trust is unchanged: consent was checked when the lock was written, and the cache cannot add an instance the lock does not name. A replay that fails is reported loudly, not swallowed: a stale mount makes local checks pass falsely.

3754.title: A changed lock re-renders the agent surface
3754.content: A mount is not done when the bytes are on disk. A newly pinned layer can bring new skills, renamed skills and new agent-memory entries, but an agent does not read the layer: it reads what is generated from it. | surface | generated by | from | . | .claude/commands/<name>.md | skill:commands | every user_invocable skill in the mounted kg graphs | . | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md, .agents/skills/, .agents/rules/ | agent-memory | the memory directories the mounted instances declare | . So when a mount:remote run changes the lock, it runs both generators from the checkout root before it exits, and a generator that fails fails the run. A re-pin commit then carries the new layers and the surface rendered from them. --no-agent-surface opts out; --check, --plan and --staging never run it, since they change no lock a commit would carry. The list lives in one place, AGENT_SURFACE_GENERATORS in cat-harness-tools/scripts/remote-mount.ts. A new generator of something an agent reads (a rule file, a settings hook) is added there, not to a checklist: a step a person has to remember is the step that gets skipped. The process step is Task_RenderAgentSurface in mount-dependency.bpmn, between writing the lock and checking against it.

3755.title: Trust: what lets a mount proceed (H8)
3755.content: A real mount needs a person’s consent for that pin (trust.consent); a --staging mount needs none. schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts has the rules. Four things to know: . | The lock records the basis for each instance: staging, or consent with who and when. mount:remote:check re-runs the trust check against the current declaration, so consent withdrawn later reads refused. | A gitlink needs consent of its own. An instance reached through a gitlink is another repository at another commit. Give its consent on overrides.<name>.trust, for the gitlink’s SHA. | Who may consent. Declare mountApprovers and a consent.by not on the list is refused. Without the list, mounts report unverified-approver: exit 0, but never shown as clean. A checkout whose mounts index.config.json lists declares the list there, as its top-level mountApprovers; declaring it on the instance declaration as well is an error. | A refused mount is not current. Its old bytes stay on disk (an agent does not delete them). The lock records them under unmounted as leftOnDisk, and the check reports them as not mounted. | . Standing consent: a site keeps itself on an upstream branch . Pins stay per site. A site may declare, on one instance’s trust.standing, that a named person consents to following a branch — {follows: "main", consentBy, consentAt, require?: "green"}. The repin tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/repin-standing.ts, run by its standing-repin.yml workflow) then moves that pin to the branch’s newest (green) commit and writes trust.consent for the new pin, by that person and marked standing. The mount accepts it only while the same rule is still declared: withdraw or edit it and those pins ask again. A pin moved by hand still asks again, rule or not.

3756.title: Publishing a remote-mounted downstream — provision gh-pages first
3756.content: A mount brings layers into a checkout; it provisions nothing on the downstream’s remote. A downstream that publishes a site needs a gh-pages branch before GitHub Pages can be switched on, exactly as a new repository does. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in the getting-started process (getting-started §5), with the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision (idempotent, never forced; without the flag it only reports unprovisioned and the exact command), then set Pages to “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)”. A worked example is in repo-conversion §5.

3757.title: Never
3757.content: . | Never add a submodule to get a dependency, and never clone into .deps/. | Never pin a branch or an abbreviated SHA. The schema refuses both. | Never edit a mounted directory and expect a re-mount to keep the edit, or to throw it away. A re-mount leaves edited bytes untouched and reports them as missing. Move the edit upstream, or delete the directory and re-mount. | Never mount over tracked files, or over a directory that no lock says this mount made. Both are refused. | Never read missing or could-not-determine as “that layer has nothing in it”. A layer that is not mounted is absent from every overlay. | .

3761.title: Staging and release are the same step
3761.content: A preview is this with a root under the release root; a release is this with the release root. What differs belongs to the caller: who may start it, what must be reviewed or verified first, what else lives on the same host and must survive the push. That is why feature-staging and docs-site-publish both call this process rather than restating it, and keep their own steps — the slug, the render log, restoring the open previews, the publication-manager alert — around the call.

3762.title: Name the Tool, not its steps
3762.content: The general process has one call activity, bound by the Tool: the activity names this skill, the Tool for the chosen target satisfies it, and the Tool lists its own subprocesses — the diagram of its steps (skills-and-tools, bpmn-processes). The general skill never lists them. | target | Tool | its subprocess | its message | . | GitHub Pages | gh-pages | bootstrap-tools processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn | the commit merged onto gh-pages + the QA of what is staged and what is served | . A target may need provisioning before it accepts a push; the Tool’s subprocess owns that. For GitHub Pages a gh-pages branch has to exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it, so the gh-pages subprocess creates it first — the general step does not. Another CDN is another Tool with its own subprocess, and nothing here changes. A CDN in front of an origin is a layer, not a publication host (kg-to-portal): the publication root URL stays the origin’s canonical one even when a CDN serves it.

3763.title: What this is not
3763.content: Not the verification of what a build produced — that is publish-verification, and it runs before a caller hands its tree over. Not the decision to release — content-publish and release-lifecycle. This step renders, pushes, and says whether the push landed.

3771.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages
3771.content: Skill render-kg-to-github-pages: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, to GitHub Pages at a publication root URL, and report the push: a status (pushed, not pushed, could not determine) and one message carrying the deployed commit and the QA result. The same steps for a staging preview and for a release; only the root URL differs. Named by: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages . Inputs, each named by whoever starts the process: . | input | what | default | . | the Knowledge Graph | an instance root, the directory holding its <name>.json | none; required | . | Subgraphs | a list of directory ids from that declaration | the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | the declaration’s iriBase, else https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ | . Output: a status and a message, and nothing else a caller must read. | status | when | . | pushed | the staged tree had no problem, the root URL answers, its README page (README.html) answers, and every document address answers | . | not-pushed | a check ran and failed: a staging problem, or a 404 at the root or at a document address | . | could-not-determine | nothing failed, but an answer was about the way here (403, 407, 5xx, no network) | . The message is one line a caller posts as it stands: pushed 1a2b3c4 to <root> — QA: staged ok (N files, M documents); root 200; README.html 200; documents M/M answer. The commit is which bytes are live: the commit on the gh-pages branch the site is served from. Staging and release are not two processes. A preview is this process with a root under the release root (…/branches/<slug>/, say) and a release is it with the release root. Anything that differs between them (who may start it, what must be reviewed first) belongs to the process that calls this one, never in here.

3772.title: The steps
3772.content: Drawn in processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Every command below is run from bootstrap-tools, with the instance as --root. | Resolve the inputs. Read the declaration; check every Subgraph id is one it declares; settle the root URL. An unknown id is refused, never rendered as a smaller site. | Make sure gh-pages exists and Pages serves it. Pages cannot be switched on to serve a branch that does not exist, so in order: . | git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages; if absent, push an orphan placeholder (index.html + .nojekyll); | Pages on, Source = branch gh-pages, folder /: gh api -X POST repos/<o>/<r>/pages -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/' when gh is signed in, otherwise the manual step (Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages, / (root)). bun run scripts/init.ts --root <instance> runs both as site:branch and site:enabled. This provisioning belongs to this process, not to the publication step that calls it. | . | Stage the rendering. bun run scripts/site.ts --root <instance> --out <dir> [--subgraph <id>]…: every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document at the IRI it names, the files as they sit, the README page as README.md — served at <root>/README.html — and index.html, a redirect to it. The redirect is only the default: an instance that carries its own index.html or index.md at its root gets that as its landing page instead. Every generated page opens with a notice naming bootstrap-tools and the script that wrote it, and its footer links the generator and its source rather than GitHub’s editor, which would edit the gh-pages copy the next publish overwrites. | Check what was staged. site.ts --check and bun run scripts/readme-book.ts --root <instance> --check. Any problem stops here: the report says not-pushed and names the problem, and nothing is deployed. A push of a tree known to be broken is not a push to report. | Deploy. Commit the staged tree onto gh-pages as a full replace with bun run scripts/publish-site.ts --site <dir> --remote <git url>: the instance’s Pages workflow runs it on a push to main, and an agent runs it with its own git credentials for an instance that carries no workflow (bootstrap). GitHub Pages builds the branch (Jekyll, unless .nojekyll). A rejected push is rebuilt and retried, never rebased. The gh-pages commit is the one the message names. | Check what is served, and report. bun run scripts/pages-status.ts --root <instance> [--url <root>] [--sha <commit>] [--subgraph <id>]… asks the root URL and every document address, and prints the message; --json gives the whole record. Exit 0 pushed, 1 not-pushed, 3 could-not-determine. | .

3773.title: What this is not
3773.content: It is one target. A harness above these tools may have several ways of putting a rendering in front of readers, and treat GitHub Pages as one of them; nothing here needs to know that, and nothing here names it. It does not decide who may publish, whether review has happened, or what happens to other previews on the same host: those are the calling process’s.

3781.title: Render logging — the publish branch keeps its own history
3781.content: Skill render-logging: Log every render to the publish branch — what was published, removed, restored or deliberately retained — to an append-only log that lives beside what it describes. Use when adding or removing anything on gh-pages, when asking “what happened to this preview”, or before writing a workflow step that deletes a published artefact. Named by: Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down .

3782.title: The question it exists to answer
3782.content: What happened to branches/<slug>, and why? . A preview can be cleaned up because its pull request closed, removed by a dispatch somebody confirmed, or deleted by an unrelated merge to main. Without a record on the publish branch itself, which one happened is not recoverable.

3783.title: Append-only, and never anything else
3783.content: A removal is a new entry, not the erasure of an old one. The pair — the rendered and the removed that follows it — IS the history. scripts/render-log.ts offers no verb that could lose an entry: no --remove, no --edit, no id to overwrite. The never-delete property is a shape of the tool, so a caller cannot be written wrongly. Emptying a log is a person’s decision, taken deliberately, with the confirmation every durable artefact here requires (deletion-requires-confirmation). No tool and no workflow does it.

3784.title: The four events, and why retained earns its place
3784.content: | event | what it records | . | rendered | published, or re-published over itself — so “when was this last built” needs no commit archaeology | . | removed | taken down. Requires a reason, refused without one | . | restored | carried across a full-replace deploy by restore-staging. Its own event, because “somebody pushed this branch” and “an unrelated merge nearly deleted it” are different facts | . | retained | a removal was considered and refused. Also requires a reason | . retained answers “why is this still up”: a preview still standing because a liveness signal fired leaves no trace otherwise.

3785.title: Where it lives, and why that is structural
3785.content: _render-log/<YYYY-MM-DD>.jsonl, at the root of the publish branch. Outside branches/, deliberately. The cleanup runs rm -rf "branches/$SLUG", and a branch named to collide with a directory under branches/ slugifies to exactly that name. A store outside branches/ is unreachable by that command whatever the slug says; a guard you have to remember is weaker than a location that cannot be reached. One file per UTC day, not one growing file and not one per entry. Six workflows publish to this branch; a read-modify-write of a single file loses whatever landed in between, and the tool appends a line rather than rewriting. One file per entry would make “what happened this week” a directory walk.

3786.title: It does NOT survive a deploy on its own — this is the part to get right
3786.content: docs-site.yml is a full replace: git rm -r --ignore-unmatch '*' over the whole branch, then copies _site in. It is the only one of this repository’s six gh-pages publishers without keep_files: true, and it is the one that fires on every push to main. So the log is carried across that deploy by restore-staging.ts, unconditionally — not gated on open pull requests the way previews are. A preview belongs to an open PR; a log entry about a closed one is exactly what nothing would carry, and exactly what a reader needs most. A log a deploy truncates is worse than no log, because a reader will believe its entries persisted. docs-site.yml runs restore-staging.ts from main, so a change to what the restore carries is not in force until it merges. --verify checks the carried prefixes as well as branches/, because a verifier blind to half of what the restore carried reports a clean run over the loss it exists to catch. A lost prefix is reported as not recoverable by re-running anything: a preview can be rebuilt from its workflow, and a record of what was already removed cannot. Only the prefixes the restore reported as carried are verified. A determined absent was never there to lose, and asserting on it would fail every deploy before the first entry is ever written. CARRIED_PREFIXES is where that is declared; it is a list, so another carried store is a new row, not a new code path. The carry runs before the preview check, so the log is carried even when there are no previews. A carry that could not be determined is not a warning. It collapses into the restore’s own unknown, exit 2, which fails the deploy step: continuing would run the full replace and delete the record. A determined absence — the branch is readable and has no log yet — is reported rather than omitted, because “there is no log yet” and “the carry never ran” look identical in a silent report and only the second is a defect.

3787.title: Who writes an entry
3787.content: Every path that can change branches/ writes one, and scripts/tests/workflow-yaml.test.ts asserts that by job rather than leaving it to be remembered: . | path | event | how it lands | . | feature-staging.yml → stage | rendered | the same commit as the deploy. The entry goes to the root _render-log/, never into _site, which would land it at branches/<slug>/_render-log/ — inside the directory a cleanup removes | . | feature-staging.yml → stage, preview cap | removed, one per rotated preview | the same commit as the deploy, written by staging-rotate.ts; the reason names the size budget, and the summary gives slug, age and size | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, confirmed | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, refused | retained | its own commit | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup-dispatch | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | docs-site.yml → restore | carried, not written | restore-staging.ts | . The reason is the gate’s own, never a restatement of one branch of it. cleanup emits merged | labelled | closed-unmerged-and-unlabelled and the entry carries that value. A hardcoded reason would name the wrong rule for some of them, and a wrong reason reads as evidence. A removal and its record are one commit. A separate log push can fail on its own and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why. The rendered and retained entries are continue-on-error. A preview that deployed and whose entry did not is a gap in the record, not a failed deploy, and failing the job there would turn a logging problem into a lost review surface. The step goes red in the run, so the gap is visible. A removed entry has no such fallback and needs none: it cannot fail separately from the removal it describes.

3788.title: Writing an entry
3788.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/render-log.ts --dir <gh-pages-checkout> \ --event rendered --kind staging-preview --path branches/<slug> --slug <slug> \ --summary "preview published" --branch "$BRANCH" --commit "$SHA" --run "$RUN_URL" . The tool writes into a directory and never pushes. The workflows that call it already hold a gh-pages checkout with their own retry and concurrency handling; a second pusher racing those is a new way to lose a deploy. One job knows how to push, this one knows what to write. Reading back: --read [--day YYYY-MM-DD]. It exits 1 when any line could not be read, and prints which — a short count must be visible as short, never passed off as complete. Same rule as ci-health: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean.

3789.title: A path is checked by VALUE, never trusted by provenance
3789.content: --path is refused unless it is / or a sequence of plain segments — no .., no leading /, no backslash. The staging slug sanitiser can emit .. (input .. gives output ..), and is safe only because git rejects every ref name containing it. That invariant holds for a slug taken from a ref and does not hold for one taken from a dispatch input — and cleanup-dispatch takes exactly that. So the check is on the value, not on where it came from.

3790.title: It is a specialisation of folio-log/v1, not a rival
3790.content: schemas/sdlc/log-entry.ts already answers “what does an entry look like”, and a render entry reuses those spellings: id, at, summary, detail, references, capture. Three things differ, each deliberately: . |   | activity log | render log | . | subject | what an agent did | what was published | . | store | fsh-guts/logs/, in the repo | the publish branch | . | published | no | yes | . An agent’s audit trail is not published; a record of what is on the publish branch belongs where its subject’s absence can be seen.

3793.title: Rendered impact — which rendered files a Change Set changes
3793.content: Skill rendered-impact: The list of rendered files a Change Set alters, and how a reviewer approves against it. Each renderer maps the input files a change touched to the rendered files of its site through its dependency cone, before any build; a build diff then confirms the prediction. Use when opening or reviewing a Change Set PR, when asked “which pages does this change”, when a prediction and a build disagree, or when adding a renderer. Named by: Review task, Human Translation Workflow, Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, A harness’s default rendering, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Adjudication, Criterion adjudication, Prose and the code it describes, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Adopting an upstream version bump, Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Editing and HCI validation, Review and publish a folio, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Skill id: rendered-impact · Package: sdlc-core . A Change Set’s PR is approved against what it does to the rendered site, not only against its source diff. A one-line FSH edit can re-render one page of 722 or all of them, and a reviewer cannot tell which from the diff. So every renderer answers one question, and the PR shows the answer.

3794.title: Scope
3794.content: . | Every renderer maps a list of changed input files to the list of changed rendered files, from its dependency cone. | The public-comment Change Set (changeset/1.0.0) is the Change Set for ANY folio change, and the rendered list is one of its fields. | The original stays in library/; a Change Set applies to the folio materialised in folio/, never to the library source. | .

3795.title: The contract: rendered-impact/v1
3795.content: Declared in cat-harness/schemas/ui/rendered-impact.ts. A renderer takes the changed input files and returns: . | field | says | . | files[] | each rendered file the change alters: path in the built site, change (changed, added, removed), role (content, data, index) and via, the chain that reached it | . | files[].anchors | for a page that assembles many units (a document page), the fragment ids the change alters; the review list links path#anchor | . | undetermined[] | each input the renderer could NOT place, with its reason, and scope: all when it can change any page | . | method | cone (predicted before a build) or build-diff (measured after one) | . Three rules, each one a refusal: . | Could-not-determine is never “no change”. An empty files with a non-empty undetermined is “not known”, and the PR says so in those words. A renderer that drops an input it cannot map is broken. | Index files are listed and marked, not dropped. The reviewer’s list (reviewList) leaves out role: index (search data, sitemaps, an artefact index) because review is of content, not indexes. The renderer marks the role; the reader filters. | A page whose bytes do not change can still change. An AST artefact page loads its resource in the browser, so the cone names the page AND its data file, and a build diff sees only the data file. That is unconfirmed, not a defect. | .

3796.title: Checking a prediction: the one comparison that matters
3796.content: comparePrediction(predicted, measured) sorts every file into three groups: . | missed: the build changed it, the cone did not predict it. A cone defect, never a pass. Report it on the PR and fix the renderer: the next Change Set relies on the same cone to tell the reviewer what to open. | confirmed: predicted and measured. | unconfirmed: predicted, not measured. Expected for content pages that load their data (rule 3). For anything else it means the cone is too wide: it is safe, but say so. | .

3797.title: The renderers today
3797.content: | renderer | maps | how | status | . | fhir-ig-pages | .fsh, .cql, input/pagecontent/*.md | fsh-cone forward cone → SUSHI’s fsh-index.json → AST artefact page + served JSON; a page → itself and every page that includes it | in the FHIR layer, documented with its AST tooling (skill_fetch ig-ast-delta) | . | document-site, public-comment-site, library-site | a block, a document/chapter/section manifest, media/*, the public-comment store, a file in a declared library entry or a folio review-anchors.json naming one (the entry’s Document view and doc.json; its structure.json also the library index) | loaded from the published changeset.json (each changed block’s label and file) and outline.json (the documents), never from source: a block lands on its document’s page, anchored at its label (anchors) — on a LAZY page (outline.json lazy) on its blocks/NNN.json chunk and index.hydrated.html instead, and a block added, removed, renamed or moved reshapes the shell and every chunk from its position on; a file no builder of the site reads is an input with no page: each builder in the folio’s build command exports siteReads (the folio; the comment store; every directory of a typology holding a kind it renders), and a file outside all of them, the submodules, .github/ and the root’s non-Markdown files reaches nothing — so beans/ reaches no page, while todos/, whose pages are rendered, still may. A step that exports no siteReads excludes nothing; never decide it from the instance’s declaration, which also declares what no builder reads | in the document layer, with the ChangeSet Tool | . | docs-site | any file | a file in the COMPOSED Jekyll tree (docsLayers, composedInstances) → its page (permalink, or .md → .html) or asset; an include → the pages that include it, transitively; _data → the pages and includes that read it; a layout, a THEME include (read from the installed theme; unreadable means every include) or an include nothing calls → any page; any page change → the search index; a file outside the tree → undetermined when the staging cone carries any directory, nothing when it reaches none | cat-harness-tools/scripts/docs-rendered-impact.ts | . | published-provenance | a mounted instance’s skill, process or schema (anything a generator renders) | the published root’s own record of what each page was generated from — the “Generated from <path>” note and data-src on the edit link — read back as source → pages; a new source has no page yet and an index names no source, so both stay for the QA diff | cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts (predictByProvenance) | . Two builds of one commit differ in every page by a ?v=<build time> cache-buster, so diffBuiltSites blanks BUILD_STAMPS before hashing; without that, every page reads as missed. A renderer’s command line belongs to the layer that owns it; this layer names none above it.

3798.title: In the review process
3798.content: content-change-review.bpmn: . | Produce: the staging build writes rendered-impact.json beside the preview and puts the review list in the PR comment. Each entry links to the preview and to main’s copy of the page. | Read: at Compare main vs staging, the reviewer opens every file on the review list, not only the pages the author mentions. Use before-after-preview for the pairs, and visual-diff for figures. | Measure: the staging job diffs its build against main’s published site (measure-rendered-impact.ts, before the banner goes on) and writes rendered-measured.json: what changed, and what the prediction MISSED. Only when that site was built from the PR’s base does it count (status: known); otherwise main’s own changes would read as misses (not-base). No published main site, no file: “not measured”, never “nothing missed”. The review page shows it under the list, as the PR comment does: a run started by dispatch finds its PR from the branch, so the comment is not lost when no pull_request event started the run. | Show: every docs-site preview also carries branches/<slug>/changes/ (cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts): the changed sources, with a re-pinned mount in index.lock.json expanded into the files its repository changed between the two pins (a re-pin handed to a renderer as one JSON line predicts nothing); the cone’s files and its undetermined inputs; and the build diffed against the site at the gh-pages root, its missed files listed as changed, not in the cone. That diff folds the preview’s base URL to the root’s, blanks BUILD_STAMPS and compares a page’s <main>, because a preview’s chrome differs on every page; a removed file is listed apart, by directory, since most are parts of the site the preview does not carry. The root records its build commit in build.json; a root not built from the PR’s base is said on the page, never read as this branch’s change. | Gate: review-coverage-gate.dmn reads three page counts beside the block counts, each with a status fact so an uncomputed count is never 0: . | unreviewedPages: review-list files nobody has reviewed at their current pin. A page is reviewed by a page: verdict, or block by block when every block anchored on it has a verdict; a data file goes with a reviewed page that shares its pin. | undeterminedInputs: inputs no renderer placed, until an input: verdict or waiver (with a reason) says somebody looked. | missedPages: measured but not predicted, until a page: verdict. | . A pin is the hash of the git blobs of the changed inputs on a file’s via (pinImpact), never the built bytes, which carry a per-build banner. An edit after review reopens exactly the pages it touched. The tag is in review-comments. | .

3799.title: Adding a renderer
3799.content: . | Map each input kind the renderer reads to the rendered files it writes, through the dependency information the renderer ALREADY has. Never re-derive a mapping the renderer’s own tool records (SUSHI’s fsh-index is the authority for FSH → resource). | Put every other input in undetermined, unless the renderer cannot read it at all: then it is an input with no file. Decide that from what the instance declares, never from a list of names here. | Test it against a real build with comparePrediction: 0 missed is the bar. | .
