3801.title: /rendered-verification — look at it, then send the picture
3801.content: Skill rendered-verification: Confirm a UI change by LOOKING at it in a browser and sending the screenshots to the author, rather than describing it. Use whenever a change touches CSS, a Liquid/HTML template, a generated page, the navbar, a board, a sticky or any rendered surface — before claiming it works, and before asking the author to review it. Covers building the site locally, taking the REAL CI build off gh-pages when the question is theme chrome or layout, driving it with Playwright in this environment, measuring computed style rather than reading the stylesheet, hit-testing a control’s centre because visible is not usable, asserting the conditions so a check cannot pass over an unstyled page, and the defect classes that are invisible to a green gate set. Named by: Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file . continual-progress holds that a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. Neither can the agent that wrote it. A stylesheet is not a rendering, a generator’s output is not a page, and a green gate set is not a screenshot.

3802.title: The rule
3802.content: A change to a rendered surface is not done until you have looked at it in a browser and sent the author the picture. Not “ran the tests”. Not “checked the CSS”. Opened it, measured the computed result, and attached the image to the turn. Sending the screenshot is part of the rule, not a courtesy: an image lets the author disagree with you in one glance.

3803.title: Why a green gate set does not cover this
3803.content: Defect classes no test catches, because the source was right and the rendering was not: . | what happens | why the suite is green | . | a generator emits raw <h3>, kramdown assigns no ids, and every heading on a page shares one anchor | the generator’s own output looks right | . | two files hold their own copy of a shared size (a rail at 40px, a sidebar at 56px) | each file has a test asserting its own copy | . | a component renders with no colour | an invalid custom-property substitution fails silently — no parse error, no console warning, just the initial value | . | a region lays out below the viewport, rendered and unreachable | the markup is correct; a !important in the theme makes the flex column inert | .

3804.title: Measure the COMPUTED result, never the stylesheet
3804.content: getComputedStyle and getBoundingClientRect are the instruments. Reading the CSS tells you what was authored; only the browser tells you what won. Measure every time: . | display, flex, min-height on a region you believe is a flex child. A !important from a theme utility class silently makes every flex value below it inert. | scrollHeight against clientHeight. A region that “does not scroll” and a region whose content is ten times its height look identical in a screenshot of the top of it. | the resolved colour, not the declaration. A custom property holding a hue substituted into color-mix() yields rgba(0,0,0,0) and no error. | . Use a control. When you suspect a value is invalid, build the minimal element in the page and read it back, rather than reasoning from the spec: the probe is a measurement, and reasoning from the spec is a claim. const probe = document.createElement("div"); probe.style.cssText = "--h:268;background:color-mix(in oklab, var(--h) 28%, transparent)"; document.body.appendChild(probe); getComputedStyle(probe).backgroundColor; // rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) -> invalid .

3805.title: A before/after pair beats an after
3805.content: Build the base branch too and shoot the same element. Without it “the dividers have colour now” is unfalsifiable. git worktree add <dir> origin/main --detach is the cheap way; symlink node_modules and the docs vendor/.bundle into it rather than re-installing. When the pair goes to a reviewer rather than confirming the change to yourself, before-after-preview governs it: one build with one variable where possible, stable capture, a k of n count with its method, the status line, and where the preview sits in the review processes. It also covers papers, FHIR IGs and slide decks.

3806.title: Running it here
3806.content: Building the site is preview:site, whose header carries the two things that make a naive bundle exec jekyll fail in this repo. It is not what CI builds — CI uses the pinned remote_theme, this uses the gem — so read a theme-chrome question off the staging preview (next section), not off this. Liquid and kramdown are identical, and so is our own stylesheet. Two environment facts: . | Serve it under its baseurl. _config.yml pins baseurl: "/folio-assistant", so every stylesheet is requested at /folio-assistant/assets/…. Serving the build directory at / returns 200 for the HTML and 404 for every stylesheet — and an unstyled page renders, so the failure looks like a CSS bug rather than a 404. Symlink <serve>/folio-assistant -> <build> and serve the parent. | Pin the browser. Chromium is pre-installed but its build number will not match whatever playwright-core resolves to, and playwright install is not available. Launch with executablePath: "/opt/pw-browsers/chromium". | . Drive the control a reader would drive. page.click(".side-bar .site-title") (the avatar, which opens and closes the sidebar from 50rem up), not element.classList.add(…). A state you set by hand is a state you have not tested the way in to. And check that the state actually changed. Setting data-fa-scheme directly does not switch the scheme — the real toggle is jtd.setTheme(name). A test that silently does nothing reports the old state as the new one. Assert the switch landed (for example, the sidebar background changed) before reading anything off it. Know what that toggle does: setTheme swaps the theme’s first stylesheet, so while the new file is in flight the page has no ground but the browser’s white canvas, and it flashes white. A scheme check that only reads the SETTLED page cannot see it — hold the new sheet in flight with page.route and read the ground then, as first-paint-scheme.e2e.ts does. The rule itself lives in theme-artefacts §”The page ground: the first paint is DARK”.

3807.title: The REAL build is reachable — take it off gh-pages
3807.content: This environment’s proxy refuses litlfred.github.io, but feature-staging.yml deploys each preview into branches/<slug>/ on the gh-pages branch, and git reaches what HTTP cannot: . git fetch origin gh-pages S=claude-my-branch-slug # the deploy comment names it mkdir -p "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" git archive "FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S" | tar -x -C "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" cd /tmp/rv && nohup python3 -m http.server 8091 >/dev/null 2>&1 & # → http://127.0.0.1:8091/folio-assistant/branches/$S/<page>.html . That is the pinned remote_theme, the composed tree, the mounted instances and the post-Jekyll steps — the thing CI publishes. A whole preview is ~90 MB; git archive FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S page.html assets takes just what a page needs. Mount it at the branches/ path, not at the site root. A staged page requests /folio-assistant/branches/<slug>/assets/…, so serving the extract at /folio-assistant/ 404s every stylesheet.

3808.title: Assert the CONDITIONS, or the check passes over nothing
3808.content: An unstyled page still renders. It still answers elementFromPoint. It still returns PASS. A run mounted at the wrong path reports a pass over a page with zero stylesheets; what gives it away is the numbers beside the verdict, not the verdict. So every rendered check reports, beside its verdict: . | document.styleSheets.length — zero or one means the page is bare; | a count of responses with status >= 400, collected from page.on("response"); | the precondition the defect needs — the class, the state, the element count. If the bug only appears when fa-has-fullwidth is set, a run where it is unset has not tested anything. | . A check that cannot tell a styled page from a bare one is not a check: could-not-determine rendered as a pass. A COUNT over the built site needs its instrument validated first . Before trusting any “N of M pages have X”, run the instrument on a known positive AND a known negative, and on one positive of each way X can appear. Naive instruments give confident wrong numbers: an exact class match misses the theme’s own variant, a substring match counts the class name quoted in prose, a link count takes a stylesheet href as a way out. For navigated pages, the instrument that holds is <nav class="fa-nav" OR id="site-nav". For a site-wide count, the gh-pages route above scales. Use a --filter=blob:none --sparse clone of gh-pages, with sparse patterns for the files counted, and exclude branches/. All HTML is about 1.7 GB and takes minutes; one directory takes seconds.

3809.title: Visible is not usable — hit-test the control’s CENTRE
3809.content: A control can have the right size, the right colour and the right label, and still be un-clickable because something is painted over it — for example a wrapper that computes to height 0 because its only child is position: absolute, letting a flow sibling paint across the field. const b = el.getBoundingClientRect(); const hit = document.elementFromPoint( Math.round(b.x + b.width / 2), Math.round(b.y + b.height / 2)); const usable = hit && (hit === el || el.contains(hit) || hit.contains(el)); . Two ways this test lies: . | It resolves INSIDE the control. elementFromPoint returns the deepest element, often an <svg> or <span> within a button. hit === el alone reports a working control as covered — which is what the contains pair above is for. | It reports a preview-only overlay. The staging banner (a <div> with no class, z-index: 9999, a child of <body>) exists only on previews. Identify the coverer (document.elementsFromPoint(x, y).slice(0, 3)) before calling it a defect: what is on top decides whether it ships. | . Where the covered control is the ONLY route back to a state — the magnifier that reopens a collapsed search — being un-clickable means an action whose inverse is not reachable.

3810.title: Two environment facts that cost cycles rather than correctness
3810.content: . | Never pkill -f "http.server" from the shell running one. The pattern matches your own process group and kills the command issuing it — exit 144, no output, looks like the tool failed. Start each server on a fresh port in its own invocation instead. | Probe scripts must not be left in the repository root. check:undeclared-files fails the gate set on a stray probe.mjs. Playwright needs the script where playwright resolves, so write it to the repo root, run it, and delete it in the same command. | .

3811.title: What to send
3811.content: The frames that answer a question the author would otherwise have to ask: . | before and after of the same element, same viewport; | the surface in both colour schemes, if the change touches colour; | the state that is hard to describe — a region scrolled to its end, a menu open, an empty case. | . Caption them with what to look at, not with what they are. “The nav crushed to a 64px sliver, no home link” is a caption; “navbar screenshot” is a filename. SendUserFile is the mechanism; write into the working directory or the scratchpad, since a file the author cannot open is not a deliverable.

3812.title: Accessibility is measured here too
3812.content: Unique heading anchors and the 3:1 bar for meaningful non-text content are rendered facts: compute the contrast from the two resolved colours rather than from the tokens, because the token you authored and the colour that won are different questions.

3813.title: Listen for pageerror, or a crash reads as a missing feature
3813.content: A throw early in a page’s init() takes the rest of init() with it. The symptom is a feature that is simply not there — which looks exactly like a feature that did not mount — and a swallowed init is silent in a screenshot. So: attach the listener, and assert zero. page.on("pageerror", (e) => errors.push(e.stack || e.message)); . And check the base branch before you claim a crash is yours — or before you claim it is not. One run against a build of origin/main tells “something I just broke” from “a live defect nobody had reported”.

3814.title: A STATIC read of a client-rendered page is not verification — in either direction
3814.content: This skill stops a false red as well as a false green. Grepping a page’s committed HTML for content the page fetches at runtime proves nothing. The content is absent whether the page works or not. A library viewer, for example, carries DATA_HREF = "../../../assets/library/index.json", fetches it, and filters by instance. Its committed index.html never holds the entry names, so grepping it for them returns the same answer for a working page and a broken one. Loading it in Chromium settles it in one command. A false red files a bug against working code and sends the next agent to rewrite a correct generator, and because the report carries measurements it reads as thoroughly evidenced. If a page assembles any of its content after load, open it. The tell is cheap to check: a fetch, an XMLHttpRequest, a DATA_HREF, a <script> that writes into the DOM. Finding one means a static read cannot answer the question, and §"Running it here" above is how to answer it instead.

3815.title: What this does NOT replace
3815.content: The gate set. This is the layer above it: gates catch what is checkable from the source, and this catches what is only true once a browser has laid it out. A change that skips either is unverified.

3817.title: /repo-conversion — folio-assistant over a repo that already has a life
3817.content: Skill repo-conversion: Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Agent activity log, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down, Merge to main, A merge train, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn, Task_ScanRepo, Task_ChooseHarnessed and Task_ConfirmImport (both non-relaxable). Scanner: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts.

3818.title: 0. The one rule
3818.content: Scan, show, ask, then move — and never in any other order. The author’s repository is the thing of value; the scaffolding is replaceable. A wrong import is not fixed by a git checkout, because the author has to work out what the agent did. Task_ConfirmImport is marked relaxable="false" in the BPMN, and a content package may not declare it away.

3819.title: 1. Scan — read-only, and honest about its limits
3819.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts # human-readable report bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts --json # same, as facts . It walks the working tree (respecting .gitignore) and sorts what it finds into three buckets: . | bucket | means | typical | . | library | external source material — something somebody else wrote, that the folio will cite or ingest | PDFs, papers, scans, datasets, references/, papers/, sources/ | . | content | material authored here, that could become folio blocks | Markdown prose, docs/, notes/, drafts/, .tex | . | unclassified | it could not tell | everything else, and it is reported, not hidden | . unclassified is reported, never forced. A two-bucket scanner’s mistakes arrive as moved files; this one reports what it could not place, and the author disposes of it. The classification is by path convention and extension only. It does not read file contents or call a model, so the author can disagree with any row of it in one word. Outside-content candidate scanning — preserving evidence and refutations . In repositories with formal, analytical, or domain-specific content, crucial verification scripts, macros, and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/); a conversion that carries only that tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts scans outside the content tree and classifies these artifacts into read-only candidate classifications (defined by the content-type layer’s conversion refinement skill), reporting source location, rationale, and linkStatus (linked when referenced by at least one content block, or unlinked when orphaned). Like the general scan, candidate scanning never writes, moves, or modifies files; it presents the candidates to the author and agent so decisions can be made before importing.

3820.title: 2. Show, then ask — three questions, all as selections
3820.content: Present the scan as counts and a handful of examples per bucket, never as a 1,400-line file list. Then three questions, each answerable by picking. Load interaction-modality first. Q1 — import at all? . | Import everything the scan found (recommended) | Import only the library bucket — sources now, prose later | Import nothing; just set up folio-assistant | Let me pick bucket by bucket | . Q2 — where does each group go? Only for groups the scan was not confident about, and only when Q1 was not “nothing”. Offer library/ vs content/ per directory, not per file (a per-file interrogation is the accessibility failure in interaction-modality §0). Q3 — leave in place, or reorganise? . | Leave everything where it is (recommended) — the folio references the files at their current paths. Nothing moves, every existing link still works, and the decision stays open. | Reorganise into library/ and content/ — tidier, and it rewrites paths. Offer this only on a clean working tree, do it in its own commit, and use git mv so history follows. | . Recommend leave in place by default: a broken relative link in somebody’s README is a defect.

3821.title: 2a. Markers — choose what the harness reads (declare, don’t slurp)
3821.content: A harness declares what it reads in a repository; it does not take all of its content. The principle is directory-conventions §”A marker declares what is read, and nothing else is”. The scan’s fourth section, markers, lists the content a harness COULD be told to read: a sushi-config.yaml (an IG: contentTypes.ig), a legacy dak.json (contentTypes.dak), .bpmn processes, a work items store, library/, uploads/, Lean (contentType: paper) and folio manifests (contentType: document). For each it gives the paths, whether it is already declared — declared, not-declared, or unknown when there is no readable index.config.json to ask — and the snippet that would declare it, with where it goes (index.config.json#contentTypes, or a local instance’s <name>.json#directories). Content types come from the registry (defaultContentTypes; an { indexSection } type is checked against contentTypes.<id>), directory facets are checked against the registered graph typologies, and only the evidence the registries cannot state is a short table in cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/content-markers.ts. Where each kind of content lives is directory-conventions. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers # the list bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers --json # same, as facts . A plain command: any agent host (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot) or a person at a shell runs it, with no MCP server. It writes nothing. Q0 — which of these should the harness read? (Task_ChooseHarnessed, non-relaxable). Ask it the interaction-modality way — the full question in the chat, then a tap card where the host has one, otherwise a numbered pick-list with its default stated. Never a typed reply. Offer only the markers that are not-declared (or unknown), one option each: . | None of these for now (the default) — nothing is declared; the scan can be run again any time | contentTypes.ig — sushi-config.yaml, input/fsh/, … (the FHIR IG) | directories: processes — processes/ (7 BPMN files) | Let me pick several — the same options as a multi-select | . The default declares nothing, and the agent never declares a marker the person did not pick. Declare exactly the picks — the scan’s suggestion snippet, at its suggestion.at — in the scaffolding commit, or in its own commit on an instance that already exists. After setup, too. The same question fits any instance at any time: “what else could this harness declare?” is --markers on the instance’s repository, then Q0. Rows already declared are shown for context and are not offered. A content type registered by a higher harness layer appears as a hint when that layer is not loaded, with a note saying where the type lives. Declaring a scoped content type is not a boolean flag: its include list states everything that layer’s readers will read, so confirm the list with the person and consult that layer’s build-pipeline skill for how additional paths are added later.

3822.title: 3. Dispatch the ingestion
3822.content: Ingestion proper is processes/library/document-ingestion.bpmn (and the content layer’s document-intake refinement skill when converting into a content folio). What this skill decides is how much parallelism, and it is a question for the author because it spends their tokens: . | scale | when | how | . | inline | under ~10 documents | do it here, no subagents | . | one agent | tens of documents, one kind | a single background agent, reporting per document | . | small swarm | hundreds, or several distinct kinds | dispatch-agent — 2–4 agents partitioned by directory, never by file count | . Partition by directory because a per-file partition puts two agents in the same manifest, and the conflicts cost more than the parallelism saves. Open one work item per ingestion front before dispatching — running the existence check in todo-manager.md §”Check before you create” first — so a session that dies mid-import leaves a plan behind rather than a half-full library/.

3823.title: 4. The conversion itself
3823.content: Once Q1–Q3 are answered, folio_init against the existing directory. It refuses rather than overwrites where a file is already present, which on this branch is the common case (README.md, .gitignore, a docs/). Read its report rather than assuming; the files it declined to write are the ones you now merge by hand: . | AGENTS.md — if one exists, merge; do not replace. It is the most valuable file in the repository for the next agent. | README.md — never replaced. readme-sections.ts only writes inside marker pairs the author has opted into, so offer to add markers rather than content. | .gitignore — append the folio entries; keep theirs. | . If the remote is empty, push main first. A repository with work locally can still have an empty remote, and GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default. Run init-folio or push main before any feature branch. If main has no harness yet, land a setup-only PR first. A fork or an existing repository whose main has no index.config.json and index.lock.json gives the full PR checks nothing to compare against: the base side fails before any test runs, and the PR’s own gates are skipped. So open one small PR with only what folio_init writes and the pins, merge it, and only then branch for content. Draft-tier checks never build the base, so this does not show until the content PR leaves draft. The setup-only PR has a Tool: instantiate-harness. It pins the harness and every layer it needs, mounts them, commits the setup on harness/<harness>, opens that PR, and renders the branch’s preview at gh-pages:branches/<branch>/. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run it from a fresh clone of the tools layer: . git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht echo "<where the author consented>" | bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts \ --repo . --harness <owner/repo> --consent-by <who> [--plan | --local] . --plan prints the closure and every step and writes nothing; --local commits on the branch and pushes nothing. The harness’s own adoption steps are its checkout scripts instantiate:<harness> (files it declares, committed with the setup) and prepare:<harness> (what the site is built from, never committed). For an IG on a FHIR harness these declare contentTypes.ig and build the IG’s first AST. A harness built on this platform may add adoption steps of its own for its kind of repository, for example about CI that already publishes a site on every push. Ask skill_list for the skill governing that kind before calling the conversion done.

3824.title: 5. Publishing — provision gh-pages first; an overlay needs it too
3824.content: An overlay never reaches getting-started §5 by itself, so this section repeats the one step a publishing route cannot skip: provision gh-pages before GitHub Pages is switched on. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in getting-started.bpmn, on the shared path after scaffolding and before the Pages build, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. The tool is pages-bootstrap: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts # reports `unprovisioned` (exit 3) and the exact command when gh-pages is absent bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision # pushes an orphan gh-pages: placeholder index.html + .nojekyll . --provision is idempotent and never forces a push, and nothing creates a remote branch without it. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — the script prints the source it expects. When the repository’s publish workflow pushes gh-pages, “GitHub Actions” is the wrong source: the workflow would push a branch Pages was never told to serve. The same holds for an overlay that remote-mounts its dependencies. A mount brings layers in; it does not provision anything on the downstream’s remote.

3825.title: 6. Anti-patterns
3825.content: . | Moving a file before Q3 is answered. | Reporting a two-bucket classification. If unclassified is empty on a real repository, suspect the scanner rather than celebrate it. | A per-file confirmation loop. See §2. | Swarming a 12-document import. The dispatch overhead exceeds the work. | Replacing an existing AGENTS.md or README.md. Merge, or leave. | Treating the scan as ingestion. It reads; it never writes. Ingestion is a separate process with its own diagram and its own gate. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. See §5. | Dropping outside-content math artifacts or unlinked audit refutations. Carrying only the primary content tree (content/ or folio/) drops outside proofs, computations, and refutations showing that some paper claims are false. See §1. | .

3827.title: Is the repository itself healthy?
3827.content: Process_RepoHealth · strict · 2 step(s) . Is the repository itself healthy — what the review previews cost the publish branch, what a clone costs, whether the work plan holds duplicates or unhonoured claims — reported in one tracking issue and never acted on. THE SAME SHAPE AS ci-health, ONE LEVEL OUT. That one asks whether the WORKFLOWS pass; this asks about the REPOSITORY — how much of gh-pages the review previews occupy, how big a clone costs, whether the work plan has duplicates or unhonoured claims. IT REPORTS AND NEVER ACTS. Four of the five checks are about artefacts accumulating, and every finding’s action names something a PERSON does. That is deletion-requires-confirmation applied to the tool that most wants to break it: the skill’s own worked example is bean plj1, a workflow whose shape deleted every open PR’s preview without anybody deciding it. There is no removal task on this diagram, and its absence is the rule being followed rather than an omission. THE REPORT IS KEPT WHETHER OR NOT THE CHECKS SUCCEED (if: always()), which is why Run the health checks says “keeping the report either way”. A sweep whose output survives only on success cannot be used to investigate the run that failed. The daily cron is at 06:41, OFF THE HOUR deliberately: GitHub’s scheduler queues heavily at :00, and a delayed run is a run whose report is stamped later than the state it describes. THE THIRD STATE IS THE WHOLE POINT, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE THAT FAILS THE JOB. Verified 2026-09-20 by reading the if: guards: unknown runs exit 1; a finding does NOT. A repository in trouble leaves this workflow GREEN and speaks through the tracking issue, while a sweep that could not look turns the job red. That inversion is deliberate and is invisible from the run list, which is the argument for drawing it. ONE TRACKING ISSUE, EDITED IN PLACE, never a comment and never a second issue — a feed nobody reads is the failure mode a watchdog invites. On unknown the issue is left UNTOUCHED: not closed, not opened, not edited. Closing it would assert the thing the sweep just failed to establish. Ensure the tracking label exists sits AFTER Could we tell? and before the split, because both issue paths need the label — the clean path filters on it too, and on a repository where nothing has ever gone wrong it would not otherwise exist. It is skipped on unknown, where neither path runs and a label hiccup must not be what fails the job. The verdict is reported through the shared tracked-watch process (Process_TrackedWatch), with the label repo-health. Its three ends say what happened: unknown (job red, issue untouched), clean (issue closed), or found (issue opened or edited, job green). i i

3844.title: Review comments — from a PR comment to a structured todo
3844.content: Skill review-comments: Reviewer comments on a folio’s edit-set, from a tagged pull-request comment to a structured todo on the review page. Covers the tag a reviewer types, how the comments are ingested into review-comment/1.0.0 todos, where the published review-comments.json comes from and when it refreshes, how a comment follows a renamed block and survives a removed one, who may change a comment’s status, and how to change this process. Use when a reviewer asks how to comment on a block, when the review page shows no comments or a wrong one, when editing the ingestion, or when a folio’s staging workflow is set up. Named by: Committee review of a content change, Data sharing agreement document life cycle . Skill id: review-comments · Package: content-lifecycle-ext Tools: folio-review-comments (ingest), folio-review-comment-move (record a decision) . A reviewer comments on one block of a folio by writing an ordinary comment on the edit-set’s pull request, starting with a tag that names the block. The review process turns each tagged comment into a todo of a special kind, review-comment/1.0.0. The review page lists those todos beside the blocks they are about.

3845.title: Design
3845.content: | rule | why | . | The channel is a PR conversation comment tagged with the block label | Needs nothing installed, sits beside the approve, and is anchored by LABEL, so it survives a block moving. A line review comment is anchored to a file line and is lost when the block moves. | . | The record is a todo subtype declared by core, in the dynamic KG | A board, heat map or reader that understands todos reads a review comment without knowing about review. | . | The preview gets comments from a file the workflow writes | Works for private and public repositories, and no token ever reaches a browser. | . | A status change is committed to the folio’s todos/ on the edit-set’s feature branch | Reviewed with the edit it is about, lands on main only when that branch merges, and is part of the KG. | . The PR comment is the write channel; the todo is the canonical record.

3846.title: Writing a comment: the tag
3846.content: Start a conversation comment on the pull request with header lines, then a blank line, then what you want to say: . block: prose:overview kind: defect role: clinical-sme The dose in the second sentence contradicts table 3. | header | required | values | default | . | block: | yes | the block’s label, exactly as the review page shows it | — | . | kind: | no | question, defect, suggestion, editorial | question, which asserts least | . | role: | no | the lane you are reviewing in, a role id from roles.json | reviewer | . | The headers must be the very first lines. The first line that is not key: value ends the header. | block: takes the rest of the line, because labels contain colons (prose:overview). It must be ONE label. | A comment without block: is conversation, not a review comment, and is left alone. A PR thread is also where people talk. | A malformed tag is reported, never dropped. An unknown kind, or two words after block:, appears in malformed with the comment’s link, so the reviewer can fix it. | . The review page shows the exact block: <label> line for every changed block, ready to copy, and links to the pull request. GitHub cannot pre-fill a comment box, so copying the line is the one manual step.

3847.title: What a review comment IS
3847.content: review-comment/1.0.0, in folio-assistant-core/schemas/review-comment.ts. It is declared with nodeKind and its one parent is the harness todo, which itself is carried-note + themed. So it IS a todo: . | targetLabel is required. A general todo may float free; a review comment is always about one block. | status is closed: open, addressed, resolved, adjudicated, withdrawn. | Everything review-specific sits under one field, review: the repository, PR, comment id and URL, reviewer, role, kind, the block’s content hash and the commit when ingested, orphaned, anchoredFrom, and the decision that closed it. | . Keeping the review fields under one key means no field here can collide with one a parent adds later, which is the collision nodeKind refuses at load.

3848.title: Who may change a status: only the process
3848.content: A status moves only through transition(comment, to, {process, task}), and only along a row of REVIEW_TRANSITIONS. Anything else throws. | move | from | to | by (BPMN task) | needs a Decision | . | ingest | — | open | Process_ContentChangeReviewCommittee#Task_IngestComments |   | . | address | open | addressed | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides |   | . | send back | addressed | open | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides |   | . | resolve | addressed | resolved | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides | yes | . | adjudicate | open, addressed | adjudicated | Process_Adjudication#A_RecordEntry | yes | . | withdraw | open, addressed | withdrawn | Process_ContentChangeReviewCommittee#Task_WithdrawComment |   | . A comment’s status is what the coverage gate counts, so a comment closed outside the process would count as reviewed when nobody decided anything. A test holds every row to a task that exists in its .bpmn. Ingestion is the review coordinator’s first step in content-change-review.bpmn’s committee phase, content-change-review-committee.bpmn; withdrawal is the reviewer’s step there after the slices come back.

3849.content: bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comments.ts \ --repo owner/name --pr 7 --out _site/review-comments.json \ --folio folio --blocks-out _site/blocks.json \ --existing <previous review-comments.json> . Declared as the Tool folio-review-comments in folio-assistant-core/tools/folio-review-comments/, whose satisfies names this skill. | Read the comments. All pages of the PR’s conversation comments, with GITHUB_TOKEN when set. --comments <file> reads them from a file instead, for offline runs and tests. | Know the blocks. Either --folio <dir>, which reads the manifests as text and executes nothing, or --blocks <blocks.json> from an earlier run. | Keep everything already ingested. Every comment in --existing is kept, status included. A comment’s id is review-pr<N>-c<commentId>, so a re-run finds it rather than adding a second one. | Add the new ones. Each tagged comment not yet ingested becomes an open todo. A defect gets priority high; the others get medium. | Re-anchor every comment against the head’s blocks (reanchorToBlocks): . | the label is present: anchored; | a block lists the label in its renamedFrom: the comment moves to that block, and the old label goes into review.anchoredFrom; | neither: orphaned: true. Kept and shown, never dropped. | . | Write review-comments.json, folio-review-comments/v1. Its comments ARE the todo kind, each validated as one. The envelope adds only what one node cannot: provenance (repo, pr, commit, generatedAt), the malformed list, and the untagged count. So “no comments” and “comments nobody could parse” can be told apart. | . Why re-anchor against renamedFrom and not the ChangeSet. A ChangeSet compares against main. A block ADDED in the pull request and then renamed inside it is “added” both times, so the comment made on its first label would be orphaned. The block’s own renamedFrom (guarded by id-stable) says where it came from whatever the base. reanchor() over a ChangeSet also exists, for a caller that has only that.

3850.title: Recording a decision: commit to the feature branch
3850.content: When an editor or adjudicator decides what happens to a comment, the decision is committed to the feature branch that carries the edit-set, the same branch the edits are on: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comment-move.ts \ --id review-pr7-c1 --to addressed \ --process Process_Review --task Task_EditorDecides \ --published _site/review-comments.json --commit . | The move goes through transition(), so --process and --task must be a task allowed to make it, and resolved / adjudicated need --decision. The command is not a back door around the table above. | A new folio already has the directory. init-folio writes todos/todos.json declaring items and feedback (todo-feedback), and creates both. An older folio that lacks it gets an error naming the remedy. | The file goes where the graph says. That is the todos graph’s directory of kind todo-feedback (“todos raised against a specific block, carrying the submitter’s identity”), read from todos/todos.json. A graph that declares none gets an error naming the remedy. | The file IS the node: <feedback dir>/<id>.json, one review-comment/1.0.0, the same object the published file carries. It is JSON, not Markdown, because the todo reader’s front matter is flat and a review comment has a nested review field. | --commit refuses the base branch (default main, change it with --base) and a detached HEAD. The check runs before anything is written, so a refused commit leaves nothing behind. A status committed straight to main would record a review outcome that no merge ever accepted. | The first move reads the published file, where a comment first exists after ingestion. Every later move reads the committed file, which is the reviewed record. | . How it reaches the page. The commit is a push to the feature branch, which rebuilds the preview. That build’s ingestion reads the committed comments (--todos) and a committed comment wins over the previously published copy. The comment-triggered refresh checks out no branch code, so it cannot read them and keeps what the last build published. Nothing is lost between the two. What it costs. One extra commit on the edit-set’s branch per decision, and a PR from a fork cannot be written to by anyone but its author.

3851.title: Verdicts: “I read this version”
3851.content: A comment asks for something. A verdict records that a reviewer read a block, and what they judged. The coverage gate needs verdicts, because comments cannot say whether a block with none was read. The channel is the same tagged PR comment, with a verdict: or waive: line instead of kind:. block: prose:dose prose:schedule verdict: ok role: clinical-sme . | line | means | . | verdict: ok | read, no objection | . | verdict: changes | read, and it needs changing. The reasons go in review COMMENTS; the verdict only records the reading | . | waive: <reason> | the block needs no review (a pure rename, say). The reason is required and kept | . | block: may name several labels, so one comment can close a slice. One verdict is recorded per label. | A comment is a verdict or a review comment, never both. A tag with kind: as well is refused and shown as malformed, so nothing is counted twice under two meanings. The comment parser passes every verdict tag over. | A verdict is pinned to the block’s hash. It counts only while the block is at that version. An edit after review reopens exactly the blocks it touched. The old verdict is kept and shown as “on an earlier version”. | A verdict on a label the head does not carry is malformed, not recorded. | . Pages and inputs no block reaches. A page changed by a manifest or media file, the comment pages and every FHIR IG page have no block to give a verdict on, and an input no renderer could place may have changed any page. The same tag takes them, beside or instead of block:: . page: en/dpi-h-ra/index.html verdict: ok . input: sushi-config.yaml waive: only the version string changed . page: names a path in the preview’s rendered-impact.json, or a page the build measured and the prediction missed; input: names one of its undetermined inputs. Each is pinned to that file’s hash there, so it reopens when an input that reaches it is edited. A page or input the build does not list, or a build that published no rendered impact, is reported malformed with the reason. See rendered-impact. The folio-review-comments Tool ingests verdicts into the same review-comments.json, as its verdicts array (folio-review-verdict/v1, folio-assistant-core/schemas/review-verdict.ts). Coverage. The folio-review-coverage Tool computes every fact GW_Covered reads (uncoveredBlocks, openDefects, and, with --rendered and --measured, the page counts with their rendered and measured statuses) and prints them as JSON on stdout, ready for workflow_complete. Every fact is always printed, because the engine refuses a missing one. With --todos <root> --commit it writes the verdicts into the todos graph’s declared review-verdicts directory and commits them to the feature branch, as comment statuses are, and it refuses the base branch and a detached HEAD. init-folio declares that directory (todos/verdicts/) for every new folio.

3852.title: Publication: where the file comes from, and when
3852.content: folio-staging.yml (the reusable workflow a folio calls) has two jobs: . | job | runs on | blocks from | what it writes | . | stage | the folio’s pull request (including a push that records a decision) | --folio, the checked-out feature branch; statuses from --todos | the site, changeset.json, blocks.json, review-comments.json | . | comments | a new or edited PR comment containing block: | the published blocks.json | review-comments.json only | . The comments job never checks out or runs the pull request’s code. It is started by anyone who can comment, and it holds a token that can write to the publish branch. Checking out a PR’s code in such a job is the well-known way to hand that token to a stranger. So it checks out only: . | the platform, at platform_ref (never a copy the PR carries); | the publish branch, which holds only what earlier trusted builds wrote. | . A comment body is parsed as data and never reaches a shell. The job also skips bot comments, so the preview comment the workflow itself posts cannot start it. Freshness. A new comment appears on the page about a minute later, after the comments job runs. A push rebuilds everything and keeps every comment. Nothing refreshes on a comment when there is no preview yet (no blocks.json), and the job says so rather than failing. The caller must opt in. A folio’s own workflow has to list issue_comment among its triggers for the comments job ever to run. init-folio writes that for a document folio.

3853.title: The review page
3853.content: en/review/index.html in the preview reads review-comments.json beside changeset.json, at the preview’s root, when it is opened: . | each changed block lists its comments: kind, status, reviewer and role, the first line, a link to the PR comment, the resolve: <id> tag for an open or addressed comment, and the recorded decision for a closed one; | a comment filter (Show comments) filters the listed comments by status (open, addressed, resolved, adjudicated, withdrawn, or open and addressed) or kind (defect, question, suggestion, editorial); | a comment on a block this PR did not change is listed separately, since a review of a whole document comments on unchanged text too; | orphaned comments are listed under their own heading, with the label they were made on; | malformed tags are listed with their links, so the reviewer can fix them; | every changed block shows its block: <label> line and a link to the PR, for writing a new comment; | no review-comments.json means the page SAYS it has no comment data. An empty list would read as “nobody commented”. | .

3854.title: Changing this process
3854.content: The process is a Skill and a Tool rather than YAML steps, so it can be changed here: . | to change | edit | and | . | the tag grammar | parseReviewTag in schemas/review-comment.ts | this skill’s tag table; the tests | . | a status or who may move it | REVIEW_COMMENT_STATUSES / REVIEW_TRANSITIONS | the BPMN task it names; this skill’s table | . | where a decision is recorded | folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comment-move.ts | the folio-review-comment-move Tool node | . | a field on the record | ReviewFieldsSchema | the page, if it shows it | . | what the ingestion does | folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comments.ts | the Tool node’s io if a flag changes | . | when it runs | folio-staging.yml and init-folio’s caller template | the trust notes above | .

3855.title: Deciding from the review page: a resolve: comment
3855.content: The page decides through the same channel it comments through. Under each open or addressed comment it shows the tag to post as a pull-request conversation comment, with the words that comment’s status allows: . resolve: review-pr7-c123 decision: resolved The dose now matches table 3. | The words are transitions of the table above: addressed (address), reopened (send-back), resolved (resolve), adjudicated (adjudicate), withdrawn (withdraw). Anything the table refuses is refused here too. | Who. A repository owner, member or collaborator (GitHub’s author_association) decides; the comment’s own author may withdraw it. Anyone else’s tag is refused, because a PR conversation is open to every GitHub user and a status is what the coverage gate counts. | The Decision that closes a comment is the decision comment’s URL. | Once. Each applied decision’s comment id is kept in review.decisions, so a rebuild, or a committed copy that already carries it, applies nothing twice. | Never dropped. A tag that cannot be read or applied is listed under “Tags that could not be read or applied”, with its reason. | . The build (folio-review-comments, and stage-local for a site.build folio) applies the tags after ingestion, so the published file and the page show the decided status. With --write-decided the Tool also writes each newly decided comment into the todos graph’s feedback directory, as folio-review-comment-move writes it; stage-local passes it and then runs state:push for a todos graph kept on its own state branch (dth-hrh’s cat/dth-hrh/todos), so the decision is recorded without anyone running a command. A todos graph in the feature branch’s tree is left for the editor to commit.

3856.title: Not yet decided
3856.content: . | Committing a page decision to an in-tree todos graph automatically. | A reviewer who edits a comment after ingest. The edit is not re-read, so a record an editor has already acted on is not silently rewritten. Whether an edit should reopen the comment is open. | Line review comments are not read. A reviewer who uses one gets no todo. | .

3858.title: Review heat map — where to look first
3858.content: Skill review-heatmap: The review page’s heat map: a section-by-metric table that tells a reviewer of a large document where to look first. Says what each column MEANS and what it must NOT be read as, where each number comes from, what a column says when a build lacks its data, and how the colour was chosen. Use when a reviewer or author asks “where do I start”, reads a number off the heat map, or asks why coverage or QA say “no data”; and before adding a column. Named by: Committee review of a content change, Draft, review and publish, Data sharing agreement document life cycle, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft . Skill id: review-heatmap · Package: folio-core . The review page (review/ in a folio’s staging preview) opens with a table. It has one row per section, in reading order, and one column per measure. The darker a cell, the more there is. Every cell also shows its number, so colour never carries the meaning alone. A section’s name moves focus to that section in the list of changes below it. It is not the block-dependency heat map in content-graph. That one draws which blocks depend on which, for a paper’s structure; this one is about a REVIEW.

3859.title: What each column means, and must not be read as
3859.content: | column | counts | from | must NOT be read as | . | Changed blocks | blocks in the section that the ChangeSet lists: added, removed or changed | changeset.json | how much text changed. A one-word edit and a rewrite each count 1. | . | Open comments | review comments still open or addressed, with defects counted in brackets | review-comments.json | how bad the section is. One comment may be about the whole section, and a question is not a defect. | . | Stale comments | open comments whose block changed AFTER the comment was made (its recorded hash differs from the block’s current one) | review-comments.json + blocks.json | wrong or obsolete. It means re-read the block before replying, because the reviewer saw an earlier version. | . | Review coverage | “3 of 5 reviewed”: the section’s added or changed blocks, and how many have a reviewer VERDICT on their current version. Shaded by what is still unreviewed. | review-comments.json’s verdicts + blocks.json | “every comment is resolved”. Resolved comments are not a verdict: a question answered is not a block judged. A verdict on an earlier version is shown on the block and does NOT count, so an edit after review reopens exactly the blocks it touched. A file with no verdicts field reads “no data”, never “0 reviewed”. | . | QA | the section’s blocks whose latest QA verdicts FAIL (with the worst severity), and those whose verdicts are STALE or that were never audited | block-qa.json, published by the folio-block-qa-summary Tool after the staging job sweeps the build | a pass. A block counts as failing only on a verdict NEWER than the block; an older verdict makes it stale, and stale outranks passing. A section gets a row for QA alone only if something there fails or is stale. | . A column with no data says so in every row (“not published”, or “no data” when a build lacks the file). It is never 0 and never blank: zero reads as “measured, and nothing there”. Orphaned comments (their block is gone) have no section. They are counted in a last row, “(listed in no section)”, because an open comment is still open.

3860.title: Where the QA column’s data comes from
3860.content: The staging workflow first sweeps the build (its qa_sweep input, on by default), then runs the folio-block-qa-summary Tool (cat-harness-tools/scripts/publish-block-qa.ts). The Tool reads each block’s block-qa/v1 verdicts, runs no checker itself, and writes block-qa.json. So the column reports THIS build’s script-checkable criteria. Criteria that need an agent’s judgement are not run by the sweep. Each block is one of: . | failing: a fresh verdict failed; | stale: nothing fresh failed, but some verdict predates the block’s files; | passing: every latest verdict is fresh and none failed; | unaudited: no verdict at all. | . “Passing” says what was judged. Each block also carries needsAgent: its applicable criteria declared automated: false that have no fresh verdict. Which criteria count comes from each criterion’s own declaration, gated as the sweep gates it (applies_to, the folio’s active voices). The column then reads either: . | “N passing on scripts only (M criteria need an agent)”; or | “passing, every applicable criterion judged”. | . A summary without needsAgent reads “passing (this build does not say whether agent-judged criteria were run)”, never “all judged”: a verdict never given is not a pass. Freshness is the QA sweep’s own rule, including the uses-graph hash that graph-scoped criteria depend on; without it every graph-scoped criterion reads stale straight after a sweep. The QA sweep writes verdicts under the instance root; the summary also reads, second, under the directory the sweep was run on, so verdicts an older sweep wrote there are still found.

3861.title: How the colour was chosen
3861.content: This follows the dataviz skill: . | Scale. One hue (blue), sequential, in three ordinal steps. Each column is scaled to its own maximum, by thirds; zero has no fill. | Light theme: steps 250 / 400 / 550. | Dark theme: steps 600 / 500 / 400, chosen for the dark surface rather than flipped from the light ones. | Validation. Both ramps pass validate_palette.js --ordinal: they are monotone, their steps are visibly apart, and the lightest clears 2:1 against the surface. | Ink. Every cell’s text colour clears 4.7:1 against its fill. | . The table is a real <table> with row and column headers, so it is its own table view for a screen reader. Every cell also has a hover title saying what it counts.

3862.title: Where it lives
3862.content: . | cat-harness-tools/scripts/review-heat.ts: computeHeat (the numbers), heatBucket (the thirds) and renderHeat (the table). The page embeds all three with toString(), so the tested functions are the ones that run. | blocks.json carries each block’s section, so a comment on an UNCHANGED block still lands in its section’s row. | .

3863.title: Adding a column
3863.content: . | Say what it counts and what it must not be read as, in the table above, before writing code. | Its data must be published in the preview, never read from an agent’s /tmp. | Add it to computeHeat and renderHeat, with a test for its “no data” state as well as its numbers. | .

3865.title: Review-log watch
3865.content: Skill review-log-watch: Poll a review log (a drafting Contributor Feedback sheet, or a public-comment sheet’s Review Change Sets) and its folio repository’s issues mechanically, with Tool review-log-watch, and start agent work only when a cell people set or an open issue changed. Each issue that no row links yet becomes a Contributor Feedback row, and a closed issue’s row is hidden with its text struck through. Use on every wake of a review-log watcher, and when setting up a watcher for a new log. Named by: Record agent step, Review-log watch . A review log is a drafting or public-comment sheet (skill review-sheet-script) for one folio repository. The steps below are for a drafting log; a public-comment log differs as set out in “Public-comment logs”. A watcher is the agent thread that keeps it moving. This skill is what the watcher does on each wake. Process: processes/content/review-log-watch.bpmn (checklist beside it).

3866.title: Why mechanical
3866.content: The watcher runs a core tool on every poll, and each issue gets a row on Contributor Feedback, including existing issues; a closed issue’s row is hidden, its text struck through. The poll wakes the watcher thread every minute. Until the tool says changed, the watcher only reads, runs the tool and does the stall pass (“Every poll”, below). It does not otherwise reason about the rows.

3867.title: Each wake
3867.content: . | Read two small ranges: . | Watch!F1:I1, where the sheet script writes Cells hash, the hash itself, and the time it last checked. The script rewrites it on every refresh and every timer tick, from the cells people set. | Contributor Feedback’s header row with its Change-set and Issue columns (A to K), so the tool can give a new row the next Change-set id. | . Save the values as JSON, with the header row and with an empty first row for each sheet row above it, so the row numbers stay the sheet’s. A sheet whose script has no Watch tab yet is read whole, from row 1, and gets no --sheet-hash. | Check: . bun run folio-assistant-core/tools/review-log-watch/watch.ts \ --repo litlfred/dth-phc --sheet values.json \ --state ~/.cache/review-log-watch/<sheet-id>.json \ --sheet-hash <Watch!G1> . | Exit 0 is {"status":"unchanged"}. Do the stall pass (below), then stop. The next wake was queued first. | Exit 10 is changed. The output has changes (an issue opened, updated or closed, or a cell’s old and new text) and append. | . Inserted rows. People may insert a row anywhere. The state keys each cell by its row’s Change-set id (CS-004:Ready for agent), and by sheet row only for a row with no id, so an insert moves no change set and reports nothing. A cell change carries cs and the row it is on now. Every row number in the output (changes[].row, closedRows) is from this read, so write only from the read you just checked, never from a row number kept from an earlier check. | Append each append[].row below the last row of Contributor Feedback. The row is already lined up with the header: . | Change-set: the next id, also in append[].agent.csId. | Title: the issue’s title. | First Contributor Feedback column: @login (#N): first paragraph. | Issue: the issue’s URL. | . The issue’s Markdown is turned into plain cell text: a [label](https://github.com/litlfred/folio-assistant-core/blob/main/skills/content/folio-document-adapter/url) shows its label, and bold, italic and code marks are dropped. Its links are in append[].links (the column and each link’s start, end and URL). Write the cell with those as textFormatRuns (updateCells), so each link is clickable. Then write append[].agent to the Agent tab as a new row: its Change-set and Issue columns. The script fills Contributor Feedback’s Issue column from the Agent tab, by Change-set, on every refresh, so an Issue written only on Contributor Feedback is cleared on the next refresh. Every other cell stays empty. This tool is the only thing that adds issue rows, so nobody adds them by hand. A row with closed: true is appended like the others and then treated as in step 4. | Closed issues. Hide each row in closedRows, plus the rows just appended for closed issues, and strike its text through. Hiding and striking are formatting only, so the row’s text and history stay. A reopened issue’s row is shown again, without the strike-through, by hand. | Agent pass. Run Contributor feedback on each changed row, and record the step on the Agent tab at once. A Ready for agent = Yes gets its edit, and a Ready for merge = Yes gets its merge. A Blue answer to a Decision needed question is taken up. Feedback on every Blue change and every new row. In every log the watcher keeps, the agent writes or rewrites Feedback (agent), in the layout of review-sheet-script (“The agent’s feedback cell has a fixed layout”), for each row that: . | is new, however it got there: from a GitHub issue (step 3), typed by a person, or copied from a TWG workbook; | has an empty Feedback (agent) cell; or | has Blue cells (Title, Selected Sections, any Contributor Feedback column, Disposition) that no longer match the Agent tab’s Feedback basis (feedbackBasis()), which is when the script shows “⚠ Stale”. It does this in the same wake, before accepting the state. A row it cannot finish keeps its stale mark and comes back on the next wake. The digest covers every row, not only issue rows, so a row with no issue still wakes the watcher. | . | Accept. Run the check again with the same inputs plus --accept, so the state file records what was handled. A row the pass could not finish still differs from the stored state, so it comes back on the next wake. | Queue the next wake. | .

3868.title: Every poll: hand new feedback on, and catch stalled rows
3868.content: New feedback goes to the agent working the row, and a stalled row is restarted or taken over; otherwise a contributor’s note can reach no one. This pass runs on every poll, changed or not, after the check: . | New feedback goes to the row’s agent. For each row whose Blue cells changed, find the thread that owns it: the one named in its Agent row or its Feedback (agent) cell, or else ask the coordinator. Send it the new text verbatim, with the CS id, the cell and the time. Then write in Feedback (agent) who has it and what happens next, so the contributor sees at once that it was heard. | Find stalled rows. A row is stalled when . | its Blue cells changed, or Ready for agent turned Yes, more than 10 minutes ago, and no Agent step has been recorded since; or | its agent has recorded no step for 2 hours while the row is open. | . | Restart or take over. Ask the owning thread once. If it gives no answer within 10 minutes, or it is done or stopped, take the row over yourself, or ask the coordinator for a new thread. Either way, write the new owner, its current step and a link into Feedback (agent). | . A row whose agent is working, but that shows nothing new, is not stalled: say what it is doing in Feedback (agent), with links to its pull requests, so the row stops looking stuck.

3869.title: Every poll: check each row against its Agent row
3869.content: After the stall pass, the watcher checks, for every row with a Feedback (agent) cell: . | a pull request or preview named in Feedback (agent) is the one in the row’s Agent row (Pull request, Staging review page); | Agent step reads <step> <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ>, not prose; | Agentic status shows no “no agent has picked this up” warning while the row’s thread is working. | . A row that fails is fixed through Record agent step (processes/content/record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent row first, then Feedback (agent), then a read-back. Another thread that owns the row sends the watcher its step and links; the watcher writes them, because one watcher owns each log.

3870.title: Finished rows: hidden and struck through, and not feedback
3870.content: A finished change set’s row (Agentic status Change merged or Closed) is hidden and its whole row struck through by the sheet script. Watchers ignore that visual change: the check compares cell values only, so hiding, unhiding and the line are never a change, and a hidden row still counts as a row: never append it again. When the check lists closedRows (rows linking a closed issue), the watcher closes each through Record agent step with Agentic status Closed; the script does the hiding.

3871.title: What counts as a change
3871.content: . | Issues: the repository’s issues, open and closed, with their state and updated_at. --author <login> keeps only the issues one person opened. | Pull requests are left out. | So are issues labelled no-sheet, which an Editor sets to keep an issue off the sheet. | . | Cells: with --sheet-hash, the script’s hash stands for them, and a change shows as one change on #hash; the watcher then reads the rows to see which changed. Without it, the tool compares the cells itself. Either way, only the cells people set count, under these headers: . | Title, Selected Sections, every Contributor Feedback column, Disposition and Change Set (human) (Blue); | Ready for agent, Ready for merge and Dispositions confirmed (Orange); | on a public-comment log also every Committee Feedback column, TWG (CS), TWG (human) and Change Set (human). | . The agent’s Green columns and the script’s Grey ones are not watched, so the watcher’s own writes never wake it. | First check (baseline: true): with no state file yet, every issue counts as new and every unlinked issue gets a row. This is how an existing sheet takes in its existing issues. The watcher appends the rows, hides the closed ones and accepts, but starts no agent pass, because a cell that is merely seen for the first time has not changed. | .

3872.title: Setting up a watcher
3872.content: A log is not set up until a watcher has both of these wakes: . | a chain of 1-minute delayed wakes (send_later), each of which queues the next before it reads anything, so no poll is skipped during long work. A send_later fires once, so a wake that does not queue the next ends the chain; | an hourly scheduled task that restarts the chain if it breaks. | . Keep the state file outside the repository, one per sheet. Without it, a fresh container treats its first check as a first check: it reports every issue as opened, and appends rows only for issues that no row links yet.

3873.title: Limits
3873.content: . | The tool reads one tab and one repository, from the issues API (up to 100 issues a page, every page). It never writes the sheet or GitHub. | The summary is the issue’s first paragraph, cut to 300 characters. A link the cut runs through keeps its target on the part that is left. Committee members may rewrite the Title and their own column. | .

3875.title: Review-log watch
3875.content: Process_ReviewLogWatch · strict (defaulted) · 7 step(s) . One poll of one review log (a drafting Contributor Feedback sheet, or a public-comment sheet’s Review Change Sets) and its folio repository. A tool decides, with no agent judgement, whether anything a person set in the sheet or any open issue changed since the last poll. Only then does the agent append rows for new issues and do its pass. 3881.title: Narrative review
3881.content: Process_NarrativeReview · advisory · 5 step(s) . Judging changed PROSE: read what the mechanical checkers flagged, decide which findings are real, then look at the two things no checker can judge — whether the editorial dependencies still hold and whether a translation still says what the source does. You are in this process when prose changed. review-code is its sibling for code nodes and review-task is what dispatches to either, so arriving here means somebody has already decided the change is narrative. Everything this lane produces is ADVICE. The reviewer records findings; accepting or refusing the change belongs to the editor’s lane in review-task, so a review can be thorough without being a veto. i i i i i

3887.title: Keep the review sheet’s Agent columns current
3887.content: Skill review-sheet-agent-columns: Whenever an agent works on a change set of a folio whose review sheet is kept by the Tool review-sheet-sync, it writes the Agent tabs’ columns for that change set and its comments as it goes: status, step, what it did, the PR, the staging page and its build, what the PR changed and when it finished. Use on every change-set edit, draft, PR, push, merge or close, in a sheet sync or not. Named by: Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . When an agent works on a change set of a sheet that has the Tool enabled, it updates the Agent columns as part of the process. The sheet’s views (Agentic status, Staging review and the ⏳ line on Review Public Comments and Review Change Sets, or on Contributor Feedback in a drafting sheet) are built from the Agent tabs, so a change set worked without writing them shows reviewers nothing, or something old as current. The tabs, their columns and who writes each are the public-comment skill’s (§”The live review sheet”) and, for a drafting sheet, review-sheet-script §”Drafting mode”. How the script reads them, and the tool that makes the cells, are review-sheet-script’s (“Stale staging previews”, “Checked by commit”, “Writing the Agent tab with the tool”, “Where the agent is”). This skill says when the agent writes and what.

3888.title: When it applies
3888.content: The folio has the Tool enabled: it carries the Tool’s config, review/public-comment/sheet-sync.json (a drafting sheet: review/drafting/sheet-sync.json), and the session can reach the sheet through a Google Sheets connector. The sheet’s id is not in the repository; it is given by the project (its scheduled sheet-sync task, or the owner). It applies to any work on a change set, however it started: a sheet sync, a card, a thread message, an issue or a review comment on the PR. If the Tool is enabled but the sheet cannot be reached, do the work, and say in the reply that the sheet was not updated and why.

3889.title: The tabs
3889.content: . | Agent - Comments (public comment only): one row per comment (No.), with Agentic status, Agentic action taken, Agentic applied in, Agentic handled by, Agentic date actioned and Change-sets. | Agent - Change Sets (a drafting sheet: Agent): one row per change set, with Pull request, Staging review page, What the PRs changed, Agent completed, Feedback basis, Staging built, PR head, Staging built from, Staging deploy and Agent step (each header ends “(change set)”). | . A public-comment sheet may instead have one Agent tab (comments left, change sets right, the Config’s AGENT_CS empty). Write it the same way, by header.

3890.title: When to write
3890.content: One move, one Record agent step. Every move in the table below is the subprocess processes/content/record-agent-step.bpmn, in this order: . | Write the change set’s Agent row: Agentic status, Pull request, Staging review page, the build columns, and Agent step. | Write Feedback (agent) from that row, linking the same pull request and preview. | Read back Agentic status, Agentic status (filter) and Staging review after the script’s next run. If they disagree with Feedback (agent), fix the Agent row, never the copied columns. | . A preview link goes in only when it is live, so a reader never gets a . | Live means the GitHub Pages deploy of a gh-pages commit at or after the preview’s publish succeeded (pages-build-deployment run, conclusion success), and an HTTP GET of each link answers 200 where the agent can reach the site. A publish that is only on the gh-pages branch is not live: deploys queue, and the next push cancels a queued one. Until then leave Staging review page empty, set Staging deploy to deploying, and write “Preview deploying” in Feedback (agent) with no preview link. Link the pull request instead. | . How to tell it is live, from where the agent runs (agents can be firewalled from github.io): gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/workflows/pages-build-deployment/runs and take the newest run whose gh-pages commit is at or after the preview’s publish; completed with success is live, queued, in_progress or cancelled is not. Then write deployed in Staging deploy. The sheet script does not fetch pages (it has no network permission, by its security review); it shows the link only when Staging deploy says deployed. Never write Feedback (agent) alone. The script builds Agentic status and Staging review only from the Agent tab, so a preview link written only in Feedback (agent) leaves Staging review empty and Agentic status naming the old pull request (CS-007, 2026-11-01). Agent step must be exactly <step> <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ> with a step from the fixed list; prose there is not read, and the row then warns “no agent has picked this up” however much work was done. A row waiting for people is idle <time>. Write as each step completes, not once at the end. Times, heads and steps come from bun run folio-assistant-core/tools/review-sheet-sync/agent-record.ts, never typed. | step | per comment (Agent - Comments) | per change set (Agent - Change Sets) | . | work starts | Agentic status Working | Agent step reading (agent-record.ts step reading) | . | proposing, editing |   | Agent step proposing or editing | . | PR opened, or a push to it | PR open; action taken, applied in, handled by, date actioned | Pull request, Staging review page, What the PRs changed; PR head, Staging deploy and Agent completed from agent-record.ts push; Agent step pushing | . | preview on gh-pages, then live |   | Staging built from, Staging built; Staging deploy pushed, deploying, deployed; Agent step staging, deploying | . | Ready for agent acted on, no new commit | date actioned | Agent completed from agent-record.ts done | . | blocked on a decision | Needs human, and what is needed in action taken | Agent step idle | . | ready for review | Ready for review | Agent completed; Agent step qa-review or idle | . | merged | Change merged | clear the Staging review page (a merged branch’s preview 404s); Agent step idle; then close the change set (below) | . | closed unmerged | Not started, and say so in action taken | remove that PR’s line from Pull request, What the PRs changed, Agent completed and PR head; Agent step idle | . Adding change sets: write the Agent tab only (2026-11-01). On a public-comment log, Review Change Sets columns A:B (Change-set, Title) are a spill, =FILTER('Agent - Change Sets'!A3:B, ...) in A3, so a new change set is a new row at the end of Agent - Change Sets and nothing else. A value typed into Review Change Sets A:B blocks the spill: every id shows #REF! and the tab looks empty (the 82 DPI-H rows written to A210:B291 did this until they were cleared). Before writing any cell, read its formula; never write over or below a formula’s spill range. Closing a change set is one step with two tools, GitHub and the review sheet. Task Task_CloseChangeSet of processes/content/contributor-feedback.bpmn: close the GitHub issue (with the merge, or the reason it closed unmerged), then set the Agent row’s Agentic status to Closed (or Change merged) through Record agent step. The sheet script hides that row and strikes the whole row through; reopening the issue and writing a new status shows it again. Never hide, strike or delete a row by hand. A disposition for the change set is written only from agent-record.ts dispositions (review-sheet-script, “Writing the Agent tab with the tool”). New feedback while you work, and stalls. The log watcher (skill review-log-watch, “Every poll”) sends new Blue feedback on your row to you, verbatim. Answer it in the same turn: record the Agent step (reading at least), and tell the watcher your step and links, so the row shows who has it. Record a step at least every time you finish one: a row with no new step 10 minutes after its feedback changed, or none for 2 hours, counts as stalled, and the watcher restarts it or takes it over. Name your thread in the row’s Feedback (agent) so the watcher knows whom to ask.

3891.title: What to write
3891.content: . | Re-read the headers first. People move columns. Find each column by its header, never by a letter remembered from an earlier run. | Write only the Agent tabs. Every other tab is people’s, or formulas, or the Apps Script’s. The exceptions are the agent’s own Green feedback column (review-sheet-script) and an explicit instruction from the owner for a named cell. | Per comment (every PC in the change set): Agentic status; Agentic action taken (what was done, in a sentence); Agentic applied in (the sections or blocks changed); Agentic handled by (the agent and its session); Agentic date actioned (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MMZ, UTC, from the clock). | Per change set: Pull request (one PR URL per line); Staging review page (branches/<slug>/en/review/ while the PR is open); What the PRs changed (one line per PR, in the same order as the URLs: what that PR changes in the document, in a reader’s words); Agent completed and PR head (one line per PR, same order). A change set may have several PRs, and a line in any per-PR column always matches the line of its URL in Pull request. | Staging built and Staging built from: when, and from which commit, the preview was last built, read from the newest gh-pages commit under branches/<slug>/. Write them on every rebuild. The script compares them with Agent completed and PR head and flags a preview built before the last push as stale. | Agent step: write idle (or the next step) before leaving a change set. A step left behind shows “no update for N min” on the sheet. | Append, never reorder. A change set new to the tab goes at the end. Review Change Sets’ typed columns sit beside rows derived from it, so moving a row moves people’s inputs onto the wrong change set. | No reviewer names or emails anywhere the agent writes, in the sheet or in the repository. Name feedback by tab, row and column header. | Only a PR that edits the document for the change set goes in Pull request (public-comment §”Which PR counts”). | .

3892.title: Checking it
3892.content: After writing, read the change set’s row on Review Change Sets (or Contributor Feedback) back. Once the Apps Script has refreshed (its timer runs every minute), its Agentic status shows <repo>#n (status, completed) · what it changed for each PR, and Staging review shows no ⚠ unless the preview really is behind. A missing or wrong line there means an Agent cell is missing or out of step.
