3914.title: Roles are swimlanes
3914.content: Skill role-model: Actors, roles and skills — who performs a BPMN task, under which swimlane, with which skills. How a role’s skill set is resolved through inherits and through a subprocess call chain, how a lane binds to a declared role, and how kg:audit finds a dangling skill, lane, role or decision. Named by: A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration . One sentence carries the whole model: . An actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Six objects, each with a home: . | object | what it is | declared in | . | Actor | a concrete participant. Human, agentic or mechanical. Persists across every process. | scenarios/actors/*.json (the declared scenarios graph, beside the roles) | . | Role | the swimlane — a persona an actor takes on because of the lane it is acting in. Carries a collection of Skills. | scenarios/roles.json | . | Skill | an instruction body: what the actor needs to know to perform the task it was handed. | skills/<pkg>/*.md (naming its input:/output: contracts, usually under schemas/skills/<name>/); JSON SkillDefinitions in each owning instance’s skills/skill-definitions/ | . | Process / Decision | BPMN and DMN. Lanes bind roles; activities name skills; gateways may compute their branch from a table. | processes/**/*.bpmn, processes/**/decisions/*.dmn | . | Requirement | a conformance obligation, pointed at by what discharges it: a skill or capability names the statement in satisfies: req:<id>#<key>. The requirement points at actors (who is bound) and derivedFrom (the broader requirement it specialises). | skills/requirements/*.json | . | Permission | what an actor is allowed to do. Cross-cuts roles. A W3C ODRL 2.2 rule, scoped by Process, Task or Role when it needs to be. | actions: skills/permissions/permissions.json; who holds them: policies/*.jsonld | . WHO’s “actor” is this model’s Role. An actor in the WHO DPI-H Reference Architecture’s conformance model (§3.7.2, an abstract information-processing role) and a DAK generic persona each map to a folio-assistant Role, never to an Actor. The RA’s system realising an actor maps to a mechanical Actor taking on that role. The comparison is on the DAK layer’s findings/dth-terms.md. Schema: schemas/process/role-graph.ts. Audit: scripts/kg-audit.ts, sidecar schema schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts. Not every skill is PERFORMED — consulted: true . Reference material belongs in no lane, by its nature. build-pdf and proof-triage are tasks somebody carries out; directory-conventions, untrusted-input and turn-reporting are what the performer READS. Both kinds are skills; only the first can sit in a swimlane. A skill that is reference material declares consulted: true in its front matter. Absent means performed: the exception is annotated, not the rule, because an axis whose default costs an edit in every skill file does not get adopted. No mechanical signal (a sibling SkillDefinition, an allowed-tools: line) tells the two kinds apart, so it must be declared. It is checked in BOTH directions, which is what stops it being an opt-out. skill-in-role-or-process skips a consulted skill; the separate consulted-skill-not-performed reports one that a role carries or an activity names, because a skill cannot be reference material and a step somebody performs. Which of the two declarations is wrong takes a person, so the criterion reports both rather than choosing. A skill does not carry roles: front matter . Do not write roles: in a skill’s front matter. bun run cat check:retired-front-matter fails if it appears, because copying an adjacent skill’s front matter brings the field back. To learn who performs a skill, read scenarios/roles.json; the registry is the only answer that resolves. A role→skill edge for a skill above the harness is an extensions entry in that instance’s role graph (§”A higher instance EXTENDS a role by id”). roles: in a folio-memory/v1 entry is a DIFFERENT field and stays. memoryForRoles filters on tags.roles, and an untagged entry would be seen by every lane. Sharing a key name across graph typologies is not sharing a field, and check:retired-front-matter keys its exemption on $schema, never on the directory. Whether a skill should declare its performer is undecided; if it ever does, the field is declared in the schema before it is written.

3915.title: Why a lane names a role, and the role is not the person
3915.content: A lane is not itself a role: a lane names the Role its tasks are performed in, not an Actor. The same actor is a different thing in two diagrams, and two different actors are the same thing in one. In crdm-requirements.bpmn the session agent acts in Lane_Agent. In bean-lifecycle.bpmn that very same session agent is, from the other diagram’s point of view, the sibling session — the lane that exists precisely to mark what is not yours to close. The skills differ because the lane differs, not because the actor did. So nothing is “a reviewer”. Somebody acts as reviewer, inside a process, for the duration of a lane. An actor carries roles[], never inherits. “Can review” and “can push” are properties of a position, not of a person, so the inherits lattice lives in the role graph. An actor lists the roles it may take on. roles: [] and an absent roles mean different things. [] says the actor takes on no role, which is the honest value for a read-only identity that never appears in a swimlane; absent says nothing has been asserted. The actor-is-not-a-role criterion reports an actor that carries inherits, because a registry written by hand reaches for inherits again. Roles played by mechanical actors are real roles, because the diagrams hand them tasks. Work plan (beans), Corpus, Publish target, a build pipeline and the external registries are roles a machine or an outside party plays. Their skills are their contract: the responsibilities they must perform, which a test can hold them to — a contract skill names its tests in front matter as tested-by:. The QA report lists a mechanical role whose skills name no test as mechanical-role-untested, and role-has-actor asks what actor plays each such role. A store is a mechanical role with a store block, and is drawn as a data store, not a lane. work-plan, corpus, log and session-record keep things rather than do them. Each stays a Role, so its skills are still its contract, and adds store: what it holds (typology ids), its api (one entry per transport, in that transport’s own format: openapi, fhir-capability, graphql, cli tools, json-schema-files, git), what it is realisedBy, and whether it is published. Only a role played by system or external actors may declare one. The role id is the store id: each layer declares <bpmn:dataStore id="<role id>"> once in processes/global-tasks.bpmn, and a process draws a dataStoreReference pointing at it, with dataInputAssociation for a read and dataOutputAssociation for a write. A system that does its own step (validates, decides, returns a result) keeps a lane; one that only keeps what others write is a data store. The same store is an ArchiMate application component (its interfaces, data objects and services hang off it) and, in a FHIR layer, an ActorDefinition of type system whose capabilities or reference points at its API. Some roles perform, but by judgement. stakeholder carries judgementOnly: true: somebody really does sign off, deliberates and is accountable — they simply cannot be handed a procedure that produces the answer. That is a different thing from a mechanical role, which has no judgement to exercise and whose skills are a contract it can be tested against. Do not give such a role a skill. The flag exists because a decision recorded only in a role’s summary is one the next agent re-litigates. activity-names-skill records n/a for activities in its lane, which lets that criterion gate on the undeclared ones.

3916.title: An actor is one of three kinds — human, agentic, mechanical
3916.content: { "id": "ci-pipeline", "title": "CI pipeline", "kind": "system", … } . kind takes one of four values, and three of them are the classification that matters. external is the fourth: a participant outside this instance, which is not ours to task at all. | kind | the kind it names | what it can be handed | . | person | human | a skill to read, and a judgement to make | . | agent | agentic | a skill to read, and a judgement to make | . | system | mechanical | a program to run, and nothing to decide | . | external | outside this instance | nothing | . The line is judgement. An agent and a person can both be handed an instruction body and asked to decide something; a mechanical system executes a procedure and decides nothing. That says whether a given step may be given to a given participant, so one value covering an LLM agent and a CI runner alike would leave “which tasks can this actor perform” unanswerable. The vocabulary is declared once, in schemas/kg/skill-package.ts (the zod-only base both the registry schema and the role graph import), and re-exported from schemas/process/role-graph.ts, where it is ACTOR_KINDS. A legacy type still loads, and is never read as agent. An unmigrated downstream registry has not said whether its non-person actors exercise judgement, so they read as system — the reading that refuses a judgement task rather than granting one on a guess. Guessing from an id ending in -agent would put an unreviewed claim into the graph wearing the appearance of data. An unrecognised kind throws: coercing a typo to system would silently disqualify an actor from every task it exists to perform.

3917.title: A task declares which actor kinds may fulfil it — mostly without saying so
3917.content: Tasks can be fulfilled by only certain actor types. activity-fulfilment-kind checks that against the lane’s role, and almost no diagram has to declare anything, because BPMN already answers it and nothing was reading the answer: . | task type | who may perform it | from | . | bpmn:userTask | person | the spec: “performed by a human being with the assistance of a software application” | . | bpmn:serviceTask | agent, system | the spec: “uses some sort of service … a Web service or an automated application” — no human in the loop | . | bpmn:task | nothing asserted | the abstract task says nothing, so neither does the check | . | bpmn:callActivity | nothing asserted | the constraint belongs to the called process’s own steps | . fulfilmentKindsForBpmnType returns undefined for the last two, never []. An empty list would read as “no kind may perform this” and fail every activity drawn as a plain task — the third state, in the place it is easiest to lose. Scoped like activity-names-skill. An activity whose lane is unbound or absent is already reported by lane-binds-role and activity-in-lane, so it is not reported twice here. Override it only when the derived answer is genuinely wrong: . <bpmn:extensionElements> <cat-harness.processes:fulfilment kinds="person agent" reason="a person or an agent drafts this; a pipeline cannot." /> </bpmn:extensionElements> . The reason is required at load time and a reasonless declaration does not parse — the same rule <cat-harness.processes:no-skill reason> follows, and for the same reason. Widening kinds is the cheapest way to make this criterion pass, so silencing it has to cost a sentence somebody reads in the diff. Read a failure as a question with three answers, not one. The task type may be wrong, the lane may be wrong, or the step may really admit that kind — and only the third is a <cat-harness.processes:fulfilment/>. Reaching for the exemption first turns it into a rubber stamp.

3918.title: Three questions about an actor, and only two are answered on the actor
3918.content: // cat-harness/scenarios/actors/admin.json { "id": "admin", "roles": ["programme-manager", "publication-manager", "editor", "author", "reviewer"], "capabilities": ["git-push"] } // policies/folio-defaults.jsonld: a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set { "permission": [ { "assignee": "admin", "action": "role-management" }, … ] } . | question | answered by | scope | . | what may it act AS? | roles on the actor | per lane | . | what may it DO? | ODRL rules in policies/ naming it as assignee | everywhere, or as narrow as a rule’s cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task and cat-harness:role constraints | . | what does its machine have? | capabilities on the actor | the environment | . What an actor may DO is not on the actor. It is a W3C ODRL 2.2 rule per action in policies/: . | Inheritance. Each action in permissions.json says which broader actions it is includedIn, ending at ODRL’s own (odrl:display, odrl:modify, odrl:execute, …). A grant of a broader action permits everything included in it. The graph need not be a tree and may have cycles. | Scope. A rule may be limited to a Process, a Task or a Role. No constraint means everywhere. | One question, three answers. permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts returns permit, deny or unknown, and unknown is never permit. Performing a task in a lane needs the permission and the lane’s role, so eligibility (roles) and permission stay separate, as below. | Anyone. cat-harness:anyone is an unauthenticated reader: a person with no login, whoever they are. It may visualize and render, and nothing else. | . Identity is not here. Which login is which actor is the data store’s to know. No actor file and no policy carries a login, and workflow history names the actor, never the login: the repository owner’s steps are recorded as owner, and the data store maps the login to owner. Who reads all three before a task runs: the BPMN executor. Before any task or decision is recorded, authorizeTask asks whether the actor is authenticated, eligible for the lane’s role (roles), and permitted by policy to perform-task here and on this content. A role mismatch or a deny refuses, and so does unknown, because the engine runs strict. The HTTP routes ask the same policies through src/core/rbac.ts. See task-authorization. Adding a permission: declare the action in permissions.json with its includedIn, then add a rule to a policy in policies/. Never add a permissions list to an actor file: the audit reads it (an unmigrated downstream registry still works), but a list there is invisible to every scoped decision. Permissions do not belong on Role either. A permission cross-cuts: one action is held by actors taking on several different roles, and not by every actor sharing a role. The line that does hold: a skill answers what the performer of this task needs to KNOW, and belongs to the lane. A permission answers what this participant may DO, and travels with the participant through every lane it enters. Both are audited and both are critical — actor-permissions-resolve (which also checks that every policy rule names a declared action and a declared actor or cat-harness:anyone) and actor-capabilities-resolve.

3919.title: Requirements are the fifth node kind, and they only point
3919.content: A requirement is not a skill and not a role. It is an obligation about them, kept in the kg graph so that every agent reads it and its joins are audited: . { "id": "req:commit-hygiene", "derivedFrom": ["req:agent-workflow"], "actors": ["author", "admin"], "statements": [ { "key": "no-secrets", "conformance": "SHALL", "requirement": "Commits SHALL NOT include secrets, API keys, tokens…" } ] } . and a skill that discharges a statement says so in its own front matter: . satisfies: - "req:commit-hygiene#no-secrets" . The statement names no satisfier: a requirement is written once, and what discharges it arrives later, so the pointer lives on the arrival. The references are audited. satisfies-resolves, requirement-actors-resolve and requirement-derived-from-resolves are critical, because a reader following a broken one gets nothing — the same test as a dangling <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>. requirement-statement-satisfied is minor coverage: a statement nothing claims is visible only from the requirement’s side. requirement-statements-graded is major: an ungraded statement is readable, it just cannot be conformance-tested, and SHALL-vs-SHOULD is the whole reason to write a requirement rather than a note. Do not fold a requirement into the skill that satisfies it. The grading, the derivedFrom lattice, the actor binding and the many-to-many satisfies are the only machine-checkable things about it, and prose in a skill doc carries none of them. satisfies is many-to-many in both directions — one skill discharges statements in several requirements — so inlining duplicates rather than relocates.

3920.title: Two compositions, and they are not the same
3920.content: inherits — a role IS-A role. qc-reviewer inherits reviewer and gets its skills everywhere, in every process, forever. Static. resolveRoleSkills closes over it breadth-first, so a skill’s reported via is the nearest ancestor that supplies it. The subprocess stack — a role acting INSIDE another role’s task. A process calls a subprocess and the actor keeps acting: it does not stop being the outer role, it additionally takes on the inner lane’s role. The skills available at that task are the union along the whole call path. resolveRoleStack takes the path outermost-first and keeps each skill’s provenance, because a reader needs to know not only that a skill was available but which level supplied it. resolveRoleSkills(graph, "qc-reviewer") // static: + everything reviewer has resolveRoleStack(graph, ["editor", "viewer"]) // scoped: the union for this call only . Do not merge them. A flat union would make reviewer permanently hold every skill any caller ever had, and a closure that broad cannot fail an audit, which is the same as not having one.

3921.title: A higher instance EXTENDS a role by id — it never edits it
3921.content: A third relation, across instances rather than within one graph. When a skill belongs above the harness (a core cataloguing skill, a sci Lean skill), the role→skill edge naming it must not stay in cat-harness/scenarios/roles.json — that is an upward reference. So the dependent holds the pointer, the way a voice points at the role it addresses and a story at the role it is told as: . // <content-core>/scenarios/roles.json { "name": "<content-core>", "roles": [], "extensions": [{ "role": "librarian", "skills": ["filing-dublin-core"] }] } . | a dependent’s scenarios/ may | it may NOT | . | add skills to a lower role (extensions) | change its title, description, inherits, actorKinds or persona | . | add a NEW role, which may inherits a lower one | redeclare a lower id — refused, “extend it instead” (one exception, below) | . | extend a lower actor: actors/<f>.json with "extends": "<id>", adding roles / capabilities | carry any other field on an extension | . | extend a capability: "extends" adding requires; or add a new probe | point an extension UP or sideways — only at an id declared below it | . The one exception — a move in flight. Moving a role, actor, capability or policy up a layer is two pull requests: the higher layer adds it, then the lower layer removes it, and in between both declare the id. A redeclaration that only adds — every field the lower declaration carries is there unchanged (the same scalar, every member of an array, a nested object by the same rule), and it may carry more, such as the skills it used to add by extension — is accepted with a warning that names the id and both layers, and the higher declaration is used. The warning is the move’s to-do: remove the lower copy. A redeclaration that changes or drops anything the lower one said is still refused. schemas/process/scenario-overlay.ts applies it (checkoutRoleGraph, checkoutActors, checkoutCapabilities, checkoutPolicies; the exception is onlyAdds); the layers are the checkout’s instances that depend on the role’s owner, deepest first. Resolved alone, the harness sees only its own roles. kg:audit, check:raci, check:fallback-roles, check:actor-reach, kg-export and the stakeholder map read the checkout’s view on the platform’s own run. The edge stays on a role graph — the graph of the instance that owns the skill — never in skill front matter.

3922.title: A lane binds its role with partitionElementRef
3922.content: Lane names are free text, and several spellings name one position, so a name alone joins a lane to nothing and an undefined lane is a silence rather than a finding. So a lane binds its role itself, with BPMN’s own partitionElementRef: the role is declared once per diagram as a top-level <bpmn:resource> whose id is the role id verbatim and whose name is its title, before the collaboration and the process. The role lists no lanes: a role is the general node and a lane the dependent one, and a general node never names its users (data-modelling step 8). <bpmn:resource id="reviewer" name="Reviewer"/> ... <bpmn:lane id="Lane_Reviewer" name="Reviewer" partitionElementRef="reviewer"> ... </bpmn:lane> . A <bootstrap.processes:role ref="reviewer"/> in the lane’s extensionElements is read, with a warning, only when partitionElementRef is absent (laneRoleRef in schemas/process/role-graph.ts); the QA report lists it as lane-role-legacy-binding. <bootstrap.processes:role variable="true"/> stays: it declares a performer who is whoever invoked the process. An explicit binding wins over name matching: a diagram that has said which role it means must not be second-guessed by a string table. A ref naming no declared role is a critical finding — it is not quietly name-matched instead.

3923.title: The audit — bun run cat kg:audit
3923.content: One criterion per join in the sentence at the top. The list below is the actor→role→skill→task core; KG_CRITERIA in schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts is the registry, and it is longer — it also covers requirements, skill bodies and the graph as a whole. activity ──names────▶ skill skill-ref-resolves critical gateway ──computes─▶ decision decision-ref-resolves critical lane ──is───────▶ role role-ref-resolves critical activity ──sits in──▶ lane activity-in-lane major task type─can be done by▶ kind activity-fulfilment-kind major lane ──is───────▶ role lane-binds-role major role ──carries──▶ skill role-carries-activity-skill major decision ──is used──▶ gateway decision-outcomes-used major role ──carries──▶ skill role-skills-resolve critical role ──is-a─────▶ role role-inherits-resolves critical activity ──names────▶ skill activity-names-skill minor role ──is used──▶ lane role-binds-a-lane minor actor ──takes on─▶ role role-has-actor minor skill ──any way in▶ anything skill-has-entry-point minor skill ──modelled?▶ role/task skill-in-role-or-process minor actor ──is not a─▶ role actor-is-not-a-role minor . | command | does | . | bun run cat kg:audit | write the sidecars, print the summary | . | bun run cat kg:audit:check | fail on a critical finding, or on a stale sidecar | . | bun run cat kg:audit:strict | …and on major too | . | bun run scripts/kg-audit.ts --json | the full report set, for a tool | . Why sidecars rather than a console report . check-workflow-refs.ts prints and exits, so its previous answer is gone. That makes “this lane has been unbound since the day it was drawn” and “this lane broke in the commit under review” indistinguishable, and a reviewer cannot separate a new defect from inherited debt. The sidecars are committed, under kg-qa/ beside whatever they audit, so the diff says exactly which findings a change introduced. Same argument and same file shape as the block sweep’s *.qa.json and the script sweep’s *.script-qa.json. Where the sidecars for another instance go — hosted, not written into it . An instance that declares no qa directory does not receive sidecars inside its own tree: kgQaHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts them in the auditing harness’s qa directory under the instance’s stub — cat-harness/test/results/bootstrap/ for bootstrap (a working copy, stored on the qa-reports branch with the rest of that qa directory; a JUDGEMENT about it is hosted the same way, under test/attestations/). A verdict ABOUT an instance is the auditor’s output, and bootstrap is the layer that must read cleanly with no harness present. The same holds once bootstrap is its own repository: the verdicts stay with the harness that computed them, against the pinned bootstrap (kg-separation §”The pair”). Three states, and what unknown costs . A criterion returns pass, fail, n/a (does not apply to this subject) or unknown (could not be evaluated — the file would not parse, a dependency was absent). unknown is never written as a pass. It counts as a failure at its criterion’s own severity. It is not promoted to major either: a diagram that will not load records unknown against its critical criteria too, so it still fails the gate, while an unevaluable minor criterion does not gate the build: a gate that fires on something nobody agreed was blocking gets switched off. Severity, and why coverage is only minor . critical is a broken reference — something names a thing that does not exist, and a consumer following it gets nothing. major is a missing join — the graph is intact but a question has no answer, e.g. a lane bound to no role. minor is coverage: a real gap with legitimate instances. A human signing something off is not implemented by a markdown file, so failing on activity-names-skill would force a fake ref onto a real step, which is worse than the gap. Never quote a count from prose — run the audit . A number written in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. Two criteria ask different reachability questions, and only one of them is about the role model: . | skill-has-entry-point — is there ANY way in: servable, in the harness, carried by a role, or named by an activity? The servable clause alone covers nearly the whole corpus, so this passes near-trivially; its green is not an answer to the coverage question. | skill-in-role-or-process — what does the actor → role → task model actually reach? This is the real coverage question, and it must never gate. A skill invoked directly by name is doing its job without appearing in any diagram, and driving the number to zero would mean inventing roles and activities to absorb tools that do not want them. Watch it move; do not read it as a defect list. | .

3924.title: What counts as a skill
3924.content: scripts/known-skills.ts is the single answer, shared by kg-audit and check-workflow-refs so the two cannot disagree. Not every group under a skills directory holds skills: actors/ holds participants, capabilities/ holds environment probes (docker, pandoc, python3), roles/ holds an assignment table and hooks/ holds a shell script. NON_SKILL_GROUPS excludes them, so <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="viewer"/> does not resolve. It is a deny-list of groups known not to hold skills, not an allow-list of local/, so a new group of real skills is picked up automatically and a new group of something else is a one-line addition.

3925.title: Administration IS a swimlane
3925.content: The role graph is the substrate every diagram’s lanes bind to. Changing it — adding an actor, opening a role, granting a permission, retiring a participant — is therefore a process like any other, and it is drawn: actor-role-administration.bpmn, in the administrator lane. Do not invent a role to make a diagram drawable. A role minted for a picture is a role no audit can fail, because nothing was ever true of it — the closure-widening failure of §”Two compositions”, from the other end. What follows from administration being a lane: . |   |   | . | administration is a lane | so role-management is exercised somewhere a reader can find | . | the lane is person-only | a permission grant is a standing decision, not a task; the agentic/mechanical line is judgement, and this one is authority | . | the mechanics are NOT re-drawn | the diagram calls code-change-review; a second description of branch-gates-review is a second thing free to disagree with the first | . | the audit runs after | every criterion is a join, so what an administrative edit breaks is never in the file it edited | .

3926.title: Adding a role
3926.content: . | Add it to scenarios/roles.json with a description that says what the position is, not what it is called. actorKinds is a SET drawn from person, agent, system and external — human, agentic, mechanical, or outside this instance. It is what activity-fulfilment-kind checks the lane’s steps against, so it is a claim about who can actually stand there, not a label. Use title/description (the two labels every knowledge-graph node carries), never summary, and actorKinds, never actorKind: Zod strips an unknown key, so a misnamed field type-checks, parses, and is silently lost. | Bind its lanes: each diagram declares <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> once, and each lane that names this role carries partitionElementRef="<role id>". The role lists no lanes, since a role is the general node and a lane the dependent one (data-modelling step 8). A lane with no ref is unbound, whatever its name. | Give it the skills its lane’s activities name. role-carries-activity-skill fails if an activity demands something its performer was never given. | bun run cat kg:audit. The kg-qa sidecars it writes are derived results whose record the CI job qa-publish stores on the qa-reports branch. | . A role that binds no lane in any diagram is reported by role-binds-a-lane: either a lane name has drifted, or the role is dead.

3927.title: Renaming a role, and a role’s other names
3927.content: Never let a name go silently. A role carries every name it goes by: . | otherNames — names in use today: synonyms, a local title, an example. The same field, and meaning, as otherNames on WHO SMART Base’s Generic Persona. Published as skos:altLabel, beside the names the role’s lanes are drawn with. | formerNames — { "name", "retiredOn" } for each name it no longer goes by. Published as skos:hiddenLabel on the role, and the old name’s concept is owl:deprecated and dcterms:isReplacedBy the role, so a reader holding the old name from older text is sent to the current one. | . To rename: change title, and add the old one to formerNames with today’s date, in the same commit. readRoleGraph refuses a name — title, other or former — that two roles share, so a retired name cannot be quietly given to a new role. The glossary ledger still records, from the harness’s side, every name a swimlane has derived; the role’s own lists are the authored record a README can show (kg:roles, written by bootstrap-tools).

3929.title: The root README, and the one fact it must carry
3929.content: Skill root-readme: Write the repository’s root README when there is none, carrying a link to the harness that was installed and the overall install status. Never replaces one that exists. It runs only once the install has succeeded. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are the Bootstrapping Agent, and the install has just succeeded. The repository now is an instance of something, and — unless somebody wrote one before you got here — nothing at its root says so. People and agents read README.md first, so the README says it.

3930.title: Writing it is not the write the layer rule forbids
3930.content: An instance-readme is read at session start and never written by a running process. That rule governs a process operating on an instance that exists; initialization brings the instance into being, so it may create the README.

3931.title: When it is absent — write it
3931.content: Two things, and no more: . | A link to the harness that was installed. Whatever reference the Requestor gave when the harness was confirmed, resolved to something clickable. | The overall install status. Not one line per location dug out of a log — the question a reader has is “is this repository set up, and as what”, and that is what you answer. Say how many locations the install touched and whether every one of them succeeded. | . Write nothing else: the harness’s own README tool fills the rest, in marker pairs, once it is installed. Say which locations, when there is more than one. “Installed” over three locations where one failed is a false statement about the repository, and the reader who acts on it is the person who set it up.

3932.title: When one is already there — do NOT replace it
3932.content: Add the link and the status inside a marker pair instead, so the harness’s README tool owns that region from then on and the rest of the file stays the author’s. If you cannot tell whether an existing file is authored or a leftover, it is authored: that is the assumption whose failure mode is a duplicated sentence rather than a lost page.

3933.title: What you do not decide here
3933.content: Whether the install succeeded — the install step decided that, and you are on the path where it did. Which harness it was — the Requestor decided that. What the README should eventually say — its author decides that, and you are not its author. If the write fails (no permission, a read-only checkout), say so and end installed anyway: the harness is installed.

3935.title: Sample import
3935.content: Skill sample-import: Testing an import of a SAMPLE of a remote source into a knowledge graph or other structured store: scope it, let materialize-remote gate it, land it in the library (permanent) or the kept, unpublished trashcan (trial), import it, and test the import. The gates are called, never copied. Named by: Sample import into a structured data store . The SDLC for trying out a remote source before committing to it: take a sample, land it, import it into the store you care about, and find out what breaks. The process is cat-harness/processes/library/sample-import.bpmn. IRIS is the worked instance (the IRIS replica); nothing here is WHO-specific.

3936.title: The gates are not here
3936.content: Size, restrictions, copyright, retention and source loss are asked once, by materialize-remote, and this process only reads the outcome. A second copy would be a second answer free to disagree with the first. What each gate refuses on is in that skill. What this skill adds is what happens around it.

3937.title: 1. Scope — three answers before anything is fetched
3937.content: | question | why it is asked first | . | Which items? By the source’s identifiers, or a subset strategy its descriptor (in the owning instance’s declared sources/, e.g. the IRIS replica’s sources/) supports. | the size gate needs a request to measure | . | Which store? The graph or database the import is tested against. | the test in step 4 is against this store’s schema | . | Permanent or trial? | it decides where the copy lands, and moving a landed copy later means moving it under the wrong obligations | . There is no default for the third. An unscoped sample goes back to the person who proposed it.

3938.title: 2. Materialize — call, and branch on the outcome
3938.content: Call Process_MaterializeRemote. referenced (any gate refused or unknown) ends the sample: nothing is imported, and the refusing gate’s reason is recorded so the next attempt does not re-litigate it.

3939.title: 3. Land it where its permanence says
3939.content: A sample that is not intended to be permanent is materialized to fsh-guts/. |   | permanent | trial | . | destination | library/ | fsh-guts/ | . | published | yes, with the library | no — kept, addressable, exported, never rendered | . | refreshed | yes, by refresh-materialized | no — it records what the source looked like when tried | . | provenance | the materialization record | $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1, plus the work item or issue it was written under. Never a movedFrom: it was not moved from anywhere, and inventing one is false provenance. | . Promoting a trial means running the process again with permanent. The gates are asked afresh; a trial’s answers were given for a trial.

3940.title: 4. Import and test
3940.content: Load the landed sample into the store and check: . | completeness — every requested item arrived (count against the request); | identifiers — the descriptor’s authoritative identifiers survived; | structure — each node validates against the store’s schema; | provenance — source, revision and fixity are attached to each node. | . A check that could not run is a failure, not a pass. That is the whole reason the gateway is labelled “no, or could not run”.

3941.title: 5. Record the outcome — every path
3941.content: . | passed → where it landed and what was checked; | failed → which check, on which items, with the evidence. The landed copy stays: a failed import is information about the source or the store, and removing the copy destroys it (deletion-requires-confirmation). | .

3942.title: Why bootstrap does not call this
3942.content: bootstrap is the floor (needs: []) and these processes live in cat-harness, which needs bootstrap. A call from bootstrap up to cat-harness is an edge layer-direction.ts reports as wrong-direction.

3950.title: Saturation meta-merge — drain the queue when the runners are full
3950.content: Skill saturation-meta-merge: When the CI runners have been full for a long time, drain a repository’s ready PRs in one step: hold the swarm, cancel the queued PR runs, stack every admitted PR onto one meta-merge branch with merge commits, and land that branch on main without waiting for CI, on the owner’s card that names each PR. Then re-run main’s checks and report. Use for “runners are full”, “cancel everything and merge what’s ready”, “meta-merge”, “consolidate the queue”, and when the queue has not moved for an hour or more. Named by: Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, Merge to main, A merge train, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Guideline Updates . This is an owner-invoked exception to merge-queue and merge-to-main. Normally every PR lands on its own green CI through merge:guard. When the runners are full, that rule is what stops the queue: each PR waits for a runner, and then a newer push to main makes its result stale. A meta-merge trades per-PR CI for one CI run on main after landing. It is only run when the owner asks for it, and on a card that names every PR. The process is sdlc/processes/saturation-meta-merge.bpmn (Process_SaturationMetaMerge), called from the merge manager’s watch loop (merge-manager-watcher).

3951.title: Trigger
3951.content: Offer the meta-merge, but do not run it, when either of these holds on a repository: . | PR runs have been queued for 60 minutes or more and no PR has landed in that time, or | the queue has 10 or more runs across the repositories the swarm shares, and the owner says the runners are full. | . Measure it with gh api "repos/<o>/<r>/actions/runs?status=queued" and the created_at of the oldest run. Offering it is a card (step 3). Running it is the owner’s tap.

3952.title: Steps
3952.content: . | Hold the swarm. Message every sibling thread that pushes to the repositories in scope: no new pushes, PRs, merges, run cancels or re-runs there until you post meta-merge done. Ask the coordinator to pass the hold on to any thread you cannot reach. A sibling that owns a PR in the batch names the head it wants merged. Check that the head you fetch is that head. | Dry run. Run the script (below) without PUSH=1 on each repository. It builds claude/meta-merge-<date> from origin/main and merges each PR head with --no-ff, in order. It skips a PR that: . | conflicts with main plus the PRs before it, generated paths included (the stacking rule in merge-queue), or | touches .github/workflows/ (an agent token cannot push a workflow file) or subscriptions/ (held, fixity-checked copies; change those upstream). | . | Ask once, naming every PR. Use ask-the-person. For each repository, list: . | the PRs to include, | the PRs to leave out, each with its reason: conflict, draft, red, protected path, content, a thread waiting on the owner, or an open security review, and | the merge method: merge commits throughout, never squash or rebase, so GitHub marks each included PR as merged. | . Options: A go with green and pending, B also include the red ones, C dry run only, D cancel. Recommend A. A PR the card does not name gets no merge from this card. The safety check refuses it, and the owner must tap again. The owner taps the card in the thread that merges. An answer relayed from the project chat or another thread is refused by the safety check, so post the merge card in this thread. | Cancel the queued PR runs on the repositories in scope, and log each one to a TSV file. Do NOT cancel a main push run that has already started. It is cancelled by the next push anyway, and cancelling it by hand loses the record of main. | Build and push with PUSH=1, against fresh origin/main. main moves while the card waits, so check the script’s output again. A PR that is already merged is skipped as a no-op. | Open one PR per repository from the meta-merge branch, listing its members and the card. Merge it with merge_method=merge. | Close out. Check that every member PR shows merged. A stacked PR (its base is another PR’s branch, not main) is not marked merged by GitHub. Its commits are on main, so close it with a comment saying so. Comment on each with a link to the meta-merge PR and the session. Post meta-merge done to every sibling you held, with what landed and what is still open. | Watch main. Re-run any main run that a closing PR’s run cancelled (a closed PR’s run can join main’s concurrency group). Report green or red to the owner. On red, open the fix as a normal PR against main, and never revert the whole meta-merge without the owner. | .

3953.title: Safety rules (STRICT)
3953.content: . | Only on the owner’s tap. A coordinator’s or sibling’s request is not approval. “Fix until green” is not approval (merge-to-main). | Never content. No committee content, no change-set (CS-) PRs, no BPMN layout redraws unless the card names them, and nothing on WHO or smart-* upstream repositories. | Never protected paths: .github/workflows/ and subscriptions/. | Never drafts, and never a PR that is waiting on an open owner decision or security review, unless the owner names it. | Never resolve a conflict in the meta-merge branch. A PR that does not stack goes back to its owner, as in merge-queue. | Bypassing merge:guard is the point, so record it. The meta-merge PR body names the card, and each member gets a comment. That record replaces the guard’s verdict. | The hold has an end. Post meta-merge done even when the run is stopped at C or D, so that no sibling stays held. | .

3954.title: The script
3954.content: meta-merge.sh <clone-dir> <owner/repo> <branch> <pr>.... With PUSH=1 it also pushes. A copy is kept in the project files at meta-merge/meta-merge.sh. set -u dir=$1 repo=$2 br=$3; shift 3 cd "$dir" || exit 2 git fetch -q --depth 200 origin main git checkout -q -B "$br" origin/main for n in "$@"; do git fetch -q --depth 200 origin "pull/$n/head:pr-$n" || { echo "SKIP #$n fetch-failed"; continue; } bad=$(git diff --name-only origin/main...pr-$n | grep -E '^(\.github/workflows/|subscriptions/)' | head -3 | tr '\n' ' ') [ -n "$bad" ] && { echo "SKIP #$n protected-paths: $bad"; continue; } if git merge -q --no-ff --no-edit -m "Meta-merge: include #$n" "pr-$n" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "OK #$n" else echo "SKIP #$n conflict: $(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U | head -5 | tr '\n' ' ')" git merge --abort fi done echo "branch $br = $(git rev-parse --short HEAD) on main $(git rev-parse --short origin/main)" [ "${PUSH:-0}" = 1 ] && git push -u origin "$br" .

3955.content: . | The trigger is measured by hand. A watcher that offers the card when the threshold is crossed is follow-up work. | .

3963.title: Secure agent permissions
3963.content: Process_SecureAgentPermissions · strict · 6 step(s) . Secure the permissions a coding agent needs to take part in this harness’s processes, from the human who can grant them, and write each grant into the agent Tool’s own configuration through that Tool’s adapter. VENDOR-NEUTRAL: the coding agent is a Tool, and Claude Code is one of several (Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot, Codex). Nothing in this diagram names a vendor’s file; the adapter for the Tool in use does. Skill: agent-permissions. CALLED FROM SESSION START (session-state-machine.bpmn, Call_SecurePermissions, after the session record opens), so it is part of initiating the harness for an actor. It also runs on demand when an agent hits a denied action: the denial is a reason to ask, never to edit the Tool’s config itself. A run that finds every needed permission already granted and recorded ends at End_Current without asking anything. NEVER SELF-GRANTED. The grant is the owner’s (Task_OwnerGrants, a person only) and the config write is done by the person, or by the agent with their explicit consent to that exact diff. An agent that edits its own permission configuration is self-modification. MERGE IS NOT A GRANTABLE PERMISSION HERE. Merging to main stays a separate owner-authorised step on every occasion (merge-to-main.bpmn); this process never writes an allow-rule for it. i i i i i i

3969.title: Security — one question, asked at every boundary
3969.content: Skill security: The security sub-KG’s entry point. What the boundaries are, which machinery already guards each one, and the single rule that unifies them — refuse, never repair. Read this before adding a check, so the answer that already exists is reused rather than rebuilt in a fourth place. Named by: Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive . This value came from outside. What may I do with it? . Everything in this package is that question at a different boundary. The split is not by attack name: the same untrusted string is command injection at a shell, path traversal at a join, and XSS at a template, and filing the rule under each name is how a correct guard ends up in one file while other call sites hand-roll it.

3970.title: The rule that unifies them: refuse, never repair
3970.content: A check returns a refusal, not a cleaned-up value. A repair silently changes which artefact is named: a slug pipeline that replaces disallowed characters can turn a branch of --- into the empty string, so rm -rf "pages/branches/$SLUG" names every preview. A refusal makes the caller decide, and only the caller knows whether that is a 400, an exit 1, or a skip. And check by VALUE, never by provenance. Re-run a guard after the value crosses a job boundary (feature-staging.yml does): “where it came from” is not a property you can read off a variable.

3971.title: The boundaries, and what guards each one today
3971.content: | boundary | the hazard | machinery | state | . | ${{ }} → a run: or script: block | the value is substituted into the script TEXT before bash or V8 parses it, so a quote is enough — and inside a JS template literal ${…} is EVALUATED, so it need not even close one. A step OUTPUT carries whatever the step put in it, so the gate resolves provenance rather than trusting the band | scripts/check-workflow-injection.ts + baseline + 2 test files | gated; two surfaces with two remedies, with:/env:/if: still ungraded | . | an external id → a path | join(base, external) escapes the store; mkdirSync + writeFileSync make it a write primitive | path-containment, src/core/safe-path.ts | guarded; narrowly gated — server-path-sinks.test.ts, a source ratchet | . | a shell string → a process | execSync("cmd " + value) gives the shell a program | injection-boundaries | partly (execFileSync at the fixed sites) | . | an archive → a filesystem | a LINK member writes through to its target, which ..-refusal does not cover | member-TYPE whitelist (tar tvzf, accept only - and d) at the one call site, tar-member-guard.test.ts against real archives | closed at one site | . | a .po catalogue → a render | translated content is authored elsewhere | scripts/translation/translation_security.py | exists, unaudited here | . | a hand-over → a model | a sub-agent report, delegated prompt, tool result or third-party comment carries an instruction the receiver follows because it trusts the sender (protocol pivoting) | bun run cat handover:screen (src/core/handover-screen.ts): field by field over a declared schema; control fields and undeclared fields refused, data fields quarantined; fenceUntrusted labels the origin | guarded and wired: every in-code site where foreign text reaches a model calls guardUntrusted or screenHandover; the sites and the deliberate gaps are in zero-trust-handover §”Where the screen is wired” | . | a remote graph → this instance | a mounted harness’s skills steer agents and its code runs, so an untrusted pin is a supply-chain compromise | bun run cat mount:remote (Tool remote-mount) refuses a mount that is neither consented for its exact pin nor signed in a declared trust network (schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts); a signature with no verifier is could-not-determine; --staging needs neither | gated at the mount; signature verification (e.g. GDHCN) not built | . | content → HTML | XSS in a rendered surface | declared XSS hints on tools and skills | open | . | a third-party action → a runner | a moved tag or rewritten branch runs new code with the job’s token and secrets | bun run cat actions:pin (pin-actions.ts) pins to a full commit SHA; security:gate blocks on any unpinned action except in a staging-only workflow that holds no write token and has no pull_request_target trigger (stagingExempt) | gated: the counts are what bun run cat security:gate reports now | .

3972.title: Where to look when adding a check
3972.content: . | Is the boundary in the table? Then the machinery exists — extend it. Adding a second guard for a guarded boundary is how they drift apart. | Is there already a helper? src/core/safe-path.ts is the path one. A correct helper in one file does not protect call sites that hand-roll the check. | Can a gate hold the property? A hand-maintained invariant drifts, and the symptom of forgetting is invisible. A guard without a gate is a guard with an expiry date. | .

3973.title: What this package does NOT own
3973.content: Shell rm -rf is not where the open surface is. The staging deletion sites are guarded by value; the surface that needed this package is the TypeScript I/O layer. Deletion policy is not security. Whether an agent may remove a durable artefact at all is deletion-requires-confirmation, and it governs cases where the path is perfectly safe and the deletion is still wrong.

3975.title: Serving a rendering — endpoints, MIME types, and what each host can enforce
3975.content: Named by: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . A rendering is what an instance publishes about itself. Running it produces one or more endpoints under that instance’s stub, and every endpoint has a media type that says what it is. This skill is about serving: the rendering already knows what it produced, and the server must say so, or a .jsonld arrives at a client as text/plain.

3976.title: One stub, several endpoints, per instance in the tree
3976.content: artefactStub() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts is the stem: stub when declared, otherwise name. Every artefact an instance publishes is named with it, so a reader who knows the repository knows the filename. The dependency tree is a set of overlaying instances, and each renders under its own stub, so an overlying instance depending on cat-harness means both are present, and both publish. <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld the knowledge graph application/ld+json <base>/<name>/<stub>.json the same bytes application/json <base>/<name>/<kind>/<id> each subject's page text/html <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json its declaration's schema application/schema+json <base>/<stub>/ the viewer text/html . So …/folio-assistant/harness.jsonld is the cat-harness instance’s rendering, served from a tree whose root happens to be folio-assistant. A consumer asking for one instance’s graph must not be handed another’s because the paths collided. The graph sits under the instance’s own directory, the host’s included. There is one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document, so a subject’s page <base>/<name>/<kind>/<id> sits next to the document that names it. Where each document goes: instance-publication §”What each instance publishes”. <stub>/ is a directory because an extensionless URL has to be. GitHub Pages resolves <base>/<stub> only to a directory index, so the viewer is what makes the bare stub openable. It climbs to the site root and reads the document’s own path, <name>/<stub>.jsonld (exportIdentity’s docPath). It never composes a neighbour’s name, because that relation is not stable across layouts. One function computes all of this, renderingPath() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts. A path a consumer dereferences — or mints as an $id — is never written out as a template literal elsewhere, so moving the renderings is one edit rather than a hunt for copies.

3977.title: Every endpoint declares its media type
3977.content: The declaration is part of the rendering, not of the server. A server is one consumer of it; an MCP server is another; a Link: header generator is a third. Writing the type at each of them is three places to disagree. | extension | media type | why not the obvious one | . | .jsonld | application/ld+json | not application/json. A JSON-LD processor keys off this type to know the document carries a @context | . | .schema.json | application/schema+json | application/json parses, but loses that it is a schema | . | .json | application/json |   | .

3978.title: What each host can enforce — three states, and they are not degrees
3978.content: A local HTTP deployment enforces it. It reads the declared type and sets Content-Type. This is where the declaration is honoured exactly. An MCP server enforces it. When it serves a rendered artefact it uses the declared default media type rather than guessing from the extension — the declaration is right there, and guessing is how .jsonld becomes application/octet-stream. GitHub Pages does not, and cannot be made to. Pages serves by its own extension table with no per-file configuration: no .htaccess, no headers file, no way to say application/ld+json. An unknown extension is served as application/octet-stream or text/plain depending on the extension. That third row is not a failure to fix. It is a property of the host, and the honest handling is the one this repository applies everywhere else: . | Do not pretend. A tool reporting “served with the declared type” must not say so for a Pages URL it did not check. | Do not fall back to a guess that looks authoritative. “Probably application/json” is worse than “this host does not declare one”, because the first is quoted and the second is investigated. | Report “could not enforce” as its own state, distinct from “enforced” and from “enforced wrongly”. | . The architectural boundary between what a static host and a local dynamic server can enforce is part of deployment awareness — see deployment-awareness for the four deployment surfaces, their constraints on tool usage, and why render-time escaping is the required line of defence on static hosts.

3979.title: Consequences a consumer must expect
3979.content: A client fetching <stub>.jsonld from Pages will receive the wrong Content-Type. A strict JSON-LD processor may refuse it. That is a known and accepted cost of publishing there, and the remedy is the local deployment. <stub>.json is an alias, not a rename. The same bytes are served at BOTH extensions: .jsonld stays canonical and is what every @id in the document names, while .json is the one path by which a correct Content-Type can come out of a static host. Renaming the artefact to .json instead would trade a wrong type for a wrong name, and the name is the part a reader uses. What that does not license is a .json whose bytes differ, or an @id pointing at it. Two documents asserting the same IRIs is the defect --base-url exists to prevent, and an alias is only an alias while it is byte-identical — which is why the staging build copies it after stamping, so the two cannot disagree about which build they came from.

3980.title: Running one — serve-rendering
3980.content: The media types and the per-host rules are the contract, in code; the server is one implementation that reads it. bun run cat serve:rendering --dir docs/_site # one site at / bun run cat serve:local --repos <repo-a>,<repo-b> # several, fetched from gh-pages . The default address is http://127.0.0.1:4007 (port 4000 is jekyll serve’s). Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost: the two are different origins, so cookies, storage and service workers split between them, and localhost may resolve to IPv6 ::1 first. The server sends localhost and [::1] requests to 127.0.0.1. Several sites on one origin, as Pages lays them out . --mount /<repo>=<dir> (repeatable) serves each built site under its own prefix, so root-relative links and IRI paths line up with https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/. It copies the Pages behaviours links depend on: <dir> redirects to <dir>/, /page serves page.html, and a miss serves the site’s own 404.html. branches/<branch>/ previews in a gh-pages checkout need no extra rule. Published IRIs open the local copy . For each mounted repo, text responses have the published base <origin>/<repo> replaced by the local one as they are served. Files on disk never change. Whole path segments only (/a never touches /ab), and a repo that is not mounted keeps its live links. <origin> is the declared canonicalUrl’s origin; --iri-origin overrides it and --iri /<prefix>=<base> adds a base on another host. Accept: application/ld+json on an extensionless IRI serves its .jsonld sibling, which Pages cannot do. Rewriting changes bytes. Check signatures and digests with --no-rewrite; a rewritten response carries X-Rendering-Rewritten: iri. One command — serve:local . --repos a,b fetches each repo’s gh-pages branch into a cache (shallow, blob-less, sparse, updated each run) and serves them all. branches/ is left out unless --staging <branch> names a preview; a repo with no published main site lists its previews. --site <repo>=<dir> serves a site you built yourself, for changes not yet published. --offline uses the cache as it is. RENDERING_MEDIA_TYPES and renderingMediaType() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts are the table, beside renderingPath(), because where a rendering LIVES and what it IS are the same kind of fact, and a table in code is one no consumer has to re-derive from prose. Obligations are skills/requirements/serving-a-rendering.json, so a second implementation is checkable against the requirement rather than against this one’s source. What a general-purpose static server actually gets wrong . Less than is often assumed, and overstating it is how a working setup gets ruled out: Python’s mimetypes and Bun.file().type both resolve .jsonld to application/ld+json. The gap is one row: .schema.json resolves to application/json in every OS table, because .json is the suffix that matches and nothing knows the compound extension means a schema. Hence longest-extension-first, and hence a declared table rather than the filesystem’s. Containment is part of the contract . A symlink inside the served root can point at a file outside it: the URL is clean, so a lexical path check passes, and resolve() never touches the filesystem. Real paths must be compared. This matters most for the self-sovereign topology, whose published directory sits beside data nobody intends to publish. The server binds loopback unless told otherwise, for the same reason.

3982.title: Session context
3982.content: Skill session-context: What a state machine tracks across a session, as against one process instance. What the record carries, why actor is required and the rest are not, why the session’s view of a node is advisory, and what a sibling session reads it for. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A session is one actor working, from the moment it picks up until it stops. A process instance is a token’s position in one diagram. They are not the same object and the difference is load-bearing: . A session starts before any instance, may open several, switches between them, and outlives each. A session with nothing open is the commonest state there is. Model the session as a field on an instance and the first process opened owns facts that belong to the actor — and the idle session, which is most of them, becomes unrepresentable. So it is its own record, referencing instances rather than containing them. Shape: schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts. Graph typology: session-state, layer state — a session writes its own record as it goes, which is exactly what content-context-and-state-graphs means by live state.

3983.title: The fields — read them off the schema, never off this page
3983.content: SessionContextSchema in schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts is authoritative. A field list in prose beside a Zod object is a second answer, wrong the first time somebody adds a field, so this page gives no field count; the sections below say what the main fields are for.

3984.title: actor is required, and it is the point of the record
3984.content: Every other field can be recovered by looking at the repository. Open instances are in the work item graph; claimed work items carry their own status; timestamps can be reconstructed from commits. WHO is acting cannot be derived from anything. The machine keeping the session cannot infer it, which is also why log-message takes actor. A sibling session needs to know who is answerable before it touches the same work item. It is a reference with a declared flag, not an ActorDefinition. An agent may act without a node under the actors graph, and requiring one would make the field unfillable in exactly the cold-start case the record is most useful for. The two facts — an id that resolves and a name nobody declared — are kept apart because a consumer acts differently on each: an audit can follow the first to a role and a permission set, and can only quote the second. And declared is written, not inferred at read time. A reader resolving it themselves gets a different answer than the writer did if the node was added or removed in between, and the record says what was true when the session acted.

3985.title: The rest of the fields, and what each is for
3985.content: | field | for | notes | . | id | naming this session | stable for its life | . | startedAt / updatedAt | telling a live session from an abandoned one | ISO-8601 UTC | . | open[] | which instances this session is inside | empty is normal, not a gap | . | claimed[] | which work items this session announced | by reference, never copied | . | waitingOn | why nothing is moving | what + since, together | . open empty is the normal state. An agent answering a question, reading, or deciding what to do next is in no process at all, and process-state calls that idle rather than broken. A record that treated empty as a defect would report every reading session as one. claimed is by reference because a claim announces rather than reserves. The work item is the authority on its own status (bean-coordination); a status copied here would be free to contradict it, and a sibling reading the copy would act on a claim that had already been released. waitingOn carries since or it carries nothing. A wait with no start cannot be told from abandoned work — the same argument bean-blocking makes for requiring an expiry. what is free text on purpose: a human answer, a CI run, a sibling’s PR is an open set no enum would survive.

3986.title: The session’s view of a node is ADVISORY
3986.content: open[].atNode is what the session believes. The instance wins. The instance is the authority on its own token; this can be stale by exactly one step — the gap between a step completing and the session noticing. It is recorded anyway for two reasons. The commonest question about a session (“what is it doing”) should not need a second file read. And a disagreement between the two is itself worth seeing: a session whose view has drifted from the instance is a session that lost track, which is one of the detectors process-state names for being out of process.

3987.title: Who reads it, and why it is parsed rather than trusted
3987.content: A sibling session, deciding whether a work item is genuinely being worked or was claimed by someone who stopped. A person, asking what is in flight. The session itself on resume, in a fresh container, where the alternative is starting a second session beside the one that already exists. The writer may be an LLM playing the part of a state machine, so the shape cannot be assumed from the writer’s care. parseSessionContext() parses at the boundary, which is what makes a non-deterministic writer safe to read from. The general rule: where a machine may be played rather than executed, the schema is the contract and the parse is where it is enforced.

3988.title: What this is NOT
3988.content: Not the work plan. A work item says what is being worked on and survives the session; this says who is working and where they are right now. Delete every session record and the plan is intact. Not a log. log-message records what an actor DID at a moment, append-only. This is the current position, overwritten as it moves. A log tells you how you got here; this tells you where you are. Not interaction preferences. cat-harness/memory/interaction.json holds how a person wants to be asked — durable, read at session start, never written by a process. That is context, and this is state: the two are on opposite sides of the layer line and must not be merged, however adjacent they look. Not a store yet. The kind is registered and the shape is defined; nothing writes one, so no directory is declared for it: a declared-but-empty directory makes a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run.

3990.title: /session-intent — durable session intent + results
3990.content: Skill session-intent: Session-start intent declaration + session-end results recording, against the work plan’s goals (milestone work items) and their open work items. Enforces the durable-handoff discipline so any agent can pick up another’s thread. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Without a durable record of which tasks are in flight, what each has already learned, and why a previous result was retracted, each new session re-discovers the same near-result and re-commits it, only to retract it again later (a flip-flop). This skill enforces the read → declare → work → record loop so the next session — possibly a different agent — picks up exactly where the previous one left off.

3991.title: Where state lives
3991.content: Each job lives in the object that already owns it: . | job | here | . | goals, and what serves each | a milestone work item per goal, with the epics parented to it — todo-manager §”A GOAL is a milestone bean”; beans roadmap renders it | . | canonical status of an item | the work item itself. There is no second copy to disagree with it | . | flip-flop history | a scrapped work item keeps the rejected approach with its reasons, and a trap node under the declared memory graph keeps the failure signature — agent-memory | . | session log | the work item’s body notes, plus the PR. Both are durable and both are read by the next session; a third place would be a third answer | . | Artifact | Purpose | . | beans/ (via the beans CLI) | the queue and the plan: goals as milestones, epics, tasks | . | memory/ | established facts and TRAPs — what not to re-derive, and what not to repeat | . | Per-PR body | session intent at branch-open; EOS results appended | . | a root dashboard file | optional, and this instance has none. See below | . The dashboard is optional, and absent is not undetermined . An instance MAY keep a STATUS.md-style dashboard. This one does not, and that is a determined absence rather than a gap: the milestones and beans roadmap answer the same question from the store, so a dashboard here would be a second copy free to drift from it. Three states, and the third is the one that gets collapsed: . | A dashboard exists → read it first, as step 1 below. | No dashboard, and the work plan reads → skip to the roadmap. Nothing is missing. | The work plan could not be read — no CLI, no store, an unreadable declaration → that is not an empty plan. Say so and fix it before declaring intent; todo-manager §”When the beans CLI is not there” has the fallback, which writes as well as reads. | .

3992.title: Session-start protocol (5 steps)
3992.content: Run these in order. Steps 1–3 are read-only; step 4 writes. 1. Read the goals . beans roadmap, or beans list filtered to --type milestone. Identify which goal the user’s request serves. A request that serves none is not thereby illegitimate — it is a finding worth one line in the turn report, and possibly a new milestone. Then find your siblings: the open PRs, and the Claude-Session: trailer on recent commits. The session API cannot see sibling sessions, so a branch and its PR are the only durable evidence that another session is working. 2. Read the goal’s epics and their open children . Walk down from the milestone: beans list and read the epics parented to it, then their open children. | Status — the work item’s own status is canonical. | What was rejected — read the scrapped work items in the archive before proposing an approach. That is what stops you re-entering a dead end, and it is why a work item is never deleted. | Traps — the memory graph’s trap nodes carry failure signatures. Do not repeat any pattern recorded there. | What is in flight — an in-progress work item, with the caveat that a claim is branch-local and announces rather than reserves (bean-coordination). | . 3. Read the queue . Run beans list to find: . | todo or draft work items not yet picked up. | blocked work items waiting on dependencies. | Who is working an item: check the work item body and its holder note. Multiple agents MAY pick the same item; coordinate with the user if you see this happen. | . 4. Declare intent (write) . Three places, all required: . a. The work item — claim the work item you are working, naming your branch: . bun run cat beans:claim <id> . A claim goes through beans:claim, not beans update: it reads the default branch first, refuses a work item somebody else holds, and records a holder note the next session’s check can read. beans update writes no such note. Then append a note to its body saying what you intend and where you got to. The work item is the durable record a sibling reads; there is no separate session log to keep in step with it. b. beans CLI — new tasks, parented by SUBJECT. No session work item. Check before you create (STRICT). beans create is not idempotent — it mints a fresh ID every call and dedupes on nothing, so re-entering this step duplicates the whole plan rather than no-op’ing. Run the existence check in todo-manager.md §Check before you create before every beans create below. | Do not create a Session: … milestone or epic. A session is a LOG, and its log is the PR body (part c) plus a work item note on each work item worked (bun run cat beans:note <id>, keyed by branch). todo-manager §”A session is a log, not a parent” has the reasoning. | For each NEW task you pick up, create it under the epic whose subject it is: beans create "<Task>" --type task --parent <subject-epic-id>, then claim it. | . c. PR body — at branch-open, the PR body must include: . ## Intent (session start) - <one line per task ID from queue you're working> - <user's stated goal in their words> ## Session results <filled at EOS> . 5. Hand off to /coordinate . After step 4, run /coordinate to post intent on relevant sibling PRs . | triage their review comments. Then start work. | . Before the first edit of any new unit of work, run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”, scaled to the blast radius and recorded in your workplan work item. A pickup (§”Hand-off pickup protocol”) runs its own.

3993.title: Session-end protocol (3 steps)
3993.content: Run these BEFORE pushing the final commit. The push triggers PR auto-subscription + sibling-coord sweep, so the EOS state must be visible from the push commit. 1. Update the queue . For each task you worked, use the beans CLI: . | If completed: beans update <id> --status completed, with a summary: beans update <id> --body-append "Completed with finding: ...". | If partial: leave status: in-progress, and append beans update <id> --body-append "Partial result: ...". | If you discovered a NEW task: create a new work item via beans create (after the existence check). | If you retract a previous claim: see step 2. | . 2. Record the results where they will be read . Append them to the work item, which is where step 4a put the intent — what was confirmed, what remains, and the PR. One object, opened and closed, rather than an intent in one place and a result in another. If the session retracted a prior claim, that is not a body note. Two objects carry it, and they answer different questions: . | the approach that was rejected becomes a scrapped work item with its reasons, so the next agent does not re-enter it; | the failure signature — what made the wrong answer look right — becomes a trap node in the memory graph (agent-memory). | . 3. Update the PR body . Replace the placeholder ## Session results section with: . ## Session results - Picked up: <task IDs> - Completed: <list> - Partial: <list with where to pick up> - New tasks added: <list> - Retractions: <list of any prior-claim retractions> - Open question for user: <if any> .

3994.title: Multi-agent same-goal coordination
3994.content: Multiple agents MAY attack the same goal simultaneously. The model is: . | Goal = product (user’s directive). | Queue = per-goal item list, all agents read + write. | Tasks are not exclusively claimed. Two agents may pick the same task; this is allowed. | Coordination is with the USER on goal-level decisions, not agent-to-agent on task-level locks. | . When you discover a task you’re working has been picked up by another agent (another holder note on the work item, or a sibling PR commit touching the same scope): . | Do not silently abandon — your independent attack is valuable (different methods may surface different findings). | Post intent on the sibling PR via /coordinate so the sibling agent sees you’re also working it. | Ask the user if they want both threads or want one to stand down, with context, options and a recommendation first (interaction-modality). Sample: . 🟡 Two agents attacking task-foo-stability — sibling PR #XXXX is at 50% with method A; I’d attack with method B. Keep both threads? . | If the user says one stands down, the standing-down agent appends its partial results to the work item and releases its claim. | .

3995.title: Hand-off pickup protocol
3995.content: If you’re the picking-up agent (someone else’s in-progress task or partial result): . | Read the work item’s notes (beans show <id>) — that’s the handoff letter and the technical state. | Read the partial PR (if open) — that’s the code state. | Declare your intent normally (claim the work item and add a note to it — bun run cat beans:note <id> — saying you picked it up and where you will start; no session work item). | Re-run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work” before your first edit, and add the result to the work item. | .

3996.title: Anti-patterns
3996.content: . | ❌ Starting work without reading the goal’s work items, scrapped work items and traps first (“just-the-prompt” agents re-commit flipped claims). | ❌ Claiming a task but not writing the EOS results (“silent abandon”). | ❌ Retracting a previous claim quietly, without a scrapped work item or a trap (“erasure” — guaranteed to re-flip next session). | ❌ Asking the user “should I pick this task?” — the queue is the authoritative list; just pick and declare. | .
