4140.title: SWOT situation analysis
4140.content: Process_SwotAnalysis · advisory · 7 step(s) . Situation analysis over two axes — internal/external and helpful/harmful — producing the raw material a decision is made from, and NEVER the decision. THE ONE STRUCTURAL CLAIM THIS DIAGRAM MAKES: there is no path through it that decides anything. Every completed run ends either at a recorded situation or at a handoff into options-analysis, which selects a decision methodology. That is not a modelling preference; it is the swot methodology’s stated refusal drawn so it cannot be skipped. Gürel and Tat’s conclusion is that SWOT gives “the raw material needed to perform more in-depth strategic analysis” but “cannot show them how to achieve a competitive advantage”, and that it must not become “an end in itself”. A diagram with a decide-here activity would contradict the methodology it implements. WHY EXTERNAL IS SCANNED FIRST: Weihrich (1982), reported in the source, holds that the only logical starting point is opportunities and threats — they are outside the organisation and largely beyond its control, and must be managed using its strengths and weaknesses. The order is his argument, rendered; it is not a house preference. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not rank the factors it finds. The source is explicit that SWOT has no way to prioritise — “quantity does not mean quality” — and the long list of quantitative extensions it surveys (AHP, ANP, their fuzzy variants, SMART, SMAA-O, MADM, TRIZ) is NOT adopted here. An activity that scored or weighted factors would be inventing the part of the method that does not exist. i i i i i i i

4142.title: Lanes — who acts
4142.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Business analyst | business-analyst | Performs the scan and the crossing. This lane owns the analysis and owns nothing else: it does not authorise, and it does not choose between options. Its deliverable is four lists, the four matched strategies, and an explicit record of what could not be classified. | . | Stakeholder | stakeholder | Consulted, in a lane of their own because the source names group discussion as a property of the method rather than as good practice around it: SWOT “promotes group discussion about strategic issues” and pools knowledge through participatory techniques. It is also the mitigation for the limitation the source states most sharply — that a list of strengths is “bound up with aspirations, biases, and hope of the individuals involved”. A single analyst producing four lists alone has performed the technique’s shape without the part that checks it. | .

4143.title: Steps
4143.content: Every one of the 7 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Name the subject and the levelA_FrameSubject | Business analyst | swot-analysis | One sentence naming WHAT is being analysed and at WHICH level — individual, organisational, national, international. The source requires this before anything is listed: “the classification of a variable also depends on the purpose of the practice”, and the criteria for assigning a variable to a quadrant “may be more difficult to clarify if the methodology is not used for a company but for a country”.It also bounds the known limitation that SWOT “is rarely deployed at lower than the organization level”, where one scan drives strategy for units its factors do not hold equally for. Naming the level does not remove that risk; it makes it visible in the record. | . | Scan the environment opportunities and threatsA_ScanExternal | Business analyst | swot-analysis | The external axis, first, per Weihrich. Work the source’s categories of environmental change rather than free-associating: societal, governmental, economic, competitive, supplier and market changes, each item recorded with what it impacts.An opportunity is an external element that gives benefit; a threat is one that could cause trouble. Both are outside the subject and largely beyond its control — that is what puts them on this axis, not whether they feel good or bad. | . | Scan the subject strengths and weaknessesA_ScanInternal | Business analyst | swot-analysis | The internal axis. Work the source’s functional checklist rather than a blank page: marketing, research and development, management information systems, management team, operations, finance, human resources.A strength gives advantage over others in the field; a weakness places the subject at a disadvantage relative to others. Both are attributes OF the subject. The source’s warning belongs to this step specifically: listing strengths on paper “is very different from testing the organization and experiencing the strengths at work”, so a strength recorded here is a claim, and where evidence for it exists it is cited. | . | Pool knowledge across participantsA_GroupReview | Stakeholder | swot-analysis | The four lists are reviewed by more than the person who wrote them. This is the method’s own answer to its own bias limitation, and it is a distinct activity rather than advice attached to the scans, because an activity can be recorded as not performed and a recommendation cannot.Disagreement about which quadrant a factor belongs in is an OUTPUT of this step, not a failure of it — it feeds A_RecordAmbiguous. | . | Record what did not classify cleanlyA_RecordAmbiguous | Business analyst | swot-analysis | Factors that sit in two quadrants, or in none, are written down as such. The source states this as inherent rather than as analyst error: “the same factor can be fitted in two categories. A factor can be a strength and a weakness at the same time.” It adds the two drifts — strengths not maintained become weaknesses, and opportunities not taken but taken by competitors become threats.A scan that silently forced every factor into one quadrant would report a cleanliness the method does not have. This is the same third-state discipline the rest of this repository applies to “could not determine”: an unclassifiable factor is a finding, not a blank. | . | Cross the axes into SO, WO, ST, WTA_Cross | Business analyst | swot-analysis | The TOWS matching step, and the only step that produces anything actionable. Strengths and weaknesses across, opportunities and threats down, and each cell names the strategy the pairing implies: SO — achieve opportunities that greatly match the strengths; WO — overcome weaknesses to attain opportunities; ST — use strengths to reduce vulnerability to threats; WT — prevent weaknesses, to avoid becoming more susceptible to threats.A SWOT that stops at four lists is the failure the source names as its central one. This step is what the process exists to reach.It produces CANDIDATE strategies, not a chosen one, and they are not ranked — see the process documentation on why no scoring activity exists. | . | Hand the candidates to a decision methodologyA_HandOff | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | The candidate strategies go to options-analysis, which selects the decision methodology by context and applies it. SWOT does not make that selection and does not make the decision.What is handed over includes the ambiguities from A_RecordAmbiguous and the fact that the candidates are UNRANKED. A receiving methodology that assumed an ordered list would be reading a priority SWOT never established. | .

4146.title: symbiotic-interaction — the three registers of author input
4146.content: Skill symbiotic-interaction: Recognize and respond to the three epistemic registers of author input — Socratic steer (known-answer correction), honest gap (flagged unknown), and intuition seed (tenuous cross-domain identification) — with the coactive-learning measurement spec (per-arc correction quality and turns-to-convergence) and the prompt-lexicon convention. Carries the STRICT rule that a steer correcting a RULE is written into the skill that governs it, in the same turn, quoted and dated — use whenever the author corrects, settles or overrules anything. Generic platform skill. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch .

4147.title: 0. Why this skill exists
4147.content: Session transcripts show the author’s inputs arriving in three distinct epistemic registers, and mis-classifying them wastes passes in three distinct ways: treating a flagged-gap question as a steer produces sycophantic confirmation; over-verifying a steer wastes the author’s good correction; demanding rigor before cheaply testing an intuition seed kills the division of labor the methodology depends on. The formal backbone is coactive learning (Shivaswamy–Joachims): the author’s feedback is α-informative — an improvement toward the target, not the gold standard — and convergence speed is governed by correction quality.

4148.title: 1. The three registers
4148.content: | register | seed lexicon (v0 — expanded by transcript mining) | agent protocol | . | steer (author knows or nearly knows) | “isn’t X essentially Y?”, “shouldn’t this be …”, “what about Z here?”, “I think the other point is …” | Treat as a correction near the truth: update the working proposal toward it, verify cheaply rather than relitigate, and do not require the author to repeat the correction. | . | gap (author doesn’t know, and says so) | “I don’t recall …”, “I wish I remembered …”, “is it true that …?”, “not sure”, typed uncertainty markers | The marker REMOVES the presumption of author knowledge: raise the evidence threshold, verify from primary sources or the corpus before adopting, never confirm sycophantically. | . | seed (author suspects a novel link) | “tenuous”, “hunch”, “could A be linked to B?”, “feels like”, any cross-domain identification offered without a citation | Corpus-grep first (is it already known here?); then the cheapest decisive (in)validation — a structural argument or a small probe per the formalize-first discipline — reported fast; survivors get rigorized. Record novelty attribution: author-origin, with a literature-absence check. | . The division of labor the third row encodes: the human is the generator of low-probability / high-value cross-domain hypotheses that exist in neither the literature nor the model’s usable priors; the machine is the fast validator and rigorizer. Once a tenuous identification is made, (in)validation is cheap — so the protocol optimizes for never letting a seed die unexamined and never letting an unvalidated seed masquerade as a result.

4149.title: 2. A steer that corrects a RULE lands in the SKILL — same turn (STRICT)
4149.content: §1’s steer row ends “do not require the author to repeat the correction.” Applied to the artefact alone, that clause is broken — just not within the session where it looks kept. The proposal is fixed, the rule that produced the proposal is not, and the next session is a fresh context that never saw the chat. It produces the same proposal, and the author corrects it again. Requiring the correction twice is requiring it repeatedly, and for an author with limited hand function that cost is keystrokes (interaction-modality §0). A steer that corrects a rule is not applied — it is WRITTEN DOWN: in the skill that governs the thing corrected, in the same turn. The rule and its reason go in the narrative; the author’s words, quoted and dated, go in that document’s provenance log. Is this steer rule-level? Three questions . A steer about the artefact in front of you is an edit. A steer about how that kind of artefact is decided is a rule, and the difference is not tone — the author says both in the same register, often in the same sentence. Ask: . | Would an agent with no memory of this chat make the same mistake again? If the correction lives only in a file that agent will not read as a rule, yes. | Does it generalise past this artefact? “Call it voices/ here” is an edit. “Voices belong to the instance that owns them semantically” decides every future placement. | Is there already a rule that this CONTRADICTS? Then the edit is not optional and not additive: the old rule is wrong and stays wrong until it is replaced; a correction filed beside it leaves the next agent two answers. | . Any yes makes it rule-level. A gap or a seed (§1) never is — a flagged unknown is not a ruling, and treating one as a rule is §3’s first anti-pattern with a durable artefact attached. Same turn, quoted, dated — in the provenance log . | Same turn. Not “noted for later” and not a work item saying the skill should be updated. A work item that records a rule is a rule in the wrong graph: beans/ is state, the skills are context, and a reader looking up how something is decided reads the skill. | Quoted. The author’s own words, verbatim, typos included — they are the primary source, and a paraphrase is the agent’s reading of them standing in for the ruling itself. | Dated. A rule with no date cannot be told from a rule that was superseded. | In the log, not the narrative. The quote and its date go in the document’s provenance log, <document>.prov.jsonld beside it (PROV-O), which the renderer shows in the page footer. The narrative states the rule and the reason the author gave, in the present tense, so a reader learns what holds without reading who said it when. | A log may name any instance. It quotes verbatim, so it carries the issue and repository names the original text did, including layers above this one. A log is a record of where a rule came from, not a reference the document depends on, so check:reference-direction exempts *.prov.jsonld. | . You do NOT ask permission to fix a rule the author just corrected . kg-contribution-offer says the agent never picks a destination silently, and that is about manufacturing a node from agreed requirements — work whose shape nobody has ruled on. This is the opposite case: the node exists, it is wrong, and the author has just said so. Asking “shall I write that into the skill?” asks them to repeat the correction, which is the failure at the top of this section. The two do not overlap, and the line is: does the rule already have a home? If yes, the correction goes there now. If the correction implies a skill that does not exist, that is a new node and kg-contribution-offer governs it — except where the author said outright it should be one. Worked examples . | the steer | where it lands | why there | . | “that should be a skill: a collision means coordinate” | the named skill (coordinate), as new triggers | rule-level on all three questions, and the author named the destination | . | “voices belong to the instance that owns them semantically” | the schema module that states voice ownership, replacing the old rule | question 3: it contradicts a standing rule, so filing it beside that rule would leave two answers | . | “the harness handler wins” (a collision between two path rules) | schema-management §”Where a viewer publishes — TWO rules, not three”, beside the two rules | question 2: it settles every such collision, not one generator’s | . A refusal is a ruling. An answer that declines your recommendation carries at least as much rule as one that accepts it — the reason it gives is a durable claim about the domain, and it goes into the governing skill or schema gloss in that turn, with the quote and date in its provenance log.

4150.title: 3. Measurement spec (new sessions and retroactive)
4150.content: An arc is (initial agent proposal y₀; author inputs u₁…u_T with register labels; terminal state ŷ). Metrics, computed offline by a discussion-corpus miner — agents do not annotate live chat: . | T — author turns to acceptance. | α̂ — mean fractional gap closed per steer (successive-proposal distance toward ŷ; the miner’s distance proxy is recorded with the estimate). This is the empirical constant of the coactive bound. | outcome ∈ {converged, abandoned, diverged}. | gap-honored? — after a gap marker, did the agent verify independently before adopting? | seed metrics — validation latency (turns to verdict), verdict ∈ {validated→rigorized, refuted, undecidable-cheaply}, and the literature-absence check for novelty attribution. | . Linkage to artifacts is via the existing commit-trailer ↔ session mapping; no extra ceremony in-session.

4151.title: 4. Anti-patterns
4151.content: . | Treating a gap-marked question as a steer (sycophantic capture). | Relitigating a steer the author has already given (wasted α). | Requiring a derivation before running the cheap probe on a seed — or the inverse, promoting an unvalidated seed into prose. | Flattening the registers: answering every input at the same evidence threshold. | Applying a rule-level steer to the artefact and not to the rule (§2) — the cross-session form of anti-pattern 2. | Filing a rule-level steer as a work item instead of editing the skill. A work item says work is outstanding; the work here is the edit. | .

4152.title: 5. Lexicon maintenance
4152.content: Register lexicons above are seeds: a corpus miner’s prompt-lexicon records expand them with observed phrasings, usage counts, and outcomes; updates land as mining PRs citing source sessions. This skill is adapter-generic.

4154.title: Task authorization — four questions before every task
4154.content: Skill task-authorization: The check every BPMN task execution runs before anything is recorded: is the actor authenticated, assigned to the role the lane binds, authorized by an ODRL policy to perform the task, and allowed access to the content it acts on? One generic check in the engine rather than a step drawn in some diagrams; strict, with GitHub as the authenticator. Also how the HTTP routes ask the same policies. Triggers on: may this actor, who may perform, authorization, authentication, access rights, permission check, RBAC, rbac.ts, workflow_complete refused, not eligible for role. Named by: A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Before an actor performs a task or answers a decision, the BPMN executor asks: who is this, may they act in this lane, does a policy let them do it, and may they touch this content? .

4155.title: The four checks, in order
4155.content: | # | question | answered from | a “no” | . | 1 | Authenticated — who is the actor, and how do we know? | the executor’s Principal (src/core/access.ts) | recorded as a finding | . | 2 | Assigned — may this actor take the role the lane binds? | ActorDef.roles in cat-harness/scenarios/actors/; the lane’s roleRef | refuses | . | 3 | Authorized — may they perform-task in this process, for this task, as this role? | ODRL policies in policies/*.jsonld | deny refuses; unknown is a finding | . | 4 | Access — the same, on the content (target) the task acts on | the same policies, rule target | deny refuses; unknown is a finding | . It is one function, authorizeTask in src/workflow/authorize.ts, run by the interpreter’s complete() and by workflow_gate. It is not drawn as a task in any diagram. A check drawn into some processes is a check missing from the others. The verdict is written into the instance history (HistoryEntry.authz) and the task-end log line, so the record of a step says who did it and on what authority, not only that it happened. Why checks 2 and 3 stay separate . A role is what the actor is acting as; a permission is what the actor may do (role-model §”Three questions about an actor”). An actor permitted to perform-task everywhere still cannot sit in a lane its roles do not include. So the role check does not wait on the policy and cannot be overridden by it.

4156.title: One action for every task
4156.content: A task always asks for perform-task, scoped by cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task and cat-harness:role constraints and by target. A step needing a narrower right gets it as a constrained rule in a policy, never as a new attribute on the diagram: . { "assignee": "content-reviewer", "action": "perform-task", "constraint": [{ "leftOperand": "cat-harness:role", "operator": "odrl:eq", "rightOperand": "reviewer" }] } . Remember the direction of includedIn: a grant of a broader action covers a narrower one. perform-task sits under odrl:execute, so granting adjudication (which is included in perform-task) does not grant perform-task. It is the other way round.

4157.title: Authentication is the executor’s job, and GitHub is today’s authenticator
4157.content: Whoever executes a process (the MCP workflow tools, a script, a swarm orchestrator) must say how it knows who the actor is. A Principal carries authenticatedBy: . | value | meaning | today | . | github | GitHub authenticated the caller | a GitHub Actions run (GITHUB_ACTOR, set by the runner) | . | http-gateway | the auth-gateway’s OAuth session, as headers | the HTTP routes, once deployed (deployment-auth) | . | asserted | an actor id the caller typed | every local agent session | . | none | nobody named | a step recorded with no actor | . The second half of GitHub as access control needs no code: the KG data store is a git repository on GitHub. An instance file, a work item or a content change becomes durable only through a push GitHub has authorised. The in-process check decides whether the step may be recorded; branch protection and push rights decide whether the record lands. Do not treat asserted as authenticated. Report it as asserted. policies/ never holds identity.

4158.title: Asking who you are: the auth_whoami Tool
4158.content: The user-auth Tool node (MCP auth_whoami, src/tools/auth.ts) answers three questions in one call: . | Who am I? It asks GitHub (src/core/github-auth.ts). With a person’s own token, GET /user gives the login and the permissions block of GET /repos/{o}/{r} gives their role. In an Actions job the token is the workflow’s, not the person’s, so it asks GET …/collaborators/{GITHUB_ACTOR}/permission instead. | What does GitHub let me do? That role, mapped onto the gateway actors policies/http-gateway.jsonld already grants: admin → owner; maintain and write → collaborator; triage and read → viewer; none → nobody. A GitHub caller and an HTTP-gateway caller therefore get the same answer from the same policy, and no login is written into the repository. | What does policy let me do here? The ODRL answer for an action, or the full four-check verdict for a BPMN step when process and task are given. | . It answers in three states: authenticated, unauthenticated, and unknown (GitHub could not be asked). unknown is never shown as a pass. A role that cannot be read stays unknown and maps to nobody; it is never guessed. An actor you name is reported as claimed, because GitHub vouched for the login, not for the BPMN actor. One resolver for preferences and permissions, two thresholds. The same identities feed both, through resolveIdentities (cat-harness-tools/src/core/identity.ts): GitHub’s answer is the one auth_whoami gives, and the other providers — GitLab CI, the agent host’s account, the user-level store, the git author — are listed beside it, each marked vouched or self-asserted. A preference may follow a self-asserted identity (interaction-modality §3.1). A permission never does: only an identity GitHub vouched for maps to an actor, and a self-asserted one maps to nobody. There is no login-to-actor table. A personal-account repository has exactly three GitHub permission levels, and they are the whole mapping (PERSONAL_ACCOUNT_LEVELS in src/core/github-auth.ts): . | GitHub level | GitHub role | actor | . | owner | admin | owner | . | collaborator | write | collaborator | . | anyone else, public repository | read | viewer | . | anyone else, private repository | none | nobody | . The consequence is stated in every auth_whoami answer: there is no read-only or triage collaborator on a personal-account repository, so every collaborator can write the whole graph. Telling an author from a reviewer is left to the per-lane ODRL rules. The actors are owner, collaborator and viewer, and nothing finer is mapped from a login. At the GitHub level author, reviewer, adjudicator and release manager are all collaborator; sign-off stays with owner by the merge, as the CRDM process has it. Access granularity is a property of the tool that holds the data, not of the actor: a GitHub-backed write is all or nothing for the whole repository, and a different tool, such as a future data store in front of the graph, may give the same actor finer grain.

4159.title: GitHub as the auth layer: what it is good at, and where it stops
4159.content: The knowledge graph’s data store is a git repository on GitHub, so GitHub is the authenticator and the outermost access control. That choice has real strengths and one structural weakness, and every answer auth_whoami gives ends by restating the weakness. Strengths . | Real identity at no extra cost. Accounts with two-factor authentication, organisation SSO where it is configured, per-repository fine-grained tokens, and a runner-set GITHUB_ACTOR in Actions. There is no second identity system to run. | Access to the graph is access to the repository. One place to grant, and revoking a collaborator takes effect on the next request. | Every write is attributable. A change lands as a commit with an author, and PR reviews and merges are recorded. That is the durable half of the audit trail that the PROV-O report (below) reads. | Write governance exists. Branch protection and rulesets can require reviews and passing checks before a merge, and CODEOWNERS makes review requirements path-scoped. | . The weakness: all of the knowledge graph, or none of it . | Read is whole-repository. Anyone with read sees every sub-graph, every node and every file. GitHub cannot say “the glossary, but not the unpublished chapters”. | Write is whole-repository too. write lets a person push to any path on any unprotected branch. Path scoping exists only for reviews (via CODEOWNERS), and it binds merges into protected branches, not pushes. | No query-path control. GitHub serves files, not queries. It cannot authorize a traversal that starts in a sub-graph you may read and reaches a node you may not, because it does not know the edge exists. | Five roles, no actions. admin, maintain, write, triage and read are its whole vocabulary. Authoring, adjudicating and releasing are all just write. The ODRL profile’s actions cannot be expressed in it. | Once read, it is copied. A clone or a fork keeps the data after access is revoked. Revocation stops the next read, not the last one. | A login is not an actor. GitHub says who pushed, not which lane or role they were acting in. | . What follows from that . | Where a boundary must hold against a reader, it is a repository boundary. Sub-graphs with different read audiences belong in different repositories. | Everything finer is ODRL, enforced in process. The engine’s four-check verdict and the HTTP routes govern callers that go through them. They are not a security boundary against someone who can clone the repository. Do not describe a scoped ODRL rule as protecting data from a GitHub reader. | Real per-node or per-query enforcement needs a data store in front of the graph (the auth-gateway, and later a relationship engine such as OpenFGA). The policies do not change when it arrives. Only the place that evaluates them does. | .

4160.title: The engine is strict
4160.content: policies/http-gateway.jsonld grants perform-task to owner and collaborator in every lane; viewer gets nothing beyond the anyone floor. The principal is the one GitHub vouches for (githubPrincipalFor), not an actor name the caller types. Together these are what make strict mode workable: without a permit in every lane and an authenticated principal, strict would stop every process. workflow_gate and workflow_complete run in strict mode (ENGINE_MODE in src/tools/workflow.ts). Strict refuses deny, a role mismatch, unknown, an asserted identity, nobody, and an undeclared actor. The actor a caller passes is still written to the history, as what it said it was acting as; it does not decide anything. With a GitHub-authenticated principal, every task and gateway in processes/ is allowed for owner and collaborator and refused for viewer (unknown) and for nobody. scripts/tests/task-authorization-strict.test.ts pins this. What strict costs: if GitHub cannot be asked (no token, no network, rate limit), no step can be recorded; that is the price of authentication being real rather than typed. authorizeTask itself still defaults to advisory, so a reader that re-checks history (the PROV-O report below) is not strict by accident.

4161.title: The HTTP routes ask the same policies
4161.content: src/core/rbac.ts asks the ODRL policies: . | a route names the action it performs: allows(req, "content-authoring"); | the gateway’s three sessions are three declared actors (viewer, collaborator, owner), and what each may do is policies/http-gateway.jsonld; | at the HTTP boundary unknown refuses. A route is a door, and a door nobody has decided about stays shut. That is the one place the two callers differ. | . | route | action | . | edit content, revert content, upload documents, save glossary curation | content-authoring | . | delete feedback | review-comments | . | adjudicate a relevance verdict | adjudication | . Every gated route allows collaborator or owner, and task-authorization.test.ts pins that.

4162.title: When a step is refused
4162.content: . | Read the verdict line: it names which of the four checks said no. | Role mismatch: you are acting as the wrong actor, or the lane binds a role you do not hold. Hand the step to an actor who may take the role (process-state). Do not edit your actor’s roles to get past it; that is actor-role-administration.bpmn, and it belongs to the administrator lane. | deny: a prohibition was written on purpose. Ask the user; never remove it yourself (deletion-requires-confirmation). | .

4163.title: The engine writes its own PROV-O record
4163.content: complete() attaches a prov:Activity to each history entry it records under an authorization context (src/workflow/prov-record.ts, HistoryEntry.prov): . | prov:agent is the actor GitHub vouched for, not a typed name; | prov:hadRole is the lane’s role, and prov:hadPlan is <process file stem>#<node id>; | cat-harness:underPolicy is every policy in force, because decide evaluated every one; | prov:used is the target, when the step names one. | . It is written at the moment it is true, which the after-check below cannot do from a name alone. The same no-invention rule applies: a refused step, a step with no actor, or a step in a lane that binds no role gets no activity.

4164.title: The after-check: the PROV-O QA/QC report
4164.content: The engine checks before a step. An agent swarm acts first, so the same policy is checked after, from the record (docs/source/concepts-agentic-harness/bpmn-execution.md). scripts/prov-qaqc.ts reads every instance in beans/workflows/, including its subprocesses, and for each history entry on an activity or decision: . | writes one prov:Activity (schemas/content/prov.ts): prov:agent is the entry’s actor, prov:hadRole is the role the lane binds (laneBinding), prov:hadPlan is <process file stem>#<node id>, and cat-harness:underPolicy is every policy evaluated. One log per instance goes to docs/assets/prov/<instance>.prov.jsonld; | re-runs authorizeTask itself. For an entry recorded under a verdict it re-checks the principal that verdict recorded (the actor GitHub vouched for); for an entry that records just a name, it uses that name, asserted; | emits the engine’s own prov:Activity when the entry carries one, and derives one only for an entry without one. | . Findings: unknown, deny, not-eligible, undeclared-actor, a recorded authz that disagrees with the recomputed one (authz-disagrees), and gaps in the record itself: no-actor, no-role, node-not-in-model, source-moved and source-missing. An entry with no actor, or in a lane that binds no role, gets no prov:Activity, because the schema requires both and a guessed value is fabrication. It gets a finding instead. bun run cat prov:qaqc # write docs/prov-qaqc/index.md and the logs bun run cat check:prov-qaqc # CI: fail when they are stale . It is advisory, unlike the engine: findings are listed on the /prov-qaqc/ page and never fail the build. check:prov-qaqc fails only on stale outputs, a prov:Activity that does not validate, or an internal error. Quote the counts from a run, not from the page you remember.

4174.title: Two kinds of test data, two declared graph directories
4174.content: Fixed and generated test data sets do not have the same provenance or audit standing, so they live in separately declared graph directories (test-data-fixed vs test-data-generated in schemas/kg/graph-typology-registry.ts) and carry self-identifying $schema and kind tags in schemas/sdlc/test-data.ts: . | Kind | Graph typology | $schema tag | Discriminator | What is stored | Audit standing | . | Fixed | test-data-fixed | test-data-fixed/1.0.0 | kind: "fixed" | Committed records, optional citations, optional SME review sign-off | Usable as certification evidence (isEvidence in schemas/sdlc/test-plan.ts) once review is present | . | Generated | test-data-generated | test-data-generated/1.0.0 | kind: "generated" | Recipe only: contentType, specialisation, template, params, seed, and canonical sha256 | Never stored materialised; synthesised at run time and hashed into folio-test-run/v1 | . Discriminate from the file content, never from the path . A consumer reading a test data node must call discriminateTestDataSet(doc) in schemas/sdlc/test-data.ts, which inspects $schema and kind inside the JSON document rather than inferring the kind from the directory path: . | FixedTestDataSetSchema is .strict() and refuses recipe fields (template, params, seed, sha256). | GeneratedTestDataSetSchema is .strict() and refuses materialised payload fields (records, cases, path, review), and verifies that sha256 equals computeGeneratedSetDigest({ contentType, specialisation, template, params, seed }). | .

4175.title: General curation process and per-content-type specialisation
4175.content: The general curation process is sdlc/processes/test-data-curation.bpmn (Process_TestDataCuration): . | Classify the data set (Task_ClassifySet, GW_SetKind) — decide whether the test case needs a small curated fixed set (audit evidence for domain logic) or a deterministic generated recipe (scale, boundary, or combinatorial coverage). | Fixed branch (Task_CurateFixed, GW_NeedsSmeReview, Call_SmeReview) — author the test-data-fixed/1.0.0 node under the instance’s declared test-data-fixed directory; if the set exercises decision support or an indicator definition, invoke sdlc/processes/sme-test-data-review.bpmn (Process_SmeTestDataReview). | Generated branch (Call_ContentTypeSpecialisation, Task_WriteRecipe) — invoke the content-type specialisation as a called subprocess (Call_ContentTypeSpecialisation), then write the test-data-generated/1.0.0 recipe and its canonical sha256 under the instance’s declared test-data-generated directory without committing materialised records. | Verify self-identification and bind (Task_VerifySelfIdentifying) — verify via discriminateTestDataSet and toTestDataRef that the file self-identifies by $schema and kind and bind its digest into the test-plan/v1 case. | . FHIR templating is one specialisation, named as such, not the design . Call_ContentTypeSpecialisation in test-data-curation.bpmn is parameterized by contentType and specialisation (TestDataSpecialisationSchema in schemas/sdlc/test-data.ts): . | fhir-templating (FHIR_TEMPLATING_SPECIALISATION) is one named specialisation for FHIR IG / DAK content (for example, Liquid or FSH/JSON templates producing synthetic patient bundles or MeasureReport cohorts). | Other content types supply their own specialisations — such as markdown-fixture for document folios, lean-counterexample for formal-proof folios, or tabular-cohort for aggregate indicator tables. | Platform schemas and processes never hardcode FHIR resources or DAK structures as the general test-data model. | .

4176.title: SME review of decision support and indicator definitions
4176.content: When a fixed test data set tests clinical or scientific decision support or indicator definitions, passing is a domain judgement: a subject-matter expert must confirm that the logic produces the right guidance on a worked case or the right value on a cohort. Two units of review in sme-case-verdict/1.0.0 . SmeCaseVerdictKind ($schema: "sme-case-verdict/1.0.0", graph typology sme-case-verdict) discriminates on subjectKind: . | subjectKind: "decision-support" — unit is a worked case (case): . | id, summary, decisionLogicRef, structured input, systemOutput, and optional expectedGuidance. | Refuses cohort. | . | subjectKind: "indicator-definition" — unit is a cohort plus an expected value (cohort): . | id, summary, indicatorRef, populationSize, inputs, expectedValue, computedValue, and optional period, numerator, denominator. | Refuses case. | . | . Attributable SME identity and review date . An audited review without an attributable reviewer and date is not audited. Every sme-case-verdict/1.0.0 node requires: . | reviewer (SmeReviewerIdentitySchema): kind: "human" (never "agent" or "script"), provider (e.g. "github", "orcid"), handle, role (e.g. "clinical-sme"), and optional displayName and actor. | reviewedAt (ReviewedAtSchema): ISO-8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD) or timestamp. | verdict: "pass" | "fail" | "needs-revision", plus a non-empty domain rationale. | . Why the SME lane in sme-test-data-review.bpmn is judgementOnly . In sdlc/processes/sme-test-data-review.bpmn (Process_SmeTestDataReview), the SME review step (Task_SmeJudge) sits in Lane_SME, bound to role clinical-sme (partitionElementRef="clinical-sme"). In scenarios/roles.json, clinical-sme declares "judgementOnly": true and carries no procedural skill on Task_SmeJudge: no procedure yields the clinical or scientific answer, which is the whole reason a person is in the lane. The preparation steps (Task_PrepareWorkedCase, Task_PrepareCohort) and the recording step (Task_RecordCaseVerdict) are mechanical and name test-data-sets; the judgement between them is the human SME’s alone.

4183.title: How to write a test
4183.content: // In scripts/tests/<suite>.test.ts import { describe, test, expect } from "bun:test"; import { REPO_ROOT, ... } from "./helpers"; describe("Feature under test", () => { test("specific behavior", () => { // Arrange // Act // Assert expect(result).toBe(expected); }); }); . Conventions . | One test file per concern: create new files for new concerns. | Use helpers.ts: Don’t hardcode paths or re-implement discovery. | Informational vs. blocking: Tests that report data quality (coverage gaps, label mismatches) should log and pass. Tests that verify contracts (JSON validity, required fields, file existence) should fail. | Comment the failure point: Each test should document what bug or failure it prevents. | Types from schemas/formalization-types.ts: Use TestResult, TestReport, CoverageEntry etc. when generating structured output. | . A test never reads test/results/ as a fixture . Derived QA results live on the orphan qa-reports branch: the checkout’s <instance>/test/results/** is an ignored working copy, and the record is the commit-keyed entry qa-publish stores. A test that reads that tree reads a file that may not be there: it fails when the corpus is absent, or worse, passes by iterating over zero files. | Build the fixture, or run the producer in-process over one, and assert on what it computed. A verdict is not a fixture: the corpus is supposed to change (see qa-witness). | If a test must read a stored result, read it through qa-store (readQa) and treat miss, corrupt and unknown as states to assert, never as an empty pass. | A loop over a corpus needs a “there are some” guard beside it, or it is green over nothing. | Never write into test/attestations/ from a test. It is the judgement store on main; a test that needs one builds it in a temporary root. | . Every test has a Gherkin (STRICT) . A test is not finished until a Gherkin Scenario says what it tests. The Scenario is the specification a reader can review without reading code; the test function is one way of executing it. A test with no Scenario is a defect, not missing documentation. | Every executable test maps to exactly one Scenario. An executable test is whatever the language’s runner discovers, ignored or skipped ones included: a Rust #[test], a Kotlin/JUnit @Test, a bun or vitest test() / it(), a pytest test_*. A parameterised test (test.each, @pytest.mark.parametrize, @ParameterizedTest) is ONE test and maps to one Scenario or Scenario Outline. A test’s title is a fixed string: a test titled by a loop variable or a ${…} template has no name a tag can carry, so the check reports it (test-name-not-static). Give it a literal title, or write the loop as test.each(…)("… %s"). | The link is a tag on the Scenario, never on the Feature: line (a Feature tag would be inherited by every Scenario under it): . @test:tools/verify/tests/signature.rs::rejects_expired_key Scenario: an expired signing key is refused . | The tag grammar is one grammar for every language — @test:<file>::<scope>::…::<name>: . | <file> is the test’s source file, relative to the repository root, with / separators; | then the enclosing scopes in source order (a Rust mod, a Kotlin or Python class, a describe() title), then the test’s own name, each segment separated by ::; | whitespace inside a segment is written as _, because a Gherkin tag ends at whitespace. The checker normalises both sides the same way and reports two tests that normalise to one tag as ambiguous. | . | runner | test | tag | . | Rust | fn parses_cbor() in mod tests of src/cose.rs | @test:src/cose.rs::tests::parses_cbor | . | Rust | fn round_trip() in tests/hcert.rs | @test:tests/hcert.rs::round_trip | . | Kotlin | @Test fun decodes() in class QrTest | @test:app/src/test/kotlin/x/QrTest.kt::QrTest::decodes | . | bun / vitest | test("reads a plan") in describe("loader") | @test:scripts/loader.test.ts::loader::reads_a_plan | . | pytest | def test_load() in class TestPlan | @test:tests/test_plan.py::TestPlan::test_load | . The pytest form is pytest’s own node id, so it can be pasted from the runner’s output. | A Scenario may name more than one test when several tests execute one behaviour, by carrying one tag per test. A Scenario with no @test: tag is specification nobody executes, and is a finding too; mark it @manual when a person executes it, and the checker counts it as linked. | Binding is by tag, and a Scenario may bind an external test case. Besides @test:, a Scenario may carry @itb:<testSuite id>/<testCase id> for a WHO-ITB (GITB TDL) test case, named by the id attribute of the <testsuite> and of the <testcase> it references: ids, not paths, since ITB reports results by id. The tag resolves against a checkout of the suites at a pinned commit; without one it is reported unresolved, never passed. External cases are checked one way only (the tag must name a case that exists), because an external suite is not this repository’s to cover. The schemes are an extensible list, so a new kind of external test is a new prefix and a resolver. | A .feature may be written in any Gherkin dialect, declared by its first-line # language: <code> comment. A translated file stays valid; the @test: and @itb: tags are not translated. | Each test-plan case names its .feature (testCases[].feature in test-plan/v1.1); the tests that execute the case are found through the @test: tags of that file, not listed again in the plan. | . bun run cat check:test-gherkin reports orphans both ways: a test no Scenario names, a tag that names no test, a test named by two Scenarios, a Scenario that names no test, a tag on a Feature: line, an @itb: tag naming no case or whose source is not held, and an unknown dialect. It reads any tree (--root, --under, --itb, --json); it is not a gate until a repository has backfilled. 4187.title: Running a test plan — from a request to a signed certification
4187.content: Skill test-plan-execution: Run a test-plan/v1 against a system under test and take it to a certification decision — the five lanes of test-plan-execution.bpmn (requester, tester, untainted checker, certifier, attestation service), how the test data is bound, what the run and the report must record, the facts the certification table reads, and the kg-audit criteria that judge a run afterwards. Read before executing a plan, re-executing a sample, or certifying a result. Named by: KG to public portal, QA report signing, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Test-plan execution, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Skill id: test-plan-execution · Package: sdlc-core · Process: test-plan-execution.bpmn · Decision: test-certification.dmn . A system is tested against a plan, by somebody who is not the system, and certified by somebody who did not run the test. Everything below is that sentence made operational. This skill is the PROCESS. How to write a test is test-engineer; how a folio’s content is tested is content-test; why the checker sees only a controlled context is untainted-verification; how a signature is routed by reach is qa-report-signing. Read those for their halves — this one does not restate them.

4188.title: The nodes, and who points at whom
4188.content: | node | schema | where it lives | . | the plan | test-plan/v1 — schemas/sdlc/test-plan.ts | authored content (test-plan kind) | . | the system under test | the systemUnderTest facet on an actor — schemas/kg/skill-package.ts | scenarios/actors/*.json | . | the run | folio-test-run/v1 with plan + sut — schemas/sdlc/test-run.ts | the declared qa directory | . | the report | test-report/v1 — schemas/sdlc/test-report.ts | the qa-reports branch, tests/<plan>/<sut>/<run>/ | . | the certification | a judgement, qa-attestations/v1 | the declared attestations graph, on main | . The run points at the plan; the plan names no run. A plan is reused across runs and systems, so a back-pointer would turn authored content into live state. Same direction for the report → run and the certification → report. The platform model is FHIR-free. FHIR R5 TestPlan informed test-plan/v1 and is a DOWNSTREAM export target, in the FHIR IG layer. Never read a FHIR TestPlan as the source of a plan here.

4189.title: The system under test is a facet, not a role
4189.content: Being tested is not a lane anybody takes on. An actor that can be executed — agent or system, never a person or an external — declares: . // an illustration, not a declared actor { "id": "example-mcp-tool", "kind": "system", "reach": "internet", "systemUnderTest": { "kind": "tool", "version": "0.1.0" } } . kind is the closed list SUT_KINDS (skill, agent, tool, machine, ig, process) — the same vocabulary as a plan’s scope.kind, so the two are compared, not translated. Reach is the actor’s own reach, read by sutRefFor; absent is unknown, never internet.

4190.title: The five lanes
4190.content: | lane | role | does | . | Requester / SUT | test-requester | asks for certification of system S against plan P, naming P’s id and version | . | Tester | tester | resolves P, binds its data, executes every case, writes the run and the report | . | Untainted checker | untainted-checker | re-executes a SAMPLE of cases, blind to the tester’s verdicts | . | Certifier | certifier | applies the plan’s exitCriteria table, then records the decision | . | Attestation service | attestation-service | signs, via qa-report-signing.bpmn, and files the certification | . The tester is untainted from the system under test. The SUT may request; it may never be the tester, the checker or the certifier, and it never writes a verdict about itself — test-report/v1 refuses a reviewer whose id or actor is the SUT’s actor, and test-sut-not-self-judged audits it. Tester . | Resolve the plan. P parses as test-plan/v1.1 (a test-plan/v1 plan still parses, deprecated), names at least one req: requirement, its exitCriteria.decision resolves to a decision in a .dmn that exists, and its scope.kind matches the SUT actor’s facet kind. A plan that does not resolve is not run. Every case names the .feature it is written in, and every test that executes it carries that file’s @test: tag (test-engineer). | Bind the test data (test-data-sets). A fixed set is a committed path and is evidence only once reviewed (isEvidence). A generated set is a template + params + seed and is never materialised into the repository. Both feed the run’s data hash; runner, configuration and scenario bank feed its process hash, and the two bases must be disjoint (buildTestRun refuses otherwise). | Execute. Every case is executed, or recorded skipped with a reason. A case with no verdict at the end of a terminal run is a finding, not an omission (checkAgainstPlan). | Write the run and the report. The run records plan {id, version} and sut {actor, version, reach}; the report rolls up per plan, never across plans, and testReportPath says where it goes. | . Untainted checker . Re-executes a sample of the cases from the plan and the data alone — never the tester’s verdicts — and reports agree, disagree or unknown. It RULES ON NOTHING (untainted-verification rule 3): the comparison is a fact the certification table reads, not a verdict the checker writes. Certifier . The gateway is computed. Pass the facts; never assert the branch — the engine refuses a hand-supplied outcome on a DMN gateway. | fact | from | . | reportStatus | the report’s status | . | dataHashKnown | the run’s data.hash is not unknown | . | unexecutedCases | checkAgainstPlan(...).filter(kind === "unexecuted-case").length | . | checker | the untainted checker’s agree / disagree / unknown | . | failedCases | rollup.fail | . | passedCases | rollup.pass | . The table returns certified, refused or undetermined. undetermined is the third state — a running or aborted report, an unknown data hash, an unexecuted case, a checker that disagreed or could not run, or a report in which nothing passed. It is never rendered as certified, and it is not a refusal either: it says the evidence does not decide, so nothing is signed. The certification decision is a judgement. The table says whether the exit criteria are met; the certifier — a person, a specialisation of stakeholder — records the decision, and it lives with the other judgements under the declared attestations graph, never on the qa-reports branch with derived results. Attestation service . Call_Sign runs qa-report-signing.bpmn unchanged; its route (API or a human release authority) is chosen there by the signer’s reach. Then the signed certification is filed under attestations.

4191.title: The kg-audit criteria
4191.content: Registered in KG_CRITERIA (schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts), implemented in scripts/test-plan-audit.ts, recorded on the graph roll-up: . | criterion | fails when | severity | . | test-plan-resolves | a plan does not parse, its exit DMN does not resolve, or a run/report names a plan, version or SUT that does not resolve (or a SUT whose facet kind is not the plan’s scope) | critical | . | test-case-executed-or-skipped | a terminal report leaves a plan case with no verdict, or names a case the plan lacks | major | . | test-data-hash-present | a plan-run’s data hash is unknown, or a report’s run carries none | major | . | test-sut-not-self-judged | any verdict’s reviewer is the system under test | critical | . | test-has-gherkin | a test no Gherkin Scenario names, a @test: tag naming no test, or a plan case whose .feature is missing or does not resolve (test-engineer) | major | . Each records n/a when there is nothing of its kind to judge — no plan, no plan-run, no report — and never a pass over nothing.

4193.title: Test-plan execution
4193.content: Process_TestPlanExecution · strict · 13 step(s) . Executing a test-plan/v1 against a system under test and taking the result to a certification decision: requested by (or for) the system, run by a tester, re-executed in sample by an untainted checker, decided by a certifier through the plan’s exit-criteria table, and signed through qa-report-signing.bpmn. You are in this process when somebody wants a system — a skill, an agent, a tool, a machine, an IG or a process — certified against a named plan. Executing a plan with no certification in view is still this process; it ends at undetermined or refused without anything being signed. The run, the report and the certification are three records, and they point backwards: the run at the plan, the report at the run, the certification at the report. The certification is a judgement and lives under the declared attestations graph, on main; the report is derived and lives on the qa-reports branch. i i i i i i i i i i i i i

4195.title: Lanes — who acts
4195.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Requester / system under test | test-requester | The system under test, or whoever speaks for it, asking for certification against plan P at a named version. Its only task is the request, and that is the design rather than an omission: the system under test never writes a verdict about itself, so after this lane it is the SUBJECT of the process and never a performer in it. | . | Tester | tester | Runs the plan against the system: resolves it, binds its fixed or generated test data, executes every case or skips it with a reason, and writes the folio-test-run/v1 and the test-report/v1. Untainted from the system under test — never the same actor — and it does not certify: what it writes is what the certifier decides on. | . | Untainted checker | untainted-checker | A second party re-executing a sample of the cases from the plan and the data alone, never from the tester’s verdicts. It rules on nothing: whether it agrees is a fact the certification table reads. One party doing both halves is not this check — it would compare a run with its own paraphrase of itself. | . | Certifier | certifier | The accountable party for the decision, a specialisation of the stakeholder. The gateway is computed from the plan’s exit-criteria table; what the certifier adds, and what makes it a judgement, is recording the decision under their name. Never the tester and never the system under test. | . | Attestation service | attestation-service | Signs the certification and files it. Reached only from certified: a refusal and an undetermined result are recorded by the certifier and signed by nobody. The signature itself is qa-report-signing.bpmn, called unchanged, whose own gateway chooses the API or a human release authority by the signer’s reach. | .

4196.title: Steps
4196.content: Every one of the 13 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Request certification of the system against plan PA_Request | Requester / system under test | test-plan-execution | Name the plan by id AND version, and the system under test by actor id. The actor must carry the systemUnderTest facet: an actor that has not said it can be tested is not run against a plan by default. The bean this instance tracks is claimed here. | . | Resolve the planA_ResolvePlan | Tester | test-plan-execution | The plan parses, names at least one req: requirement, its exitCriteria resolves to a decision in a .dmn that exists, and its scope.kind is the system’s facet kind. A plan that does not resolve is not run — test-plan-resolves audits the same join afterwards. Reads a test-plan/v1. | . | Bind the test dataA_BindData | Tester | test-plan-execution | Per bean vm6m: a fixed set is a committed path and counts as evidence only once reviewed; a generated set is template + params + seed and is never materialised. Both feed the run’s data hash, and nothing that feeds the process hash may feed it too. | . | Execute every case, or skip it with a reasonA_Execute | Tester | test-plan-executiontest-engineer | Every case in dependency order. A case is executed or explicitly skipped with its reason; a case that simply has no verdict is a finding, because it cannot be told from a case nobody ran. | . | Write the test run and the test reportA_WriteRun | Tester | test-plan-execution | The run records plan {id, version} and sut {actor, version, reach} with its data and process hashes; the report rolls up per plan, never across plans, and goes to the qa-reports branch at tests/plan/sut/run/. No verdict in it may name the system under test as its reviewer. Writes a folio-test-run/v1 and a test-report/v1. | . | Re-execute a sample, blind to the tester’s verdictsA_ReExecuteSample | Untainted checker | untainted-verificationtest-plan-execution | Given the plan, the bound data and a sample of case ids — not the report. Says agree, disagree or unknown; unknown (could not run) is said as plainly as a disagreement, because the table reads both the same way and an unknown read as agreement certifies on one party’s word. | . | Record the certification decisionA_RecordCertification | Certifier | test-plan-execution | The judgement: the certifier records, under their own name, that the system meets plan P at this version on this run. It is written under the declared attestations graph beside the other judgements, never on the qa-reports branch with derived results. A user task, so no agent or pipeline can fill it. | . | Record the refusal, with the failing casesA_RecordRefusal | Certifier | test-plan-execution | A complete, trusted run in which a case failed. The refusal names the failing cases and is the end of this request; nothing is signed. The bean resolves here because the process has finished — what to do about the failure is a new piece of work. | . | Record why it could not be decidedA_RecordUndetermined | Certifier | test-plan-execution | The third state: which fact kept the table from deciding — a run not finished, an unknown data hash, an unexecuted case, a checker that disagreed or could not run, or nothing passed. A note and not a resolution, because the request is still open: it needs a re-run or an adjudication, not a verdict. | . | Sign the certificationCall_Sign | Attestation service | calls QA report signingqa-report-signing | qa-report-signing.bpmn, unchanged: it builds the signable run record, resolves the signer’s reach, and routes the signature to the API or to a human release authority. | . | File the signed certificationA_FileCertification | Attestation service | test-plan-execution | The signed certification goes under the declared attestations graph on main (owner ruling D2 (a), D5 default), pointing at the report it certifies. The bean resolves here, once the process has actually finished. Files it as qa-attestations/v1. | . | Open the beanCall_BeanOpen | Requester / system under test | calls Open the beanbean-coordination | Process_BeanOpen: check before you create, find out whose the bean is, and claim it — or leave it alone when it is someone else’s. The one place a claim is drawn (bean m8gz, owner 2026-10-24); the gateway after this reads which end it reached. | . | Close the beanCall_BeanClose | Attestation service | calls Close the beantodo-manager | Process_BeanClose: end the bean in a state that says why — complete and archive it, scrap it with its reasons and archive it, or record the blocker and hand it back. The one place resolve and archive are drawn (bean m8gz, owner 2026-10-24); placed straight before the end so the engine’s resolve sees nothing left but the archive step. | .

4197.title: Decisions
4197.content: Every one of the 3 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Exit criteria met?GW_ExitCriteria | Computed from six facts read off the records — report status, data hash known, unexecuted cases, the checker’s agreement, failed and passed cases — by the table the plan’s exitCriteria names (resolved dynamically; if unresolvable, routes to undetermined and never silently falls back to default). Supplying the branch by hand is refused. | certified → Record the certification decisionrefused → Record the refusal, with the failing casesundetermined → Record why it could not be decided | . | Bean claimed?GW_BeanYours | Reads which end Process_BeanOpen reached. claimed: the bean is in progress and this process works it. not yours: a sibling session or a human holds it, nothing was written to it, and this process stops here rather than work a bean it does not own (bean-coordination). | claimed → Request certification of the system against plan Pnot yours → Not yours — left alone | . | How did it end?GW_BeanClosedHow | Which outcome the bean was closed with, so each ends at its own named end event. 4199.title: Theme art intake
4199.content: Skill theme-art-intake: Accept or refuse a set of three theme/avatar layouts arriving through document ingestion, with a named reason for every refusal. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph . Art arrives — three crops for a theme or an avatar — and the answer is either accepted, with the declaration written, or refused, with what to fix.

4200.title: This is a step in document ingestion, not a process beside it
4200.content: Document ingestion already answers the question art arrival poses — something unstructured has arrived; is it acceptable, and if not, why not — with a pipeline and a completeness gate. Theme art is the same event with a different payload, so what exists is a check keyed on the payload, not a second pipeline: a parallel “avatar ingestion” would be a second answer to one question, free to disagree with the first. |   | where | . | the check | schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts — pure, no I/O, no clock | . | the CLI face | scripts/check-theme-art.ts, bun run cat check:theme-art | . | the arrival | uploads/, per content-acquisition and document-intake | .

4201.title: The constraints
4201.content: Each constraint answers a failure that has happened. Do not add one that has not: a rule with no failure behind it is one whose next maintainer cannot tell whether it still matters. | constraint | verdict | why | . | all three layouts | refuse | resolveThemeBackdrop refuses an incomplete backdrop wholesale, so a theme missing one crop renders with no art — not two thirds of it. | . | distinct content | refuse | two byte-identical files for two named layouts or avatars means one is missing. | . | orientation per layout | refuse | a portrait crop is not a landscape crop scaled down. The quiet area the sticky’s text sits in moves. | . | a declared destination | refuse | art outside a declared directory (at the repository root, say) is seen by no gate: check-declared-assets walks declared→disk. | . | dimensions measured | structural | intake takes bytes and emits the declaration, so there is nowhere for a retyped (or copied) number to enter. | . | weight and format | report | heavy PNGs still render, so refusing them would block work over a bandwidth judgement. | .

4202.title: Refuse, report, or neither
4202.content: . | Refuse when the art cannot do its job, or when intake cannot tell which of two readings is intended. A missing crop and two identical files are both “somebody has to decide something”. | Report when the art works but costs. Weight and format are the cases: a 1.6 MB PNG renders correctly. | Neither — say nothing — for anything intake did not actually measure. | . remedy is a required field on every failure: a refusal that says invalid teaches nobody what to fix. All failures are collected rather than thrown one at a time, because art arrives as a batch, and reporting the first problem of three means three round trips to learn three things.

4203.title: Do not repair somebody’s art
4203.content: deletion-requires-confirmation applies, and so does its spirit. When intake refuses, the outputs are the report and a work-plan item — not a re-crop, not a converted file, and not a quietly removed declaration. What looks like a missing crop may be a duplicate that was uploaded by mistake, and that is a question for the person who has the original. check:theme-art:check runs in CI, so a refusal of declared art is a regression.

4204.title: Reading the report
4204.content: ✓ landing-engineer: 3 layouts accepted · laptop 1672×941 docs/assets/img/harness/landing-engineer-laptop.png ! [heavy] laptop: … is 1560 KB, over the 391 KB budget → convert to webp — the measured gap on this art was about 16× ✗ landing-architecture: refused, 1 problem(s) · [missing-layout] mobile: no file offered for the mobile layout → supply all three layouts … . Three rules for reading it, the same three ci-health states: . | declared-but-absent is not a refusal and not a pass. The declaration names a file that is not on disk. It is reported on its own line because “the file is not there” and “the file is the wrong shape” are different facts, and a reader who cannot tell them apart fixes the wrong one. | A check that fires on every subject is wrong. docs/ is not a declared directory, and should not be — a declared entry names a graph, and the site is the render target — so art under it is not undeclared-destination. When a new check’s first run lights up broadly, ask which of these are correct? before how do I fix the repository?, and test any exclusion in both directions: a test of the excluded case alone passes equally for a check that never fires. A check that fires on legitimate subjects gets switched off, and a switched-off check still reads as coverage. | Warnings do not accumulate into a refusal. Twelve heavy files are twelve reports, not a failure. | .

4205.title: Adding a constraint
4205.content: . | Name the failure it answers. No failure, no constraint. | Decide refuse vs report by the line above — can the art do its job? | Write the remedy before the detection. If you cannot say what to do about it, the check is not ready. | Prove it fires, with a test that fails when the check is removed. | Check it against art already shipped. The aspect bands are deliberately wide because the shipped laptop crops run 1.50–1.78; a tighter band would refuse work that is fine. | . The stages of theming, and which owns which question, are in theming.

4208.title: At ingestion, and only at ingestion
4208.content: Skill theme-ui-review: Review graphical assets AS THEY ARE INGESTED, in the context of the website or app design they are for — accessibility, branding, languages — to determine what the assets and the UI will be. At ingestion only; called from ingest-theme. Measures rather than asserts, and raises findings rather than fixing them. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph . This skill runs in exactly one place: theme-ui-review.bpmn, called from ingest-theme.bpmn Task_Review, whose agent lane is ingestion-agent. It is not part of a post-MVP SDLC step and is not called from crdm-deliver.bpmn.

4209.title: What it reviews
4209.content: It looks at the arriving graphical assets laid out in the design they are for, so a finding is a decision about what the assets will be, taken while it is still cheap. The questions: accessibility measured rather than asserted, branding against the instance’s own declaration, and every declared locale. Theme choice is an authoring judgement. There is no role-to-theme mapping (theme.ts records why), so nothing here checks a binding. What gets reviewed is the ingested art in its design context.

4210.title: What this gives up — accepted
4210.content: An ingestion review answers “what will this turn into?” only as far as the assets can be laid out in their design before the site exists — not how a crop reads in the finished page. That gap is accepted; do not add a post-MVP review call on your own initiative.

4211.title: A person is in the loop, inside ingestion
4211.content: R_Judge is a human step: a person looks at the assets laid out at a web and a mobile width, so ingesting a theme source is attended at that step. Ingesting anything else stays unattended — Gateway_ThemeSource in document-ingestion.bpmn routes non-theme documents past ingest-theme.bpmn entirely.

4212.title: Measure; do not assert
4212.content: Contrast is computed, against the real ground. A theme with a backdrop has no single ratio — ink over a photograph varies pixel to pixel — so the number that matters is the worst case the art can present. Every shipped scrim in this repository is measured over pure black for that reason, and the check is written so it can fail: without a case that fails at a thin scrim, passing assertions prove nothing about the value. Colour is never the sole carrier (SC 1.4.1). Where it carries meaning, look for the second channel — the priority stripe is a width as well as a hue precisely so a monochrome reader still sees it. An automated pass is necessary and not sufficient: . | axe accepts a non-empty placeholder as an accessible name, so a label removed from the accessibility tree can pass the automated check. | A CSS selector that matches nothing raises no error in any tool, and can leave a backdrop at its intrinsic size across the viewport with every gate green. | . So a person looks at the assets laid out in their design (R_Judge). That is a step in the diagram, not an optional extra, because no automated check catches either case above.

4213.title: Branding is a question about the INSTANCE, not about taste
4213.content: Marks, palettes and art are checked against the instance’s own declaration rather than a remembered style. The sharpest form of the question comes from downstream: would a folio depending on this platform inherit something it did not choose? landing.html states it as a rule — “a downstream folio should not inherit a grumpy cat it did not choose” — and it is why a theme names an image role rather than a path.

4214.title: Languages: new UI is where untranslated strings enter
4214.content: Check that every user-facing string reaches the .pot, that each declared locale renders without clipping, and that right-to-left is laid out rather than mirrored by accident. The distinction worth keeping: a name is translatable and a value is not. A theme’s display name goes through the pipeline; its palette does not, because a colour is not language-dependent and translating one invites a locale to diverge on a value the CSS must agree on.

4215.title: Raise findings; do not fix them
4215.content: A finding goes back to whoever authored the choice, because the choice was theirs. There is no mapping to correct instead, and a reviewer who quietly re-themes a note has substituted their judgement for the author’s without saying so — which is the same objection decision-audit makes to editing a finding rather than overruling it with a note. The one exception is the one this repository already allows everywhere: a defect that is not a judgement call at all — a selector matching nothing, a string missing from the .pot, a contrast ratio below the floor — is a bug, and bugs get fixed.

4216.title: What this does NOT cover
4216.content: Not the choice itself. Whether a sticky should be engineer or library is an authoring decision, and this review does not second-guess it; it asks whether what was ingested will render legibly, consistently and in every declared language in the design it is for.

4217.title: Both viewports, always
4217.content: . | Every surface is inventoried and judged at a web width and at a mobile width. | A review done at one width is incomplete, not passed. | The surface’s wireframe, in wireframe-design-review, states what each layout was meant to be, so the review compares the build against an intent rather than against memory. | .

4225.title: Session Task Manager (beans)
4225.content: Skill todo-manager: Maintain and display work-in-progress task lists using the beans CLI issue tracker. Track implementation progress, open tasks, missing artifacts, and blocked items across a session. Named by: Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase
