4346.title: The registry is the tenant list, and it does not hold the version
4346.content: upstream/upstream-pins.json — in this harness’s declared upstream/ directory — declares each pinned dependency, with each pinnedIn resolved against the harness root: the upstream repo, the file the pin literal actually lives in, the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to it, and the commands that constitute its MVP. It deliberately does not store the pinned version. The version lives in exactly one place — site-chrome/_config.yml for the theme — and the registry says how to read it from there. A registry that carried its own copy would be a second answer to “what are we running”, free to disagree with the build. bun run cat check:upstream-pins reads the literal out of the declared file; a pattern that matches nothing is reported as an error, not as “no pin”. binds and mvp are the reason the registry exists at all rather than the check simply grepping for version strings. They are what turn impact analysis and MVP from words in a box into a list somebody can work through.

4347.title: 1 — Watch
4347.content: bun run cat check:upstream-pins, weekly from .github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml and on demand. For each row: read the pinned ref out of its declared file, list the upstream tags that match tagPattern, and compare. Exit codes, and the middle one is the point: . | Exit | Meaning | What the workflow does | . | 0 | every pin is at the newest matching release | closes the tracking issue if one is open | . | 1 | at least one pin is behind | opens one issue labelled upstream-pin, or edits the existing one | . | 2 | could not determine — upstream unreachable, pattern did not match | leaves the issue untouched and fails the job | . Three rules it inherits from check-ci-health.ts, and they are not optional: . | “Could not check” is never rendered as current. An unreachable upstream is exit 2, not exit 0. A watchdog that goes blind must not read as good news. | One issue, edited in place. An edit does not notify, so a pin that stays stale for months stays one unread item rather than many. | The job fails on exit 2, which makes this workflow itself red on the default branch, which check:ci-health reports. The watchdog is watched. | .

4348.title: 2 — Impact analysis
4348.content: Scope the delta first, and scope it to what reaches our output. The upstream changelog is the claim; the diff is the evidence. For a Jekyll theme that means _sass, _includes, _layouts and assets — a change to upstream’s own docs, CI or tests cannot reach us: . git -C <upstream-clone> diff --stat <pinned>..<candidate> -- _sass _includes _layouts assets . Then ask what of ours binds to it, from the row’s binds list. This is the half that a changelog cannot tell you, because upstream does not know what you reached into. For the theme it is concrete and small: site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js moves the theme’s own search markup into the action launcher, binding .search, #search-input and .search-label; site-chrome/assets/css/docs-ui.css overrides .side-bar, .site-header and .main-header; and three e2e specs assert the structure the theme emits. An upstream rename of any of those is not a build failure — it is a shipped feature that quietly stops working, which is the failure mode a pin exists to convert into a decision. Write the analysis down as the work item’s note before building anything. A candidate that touches nothing we bind to is a different conversation from one that renames a selector we depend on, and the reviewer needs to know which they are looking at before they look.

4349.title: 3 — MVP
4349.content: An MVP is a deployed build, not a description of one. Move the pin on a branch, let feature-staging.yml publish it under branches/<branch-slug>/, and run the row’s mvp commands. For the theme: . rm -rf _kg _site bun test # unit tests CI=1 bun run cat test:e2e # a11y, action tiles, sidebar panels, qa panel bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/site-links.ts --site ./_site # every navbar tile resolves in the BUILT site . site-links.ts checks the tiles against the real _site rather than against the attribute, which is what catches a tile that 404s. A red gate is evidence, not an exit. It does not end the process and it does not loop on its own — it goes to the reviewer with everything else, because “this version breaks us” is a finding the decider needs, not a reason to stop before they see it.

4350.title: 4 — Review
4350.content: Post the staging URL, the gate results and the impact analysis on the PR, then hand it over. The reviewer’s question is narrower than “is the new version good”: it is does anything in binds still hold, checked against the deployed page rather than against a screenshot. Findings the agent can fix — our overlay adapting to a renamed class, a test fixture updated to the markup the theme now emits — loop back into impact analysis on the same branch. Findings that are upstream’s behaviour rather than ours go to the decision as they are.

4351.title: 5 — Decide
4351.content: A person decides, and the diagram says so. PM_Decide is a bpmn:userTask in the publication manager’s lane, and that role admits person only, so activity-fulfilment-kind fails the moment somebody tries to make an agent the accepting party. It also carries <cat-harness.processes:policy relaxable="false"/>: no package may relax it. The lane is the publication manager’s rather than the editor’s because the pin is not a change to the corpus — it is a change to what the published artefact is built from, and that role is the one “accountable for what is live”. The gateway is not DMN-backed, and that is deliberate. Every other computed gateway in this repository reduces to arithmetic over tool output; this one weighs a rendering nobody can score against the cost of staying behind. A table here would look authoritative and would not be. Three outcomes: . | Adopt — move the pin, open the PR, and say in the body what the version range changed in rendered output. Record the evidence you used, not just the verdict. | Hold — record it as a block with an expiry and a revisit trigger (bean-blocking.md). A hold with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work, and the next watcher run will re-raise the same pin with no memory of why it was left. | Decline — record the reasons on the work item and scrap it. A scrapped work item is what stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end; a deleted one leaves them unable to tell a decision from an accident. | . In every case the decision is written down before the process ends. The work item is resolved from the terminal step, so a run that stops at “we looked and said no” is as finished as one that moved the pin.

4352.title: Adding a tenant
4352.content: . | Pin the literal wherever the tool reads it, with a comment saying which process governs moving it. | Add a row to upstream-pins.json: repo, pinnedIn, pattern, tagPattern, binds, mvp. | Run bun run cat check:upstream-pins and confirm it reads your pin back. A pattern that does not match is exit 2 — “could not determine” — and the row is not watched until it does. | . No diagram changes. That is what reusable means here.

4353.title: How to pick the pinned version when you first pin something
4353.content: Pin what is running, not what is newest. Those are different changes, and doing both at once means neither is reviewable — a regression cannot be attributed to the pin or to the bump. Establish what is running by fingerprint, not by assumption. For the theme that meant finding a declaration in the deployed CSS on gh-pages (text-wrap: balance, in _sass/navigation.scss) that entered upstream after the newest release, which proved the live site was tracking the default branch rather than any tag. The newest release at or below that point is the pin, and the PR states the residual delta — one CSS declaration — rather than claiming there is none. If no fingerprint discriminates, say so and pin the newest release anyway; an unverified pin is still strictly better than an unpinned dependency, and “could not determine” written down is worth more than a confident guess.

4361.title: uses[] Editorial Review
4361.content: Skill uses-editorial-review: Adjudicate uses-editorial-completeness — read a block as a reader would and judge whether its uses[] is complete and genuinely expository. The human/agent half of the uses QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-uses.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review, Committee review of a content change .

4362.title: The relation you are auditing
4362.content: uses[] is the editorial dependency relation: what must a reader have read to follow this block? It is authored content — a deliberate judgement about narrative order — and it is maintained by agents and humans, not generated. The same relation exists at term scale: a glossary term’s requires, and a schema term’s uses in bootstrap’s graph.schema.json, say what a reader must know before the definition. Same discipline — AUTHORED, never inferred, with a text matcher kept only as a guard that list and prose agree (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”). It is not any machine-derived dependency graph. A content type with a formal layer also derives a formal relation, from what its proofs actually invoke, and the two relations answer different questions and diverge in both directions, correctly. The layer that ships such a content type holds that comparison and names this skill from its side (for a paper folio, the science layer).

4363.title: interprets is the same relation under a second field name
4363.content: uses[] is the curated list. interprets states the same reader-facing fact for a remark or example about one specific block, and the content graph counts both. Each editorial edge carries editorialField so a tool proposing an edit can still tell which field an author wrote: they are interchangeable to a reader and not to a writer, and collapsing them would make an automated edit rewrite the wrong field. Two caveats, both of which change what a number means: . | detangler-no-forward-ref builds its own uses-only adjacency and does not consume the shared graph, so forward-pointing interprets edges are outside what it counts. | The editorial graph is not acyclic. Counting both fields reveals genuine editorial cycles. Do not “fix” one without reading whether it is real. | . Do not quote a count from prose — run the check against the corpus in front of you. A number in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. For impact questions — what breaks if this changes? — use the union, via the content graph’s accessors, which default to it.

4364.title: The prime directive
4364.content: Never populate uses[] from a machine-derived dependency graph. Copying derived dependencies in destroys the editorial signal and inflates every ordering metric computed from it (graph energy, forward refs, cone size, PageRank). Never “sync” the two. When reviewing, do not open a block’s formal or generated sibling to decide what belongs in uses[]. The question is about the reader.

4365.title: Workflow
4365.content: . | Read the .md as a reader. Cold. Do not read the .ts first — you want your own sense of what the block presumes before you see what the author declared. | List what the narrative actually leans on. Note every point where the prose: . | uses notation it does not introduce, | names an object (“the canonical $X$”) defined elsewhere, | argues against or refines a prior result, | presumes a construction the reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. | . | Now read uses[] in the .ts manifest and compare both ways. | Judge completeness. Anything from step 2 missing from uses[] that a reader would genuinely stumble over ⇒ fail (major). A reader who could carry on unbothered ⇒ at most warn. | Judge editorial fitness. For each listed entry, ask: would a reader be worse off having not read this first? . | Yes ⇒ fine. | No, and it looks like a derived artefact (an entry the prose never mentions, copied from a generated dependency list) ⇒ fail (major). This is the pollution case. | No, but it is defensible context ⇒ warn. | . | Write the sidecar entry under uses-editorial-completeness with reviewer.kind: "agent" (or "human"), citing file:line and a verbatim quote for every finding — the block-QA evidence contract. | .

4366.title: Verdict rubric
4366.content: | Verdict | When | . | pass | List reads as a deliberate editorial judgement; nothing a reader needs is missing; nothing present is dead weight. | . | warn | A marginal entry, or a missing dependency a reader could shrug off. | . | fail | A missing dependency a reader would stumble over, or an entry that is plainly a copied-in derived dependency. | .

4367.title: Forward references and foreshadows[]
4367.content: A uses[] entry pointing at a block that appears later in the chapter is a detangler-no-forward-ref finding. Sometimes that is right — the exposition really does defer — and foreshadows[] records it. foreshadows[] is independent of uses[], so a chapter overview can name results it previews without asserting a dependency that is not real. It covers two cases you must keep apart: . | case | in uses[]? | who records it | cost | . | Pure forward pointer — the prose names something coming later and does not depend on it | no | derived from the .md, not authored | zero by construction: it never enters the dependency graph | . | Deferred prerequisite — a real dependency the paper states later on purpose | yes | declared by the author, and only the author | exempt from ordering cost; still counted for cycles, cones and depth | . Do not hand-author the first case. deriveForeshadows reads the block’s own markdown links and backticked labels, keeps those that resolve to a real block sitting later in reading order and are not already in uses[], and loadChapterGraph re-derives on every load. Writing them into the manifest duplicates the prose into metadata, where it goes stale. The derivation never reads deferral language; it matches links and labels only (phrasing detection misreads e.g. “Below $n^*$”, a numeric comparison).

4368.title: Declaring the second case
4368.content: Only a deferred prerequisite needs your judgement: it exempts a real uses[] edge from the ordering metrics, hiding a genuine defect behind an authored claim that the disorder was intended, and nothing downstream re-opens it. The contract in BlockBase.foreshadows is strict — the prose must frame the reference as deferred (“we will need X, proved in chapter 9”). The bar is a first-person authorial hand-off that says the treatment happens elsewhere: “we establish this in X”, “we work this out separately”, “the derivation is recorded in X”. | Looks like a deferral | Actually | . | Bare cross-reference — “See [X] in Chapter 7” | ordering. Says nothing about direction. | . | Organizational pointer — “these tables are projections of this master table” | ordering. About structure, not sequence. | . | Block asserts the target’s conclusion as background, then reasons onward from it | ordering. Consuming a result is the opposite of deferring it. | . | Target listed under “## Rigorous results” / “## Consumers / downstream” | ordering — and check the direction; these often run target→source. | . | A forward-looking word (“below”, “later”, “we must show”) | ordering unless the sentence is about this target’s placement. “Below $n^*$” is a numeric comparison; “we must show” is usually about research, not chapter order. | . Two failure modes survive a verbatim quote, so check both before declaring: . | False locator. “the functor of the next subsection” where the target is 21 sections and ~300 blocks away. The prose defers; it does not defer this far, and the edge is a real defect. | Mis-aimed deferral. The quoted sentence hands off to a different block than the edge under review. A deferral pointed elsewhere cannot exempt this one. | . Both are about the declared case only. A derived pointer is aimed by the link itself, so it cannot be mis-aimed, and it carries no exemption to abuse. Two rules police the field: foreshadows-resolve (every target must exist) and foreshadows-not-self. The foreshadows-point-forward criterion catches a target the reader has already passed, which is either a prerequisite filed in the wrong field or an inert back-reference.

4369.title: A block’s uses[] may be carrying the whole family
4369.content: Never judge an entry from the block’s own .md alone. A block is the head of a family — X-proof, X-interpretation, X-tableN-data — and the dependency you are looking for is often in a child while the declaration sits on the parent. | Table children. Pointer-style blocks (“See Table 3”) keep their substance in tbl:…-data. A name-and-notation search of the parent’s .md reports an absence that is not real. | Proof children. A proof cites what the statement assumes. The parent’s prose may never name a target its proof child cites by label; if the proof declares no uses[] of its own, the parent’s entry is the sole record of the dependency, and deleting it as “unsupported by the prose” erases the edge entirely. | . So before removing an entry, check whether any child leans on the target, and whether that child declares anything itself. An entry that looks like dead weight on the parent may be the family’s only declaration. Searching for the target’s words also misses a lean on the target’s object — a source writing “the canonical $\tilde w_\lambda$” depends on whatever defines the undeformed $w_\lambda$, whether or not it ever says so.

4370.title: Sibling parity is evidence only until a bulk edit touched the family
4370.content: “All the siblings declare nothing, so declaring it here would be the anomaly” is evidence only if no bulk operation has run over the family: a bulk edit (for example a transitive-prune pass) produces parity by construction, so parity cannot distinguish a shared convention from shared damage. Before resting on it, check the family’s history, not just the block’s: . git log --oneline -- <chapter>/<sibling>.ts # for two or three siblings . A convention shows up as blocks that were authored empty. Damage shows up as one commit emptying all of them on the same day. If the emptiness has a single commit behind it, parity tells you nothing about intent. The same caution applies to any evidence drawn from what “the corpus does”: a corpus that has been swept is a record of the sweep as much as of the authors.

4371.title: One reading is not the standard
4371.content: A single careful pass is not enough: on re-review, destructive uses[] verdicts and foreshadow declarations are overturned often, and keyword search over the .md alone misses real dependencies. Use two readers who cannot see each other’s verdicts for anything that edits the graph, and treat agreement as the signal. Where they disagree, or where either is unsure, leave the edge alone: a wrongly deleted editorial edge silently corrupts every ordering metric computed from the graph. A retarget carries both burdens. It asserts this edge is wrong and that one is right, so it needs evidence for each half separately. When only the second half holds, it is an addition, not a swap.

4372.title: Reading the mechanical findings first
4372.content: Run the script half before adjudicating — it is cheap and it changes what you should look at: . bun run pipeline/qa-checkers-uses.ts # via qa-sweep --axis uses . | Mechanical finding | What it means for your review | . | uses-editorial-hygiene fail — unresolvable label | A dangling reference. Fix the label or add the missing block before judging completeness; the graph is wrong until you do. | . | uses-editorial-hygiene warn — transitive redundancy | Tidiness only. The graph is correct, just not minimal. Do not let it distract from the completeness question. | . A content type with a formal layer adds its own advisory finding here; the layer that ships it says how to read it.

A content type’s own skills that consume or extend this relation are named by the layer that ships the type, which links down to this skill.

4376.title: Design rules
4376.content: . | A Skill and a Tool, built into the processes. The steps live in the folio-block-screenshots Tool and in this skill. The staging workflow and the review process CALL them; nobody copies them. | No new dependency. The pictures are taken with Playwright, which the platform already uses, and the comparison runs in Chromium’s own canvas, so nothing new needs a licence. | One key or one click; never a drag. The page offers four views as radio buttons, not a slider. | .

4377.title: What the reviewer sees
4377.content: On the review page, a visual block opens on “Pictures, before and after”. It shows: . | a sentence stating how much changed: “12.3% of the block’s pixels changed”, or “No pixel changed beyond anti-aliasing”, or “Only one side could be pictured”; | four views, each one click (or an arrow key): | . | view | shows | . | Changed pixels | the after picture faded to grey, with every changed pixel marked in magenta | . | Before | the block on the published site | . | After | the block on this preview | . | Both | before and after side by side | . When a build published no pictures, the block opens side by side (the live pages in frames) instead, because the page takes the first view that can run and lists the block’s kind.

4378.title: What the percentage means, and must NOT be read as
4378.content: | it is | it is not | . | the share of the block’s pixels, in the larger of the two pictures, that differ by more than a small tolerance (24 of 255 per channel, to absorb anti-aliasing) | whether the change is right. A one-pixel line through a chart can be the whole point | . | counted over the larger picture, so a block that grew counts the new area as changed | a measure of text change: a reworded caption moves many pixels | . | of the light theme only | a check of dark mode | . Zero means nothing changed that the eye would see. A block the ChangeSet lists as changed with 0% is still worth a look at its markup: the change may be in alt text, a label or a link.

4379.title: When a picture is missing
4379.content: A missing picture is said, never drawn blank: . | message | means | what to do | . | “Not on main: this block is new.” | an added block has no before | nothing: there is nothing to compare | . | “Its page is not in the published site” | the before side has no page for the block’s document | the document is new, or main was never published. A folio publishes main when its staging caller lists push to main; the build log warns when _main-site.json is absent | . | “Its anchor is not on the … page” | the page exists, but has no <a id="<label>"> for the block | the block was renamed without renamedFrom, or the build dropped it. Check the id-stable QA criterion | .

4380.title: How a picture is taken
4380.content: The site build writes an empty <a id="<label>"> before each labelled block. There is no element that wraps the block. So a block’s picture is the region from its anchor down to the next anchor, as wide as the anchor’s container. A page with anchors out of order pictures the wrong region, so if a picture looks wrong, check the anchors first.

4381.title: The Tool

It writes visual-diff.json (folio-visual-diff/v1) and visual/*.png next to the site. The review page reads ../visual-diff.json.

It runs after the step “Choose the before side”, which picks: . | main’s site, at the publish branch’s root, published by the same workflow’s publish-main job on every push to main; | for a stacked PR, its base branch’s preview, branches/<base-slug>/, so the pictures and the ChangeSet compare with the same branch. 4385.title: Visualizer loading — the page is layout, the graph is fetched
4385.content: Skill visualizer-loading: The general strategy for a complex visualizer: the generated page carries identity, layout and a pointer, and its bulky or repeated content is fetched from the Knowledge Graph in the browser rather than baked into every page. What must stay server-side, how to fetch, how to stay equivalent to the render being replaced, and how to verify a page whose content is not in its HTML. Read before generating any page that shows a KG node’s data at length: an IG artefact view, a graph viewer, a schema or sidecar view. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Skill id: visualizer-loading · Package: ui-core .

4386.title: The rule
4386.content: A generated page for a complex visualizer holds three things: . | Identity: the title, description and front matter that navigation, search and a link preview read. | Layout: headings, tabs and links, arranged by a template (liquid-templates). | A pointer: the KG file the content comes from, resolved by the generator. | . The content (a sidecar file, a node’s properties at length, a table derived from the graph) is fetched by the browser from the committed KG artefact. It is never copied into the page. Each copy is a second answer, free to drift from the first, and copied into a thousand pages it is most of the site’s bytes. kg-viewer is an instance of the pattern: one page that fetches its sibling graph document and computes back-links at load.

4387.title: What stays server-side
4387.content: Moving content client-side has costs: a reader without JavaScript loses it, a search index loses it, and so does the first paint. So these stay in the page: . | What navigation and search need: title, description, headings, and the link labels a reader scans for. | The way to reach the data without JavaScript: a link to the raw file, under <noscript> if nowhere else. A view that renders nothing without scripts must still say where its content is. | Anything short and unique to the page. A one-line value is not bloat, and fetching it costs a request to save a few bytes. | . Move a block when it is large or repeated and already a KG file. A block that would need a new file published just to be fetched is a design question for the owner, not a default.

4388.title: Where the data is served from — served: true
4388.content: The fetched file is the KG’s own, published verbatim. A directory declares served: true in its instance’s <instance>.json, and mount-instance-docs copies its bytes to /<instance>/<path> after Jekyll: no Liquid, no layout, no index page. Pages under the instance’s composed docs then reach it with a relative path. Never copy the file into docs/ beside the page instead — a gate flags it as an unknown file family in a docs directory. A generator whose data is not served writes no page that would fetch it, and says why.

4389.title: How to fetch
4389.content: . | Relative to the page’s own location, never via a configured base URL, so the same bytes work in production and in a staging preview (kg-viewer §”The page is generated, not committed”). | One shared loader per visualizer kind, published once and referenced by every page, never inlined in each page. | No dependencies: no CDN or framework. Same reason as kg-viewer: the data is this repository’s, and a third party in its trust boundary is at odds with that. | Three states on the page: loading, loaded, and could not load, which names the file and the error. A failed fetch that leaves a blank or a permanent “Loading…” is the silent-gap defect in another form. | .

4390.title: Stay equivalent to the render you replace
4390.content: When the page replaces another renderer’s page (for example the IG Publisher’s, which every phase must render equivalent to), compute the display the same way that renderer does, and then check it. For example, a page that shows a file as JSON.stringify(parsed, null, 2) differs from the file’s own bytes whenever the file has integer-like keys, which JavaScript orders first; showing the raw bytes would look right and be wrong.

4391.title: Printing and PDFs
4391.content: A browser prints the page as it is at that moment, so fetched content prints once it has loaded and not before: a PDF taken at domcontentloaded holds “Loading…”. | Every loader signals completion. Each counts itself in and out of window.__kgLoads, and the last one to finish sets <html data-kg-loaded>, on success or failure. A failed fetch still ends the wait, and its message is what prints. | Anything that prints or renders a PDF waits for that attribute, never for a fixed delay. That includes a Playwright page.pdf(), a PDF build step and a screenshot test. A page with no loader never sets it, so a tool that waits must first check whether the page loads one of the loader scripts. | A reader pressing Ctrl+P gets the page as loaded. The loaders are fast, but a print from a cold cache can still catch “Loading…”. That is a visible, honest state, not a blank. | .

4392.title: Verify in a browser, not in the HTML
4392.content: A static check cannot see fetched content: the built HTML holds only “Loading…”. Verification therefore means loading each page in a browser (Playwright, with the pre-installed Chromium) and comparing what it displays against the reference, as rendered-verification requires of any rendered artefact.

4393.title: Finding what to move
4393.content: A QA review over a built site: . | The mechanical half measures per-page bytes, blocks repeated across pages, and blocks matching a committed KG file, and writes a QA sidecar. | The agentic half judges each candidate against §”What stays server-side”. | . Repetition is a measurement, but whether a block may leave the page is a judgement.

4394.title: Do not
4394.content: . | Bake a KG file’s text into a page “for now”. That copy is what the next person will have to find and remove. | Move navigation or search terms client-side to save bytes. The saving is small and the loss is the page being findable. | Add a framework to fetch a JSON file. fetch and textContent are the whole loader. | .

4397.title: Read the voices before the first sentence, not after the first review
4397.content: A voice is an editorial register — spelling, punctuation, terminology, how a normative statement is phrased. Get it right while drafting; correcting it afterwards means rewriting prose somebody has already reviewed. bun run cat check:voices # what this instance ships, and how many rules each carries . The active set is in the instance’s config, its index.config.json entry: . { "voices": { "active": ["milnor"] } } . An empty or absent list means no voice, and that is a real answer. The platform’s own documentation activates none. Do not add one because a voice exists.

4398.title: What to load, and what to do with it
4398.content: Each voice’s rules carry three things you need while writing: . | terminology — preferred/deprecated pairs. Apply these as you type; a terminology change ripples into every sentence built around the old word. | patterns — what the mechanical check will look for, i.e. which constructions will be questioned. | judgementOnly: true — no lexical check can decide it, so nobody will catch it for you. These are the rules to hold in mind rather than fix on a later pass. | .

4399.title: The rules most often broken by drafting on instinct
4399.content: The rules worth knowing in advance are the ones where instinct is wrong. For example, under the science layer’s milnor voice, “clearly” is fine in a mathematical block when it routes the reader away from a routine verification; do not write around it to appease the checker. This skill restates no voice’s rules: each rule belongs to the instance that derived it, with the publication, page and verbatim quote it was read from, and a copy here would lose that citation — and the uncited copy is the one a reader meets first and nothing can check. To learn which of your voices’ rules are counterintuitive, open the voices.

4400.title: When two active voices disagree
4400.content: Rules are unioned, not merged, and both stand. If honouring one would break the other, that is a finding for the author and not something to resolve silently in the prose — say which two rules and which voices, and let the editor decide. A silent choice hides a genuine conflict between two documents the folio has adopted.

4401.title: Do not
4401.content: . | Do not apply a voice the folio has not activated. An unasked-for register produces confident findings against prose never written to it. | Do not treat a voice as a substitute for the base house voice. Voices overlay one-voice-style-guide.md; they do not replace it. | Do not add a rule to a voice while drafting. A voice rule needs a citation that resolves (check:voices enforces it) — a rule you inferred from the prose you are writing is circular. | .

4403.title: Voice editorial review
4403.content: Skill voice-editorial-review: Adjudicate a voice-* finding — read the flagged passage as a reader of THAT genre would and decide whether the register is wrong, the criterion is out of scope, or the block is a stated exception. The human/agent half of the voice QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-voice.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review .

4404.title: The axis you are adjudicating
4404.content: Six criteria in pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts describe one house voice: . | criterion | what it matches | severity | . | voice-status-leak | status markers and derivation-status speech in body prose | critical | . | voice-scholarly-default | second-person address, lecturer-cadence openers, paper-past-tense narration | major | . | voice-author-notes-pollution | status banners, PR/commit refs, agent names, ISO dates | major | . | voice-emoji-content | emoji as content outside tables | major | . | voice-first-person-work | first-person work tone — “we’ll add”, “let me”, “needs more work” | major | . | voice-editorializing | “surprisingly”, “it is worth noting that”, “rather than merely …” | minor | . They are heuristics over phrase lists. A match is a question, not a verdict; a reviewer entry on the same sidecar confirms or overrules it.

4405.title: The scoping question comes first, and it is usually the answer
4405.content: Every criterion above was written for a paper: a scholarly artefact in third person, where a status marker really is a leak of the work tracker into the published text. A criterion without profiles scoping also runs over documentation, whose register addresses the reader: “you need bun, latexmk and Lean” is a correct sentence in a prerequisites page and a voice-scholarly-default match. Ask which is true before touching the prose: . | The register is wrong for this genre. Fix the passage. | The criterion does not belong in this genre. Add profiles: ["paper"] to it in the registry. One edit clears the finding for every document folio and records why. | The criterion belongs and this block is an exception. Record a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached, and nothing is silently rewritten. | . Many instances of one criterion across many guide pages is evidence about the criterion’s scope, not about the authors.

4406.title: What the criterion cannot know
4406.content: The checkers match text. They do not know what the page is about. Typical false positives: . | voice-status-leak on a page that is a deliberate inventory of gaps (**Not yet implemented:** is its subject, not a leak). | voice-status-leak on prose about a work-plan lane: prose about a to-do store contains the words of a to-do store. | voice-emoji-content inside a transcript of an agent session, quoted as data. | . Each is a criterion reading a quotation as an assertion, and the reviewer entry says so in those words.

4407.title: Adjudicating one finding
4407.content: . | Open the block, not just the evidence line. The sidecar quotes one line; the register is a property of the passage around it. | Name the genre. Paper, guide, reference, transcript. That decides which of the three outcomes applies before you read another word. | Record the outcome where the next reader will find it — a prose edit, a registry edit with profiles, or a reviewer entry. A finding left open comes back on the next sweep. | Re-run the sweep — bun run pipeline/qa-sweep.ts --root docs/source — so the sidecar, the icon and the panel agree with what you decided. | .

4408.title: Where the open findings are
4408.content: Tracked in the work plan, one item per criterion, each carrying its blocks with file, line and the matched text: . beans list | grep "Voice axis" . The evidence itself lives in <block>.qa.json beside each block, and is published per block on the docs site: the QA icon opens the criterion, and the criterion opens the witness that ruled on it — which checker, at which script_hash, and whether the verdict still matches the file on disk.

4409.title: Do not
4409.content: . | Do not edit prose to silence a criterion you believe is out of scope. That hides the scoping defect and costs the next folio the same argument. | Do not mass-apply one finding’s resolution across its siblings without reading them; one criterion can fire for different causes. | Do not treat critical as “fix first”. Severity ranks the criterion’s authors’ concern, not the confidence of this match. | Do not delete a finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one comes back with no record that anyone looked. | .

4412.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
4412.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The instance’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

4413.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
4413.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

4414.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
4414.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

4415.title: A mechanical match is a question
4415.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

4416.title: Recording the verdict
4416.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

4417.title: Do not
4417.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

A unified watcher that handles branches (poll git ls-remote) and change proposals — pull requests, PRs — (subscribe to their activity through the session platform; subscribing is not a forge operation). On every event, walk the §3 integration checklist and either act, defer, or flag the user.

4426.title: Invocation
4426.content: The user’s request maps to one of three modes; pick the right one without asking: . | user phrase | mode | how | . | “watch main” / “watch upstream” / no target | branch:main | poll origin/main every 5 min | . | “watch PR 516” / “watch the PR” / “watch this PR” | pr:N | subscribe to its activity — the session platform’s subscription (event-driven) | . | “watch branch foo/bar” / “watch claude/x-y” | branch:foo/bar | poll origin/foo/bar every 5 min | . | “watch foo/bar PR 42” | pr:42 + maybe branch | subscribe + poll | . If ambiguous, default to branch:main.

4427.title: 1.  Stash the baseline
4427.content: Before arming anything, record the current state so the §3 review compares cleanly: . # Explicit refspec, ALWAYS. `git fetch origin <BRANCH>` writes FETCH_HEAD and # refreshes refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH> only when the clone's configured # refspec covers it — and exits 0 either way. A baseline read from a tracking # ref that was never updated is not a baseline. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null # Sanitize branch name for use in a file path: replace `/` with `_` # (e.g. `feature/foo` → `feature_foo`). Without this, branches with # slashes silently land in non-existent directory trees. SAFE_BRANCH=$(printf '%s' "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') git rev-parse "origin/<BRANCH>" > "/tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE_BRANCH}.sha" . For PR mode, instead capture the latest PR head SHA: read PR N with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool and stash its head commit SHA.

4428.title: 2.  Arm the watcher
4428.content: Branch mode — Monitor with poll loop . Use the Monitor tool, persistent: true, 5-minute poll: . Monitor: description: "origin/<BRANCH> new commits" persistent: true command: | BRANCH="<BRANCH>" last=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" | cut -f1) while true; do cur=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) if [ -n "$cur" ] && [ "$cur" != "$last" ]; then git fetch origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null # one line per new commit, oldest first git log --reverse --oneline "$last..$cur" | head -20 last=$cur fi sleep 300 done . Each new commit becomes one notification line. PR mode — activity subscription . Subscribe to the PR’s activity through the session platform (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription). This is not a forge operation, so no forge Tool node offers it. Already event-driven — no polling needed. The harness delivers <github-webhook-activity> events for comments, CI status, reviews, and merges. See the existing PR-subscription guidance in the system prompt for handling.

4429.title: 3.  Per-event integration checklist
4429.content: For every notification (branch commit or PR event), run through these four questions in order — stop at the first “no” or “no action”: . Q1 — Should we integrate? . | Is the change on a file we touch in this branch? Quick check: git diff --name-only HEAD <NEW_SHA> -- $(git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD). | If yes and the change is small, rebase / pull now. | If yes but large, defer until the immediate task ships and add a TODO. | If no overlap, skip Q2/Q3/Q4 and acknowledge with a one-liner. | . Q2 — Does it conflict? . | Try a dry rebase in a fresh worktree. Use mktemp -d so the path is unique (avoids collisions with previous failed runs and with parallel /watch invocations) and clean up unconditionally via trap: . PROBE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rebase-probe.XXXXXX) trap 'git worktree remove --force "$PROBE" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$PROBE"' EXIT git worktree add "$PROBE" HEAD >/dev/null ( cd "$PROBE" && git rebase "origin/<BRANCH>" ) status=$? # trap fires on EXIT . | Conflicts (status != 0) → first attempt auto-resolve for the recurring drift-conflict pattern (see §2a below); only flag the user if auto-resolve fails or the conflict is non-trivial (overlapping logic edits, schema rewrites, etc.). | . §2a — Auto-resolve drift-conflict pattern (CI-regenerated artifacts) . Some artifacts (*.witness.json sidecars, generated caches, derived reference files) are routinely regenerated by the CI validate job and frequently conflict on rebase against fast-moving main. These conflicts are always the same shape: our branch’s committed artifact was regenerated against an older main; main now has a fresher version. Resolution is mechanical: regenerate against current main and recommit. The recipe (run on the real branch, not the probe worktree): . # When `git rebase origin/<BRANCH>` halts with a regenerated artifact # in the conflict list, do NOT hand-merge the JSON. Instead: # 1. If the conflicting commit was a pure regen of these generated # artifacts (no other changes), skip it — main already has the regen: git diff --name-only --cached | grep -qE '\.witness\.json$' && \ ! git diff --name-only --cached | grep -vE '\.witness\.json$' && \ git rebase --skip # 2. Otherwise, abort the rebase, regenerate the artifacts # on the rebased branch, then re-rebase. This produces a clean # apply because the regenerated artifact now matches main. git rebase --abort git rebase origin/<BRANCH> # re-rebase, skipping bad commits as above # regenerate the affected artifacts via the project's generator(s), e.g. bun run cat regen git add <regenerated-artifact-paths> git commit -m "Regen generated artifacts post-rebase against latest main" git push --force-with-lease . Only flag the user if: . | The conflict is in a source file (.py, .lean, .ts, .md) — those are real semantic conflicts that need human judgment. | The conflict is in a generated artifact whose regenerated content differs substantively from a simple drift (e.g. a numerical value changed, not just a timestamp/hash) — that means a CI-run generator on main produced different output, which deserves a closer look before blindly accepting. | The auto-resolve recipe itself fails (regen script errors out, push rejected for non-fast-forward reasons, etc.). | . For generated artifacts specifically: if upstream regenerated files our branch also touched, prefer rebase-and-regenerate over hand-merging. Drift is structural; merging is fragile. Q3 — Can we reuse? . Apply four reuse questions: . | Definitions / lemmas / helpers / witnesses — does the new commit add something our branch is duplicating, paraphrasing, or reinventing? Replace with uses[] / a citation and delete the local stand-in. | Proofs — does a new lemma or tactic discharge a hypothesis, collapse a chain, or close a gap? Apply via the project’s proof-simplification / build-fix skills. | Exposition — does our .md re-derive what main now defines upstream? Replace with a forward-reference; route through the project’s accuracy / readability skills. | Computation — does a new script or witness supersede a hand-rolled loop or stale witness in our branch? Swap in and regenerate the artifact. (See §2a for the routine drift-conflict pattern.) . | When the upstream commit adds or modifies a prop: / thm: / lem: / cor: block (or its sibling formalization), delegate to the project’s compute-integration watcher to check whether the new claim is wired into the production compute chain. Capture the verdict here and feed it into Q4. | . | . Q3a — Did upstream land a new skill file? . For each main-refresh, check whether a skill directory the instance declares in its kg graph (skill_list names them) gained a new file between this branch’s prior baseline and the new origin/main: . git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "$LAST_BASE..origin/main" -- <skill-dirs> . For each new skill file: . | Read its frontmatter — extract name, roles, description, and any inherits field. | Match against branch scope — does the skill’s description overlap with what this branch is doing? Heuristics: . | skill description mentions a file kind / domain / pattern that appears in this branch’s git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only, OR | skill is a new integration-watcher child (inherits: local/integration-watcher) and your branch is itself an integration-watcher PR, OR | skill is a content-block QA skill (e.g. one-voice-*, proof-*, compute-*) and your branch touches .md / .ts / .lean content blocks. | . | Surface to the user via AskUserQuestion with the standard 3-chip pattern: . New skill <name> landed on main: . <one-line description from frontmatter> . This branch’s scope overlaps because <one-line match rationale + file paths>. 1) Adopt now — invoke the skill on the relevant subset of this branch’s diff before continuing. 2) Defer to follow-up branch — record the decision and note for the next branch; don’t change this branch. 3) Not relevant — record so the watcher doesn’t re-prompt on future main-refreshes. | Record the decision as a note on the watcher’s work item (or in chat for the bare /watch flow) so subsequent main-refreshes don’t re-prompt for the same skill. | . This rule applies to skill files only. Skills landing on sibling PRs that haven’t merged yet do NOT trigger this check — only main commits count, mirroring the §2 “watch origin/main” scope. Q4 — Report or act? . | Acted (made the change): one-line summary + the new commit SHA. | Will act after current task: add a TODO with what + why. | Skipped: one-line reason (“no overlap”, “blocked on $TASK”). | .

4430.title: 4.  Stop the watcher
4430.content: Stop when the branch ships (PR merged, or you switch branches): . | Branch mode: call TaskStop on the Monitor task ID. | PR mode: the harness auto-unsubscribes when the PR merges/closes; otherwise unsubscribe through the session platform. | .

4431.title: 5.  Common upstream patterns (heuristics)
4431.content: . | Artifact drift: upstream regenerated generated artifacts (*.witness.json, caches) while we also modified them → rebase-and-regenerate, never hand-merge. | Toolchain version bumps: a dependency/toolchain hash changed → check our branch’s toolchain pin aligns before continuing a build. | Schema or generator changes: run bun run cat regen before continuing. | Routine review-cycle commits (Gemini/Copilot fixes on unrelated PRs): almost always Q1 = no overlap = skip with one-liner. | .

4432.title: 5b.  Monitor-timeout recovery (MANDATORY when re-arming)
4432.content: Background Monitors time out ([Monitor timed out — re-arm if needed]). Do not just re-arm and continue — between the last event and the timeout, main may have moved substantially. Mandatory steps on timeout-recovery: . # Compare the stashed baseline against the WATCHED BRANCH's actual head. # # This fetched `main` and then measured `origin/<BRANCH>` — a different ref # from the one it refreshed. The recovery step that exists to catch what was # missed while the watcher was down therefore compared the baseline against a # tracking ref nothing had updated, found them equal, and reported 0 missed # every time. Fetch the ref you are about to read, with an explicit refspec so # the tracking ref is actually written. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null SAFE=$(echo "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') LAST=$(cat /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha 2>/dev/null || echo "") CUR=$(git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH>) if [ "$LAST" != "$CUR" ]; then MISSED=$(git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) echo "MISSED $MISSED commits while watcher was down" git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" | head -10 # Update baseline AFTER reporting git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH> > /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha fi . If MISSED >= 5 OR any missed commit touches a file in your branch’s diff, run the §3 integration checklist on the missed range BEFORE arming a fresh monitor. This catches main moving many commits ahead during a long focused session while the watcher is timed out.

4439.title: 1. Intent
4439.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

4440.title: 2. Candidates
4440.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

4441.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
4441.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

4442.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
4442.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

4443.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
4443.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

4444.title: Staging links
4444.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: staging-review §”The deep-link rule”.

4445.title: Showing it to the requester
4445.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (staging-review, the deep-link rule, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .

4454.title: Restructuring a work plan — a reviewed plan, not a bulk edit
4454.content: Skill work-plan-restructure: Reorganise a work plan that has outgrown one-bean-at-a-time repair — session logs typed as epics, duplicate families, generated template work items, stale claims, unparented work — through a reviewed PLAN rather than in bulk. The taxonomy is stated as data, a dry-run plan lists one row per work item (action, new parent, new status, evidence, note) with its before-state so the plan is its own inverse, the owner approves it by class or by row, and the apply is batched and reversible. Scrap, never delete. Read before changing the parent, type or status of more than a handful of work items at once. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . lsi-indexing §”Epic filing” ends with “never apply the proposal in bulk”. A store that needs thousands of moves — session logs typed as epics, stale claims, duplicate groups, generated template families — cannot be repaired one work item at a time either. This skill is the middle path: a plan file a person reads, approves, and can undo. Applying a rule across thousands of work items unread is what deletion-requires-confirmation and the lsi method’s refusal 3 forbid; the plan is how the rule gets read without each work item being read alone.

4455.title: 1. State the taxonomy as data, first
4455.content: A restructure is a claim about what each level MEANS. If that claim stays implicit, the plan cannot be reviewed: the owner would be approving moves whose criterion they never saw. So the plan file opens with the taxonomy it applies: . { "taxonomy": { "milestone": "a GOAL, in the owner's verbatim words (todo-manager §A GOAL is a milestone bean)", "epic": "a SUBJECT that outlives any session; >= 2 children, or it is a task", "feature": "a deliverable a person can accept or reject on its own", "task|bug": "one pull request's worth of work", "never a level": ["a session", "a handover", "a generator run", "a PR"] }, "rules": { "max-depth-below-milestone": 3, "epic-min-children": 2 } } . Defaults are the ones this repository already states: todo-manager for goals, subjects and a session is a log, and release-epic-planning for epic → feature → task. The types must be the ones .beans.yml lets the CLI write. A level the store cannot hold, such as a story type it does not configure, is a proposal to the owner. It is not a row.

4456.title: 2. Generate the dry-run plan — one row per bean, with its before-state
4456.content: | column | what it carries | . | bean | the id, or new:<slug> for an epic the plan creates | . | action | keep · reparent · retype · scrap-duplicate · scrap-generated · close-landed · reset-claim · create-epic | . | from-parent → to-parent | before and after | . | from-type → to-type | before and after | . | from-status → to-status | before and after | . | evidence | explicit · rule:<name> · latent:<cosine>/<margin> — never blank | . | note | what a reviewer needs: the survivor of a duplicate, the commit that landed it, the rule that fired | . The from- columns make the plan its own inverse. Swap every from-* and to-* and you have the plan that undoes it. Nothing has to be remembered to reverse it, and that matters most when the session that applied it is gone. The evidence comes from tools that already exist. Do not re-derive any of it: . | row source | tool | evidence class | . | reparent an open work item | lsi:epics: a parent: chain or a work item id in commits first, cosine second | explicit, else latent | . | session log typed as epic or milestone | sessionLogRootBeans in test/health/checks.ts (the bean-session-log-roots finding) | rule:session-log | . | duplicate | the bean-store duplicate groups; the target-object key in todo-manager §”Check before you create” | rule:same-title, rule:same-target | . | landed work still open | branch-archaeology: patch-id equivalence on main | explicit | . | stale claim | bean-stale-in-progress / bean-quiet-claims in bun run cat health, network-checked by check:quiet-claims | rule:stale-claim | . | unparented | check:bean-parents | rule:orphan | . lsi:epics prints a calibration line, and the plan carries it. Its agreement rate is well short of certain, so a latent row is a proposal, never presented as a finding. Write the plan as a work item note on the work item that owns the restructure (bun run cat beans:note <id>), with the summary first and the rows as a table. The notes directory is declared and keyed by branch, so the plan is committed and reviewed in the PR diff without inventing a new directory. A plan too large for one note is split by action class, one note per class, because that is how the owner approves it.

4457.title: 3. The owner gate — approve by class, never by silence
4457.content: Present the summary before any row, following interaction-modality §4.1 (context → options → recommendation → question): . | counts per action; | open children per epic, before and after; | orphans after (it must be 0); | every row whose to-status is scrapped or completed. | . Then ask: . | A class approval covers explicit and rule: rows only. Latent rows are approved row by row, or by the owner’s explicit words extending the approval to them. A latent row that was not approved stays keep. It is never applied on the strength of its cosine. | Scrap and close are the deletion-shaped actions. They take the owner’s word under deletion-requires-confirmation, or a recorded confirmation-waiver for the deletion gate that names this plan. | No answer is not approval. Say what happens if they say nothing: the plan stays a note, and the store is untouched. | .

4458.title: 4. Apply in batches, re-reading each bean first
4458.content: . | One action class per commit, at most ~100 rows. The commit message names the plan note and the class. A bad batch is then one git revert. | Re-read each work item before you write it (todo-manager §”Check before you WORK”). If its current parent, type or status differs from the row’s from-*, a sibling moved it after the plan was made. Skip the row and report it; do not overwrite. | Respect live claims. Leave alone any work item that is mid-flight under bean-coordination: touched within 72 h, or named by an open PR. The exception is the owner naming that work item. | One flag per beans update, then read the front matter back. A multi-flag update can apply only some of its flags and still report success (todo-manager §”After you create”). | Notes go in by note or --body-append, never --body-file. --body-file replaces the body silently. | Scrap, never delete. scrap-duplicate names the survivor in the scrapped work item. scrap-generated names the generator and the sidecar or queue that should have held the item instead (work items are not sidecars). A session log is closed or scrapped with a pointer to where its children went. Archiving is a view, not an exit (bean-coordination §”Archiving is a VIEW”). | After each batch: bun run cat check:bean-parents, bun run cat readme:subgraphs and bun run cat health. The batch is not done until the guards agree with the plan’s “after” column. | .

4459.title: 5. Reversing it
4459.content: If nothing has landed on the store since, revert the batch commits; the store is committed, which is what makes that possible. If siblings have edited it since, apply the swapped plan: the from-* columns become the targets. Its rows go through the same re-read rule in step 4.2, so a row that a sibling has since moved is skipped rather than clobbered.

4460.content: . | Decide the taxonomy. It states one for the owner to accept or amend. A disputed filing (symptom against subject, as lsi-indexing puts it) is the owner’s call, not the score’s. | Run unattended. No step from 3 onward happens without the owner’s approval for that plan. | Fix the cause. If a generator or a skill is minting the work items being scrapped, fix that first. Otherwise the plan is repaired again next week. | .

4462.title: The work plan’s contract
4462.content: Skill work-plan-store: The contract the work plan (work items) keeps as a data store, as operations any Tool must provide: get, list, create, update with ifMatch, note, history, and where a work item is in its processes. Give back a work item exactly as written, keep ids unique and links whole, keep status and type to their closed lists, lose nothing to concurrent writers, and answer a work item’s history. A mechanical Actor plays this Role through whichever Tool the deployment names. Named by: Authoring a document . The work plan is a data store, and this is its contract. work-plan in scenarios/roles.json is a mechanical Role with a store block: what it holds, and how it is reached. This skill is the other half, what it must do. How an agent USES the plan is todo-manager; this file says what the plan promises back. This contract names no Tool. A process or skill that touches the work plan says which operation below it performs (“note the bean”, “claim it”), never which command does it. How one Tool performs an operation belongs on that Tool’s page, listed in §”Tools”. The Tool in use is chosen by the deployment description, per checkout. A diagram draws the store as a data store, never a lane: a dataStoreReference with dataStoreRef="work-plan", declared once in processes/global-tasks.bpmn. A task that opens or closes a work item writes to it with a dataOutputAssociation; a task that reads the plan has a dataInputAssociation from it. The task sits in the lane of whoever does it.

4463.title: What it holds
4463.content: | Kind | What | . | bean-defs | work items ($schema: bean/1.0.0), shaped by schemas/kinds/bean-defs.schema.json | . | bean-notes | addenda to a work item, one per writer, never rewritten | . | workflow-state | running and finished BPMN instances (folio-workflow-instance/v1) | .

4464.title: Operations
4464.content: Every Tool provides these. Each line says what a caller can rely on. | Operation | Guarantee | . | get(id) | the work item as last written, or “none”. A short id resolves to exactly one work item or to none | . | list(filter) | work items by status, type, tag or parent; archived work items only when the filter asks for them | . | create(bean) | the id is unique; the work item is readable by get once create returns | . | update(id, change, ifMatch) | refused when ifMatch names a version that is no longer current; a retry on the current version lands. archived: true archives the work item | . | note(id, text, by) | appended to the work item’s notes, never rewriting earlier ones | . | history(id) | every change to the work item, oldest first: when, by whom, what changed, and which process step made it when one did | . | positions(id) | every workflow instance that names the work item: process, step(s), instance status, last move | . | beansAt(process, step?) | the work items with a token at that process (and step) | . Archiving is a field, not an operation. update(id, { archived: true }, ifMatch) is refused unless the work item is completed or scrapped, and the work item keeps its status. get still finds an archived work item; list leaves it out unless asked. Where an archived work item lives is the Tool’s choice, stated on its page. A work item’s position lives only in the workflow instances. The work item records no process or step of its own; positions and beansAt read the instances the store holds. A tag such as process:code-change-review may label a work item for people, and is never read as its position.

4465.title: Responsibilities
4465.content: Each line is something a test can check against any Tool. | Give back what was written. get after create or update returns, byte for byte, the work item written. | Keep ids unique. No two work items share an id. | Keep links whole. parent, blocking and blocked_by name work items that exist. | Keep the lists closed. status and type take only the values the schema declares. | Lose nothing to a race. Two writers at once both land: the second update with a stale ifMatch is refused, retried on the current version, and lands. Nothing is overwritten unread. | Keep the history. history(id) answers who changed what and when, and which process step did it. | Archive only what is finished. archived: true on a work item that is not completed or scrapped is refused. | Know where a work item is. positions and beansAt agree with the instances the store holds. | .

4466.title: Tools
4466.content: | Tool | Backed by | Page | . | git state branch | a branch per graph (cat/<harness>/beans), mounted at beans/, written with the beans CLI (beans-cli) or by hand (beans-manual), read with bean-query | work-plan-store-git-branch | . | work items server | beans-serve GraphQL (schema); its mutations already take ifMatch | proposed | . | MCP service | an MCP server over the same operations | proposed | . | run-scoped store | in memory or a scratch branch, one per benchmark run, never the real plan (req:model-benchmark) | proposed | .

4467.title: Tests
4467.content: The conformance suite lives in the tools layer (scripts/tests/sdlc/work-plan-store-conformance.ts, one describe per responsibility above) and runs against both of the git Tool’s access modes. Until this file carries a tested-by: line, kg-audit reports this role as mechanical-role-untested.

4468.title: Not its responsibility
4468.content: Deciding what to work on, who claims a work item, or whether work is done. Those are judgements made in the lanes of the people and agents who read and write the plan.

4470.title: State in a running process
4470.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Execute audited named queries over partitioned W3C N-Quads distributions, Package and distribute partitioned W3C N-Quads and named queries, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Editing and HCI validation, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

4471.title: Which store answers which question
4471.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

4472.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
4472.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

4473.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
4473.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

4474.title: What state does NOT buy you
4474.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

4475.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
4475.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

4476.title: Reading the state you did not write
4476.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
